Neuroblastoma

MONDO:0005072 Pathograph 67 Show in embeddings browser neuroblastic tumor

Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood, arising from neural crest-derived sympathetic nervous system precursors. It demonstrates remarkable clinical heterogeneity, ranging from spontaneous regression in infants to highly aggressive metastatic disease in older children. MYCN amplification, present in approximately 20% of cases, is among the most powerful adverse genomic prognostic markers and drives aggressive tumor behavior. Risk stratification in the INRG system combines stage, age, histologic category and grade of differentiation, MYCN status, chromosome 11q status, and DNA ploidy to guide treatment intensity. A distinct axis of neuroblastoma biology is the mechanism of telomere maintenance: telomerase is activated through TERT rearrangement, MYCN amplification or high TERT expression without either alteration, while alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT), often with ATRX alteration, maintains telomeres without telomerase. The two mechanisms are almost mutually exclusive. ATRX-altered disease is enriched in older children, adolescents and young adults and often runs a slow but progressive course, with poor response to induction chemotherapy reported for large ATRX deletions and truncating mutations. Low-risk neuroblastoma may require only observation, while high-risk disease requires intensive multimodal therapy with immunotherapy.

Mappings

MONDO
MONDO:0005072 neuroblastoma
skos:exactMatch MONDO
Primary MONDO identifier for this entry. MONDO defines the class as an extracranial childhood cancer that originates from neural crest tissues of the sympathetic nervous system, matching this entry's scope, and records NCIT:C3270 and Orphanet:635 as exact matches. MONDO also files olfactory, cerebral and retinal neuroblastoma, and adrenal gland and mediastinum ganglioneuroblastoma, beneath the class; this entry does not cover them (see notes).
NCIT
NCIT:C3270 Neuroblastoma
skos:exactMatch NCIT
NCIT concept that MONDO records as an exact match of MONDO:0005072. NCIT defines it as a malignant neuroblastic tumor with neuroblastic cells, no ganglion cells and no prominent Schwannian stroma, matching this entry. NCIT also files olfactory neuroblastoma (NCIT:C3789), CNS neuroblastoma with FOXR2 activation (NCIT:C186547) and retinal neuroblastoma (NCIT:C6956) beneath it; this entry does not cover them (see notes). NCIT also has a narrower Peripheral Neuroblastoma class (NCIT:C6591); C3270 is used because it is the class MONDO records as an exact match, and NCIT files this disease's stage, risk-group and differentiation-grade classes under C3270 rather than under C6591.

Inheritance

2
Sporadic occurrence in most cases HP:0003745
Most neuroblastoma arises sporadically, with no family history and no identified germline predisposing variant. About 1% of cases have a positive family history, so the heritable forms below describe a small minority of the disease even though they are what the genetic section characterises in most detail. A sporadic presentation is the default and is not a statement that no germline contribution exists: common susceptibility variants and de novo events are not excluded by an absent family history.
Sporadic
Show evidence (1 reference)
PMID:21734404 SUPPORT DIRECT BACKGROUND Human Clinical
"Most NBs arise sporadically, but approximately 1% of all cases have a positive family history"
Gives both halves of this block: sporadic occurrence is the usual case, and the familial share is about 1%. The sentence is the introduction of a study about penetrance modifiers rather than that study's own result, so it restates the established epidemiology and is graded BACKGROUND.
Autosomal dominant familial neuroblastoma with incomplete penetrance HP:0000006
The familial form is transmitted as a dominant trait with markedly incomplete penetrance. Germline activating ALK variants account for the majority of familial cases and germline PHOX2B variants for a smaller share; both are detailed in the genetic section rather than here. The penetrance figure is what makes this block worth stating separately from the gene records: in the pedigrees used to map ALK, only about half of mutation carriers developed neuroblastoma, so carrier status is not a prediction of disease and a transmission probability is not a risk of illness. Reduced penetrance is itself under genetic investigation, with modifier variants proposed at or near the ALK locus.
Autosomal dominant inheritance Penetrance: INCOMPLETE
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:21734404 SUPPORT DIRECT BACKGROUND Human Clinical
"Dominant mutations in ALK are found in more than 50% of familial NB cases. However, in the families used for the linkage study, only about 50% of carriers of ALK mutations are affected by NB."
Both claims this block makes: the mode of transmission is dominant and accounts for more than half of familial cases, and penetrance is about 50% in the mapping pedigrees. Graded BACKGROUND because the sentences introduce a penetrance-modifier study by restating its predecessor's findings rather than reporting this study's own linkage result. The penetrance figure is from the specific families used for linkage, so it is not a population estimate.
PMID:18724359 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"Resequencing of regional candidate genes identified three separate germline missense mutations in the tyrosine kinase domain of ALK that segregated with the disease in eight separate families."
The segregation observation the dominant model rests on: three germline ALK missense variants tracking the disease through eight pedigrees. Segregation in families is what establishes heritable transmission here, and the dominant mode is read from it together with the carrier frequencies above rather than from this sentence alone. Graded HUMAN_CLINICAL to match this sentence's grading in ALK-Related_Neuroblastic_Tumor_Susceptibility, which cites it for the same families.

Subtypes

3
molecular
MYCN-Amplified Neuroblastoma
Approximately 20% of neuroblastomas harbor MYCN gene amplification, associated with rapid tumor progression and poor prognosis. MYCN amplification is one of the earliest oncogene amplifications discovered.
Show evidence (4 references)
PMID:41560679 SUPPORT BACKGROUND Human Clinical
"MYCN amplification is a key factor contributing to the poor prognosis of NB."
States the adverse prognostic association of MYCN amplification. The sentence is background in the abstract of an iPSC-derived neural crest model study, restating the clinical picture; it is not something that study measured. The patient-derived support is the Brodeur and INRG evidence below.
PMID:6719137 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Furthermore, N-myc amplification is highly correlated with advanced stages of disease (P less than 0.001) and with the ability to grow in vitro as an established cell line, both of which are associated with a poor prognosis."
Human clinical support for the rapid-progression and poor-prognosis claim, from untreated primary neuroblastoma tissue.
PMID:19047291 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Stage, age, histologic category, grade of tumor differentiation, the status of the MYCN oncogene, chromosome 11q status, and DNA ploidy were the most highly statistically significant and clinically relevant factors."
Confirms MYCN status as a statistically significant, clinically relevant prognostic factor in the 8,800-patient INRG cohort.
+ 1 more reference
risk group
High-Risk Neuroblastoma NCIT:C150281
A pretreatment risk group that sets treatment intensity, not a histologic or molecular entity; which tumors it contains depends on the classification system. In the International Neuroblastoma Risk Group (INRG) classification (2009), which defines 16 pretreatment groups, high risk denotes the groups with 5-year event-free survival below 50%, and 18 months was selected as the age cutoff. The Children's Oncology Group (COG) classifier version 2 (2021) uses the INRG Staging System (INRGSS) and adds segmental chromosome aberrations. Among stage L1, L2 and M tumors, it classifies as high risk stage M at 18 months or older, MYCN-amplified stage M at any age and stage M in toddlers aged 12 to under 18 months with any unfavorable biomarker, as well as MYCN-amplified L2 tumors, L2 tumors without MYCN amplification but with unfavorable International Neuroblastoma Pathology Classification (INPC) histology at 18 months or older, and incompletely resected MYCN-amplified L1 tumors. Its rules for stage MS are set out separately; for stages M and MS together, MYCN status affected risk group assignment in children younger than 12 months, and MYCN status, histology, ploidy and segmental chromosome aberrations did so at 12 to 18 months. The International Society of Pediatric Oncology European Neuroblastoma Group (SIOPEN) high-risk trial HR-NBL1 took patients older than 12 months with International Neuroblastoma Staging System (INSS) stage 4 disease and patients with MYCN-amplified stage 2, 3 or 4 disease. In the SIOPEN HR-NBL1.5 study, random assignment between two induction regimens used a 1-year age threshold: it was open to patients aged 1 to 20 years with stage 4 disease and to infants younger than 1 year with MYCN-amplified stage 4 or 4S disease. High-risk treatment typically includes myeloablative therapy and immunotherapy.
Show evidence (7 references)
PMID:19047291 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"The optimal age cutoff was determined to be between 15 and 19 months, and 18 months was selected for the classification system. Sixteen pretreatment groups were defined on the basis of clinical criteria and statistically significantly different EFS of the cohort stratified by the INRG criteria...."
The INRG Task Force report found the optimal age cutoff to lie between 15 and 19 months, and the Task Force selected 18 months for the classification system. In its cohort of 8,800 children diagnosed in 1990-2002, sixteen pretreatment groups were defined, and groups with 5-year event-free survival below 50% were classified as high risk. The risk categories are survival bands from this pooled cohort.
PMID:34319759 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"A revised 2021 COG neuroblastoma risk classifier (version 2) that uses the INRGSS and incorporates SCAs has been adopted to prospectively define COG clinical trial eligibility and treatment assignment."
The conclusion of this COG analysis of 4,832 patients on the ANBL00B1 biology study states that the revised 2021 COG classifier (version 2) uses the INRGSS, incorporates segmental chromosome aberrations and has been adopted to define COG trial eligibility and treatment assignment. High risk is one of the groups this classifier assigns; the paper notes that risk schemas differ across cooperative groups.
PMID:34319759 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"Thus, L1 tumors are classified in v2 as LR except rare MYCN-A tumors (4%) that are incompletely resected (macroscopic residual tumor), which are considered HR. ... INPC was prognostic for most L2 subsets, with the largest impact in patients age >= 18 months with MYCN-NA tumors ... In this group,..."
The results of the COG ANBL00B1 analysis state the three locoregional groups that COG version 2 classifies as high risk: incompletely resected MYCN-amplified L1 tumors, MYCN-amplified L2 tumors, and MYCN-non-amplified L2 tumors with unfavorable INPC histology in patients aged 18 months or older ("these patients" refers back to that subset). These are COG-specific rules.

anatomic
Adrenal Gland Neuroblastoma MONDO:0006076
Neuroblastoma whose primary tumor arises in the adrenal gland. In the INRG database, 47% of 8,369 children with neuroblastoma or ganglioneuroblastoma and a known primary site had adrenal tumors. After adjustment for age, stage and histologic grade, adrenal primaries had about twice the odds of MYCN amplification of non-adrenal primaries (adjusted odds ratio 2.09), and after adjustment for age, MYCN status and stage they carried a modestly higher risk of events (hazard ratio 1.13).
Show evidence (1 reference)
PMID:25154816 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"Among 8,369 children, 47% had adrenal tumors. ... Adrenal tumors were more likely than nonadrenal tumors (adjusted odds ratio, 2.09; 95% CI, 1.67 to 2.63; P < .001) and thoracic tumors were less likely than nonthoracic tumors (adjusted odds ratio, 0.20; 95% CI, 0.11 to 0.39; P < .001) to have..."
In the INRG database cohort of children younger than 21 years diagnosed with neuroblastoma or ganglioneuroblastoma in 1990-2002 with a known primary site, 47% of the 8,369 children had adrenal primary tumors. Compared with non-adrenal primaries, adrenal tumors had about twice the odds of MYCN amplification after adjustment for age, stage and histologic grade (adjusted odds ratio 2.09), and a higher risk of an event after adjustment for age, MYCN status and stage (hazard ratio 1.13). Because the cohort includes ganglioneuroblastoma, the 47% is a share of this cohort, not a frequency among neuroblastoma alone.

Mechanistic Hypotheses

4
Withdrawal of NGF-dependent TrkA signalling triggers developmentally programmed cell death in TRKA-expressing tumours
regression_trka_ngf_deprivation ALTERNATIVE
Evidence balance 3 support
Spontaneous regression is the delayed activation of developmentally programmed cell death in a tumour whose cells have become dependent on NGF through the TrkA receptor, occurring where NGF is not available in the tumour's microenvironment. Of the candidate mechanisms the reviews name, this is the one a 2014 review judged the available data most consistent with, and the 2018 review by its first author says a switch in TrkA dependence could explain regression while adding that further mechanisms explain the phenomenon as well. Both reviews also state that the exact mechanisms of regression are uncertain, which is why this group is recorded as an alternative rather than a canonical model. Edges belonging to it opt in via hypothesis_groups: [regression_trka_ngf_deprivation]; in this entry that is the edge from NGF-TRKA Trophic Signaling Withdrawal to Spontaneous Tumor Regression, whose intermediate mechanisms state what has been measured and where.
Pathograph links
NGF-TRKA Trophic Signaling Withdrawal -> Spontaneous Tumor Regression INDIRECT UNKNOWN INTERMEDIATES The neurotrophin-deprivation account of spontaneous regression: a tumour whose cells have become dependent on NGF through TrkA regresses when NGF is not available in its microenvironment. The edge is indirect because no study has observed NGF becoming limiting in a regressing patient tumour; what the cited work measured is stated in the intermediate mechanisms below. Intermediates: Programmed death of TRKA-expressing tumour cells deprived of NGF, shown in cells cultured from TRK-expressing primary tumours rather than in a regressing tumour; Induction of the dependence receptor UNC5D with E2F1 and p53 on NGF withdrawal, shown in cultured cells from two primary favourable-biology tumours rather than in a regressing tumour
Show evidence (3 references)
PMID:25331179 SUPPORT DIRECT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Other
"However, the available data regarding the possible mechanisms of neuroblastoma regression are most consistent with a TrkA dependence mechanism."
Closing its discussion of the Trk receptors, Brodeur and Bagatell's 2014 review states that the available data on the possible mechanisms of neuroblastoma regression are most consistent with a TrkA dependence mechanism. This is the sentence that ranks the TrkA mechanism as an explanation; both reviews' abstracts rank the same mechanism first as a drug target, which is a different claim. It is a 2014 judgement, and in the matching paragraph of the 2018 review the first author instead says that a switch in TrkA dependence could explain regression but that additional mechanisms do as well. Graded OTHER because the sentence is the authors' synthesis across cultured tumour cells, developmental biology and clinical associations rather than a report of any one study type.
PMID:29305654 SUPPORT DIRECT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Other
"Thus, a switch in TrkA dependence could explain spontaneous regression of neuroblastomas but there are additional mechanisms to explain this phenomenon as well."
Brodeur's 2018 review closes its TrkA section by saying that a switch in TrkA dependence could explain spontaneous regression of neuroblastoma, but that additional mechanisms explain the phenomenon as well. It supports this hypothesis as a candidate explanation while stating that it is not the only one, which fits a status of ALTERNATIVE, a plausible competing or superimposed hypothesis with supporting evidence, rather than CANONICAL. Graded OTHER because the sentence is the review's own assessment, drawn from developmental work in animals, primary culture of tumour cells and the association of high TrkA expression with favourable tumours, and reports no single study type.
PMID:25331179 SUPPORT DIRECT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Other
"This evidence also suggests several possible mechanisms to explain the phenomena of spontaneous regression in neuroblastomas, including neurotrophin deprivation, humoral or cellular immunity, loss of telomerase activity and alterations in epigenetic regulation."
The abstract of the same 2014 review names neurotrophin deprivation first among several possible mechanisms of spontaneous regression, alongside humoral or cellular immunity, loss of telomerase activity and altered epigenetic regulation. In the body of the review, neurotrophin deprivation is the death of TrkA-expressing tumour cells when NGF is absent from their microenvironment, which is the mechanism this group records. The sentence supports the group as one candidate among several, which is its ALTERNATIVE status, and not as an established mechanism. Graded OTHER because it is the review's synthesis of earlier work rather than a report of any one study type.
Absence of a telomere maintenance mechanism is a prerequisite for spontaneous regression
regression_absent_telomere_maintenance ALTERNATIVE
Evidence balance 2 support
Tumour cells with neither telomerase activation nor ALT have a finite telomere reserve, and this absence is proposed as a precondition for spontaneous regression or differentiation, because telomere maintenance is essential for cancer cells to achieve immortal proliferation capacity. The claim the source makes is that the absence is likely a prerequisite, a necessary condition, so it is equally consistent with the absence permitting a regression that one of the other mechanisms drives. Absence of a detectable mechanism is not sufficient for regression: this entry's Unlimited Replicative Potential node records high-risk tumours lacking significant telomere lengthening activity whose cells kept proliferating for more than 200 population doublings while their telomeres shortened (PMID:28636942). The observational basis is that 99 of 208 assessed pretreatment tumours lacked any maintenance mechanism, 57 of those patients were never given cytotoxic treatment, and 18 had documented spontaneous regression. Edges belonging to this group opt in via hypothesis_groups: [regression_absent_telomere_maintenance].
Pathograph links
Absence of a Telomere Maintenance Mechanism -> Spontaneous Tumor Regression INDIRECT UNKNOWN INTERMEDIATES The telomere-shortening account of spontaneous regression: a tumour that maintains its telomeres by neither route cannot sustain indefinite proliferation, so its telomere reserve is drawn down. The absence is proposed as a precondition for the tumour to involute or differentiate rather than as a sufficient cause: this entry's own Unlimited Replicative Potential node records high-risk tumours without significant telomere lengthening activity whose cells kept proliferating. The edge is indirect because the steps between the missing mechanism and the regression have not been observed in a regressing tumour, and because the source states the absence as a prerequisite, a necessary condition, rather than as a cause. Intermediates: Progressive telomere attrition ending in senescence, crisis or cell death, inferred from the absence of a maintenance mechanism rather than observed in a regressing tumour
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:30523111 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"Because telomere maintenance is essential for cancer cells to achieve immortal proliferation capacity (8, 28), its absence is likely a prerequisite for spontaneous regression and differentiation in neuroblastoma."
Ackermann et al. assessed telomerase activation and ALT in 208 pretreatment neuroblastomas; the 99 patients whose tumours lacked a telomere maintenance mechanism had an excellent outcome, and 18 of them had documented spontaneous regression. In the concluding paragraph the authors state this claim: because telomere maintenance is essential for cancer cells to achieve immortal proliferation capacity, its absence is likely a prerequisite for spontaneous regression and differentiation. The premise is cited to earlier work and the conclusion is the authors' own hedged inference rather than a measured result, since the study recorded telomere maintenance status and patient outcome rather than how tumours regress. A prerequisite is a necessary condition and not a cause, so the sentence is equally consistent with the absence permitting a regression that another mechanism drives.
PMID:36030273 SUPPORT INDIRECT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Human Clinical
"In short, the critical importance of telomeres in NB malignancy is underscored by (i) the poor prognosis of tumors that harbor telomerase or ALT and (ii) the spontaneous regression and/or maturation of low stage tumors that harbor no TMM."
A 2022 review of telomere biology in neuroblastoma sums up the clinical picture: tumours with telomerase or ALT have a poor prognosis, while low-stage tumours with no telomere maintenance mechanism undergo spontaneous regression or maturation. That places both regression and maturation on the telomere-maintenance-negative side, which is the pairing this hypothesis rests on. Indirect because the quoted sentence records which tumours regress or mature rather than that the absence is required for regression, and it covers low-stage tumours only. Elsewhere the review proposes that such tumours regress once their telomere reserves are exhausted, but it presents that as a model rather than a measured result. The review reports no new data and the cohort studies it draws on include Ackermann et al. 2018, cited above, so it is not independent replication.
An anti-tumour immune response destroys the tumour
regression_immune_mediated EMERGING
Evidence balance 2 support 1 refute
Spontaneous regression is tumour destruction mediated by a humoral or cellular anti-tumour immune response. The human evidence is associational: in 107 untreated tumours, expression of the iNKT-cell-specific T-cell receptor was higher in the lower-stage and lower-risk group, in tumours with high TrkA expression and favourable histology, and in younger patients, and overall survival was higher where iNKT cells had infiltrated. No study cited here observes an immune effector producing a regression. In the TH-MYCN transgenic mouse model of aggressive disease the natural antitumour antibody did not correlate with spontaneous regression and B-cell depletion left tumour incidence unchanged, which bears against the antibody-mediated arm in that model while leaving cellular immunity untested. The group carries no causal edge in this entry, because no pathophysiology node is annotated for an immune effector here.
Show evidence (3 references)
PMID:29018959 SUPPORT INDIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"Vα24-Jα18 receptor was detected in 62 untreated cases (57.9%). The expression was significantly higher in stages 1, 2, 3, or 4S (P = 0.0099), in tumors with low or intermediate risk (P = 0.0050), with high TrkA expression (P = 0.0229), with favorable histology (P = 0.0026) ... and in younger..."
Hishiki et al. used real-time quantitative PCR to quantify expression of the iNKT-cell-specific T-cell receptor in untreated tumour samples from 107 neuroblastoma patients and detected it in 62 (57.9%). Expression was significantly higher in tumours of stage 1, 2, 3 or 4S, reported as one pooled group, in low- or intermediate-risk tumours, in tumours with high TrkA expression, in tumours with favourable histology and in younger patients, and overall survival was significantly higher in patients whose tumours showed iNKT-cell infiltration. This is evidence from human tumours that an innate-like T-cell population is more abundant in the favourable-biology group that contains stage 4S. It supports immune-mediated regression only indirectly: the abstract reports no regression outcome, it does not report stage 4S separately from stages 1 to 3, and it gives each association on its own, so infiltration may mark lower stage, lower risk, younger age or high TrkA expression rather than act independently of them. The ellipsis skips the association with aneuploidy.
PMID:30054041 SUPPORT INDIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Model Organism
"Mice with no or small (<5 mm) tumors showed higher antibody titers in plasma than mice with large (>5 mm) tumors. A significant negative correlation was observed between the tumor diameter and the titer of antitumor antibody. This antibody had complement-dependent cytotoxicity but not..."
The half of Kawakubo et al.'s result that is consistent with an antibody arm, quoted separately from the half that is not. In homozygous and heterozygous TH-MYCN mice the natural antitumour antibody titre was higher in animals with no or small tumours than in those with large ones, with a significant negative correlation between tumour diameter and titre, and the antibody killed neuroblastoma cells through complement but not through antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity. Indirect because an inverse correlation with tumour size is not an observation of regression, the direction of the association is not established, and the cytotoxicity was measured in cultured cells. The companion item below carries the result that cuts the other way.
PMID:30054041 REFUTE INDIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Model Organism
"Moreover, B-cell depletion had no effect on the tumor incidence in vivo. We revealed that TH-MYCN transgenic mice have a natural antibody against neuroblastoma that correlate with tumor size. However, this antibody does not correlate with the spontaneous regression of neuroblastoma."
The authors' own negative result, split from the supporting half above because one evidence item cannot carry both directions: depleting B cells left tumour incidence unchanged, and the natural antibody tracked tumour size without tracking spontaneous regression. This contradicts the antibody-mediated arm of the immune hypothesis in this model. It does not refute the hypothesis as a whole: only natural antibody was tested, so cellular immunity is untested, and the model is MYCN-driven aggressive disease rather than the favourable-biology tumours that regress in patients, which is why the item is graded indirect.
Altered epigenetic regulation, including subtelomeric promoter hypermethylation, contributes to regression
regression_epigenetic EMERGING
Evidence balance 1 support
Spontaneous regression follows from altered epigenetic regulation of gene expression rather than from a genomic change. The specific finding recorded here is that stage 4S tumours carry a characteristic DNA methylation portrait, with hypermethylation of specific subtelomeric promoters, which the authors suggest may be an additional mechanism by which telomere length and spontaneous regression are controlled; that suggestion connects this group to the telomere group above rather than standing apart from it. Stage 4S is used as a surrogate for tumours likely to regress, so the comparison is by stage rather than by observed regression, and the subtelomeric result rests on 14 stage 4S tumours. The group carries no causal edge in this entry, because no pathophysiology node is annotated for a methylation state here.
Show evidence (1 reference)
PMID:27599161 SUPPORT INDIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"In this study, we have shown that specific subtelomeric promoters are hypermethylated in stage 4S tumors compared to stage 1/2 and stage 4 tumors, which suggests that subtelomeric DNA methylation may represent an additional mechanism by which telomere length and spontaneous regression are..."
A re-analysis of methyl-CpG-binding domain sequencing data from 41 MYCN-non-amplified primary neuroblastomas (14 stage 4S, 14 stage 4 and 13 stage 1/2) found specific subtelomeric promoters hypermethylated in stage 4S tumours compared with both other groups. From this the authors suggest that subtelomeric DNA methylation may be an additional mechanism by which telomere length and spontaneous regression are controlled. Indirect for this hypothesis on three counts: tumours were grouped by stage, used as a surrogate for regression, rather than by whether they regressed; telomere length was not measured in these tumours, and the authors note that this route of telomere-length regulation is unexplored in neuroblastoma; and the stage 4S group is small, at 14 tumours.

Discussions and Knowledge Gaps

6
Why do MYCN-amplified neuroblastomas respond worse to Aurora A inhibition than non-amplified ones, when the preclinical mechanism makes them the tumours that depend on Aurora A most?
HUMAN MODEL MISMATCH OPEN mismatch_nb_aurora_a_mycn_amplified_benefit
Attached to
pathophysiology#Aurora A-Mediated N-Myc Protein Stabilization treatments#Alisertib (Aurora A Inhibition)
The preclinical case is specific about direction. An shRNA screen found AURKA required for the growth of MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma cells and largely dispensable for cells without amplification, and Aurora A stabilises N-Myc by binding it and the SCF(Fbxw7) ligase. The prediction that follows is that amplified tumours should be the ones Aurora A inhibition helps. The trial predicted exactly that, in its own words, and found the opposite: activity concentrated in MYCN non-amplified tumours, with MYCN amplification associated with inferior progression-free survival. Three readings are open and the entry does not choose between them. Alisertib inhibits the catalytic site, while the stabilisation is kinase-independent and is undone by compounds that distort Aurora A's conformation, so the drug may simply be the wrong tool for the mechanism. Or the clinical comparison may be confounded, since MYCN amplification predicts worse outcome whatever the treatment, and the association comes from an exploratory analysis pooling three cohorts rather than a randomized comparison. Or the dependency shown in cell lines may not hold in patient tumours. What would separate them is a conformation-disrupting Aurora A compound tested in MYCN-amplified disease with N-Myc protein measured on treatment, rather than a catalytic inhibitor assessed by response rate alone.
Posed by dismech curation (issue #14976) Posed 2026-10-27T00:00:00Z
Does a high mesenchymal cell-state signature predict worse outcome in neuroblastoma, better outcome, or neither?
CONTROVERSY OPEN controversy_nb_mesenchymal_state_prognosis
Attached to
pathophysiology#Adrenergic and Mesenchymal Cell-State Plasticity pathophysiology#Mesenchymal-State Chemotherapy Resistance
Three patient-level studies published within two years point in three directions, which is why no node in this entry asserts a prognostic direction for the mesenchymal state. A spatial-omics study of 54 profiled tumours, using signatures built from early-passage orthotopic patient-derived xenografts because established cell line-derived signatures failed to identify mesenchymal tumour cells, reports that high mesenchymal gene expression correlates with worse event-free and overall survival. A longitudinal single-cell multiomic study reports a tested null in the other direction: in 498 diagnostic bulk transcriptomes the mesenchymal signature was not significantly associated with prognosis. Two things bound that null. It is adjusted for age, sex and MYCN amplification in a cohort spanning all stages, and the same paper finds the mesenchymal state enriched in patients with MYCN amplification, so it is a null conditional on those covariates rather than an absence of any association. In the paper's own high-risk cohort a higher mesenchymal proportion at diagnosis correlated with a poorer response to induction chemotherapy and with adverse clinical events. Those two findings come from different analyses on different cohorts: the post-therapy increase from 22 paired longitudinal patients, the survival null from the bulk transcriptome cohort. A hypoxia study reports the opposite direction again, with better three-year overall survival for high scores in both a discovery and a validation cohort. It scores a composite signature of 94 mesenchymal signature genes selected because they rose in adrenergic cells under hypoxia, and it scores it only within hypoxic tumours, where the same score was not prognostic in the low-hypoxia subsets. So it is not a head-to-head contradiction of a pure mesenchymal signature, but it is a published, two-cohort, patient-level result pointing the other way. The three studies also score different things under one word: established cell line-derived signatures, xenograft-derived signatures, a single-cell-defined state signature scored in bulk tissue, and a hypoxia-conditioned composite. None of them measures a mesenchymal cell fraction directly.

"In patients, high MES gene expression correlates with worse event-free and overall survival."
The adverse-prognosis position, stated directly: in patients, high mesenchymal gene expression correlates with worse event-free and overall survival. This is a prognostic correlation and not evidence that the mesenchymal state causes poor outcome. The abstract reports no effect size, does not identify the patient cohort or the signature used for the survival analysis, and does not say whether the association holds after adjustment for established risk factors; the 54 tumours it describes are its profiling cohort, which may or may not be the survival cohort. The finding follows the authors' development of mesenchymal and adrenergic signatures from early-passage orthotopic patient-derived xenografts, which they introduced because established cell line-derived signatures failed to identify mesenchymal neuroblastoma cells.
PMID:40229600 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"The MES signature was not significantly associated with prognosis in the diagnostic samples"
The tested-null position, which is what stops a reader assuming the adverse one. In the authors' survival analysis of 498 diagnostic neuroblastoma bulk transcriptomes the mesenchymal state signature was not significantly associated with prognosis. Its scope: a signature score from bulk tumour RNA rather than a measured mesenchymal cell fraction, split at the median and modelled against overall and event-free survival with age, sex and MYCN amplification as covariates, in a cohort spanning all stages rather than the high-risk cohort the paper profiled by single-nucleus sequencing. The authors also report the mesenchymal state enriched in patients with MYCN amplification, so the null holds conditional on MYCN status. The same paper qualifies it twice: in its alternative stratification, patients assigned to the mesenchymal state had an intermediate prognosis, and in the diagnostic samples of its own high-risk cohort a higher mesenchymal proportion correlated with poorer response to induction chemotherapy and with adverse clinical events (one-sided t-tests, P = 0.02 and 0.05). PMID:41724733 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical

The opposite-direction position, in the discovery cohort: among high-risk patients whose diagnostic tumours scored high for hypoxia, a high composite mesenchymal and hypoxia score went with significantly better three-year overall survival than a low score. Two caveats must be read with it. The score is a composite of 94 mesenchymal signature genes selected because they were upregulated in adrenergic cells exposed to hypoxia, so it is not a pure mesenchymal signature; and the comparison is made only within hypoxic tumours, where the same score was not prognostic in the low-hypoxia subset. The authors note that their cohorts are retrospective with treatment received unknown, and that the signature would need prospective confirmation before any use as a clinical prognostic biomarker.

Which intermediate noradrenergic and mesenchymal population do patient tumours contain, and does it lie on a trajectory between the two states?
CONTROVERSY OPEN controversy_nb_intermediate_adrenergic_mesenchymal_state
Attached to
pathophysiology#Adrenergic and Mesenchymal Cell-State Plasticity
The disagreement here is about definition, markers and trajectory, not about whether an intermediate population exists. Framing it as one study reporting an intermediate state and another denying it would misstate the dissenting source, which reports an intermediate population of its own. Trajectory modelling of single-cell data from peripheral neuroblastic tumours places malignant neuroblasts moving between the adrenergic and mesenchymal states via an intermediate state its authors term transitional, defined in part by MYCN, NEUROD6, EZH2 and SOX11. The dissenting study reports a bridge cluster of noradrenergic tumour cells co-expressing mesenchymal features, found in a subset of an 18-biopsy series and running towards normal Schwann and mesenchymal cells, and marked by FOXC1, TIMP3, ETV1 and HGF. What it disputes is the other study's transitional state specifically: that those cells did not appear in a path or a cluster between the two identities, and that its own noradrenergic and mesenchymal signature does not include the genes defining that transitional state. Its own data place EZH2 and SOX11 in cycling-cell clusters instead. A third patient dataset independently reports an intermediate cluster with moderate adrenergic and mesenchymal signatures, so the population is reported more than once; what differs between the studies is which cells are being named, which markers define them, and whether they sit on a trajectory.

pathophysiology#c-MYC Activation by Enhancer Hijacking or Enhancer Amplification
The model makes a two-part claim and the patient data answer one part of it. In transgenic zebrafish the expansion driven by c-MYC was rapid and sustained where MYCN-driven lesions regressed after five weeks, which the authors attribute to reduced apoptosis together with a higher proliferative fraction; and disrupting c-MYC in SKNAS, a MYCN-non-amplified line with high c-MYC, costs viability and colony formation while leaving the MYCN-amplified line Kelly unaffected. In patient tumours the only index reported for this subset is the mitosis-karyorrhexis index, which counts mitotic and karyorrhectic figures together, and the MYC-protein-positive tumours tend to low or intermediate values where the MYCN-protein-positive ones are high. That series separates the two components rather than leaving them merged: it places the difference in karyorrhexis rather than in mitosis, and reads it as a functional difference between the two proteins in their apoptotic and karyorrhectic pathways. So the apoptotic half of the model's claim is matched in the patient tumours, and the proliferative half is left unmeasured rather than contradicted. A mitotic-figure count reported only as not being the driver of the index difference, with the data not shown, is not a proliferation fraction, and no Ki-67 or other labelling index stratified by MYC against MYCN protein appears in that work. The cohorts also differ: the index comes from a series restricted to undifferentiated and poorly differentiated tumours with the subset defined by immunohistochemistry, while the zebrafish and cell-line work follows a subset defined by expression rank. Until a proliferation fraction is measured in MYC-high patient tumours, a proliferation node for this subset would rest on the fish and the cell line alone, which is why this entry does not carry one.
Proposed experiments
Proliferation fraction in MYC-protein-positive versus MYCN-protein-positive primary neuroblastoma
nb_myc_high_proliferation_fraction_vs_mycn
Measure a proliferation fraction separable from apoptosis in archival primary tumours stratified by MYC and MYCN protein immunohistochemistry: a Ki-67 or MIB-1 labelling index, and a mitotic count scored by phospho-histone H3 so that mitotic figures are read independently of karyorrhectic ones, with apoptosis recorded separately by cleaved caspase-3 or TUNEL. Draw the series without restricting it to undifferentiated and poorly differentiated histology, so that the result is not conditioned on the inclusion criterion behind the existing index comparison.
Decision criterion
Whether MYC-protein-positive tumours differ from MYCN-protein-positive tumours in proliferation fraction once the mitotic and karyorrhectic components of the mitosis-karyorrhexis index are measured separately.
Supporting outcome
  • A proliferation fraction in MYC-protein-positive tumours at or above that of MYCN-protein-positive tumours, with the lower mitosis-karyorrhexis index accounted for by reduced karyorrhexis, would carry the zebrafish and cell-line result into human tumours and make a proliferation node for this subset curatable.
Refuting outcome
  • A proliferation fraction genuinely lower in MYC-protein-positive tumours, with the mitotic component itself reduced, would place this subset's aggressiveness somewhere other than proliferative rate and leave the zebrafish proliferative advantage as a property of that model.

Which consolidation gives better event-free survival in high-risk neuroblastoma, a tandem transplant built on carboplatin, etoposide and melphalan or a single busulfan-melphalan transplant?
KNOWLEDGE GAP OPEN gap_nb_consolidation_tandem_versus_busulfan_melphalan
Attached to
treatments#Autologous Stem Cell Transplant
Two randomized phase 3 trials each improved on a carboplatin-etoposide-melphalan comparator, and neither tested the other's winner. The Children's Oncology Group's ANBL0532 randomized tandem transplant, thiotepa and cyclophosphamide followed by dose-reduced carboplatin, etoposide and melphalan, against a single carboplatin-etoposide-melphalan transplant, and found three-year event-free survival from randomization of 61.6% against 48.4%. SIOPEN's HR-NBL1 randomized busulfan with melphalan against carboplatin, etoposide and melphalan as single high-dose regimens, and found three-year event-free survival of 50% against 38%, with fewer severe adverse events on busulfan-melphalan but more veno-occlusive disease. So both beat the same regimen, and the arm that won each trial has never met the arm that won the other. The comparison is not recoverable from the two results: the trials differ in their induction regimens and their eras, and they randomize different populations. HR-NBL1 randomized only patients who had completed induction and achieved an adequate disease response, whereas ANBL0532 randomized 355 of its 652 enrolled patients, 207 of them withheld by physician or parent preference, and reports event-free survival from the time of randomization. The absolute percentages are therefore not comparable across them, and ANBL0532's authors say its result may not represent all patients with high-risk neuroblastoma. Resolving this needs a randomized comparison of tandem carboplatin-etoposide-melphalan consolidation against single busulfan-melphalan, in one induction backbone, with anti-GD2 maintenance in both arms.

Does alternative lengthening of telomeres mark the neuroblastomas that benefit from WEE1 inhibition?
OPEN QUESTION OPEN question_nb_alt_status_and_wee1_inhibitor_benefit
Attached to
pathophysiology#Replication-Stress Checkpoint Dependence pathophysiology#Alternative Lengthening of Telomeres treatments#Adavosertib (WEE1 Inhibition)
In the ADVL1312 neuroblastoma cohort, two of the three patients with an objective response had tumours with alternative lengthening of telomeres. The observation is worth recording because it joins two things this entry already models separately: ALT is a telomere-maintenance mechanism that runs on homologous recombination at telomeres, and the checkpoint dependence this treatment targets is a response to replication stress, so a tumour already carrying that burden is a plausible place for the drug to work. It is two patients. The trial analysed ALT and ATRX in tumour tissue but was not designed or powered to test ALT as a predictive marker, there is no comparison with the response rate in non-ALT tumours, and the second adavosertib trial reports its own candidate markers instead, finding clinical benefit in seven of eight patients with alterations in homologous recombination, replication-stress or RAS-pathway genes. Nothing here establishes ALT as a biomarker, and the entry does not claim it. What would settle it is a trial that stratifies on ALT status up front, or a pooled reanalysis across adavosertib studies with ALT called by a single assay.

Pathophysiology

LIN28B Overexpression
LIN28B, an RNA-binding protein normally restricted to fetal tissue, is overexpressed in high-risk neuroblastoma. It binds the terminal loop of primary and precursor let-7 transcripts and blocks their maturation, so less mature let-7 is produced. This is one of three routes into let-7 depletion rather than the only one: in MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma cell lines LIN28B can be removed without loss of MYCN protein or cell growth even though let-7 is de-repressed, which the same study reads as LIN28B serving a redundant let-7-suppressive role where the MYCN transcript is abundant.

let-7 Depletion
The mature let-7 microRNA family is depleted in neuroblastoma by three routes that substitute for one another rather than acting in series: LIN28B blockade of let-7 maturation; sponging of let-7 by the MYCN transcript, which in MYCN-amplified disease reaches levels high enough to titrate the family; and genetic loss of let-7 loci, which is common in neuroblastoma, inversely associated with MYCN amplification and independently associated with poor outcomes. let-7 represses MYCN post-transcriptionally, so depleting it de-represses MYCN and lifts the let-7 restraint on neuroblast differentiation. The routes converge on this node, which is why an entry whose flagship subtype is MYCN-amplified disease cannot model the LIN28B route alone.

MYCN-Driven Proliferation MYCN amplification drives aggressive proliferation
Adrenergic and Mesenchymal Cell-State Plasticity The arrested neural crest-derived sympathoadrenal progenitor is the lineage within which the two tumour cell identities are defined. The noradrenergic pole carries the committed sympathetic core regulatory circuitry, while the mesenchymal (NCC-like) pole sits close to the undifferentiated neural crest cell, so the two states map onto different points of the same blocked differentiation programme. The evidence cited here locates the two identities in that lineage; it does not show that the arrest itself drives switching between them.
Norepinephrine Transporter (NET/SLC6A2) Expression Arrest at an immature noradrenergic sympathoadrenal stage leaves the lineage's norepinephrine-uptake machinery in place. The edge is retention, not induction: the transporter is inherited from the sympathetic neuronal precursor rather than switched on by the arrest, and the cited sources state lineage-linked expression rather than any inducing step. It is recorded as an edge because the arrested lineage state is what accounts for the transporter still being there, which is the fact the therapy depends on.

Norepinephrine Transporter (NET/SLC6A2) Expression
Neuroblastoma arises from sympathoadrenal and sympathetic neuronal precursors, and the tumor retains those precursors' norepinephrine transporter (NET, encoded by SLC6A2), a transmembrane protein that carries norepinephrine into the cell. That retained transporter is the route by which both the 123I-MIBG diagnostic tracer and therapeutic 131I-MIBG enter the tumor cell, with vesicular retention through VMAT once inside. The node claims only that the transporter is expressed and is what MIBG uses; the uptake and expression measurements themselves are curated on the MIBG-Avid Disease row of imaging_findings, and are not restated here.

Animal models
Xenopus anteroventral noradrenergic (AVNA) cell differentiation model Xenopus laevis perturbs Positions MYCN upstream of the differentiation block: MYCN overexpression prevents Ascl1-driven differentiation, and loses that ability when Ascl1 cannot be phosphorylated.
Downstream
T-Cell-Poor Tumor Microenvironment Amplified MYCN tracks a T-cell-poor microenvironment. In primary tumours from patients with metastatic disease a T-cell-poor microenvironment was associated with genomic MYCN amplification, and in a separate patient series high-risk MYCN-not-amplified tumours carried significantly higher cytotoxic tumour-infiltrating-lymphocyte signatures than MYCN-amplified tumours. The route recorded here runs through suppressed interferon and pro-inflammatory signalling and the chemokine output that recruits T cells: in human and murine neuroblastoma cell lines N-Myc suppresses interferon and pro-inflammatory pathways, and N-Myc depletion amplified the interferon response to a cGAS-STING agonist, which in turn raised chemokine expression including Cxcl10 and drew T cells in a microfluidics migration assay. The limits sit on both halves. The patient half is an association in cross-sectional cohorts and does not establish direction, and the second series contrasts MYCN-not-amplified against MYCN-amplified tumours, so the direction is read off that contrast rather than measured within tumours over time. The intermediates are cell-line and microfluidics results; the cGAS-STING agonist used is specific for mouse and not human STING, so that arm was run in murine lines, and nothing in the model half was measured in patient tumours.
Telomerase Activation Amplified MYCN raises TERT transcription, which makes MYCN amplification a route to telomerase activation rather than a separate telomere maintenance mechanism. TERT expression was higher in MYCN-amplified tumours, and in a MYCN-amplified cell line TERT was the gene most strongly downregulated when MYCN was knocked down. Not every MYCN-amplified tumour takes this route: some express TERT as low as ALT tumours do, and forced MYCN overexpression did not induce TERT where the promoter was repressed.
Compensatory Polyamine Uptake from the Microenvironment MYCN regulates SLC3A2, the transporter that carries polyamine uptake in neuroblastoma, alongside other components of the polyamine pathway, so amplified MYCN raises the import route as well as the synthesis route. As with the synthesis edge below, no return edge is drawn from the uptake node into this one, to avoid a two-node cycle in the pathograph.
Polyamine Biosynthesis Dependence ODC1, the rate-limiting enzyme of polyamine synthesis, is a direct transcriptional target of MYCN, so amplified MYCN raises flux through the pathway. The dependence runs the other way as well, which is what makes the pathway a target rather than only a consequence, but that return relation is recorded in the downstream node's description rather than as a second edge, because an edge back into this node would make a two-node cycle in the pathograph.
let-7 Depletion In MYCN-amplified tumours the MYCN transcript is itself abundant enough to act as a competing endogenous RNA for let-7, which is why deleting LIN28B from amplified cell lines leaves MYCN protein and growth intact. This is the least established of the three routes into let-7 depletion: the authors raise the stoichiometric question themselves, whether a rise of more than 100-fold in MYCN mRNA, which lifts the total pool of let-7 target sites by only about a quarter, suffices for a competing-endogenous-RNA effect, and answer it with their own 3-prime-UTR-loss reporter and let-7-target mRNA sequencing. The quantification is in MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma cell lines.
LIN28B Overexpression Amplified MYCN also raises LIN28B itself, closing a loop with the let-7 node: MYCN binds the LIN28B promoter directly in a neuroblastoma line carrying inducible MYCN, and acts in parallel through miR-26a-5p. This edge records the transcriptional arm only and makes no claim about which arm dominates in a given tumour.
Replication-Stress Checkpoint Dependence N-Myc is what puts the replication checkpoint under load, so the dependence on CHK1 and WEE1 follows the oncogene rather than sitting beside it. Two results in one study carry the link: CHK1 inhibitor sensitivity tracked total MYC(N) protein, and inducing MYCN in untransformed retinal pigment epithelial cells was by itself enough to phosphorylate CHK1. The second is the causal half, and it is deliberately run outside neuroblastoma, because isolating what MYCN alone does requires a cell that does not already carry the amplification. That is also what keeps it a model rather than a measurement in the disease, which is why the edge is graded indirect. What this edge leaves out is the replication stress itself, the step between the oncogene and the checkpoint it activates.

Aurora A-Mediated N-Myc Protein Stabilization
Mechanism confidence: Established
N-Myc protein is short-lived: degradation requires sequential phosphorylation by cyclin B/Cdk1 and GSK3, after which the SCF(Fbxw7) ubiquitin ligase ubiquitinates it for proteasomal destruction. Aurora A binds both N-Myc and that ligase and counteracts the degradation, which uncouples N-Myc abundance from the growth-factor signalling that would otherwise set it. The stabilising action does not need Aurora A's kinase activity: it is a protein-protein interaction, and inhibitors that merely block the catalytic site lower N-Myc only modestly, whereas compounds that distort the kinase's native conformation drive N-Myc degradation. An shRNA screen found AURKA required for the growth of MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma cells and largely dispensable without amplification, which is what makes the interaction a dependency rather than an incidental one. What does not follow is the therapeutic corollary: in the clinic, alisertib has done worse in MYCN-amplified disease than in non-amplified disease, the opposite of what this mechanism predicts. That tension is recorded as a human-model mismatch discussion rather than smoothed over here.

Extrachromosomal MYCN Amplicon Architecture
In MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma the supernumerary MYCN copies are commonly carried on extrachromosomal circular DNA (ecDNA), which can be highly rearranged. The extrachromosomal form is the common state and not the only one: the same paper reports a MYCN amplicon carried as a linear intrachromosomal array, a homogeneously staining region. Amplicon composition is not random. Across a copy-number meta-dataset of 240 MYCN-amplified neuroblastomas, a 290 kb region downstream of MYCN was co-amplified in more than 90% of tumours, and the distal MYCN-specific enhancer e4, driven by the noradrenergic core regulatory circuit (CRC), lay inside the consensus amplicon in 90% of cases. Two amplicon classes follow. The first always co-amplifies a proximal CRC-driven enhancer; the second is structurally complex, lacks the key local enhancers and instead carries distal chromosomal fragments harbouring CRC-driven enhancers, which the authors read as ectopic enhancer hijacking replacing the missing local elements. That classification was made on primary-tumour copy-number profiles, which cannot separate extrachromosomal from intrachromosomal amplicons, so it applies to both forms. The two classes were prognostically indistinguishable in the same series, so amplicon class sets the regulatory route to MYCN overexpression rather than clinical behaviour. Separately, rearrangements derived from extrachromosomal circles can give rise to cancer-causing lesions and are associated with adverse clinical outcome; that association belongs to the circle-derived rearrangements and not to amplicon class.

MYCN-Driven Proliferation The two amplicon classes are what account for the regulatory requirements of MYCN overexpression, so the amplicon's architecture sits upstream of MYCN protein dosage and thereby of MYCN-driven proliferation. The architecture sets the regulatory route rather than gating the outcome: class II amplicons lacking the key local enhancers nevertheless expressed relatively high MYCN per gene copy, which is what the authors mean by ectopic enhancer hijacking compensating for the loss of local elements. Neither cited sentence reaches proliferation, so MYCN overexpression is named as the intermediate.
ecDNA Oncogene Dosage Heterogeneity Because ecDNA segregates asymmetrically at mitosis, carrying the amplicon extrachromosomally rather than in a chromosomal array is what produces variation in oncogene dosage between cells of the same tumour. The cited sentence is the general statement of that property of ecDNA rather than a measurement in neuroblastoma; the measurements sit on the downstream node.

ecDNA Oncogene Dosage Heterogeneity
Mechanism confidence: Provisional
MYCN copy number on ecDNA varies greatly from cell to cell, whereas copy number in cells carrying a linear homogeneously staining region appeared more evenly distributed, and in near-isogenic cell lines higher ecDNA copy number tracks greater colony-forming output. The second arm of the same biology runs the other way. ecDNA that is damaged and mis-segregated into a micronucleus is a constraint rather than a driver: the daughter cell inheriting an ecDNA-positive micronucleus divides later and dies more often, and a higher frequency of ecDNA-positive micronuclei in the diagnostic biopsy is associated with longer survival in MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma. The node is provisional because the measurements are recent, the clinical association rests on a single cohort with no independent replication, and the two arms point in opposite directions, so what the net effect of dosage heterogeneity on tumour behaviour is remains open.

Gives the cell-level arm of the claim: a daughter cell that inherits an ecDNA-bearing micronucleus reaches its next division later and dies more often than the sister cell that inherited none, so mis-segregation of the amplicon is a fitness penalty rather than only a dosage fluctuation. The underlying measurement is narrower than the sentence: micronuclei were enriched by hydroxyurea exposure before live-cell imaging, so the penalty is measured under induced replication stress; the comparison is between daughter and sister cells; and the delay and excess death were quantified for large ecDNA-containing micronuclei over 2 micrometres in diameter, being strongest where micronuclear ecDNA content was high while independent of copy number in the primary nucleus. The route the authors propose is loss of oncogenic transcription after micronucleation, and they state that the exact mechanism by which micronuclei affect cancer cell fate remains to be determined.

c-MYC Activation by Enhancer Hijacking or Enhancer Amplification
Mechanism confidence: Provisional
In a distinct subset of high-risk neuroblastoma, about 10% of cases when the subset is defined by high MYC expression, the MYC paralogue rather than MYCN is the driver. Activating mechanisms identified in some of these tumours are focal amplification of distal enhancers lying downstream of the MYC coding sequence, and translocation that brings a highly active enhancer from another locus into a topologically associating domain containing MYC. The subset is defined by expression rather than by lesion: MYC and MYCN expression are reciprocal across the cohort, some high-MYC tumours carry no detectable enhancer lesion, and of the primary tumours that do carry one only part rank in the high-expression group. Patients with high MYC expression had unfavourable outcomes that did not differ significantly from those of patients with MYCN-amplified tumours, which the authors describe as virtually identical.

Polyamine Biosynthesis Dependence
Mechanism confidence: Provisional
Neuroblastoma cells raise flux through polyamine biosynthesis, with ODC1 as the rate-limiting enzyme and a direct transcriptional target of MYCN. Transcriptome analysis of MYCN-amplified tumors shows the whole pathway deregulated rather than ODC1 alone, and high-risk tumors without MYCN amplification overexpress ODC1 as well, so the dependence is not confined to the amplified subset. Elevated ODC1 tracks reduced survival independently of MYCN status in two patient cohorts. The node is marked PROVISIONAL because the step from this pathway to the clinical effect of the approved drug is not established: at the approved low dose, polyamine depletion has not been shown to be the operative mechanism, and sensitivity to the inhibitor does not track MYCN or ODC1 copy number. See the Eflornithine treatment record for that evidence.

Compensatory Polyamine Uptake from the Microenvironment
Mechanism confidence: Provisional
Neuroblastoma cells import polyamines from the surrounding microenvironment, which is the reason blocking synthesis does not deplete them. Treating neuroblastoma cells with the ODC1 inhibitor eflornithine (DFMO) is only partially effective against cell growth, because compensatory mechanisms raise polyamine uptake; in culture, polyamines taken from the medium rescue the deficit the drug creates. SLC3A2 was identified as the key transporter carrying that uptake in neuroblastoma, knocking it down lowered uptake of radiolabelled spermidine, and DFMO treatment itself raised SLC3A2 protein, so the drug induces the route around its own target. Blocking uptake with AMXT 1501 alongside DFMO prevented or delayed tumour development in neuroblastoma-prone mice and extended survival in rodent models of established tumours, and in a second laboratory the same combination deepened the inhibition of protein synthesis even in cell lines resistant to high-dose DFMO alone. Marked PROVISIONAL because every result here is from cell lines or rodent models: nothing establishes that uptake limits the approved drug's effect in patients. The synthesis arm is the Polyamine Biosynthesis Dependence node, and what the approval does and does not settle is in the Eflornithine treatment record.

ALK Signaling Activation
ALK (anaplastic lymphoma kinase) is activated by point mutations in approximately 8-10% of neuroblastomas at diagnosis, and by amplification in additional cases. In neuroblastoma cells, high expression of the wild-type receptor can also lead to its constitutive activation. Intragenic rearrangement of the ALK locus is a third and rare route, found in four of 332 primary tumours screened, where the receptor is phosphorylated although no fusion protein is predicted. ALK mutations are enriched in familial neuroblastoma and represent a therapeutic target for ALK inhibitors.

GD2 Surface Antigen Expression
The disialoganglioside GD2 is expressed on the surface of nearly all neuroblastoma cells and only sparsely on normal tissue, which is what makes it the target of antibody therapy. Expression is not uniform, and it can be absent: in a series of 474 patients with unequivocal bone marrow infiltration, tumor cells showed complete or partial negative GD2 staining in 12.0% across diagnosis, treatment and recurrence, and 21 cases converted from positive to negative. That series found no event-free or overall survival difference between negative and positive staining, so loss of the antigen is recorded here as a property of the tumor rather than as a prognostic marker.
Downstream
Anti-GD2 Antibody-Mediated Tumor Cell Killing Surface GD2 is the antigen the therapeutic antibodies bind, so it is the precondition for antibody-mediated killing. This edge is intervention-conditioned: it carries flux only while an anti-GD2 antibody is being given, and the downstream node describes what the drug then does rather than anything the untreated tumor does.

Anti-GD2 Antibody-Mediated Tumor Cell Killing
An anti-GD2 antibody bound to surface GD2 recruits the host's innate effector arms: Fc-receptor-bearing innate immune cells kill the opsonized cell by antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, and bound antibody also triggers complement-dependent cytotoxicity. This node exists only under treatment, and it is the node the antibody treatments point at.

Low Tumor Mutation Burden
High-risk neuroblastoma carries few somatic coding mutations. Across the coding regions of 240 high-risk tumours the median exonic mutation frequency was 0.60 per Mb (0.48 nonsilent), with few recurrently mutated genes, a rate the authors place alongside medulloblastoma and haematopoietic malignancies and well below adult solid tumours. It is low on average rather than uniformly low: per-tumour counts ranged from 0 to 218, and two tumours carrying DNA-repair gene alterations reached 7.27 and 4.29 mutations per Mb. Two reviews of neuroblastoma immunotherapy name that burden as a hurdle to checkpoint blockade, one of them alongside the reduced tumour-cell MHC class I carried by the Low Tumor-Cell MHC Class I Expression node. Nothing cited here measures neoantigen load, antigen presentation or immune infiltration, so the step from few mutations to few mutation-derived neoantigens is an inference those reviews state rather than a result any of these sources tests.

PMID:23334666 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"To determine the spectrum of somatic mutation in high-risk neuroblastoma, we studied 240 affected individuals (cases) using a combination of whole-exome, genome and transcriptome sequencing as part of the Therapeutically Applicable Research to Generate Effective Treatments (TARGET) initiative...."
In the TARGET initiative, 240 matched tumour and normal (blood leukocyte) pairs from patients older than 18 months at diagnosis with metastatic stage 4 disease were sequenced: 221 cases by whole exome, 18 by whole genome and one by both, with RNA sequencing on ten of the genome cases. Across their coding regions the median somatic mutation frequency was 0.60 per Mb (0.48 nonsilent) and few genes were recurrently mutated, a rate the authors call consistent with unselected neuroblastomas and significantly lower than adult solid tumours, so low here means low relative to adult solid tumours. The figure describes high-risk stage 4 tumours at diagnosis rather than neuroblastoma as a whole, and it is a median: per-tumour counts ranged from 0 to 218, and two tumours with DNA-repair gene alterations reached 7.27 and 4.29 mutations per Mb. Graded DIRECT because the quoted sentence reports the mutation frequency this node is named for. What it does not establish is any immune consequence: the study measures neither neoantigen load, antigen presentation nor immune infiltration, so the inference from few mutations to few mutation-derived neoantigens for T cells to recognise is carried by the two reviews cited below and not by this series.

Abstract sentence of a review of antibody immunotherapy for high-risk metastatic neuroblastoma, making a general point about immunotherapy: low tumour mutational burden is a major hurdle for immune checkpoint inhibitors, and an immature or impaired immune system and an inhibitory tumour microenvironment can further complicate the prospects for successful immunotherapy. Graded INDIRECT because the sentence names no tumour and the sentence before it concerns paediatric cancers in general, so applying it to neuroblastoma is an inference from the review's subject and from its next sentence, which calls neuroblastoma poorly immunogenic. The review also scopes the cold phenotype to high-risk metastatic disease and describes low-risk neuroblastoma as having the characteristics of a hot tumour, so the claim does not extend across the disease, and the authors' hedge that these factors can further complicate immunotherapy is kept.
Low Tumor-Cell MHC Class I Expression
MHC class I on neuroblastoma tumour cells is low rather than absent. Immunohistochemistry with a panel of antibodies to the HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C loci, beta-2-microglobulin and HLA-DR found none of 17 evaluable diagnostic specimens immunopositive for MHC class I or class II, and an earlier series of ten tumours detected no HLA class I or beta-2-microglobulin reactivity on more than 94% of the small round cells in each tumour while a population under 6% did stain. Yet HLA class I tumour-cell density was quantified across tumours by in situ immunohistochemistry in 77 specimens and, combined with PD-L1, carried outcome information, being prognostic for overall survival, which is why this node says low and not absent. Two caveats bound the node. The two series that detected none are small, 17 and ten tumours, and date from 2005 and 1985. And nothing cited here measures T-cell infiltration or stratifies class I by MYCN status: the 2005 series states that its own result does not support a direct correlation between MYCN amplification and loss of MHC class I, so this node takes no incoming edge from MYCN-Driven Proliferation.

Immunocytochemistry for beta-2-microglobulin and HLA class I on ten solid neuroblastoma tumours from patients. In frozen sections of every tumour, blood vessel endothelium and a small population of cells, under 6% of the small round cells, stained, while no reactivity for either molecule was detected on the remaining more than 94%. The endothelial staining acts as an internal positive control in each section, so the negative small round cells are unlikely to reflect a failed stain. The authors report that the localisation of most positive cells near stromal tissue and blood vessels suggests most of them may be of non-tumour origin, so the stained minority is not shown to be tumour cells presenting class I. Patients differed in degree of disease involvement, yet no differences in beta-2-microglobulin or HLA class I expression were found among the tumours, and the paper describes a method for formaldehyde-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue alongside the frozen-section result. The authors present the finding as extending earlier reports of weak beta-2-microglobulin and HLA class I levels in cells of neuronal origin, so not detected means below what this 1985 immunocytochemical assay could detect rather than proven absence. The denominator is ten tumours, the readout is a stain scored on morphologically defined small round cells, and nothing here measures T-cell infiltration.

What it establishes for this node is that class I density on tumour cells was quantified across a patient series and carried outcome information. The result is for the combination of the two markers rather than for HLA class I density alone, it rests on a single cohort with a borderline p value and no independent validation cohort, and the abstract does not name the covariates, so it should not be read as class I density being independently prognostic. T-Cell-Poor Tumor Microenvironment
Tumours are T-cell-poor, and that poverty tracks MYCN amplification: in primary tumours from patients with metastatic disease the T-cell-poor tumours showed lower interferon-response and chemokine signature expression, in line with reduced immune cell infiltration. The contrast with MYCN-not-amplified tumours in a second patient series, and the interferon and chemokine route proposed for the MYCN link, are recorded on the incoming edge from MYCN-Driven Proliferation rather than on this node. The clinical corollary is cited here as patient evidence and not as a treatment claim: in the ADVL1412 phase 1-2 trial of single-agent nivolumab in children and young adults with relapsed or refractory non-CNS solid tumours or lymphoma, objective responses were confined to the lymphoma cohorts and were not observed in any other tumour type, neuroblastoma being one of the part-B expansion cohorts. Two caveats bound the node. The patient evidence is association and signature-based description rather than a demonstrated mechanism, with the T-cell content inferred from bulk-RNA signatures rather than counted in tissue. And the trial result is a non-response to one checkpoint antibody in heavily pretreated relapsed or refractory disease, with no per-cohort response rate reported for neuroblastoma, so it corroborates the T-cell-poor phenotype rather than measuring it.

Tumor-Associated Macrophage Infiltration
Mechanism confidence: Provisional
Tumour-associated macrophages are more abundant in metastatic than in locoregional neuroblastoma, and macrophage-associated gene expression carries prognostic weight in one stratum of the disease. In 71 localised and metastatic tumours assessed by immunohistochemistry, significantly greater numbers of infiltrating macrophages were seen only with CD163 staining, which identifies the alternatively activated (M2) phenotype, and only in stage 4 against locoregional tumours (t test P = .003); the excess did not reach significance with the other macrophage marker used, AIF1, and stage 4S tumours, which undergo spontaneous regression, did not differ from locoregional ones. Among metastatic MYCN-non-amplified tumours, those diagnosed at 18 months or older carried higher expression of inflammation-related genes than those diagnosed earlier, and in 133 such tumours the expression of five genes representing tumour-associated macrophages contributed 25% of the accuracy of a novel 14-gene tumour classification score. Among children diagnosed at 18 months or older, that score's low- against high-risk groups separated 5-year progression-free survival in the 94-patient subgroup of the CCG training cohort (47% against 12%, by leave-one-out cross-validation) and in two independent validation cohorts (57% against 8% in 39 patients treated on GPOH protocols, 50% against 20% in 52 treated on COG protocols). The 39 CCG patients diagnosed before 18 months are part of the 133-tumour training set behind the 25% figure but not of those survival comparisons. That score is a prognostic tumour score with a macrophage-associated part rather than a macrophage signature: in the authors' permutation analysis the tumour cell-related genes explained 63% of its accuracy and age at diagnosis a further 12%. The stratum here is metastatic MYCN-non-amplified disease, a different stratum from the MYCN-amplified association recorded on T-Cell-Poor Tumor Microenvironment, and the source's own conclusion is hedged: interactions between tumour and inflammatory cells may contribute to the clinical metastatic neuroblastoma phenotype.

In metastatic MYCN-non-amplified neuroblastoma the authors selected a 14-gene score from 44 candidate genes, 31 tumour-related and 13 inflammation-related, quantified in 133 tumours of the CCG training cohort, and validated it in 91 further tumours from patients treated on GPOH (39) and COG (52) protocols. In a permutation analysis the inflammation-related genes explained on average 25% of the model's accuracy in predicting progression-free survival, against 63% for the tumour cell-related genes and 12% for age at diagnosis, so the 14-gene score is a prognostic tumour score with a macrophage-associated part and not a macrophage signature. The gene levels are measured in tumour samples rather than as macrophage counts, and the result shows that macrophage-associated expression adds prognostic information alongside tumour genes, not that macrophage content alone predicts outcome.
Telomerase Activation
Telomerase-mediated telomere maintenance, one of the two telomere maintenance mechanisms in neuroblastoma. TERT rearrangements at 5p15.33 juxtapose the TERT coding sequence to strong enhancer elements, with chromatin remodelling and DNA methylation of the affected region, and despite their structural diversity they all induced massive transcriptional upregulation of TERT. MYCN amplification raises TERT transcription, and some tumours have high TERT expression with neither alteration. In 457 pretreatment neuroblastomas, TERT rearrangement was found in 46 and MYCN amplification in 93, and high TERT expression without either in 10 of 223 tumours with expression data. TERT promoter mutations are rare: none was found in 131 primary tumours representing the whole spectrum of the disease, and a single-centre series found them in 17 of 603 tumours. Activated telomerase, defined by these routes, was associated with the poorest overall survival and was an independent prognostic marker in multivariable analyses. Enzymatic telomerase activity has been shown in neuroblastoma cell lines that carry a TERT rearrangement or MYCN amplification.

p53 Pathway Inactivation
Loss of p53-axis control, through an inactivating TP53 mutation, MDM2 amplification (in the SIOPEN cohort cited here as CDK4/MDM2 co-amplification, the two genes lying at 12q14.1 and 12q15; in the relapse series cited here as MDM2 amplification alone at 12q15), or homozygous CDKN2A deletion removing p14ARF. In 84 tumours from 41 patients with relapsed neuroblastoma, a p53-pathway abnormality was detected in 20 of 41 (49%) cases. That is a share of patients who relapsed rather than of relapse tumours, and it is a floor, because MDM2 amplification was assessed in only 23 of the roughly 35 patients whose relapse tumour was p53-wild-type and TP53 sequencing covered exons 4-9. The parts of the pathway differ in timing: TP53 mutations were first detected after chemotherapy in all but one of the six mutated cases, whereas MDM2 amplification and p14ARF inactivation were present at both diagnosis and relapse in most cases, so this is not a uniformly therapy-era lesion. The p14ARF readout in that series was specific to CDKN2A exon 1-beta, the p53-arm product, whereas p16INK4a from the same locus acts in the RB arm. The pathway is not confined to MYCN-amplified disease: in a SIOPEN series of 98 non-MYCN-amplified, localized unresectable or stage 3 tumours of unfavourable histology, classed as intermediate risk under the European criteria used there and, in the paper's own words, as high risk in most of North America, 10 tumours carried a p53-pathway abnormality and those patients had inferior event-free and overall survival. That study's definition of the abnormality also admits a pathogenic ATM mutation, which this node does not bind.

Therapy-Resistant Relapse
The clinical state the relapse-enriched lesion classes converge on: disease that responds to initial treatment and returns resistant to it. Most patients with high-risk neuroblastoma respond initially, yet up to 60% of them relapse with therapy-resistant tumours despite chemotherapy, surgery, radiotherapy and immunotherapy, and over half of high-risk neuroblastomas relapse with chemoresistant disease. Relapse can be the outgrowth of clones established early: genomic profiling of 470 sequential and spatially separated samples from 283 patients found metastatic clones already at distant sites by diagnosis that could stay dormant and cause relapse years later, although the authors describe years-long dormancy as rare and most relapses in that cohort also carried additional genomic changes.
