Reduced ATRX/DAXX Complex Abundance
Reduced abundance of the ATRX/DAXX chromatin remodelling complex, a recurrent molecular feature of alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) in neuroblastoma. ATRX encodes an ATP-dependent helicase of the SWI/SNF family of chromatin remodellers and, with DAXX, deposits the histone variant H3.3 at telomeric regions. ALT-positive neuroblastomas show reduced ATRX/DAXX complex abundance, due either to ATRX mutation (55% of them in one cohort) or to low protein expression, while mutations in the complex members DAXX and H3F3A were extremely rare. In a pooled analysis of published ATRX-altered neuroblastomas, 68% of ATRX aberrations were multi-exon deletions, and 75% of these were predicted to be in-frame. ATRX mutation is strongly age-dependent: in 104 patients with metastatic disease, sampled to represent each age group, it was found in tumours from 14 of 32 adolescents and young adults, 9 of 54 children and none of 18 infants, although infant cases are reported. In the pooled analysis, each of the three types of ATRX aberration was more frequent in patients diagnosed at an older age, yet about 40% of the ATRX-aberrant patients were five years or younger at diagnosis.

Alternative Lengthening of Telomeres Loss of ATRX/DAXX complex function permits alternative lengthening of telomeres. ATRX mutation is associated with loss of nuclear ATRX protein and with ALT, and in one series every ALT tumour carried an ATRX or DAXX alteration. Without ATRX, histone H3.3 is not efficiently deposited at telomeric repeats, replication forks stall there, and the telomeres undergo the homologous recombination that leads to ALT.

Intratumoral Lymphoid Infiltration with Lymphoid Follicles
Most neuroblastic tumors from children with opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome (OMAS) carry a heavier lymphoid infiltrate than other neuroblastic tumors. In a blinded review of 13 such tumors against 41 age- and stage-matched controls, 12 had diffuse and extensive lymphocytic infiltration with lymphoid follicles, a pattern the authors call characteristic; no control had diffuse or extensive infiltration, although 18 had focal infiltrates and 6 had lymphoid follicles. In a comparison of OMAS-associated neuroblastomas with neuroblastomas from children without OMAS (38 against 26 tumors by RNA sequencing, fewer for repertoire sequencing and histology), B- and T-cell infiltration was greater and polyclonal; B cells were more numerous and, in the authors' summary, activated, and lay in tertiary lymphoid structures rich in T cells; and tertiary lymphoid structures were more frequent (10 of 14 OMAS-associated tumors against 2 of 6 low-risk and 1 of 5 high-risk controls), though not confined to OMAS. The infiltrate is not uniform: on clustering by immune gene signatures, several OMAS-associated tumors grouped with high-risk tumors from children without OMAS that had low immune-marker scores.

Cerebellar and Brainstem-Directed B- and T-Cell Autoimmunity This entry reads the tumor's lymphoid response as feeding the autoimmunity. In a model drawn from tumor studies, polyclonal autoreactive B cells act as antigen-presenting cells and drive tertiary lymphoid structure formation, thereby supporting the paraneoplastic neuropathology; the authors present tumor and nervous-system involvement as parts of one systemic autoimmune process, the step from the tumor to the brain was not tested, and whether the tumor infiltrate arises from lymphocytes entering from the circulation is unsettled. Cerebellar and Brainstem-Directed B- and T-Cell Autoimmunity
Autoimmunity held to be directed at the cerebellum and brainstem and to involve B and T lymphocytes. Children with opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome (OMS), most with normal cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cell counts, have expanded B-cell and gamma-delta T-cell subsets and a higher percentage of activated T cells in the CSF. In a cross-sectional cohort the subset expansion was found even years after onset and conventional treatment, the abnormalities correlated with neurological severity and disease duration, they did not differ significantly between children with and without a tumor, and, in children with neuroblastoma, tumor resection or chemotherapy did not alter them. In a larger cohort of 389 children from the same investigators, commercial serum paraneoplastic antibody panels were negative apart from subclinical titers in four children, whereas in untreated children CSF oligoclonal bands (58%) and a raised CSF B-cell percentage (93%) were common. No specific antibody is associated with neuroblastoma-associated OMS, and a study of OMAS-associated tumors identified no unifying single antigen behind their lymphoid infiltrate. Most of the CSF findings come from cohorts of children with and without a detected tumor.

Flow cytometry of CSF and blood lymphocytes from 36 children with OMS and 18 control subjects, in a cross-sectional study. These are OMS-wide data: the cohort includes children with and without a tumor, not only neuroblastoma-associated OMS. The expanded B-cell and gamma-delta T-cell subsets are given as subset percentages, and most children had normal CSF cell counts. The abstract reports no significant differences between the tumor and no-tumor groups, which is what lets OMS-wide data stand for the paraneoplastic autoimmunity node, but it does not give the size of the tumor subgroup or say which measures were compared, and a non-significant difference in 36 children does not show that the groups are the same. Because the design is cross-sectional, the persistence of the abnormalities and their being unaltered by resection or chemotherapy most likely come from comparing children sampled at different disease durations and treatment states, not from following the same children over time. The quote shows B- and T-cell changes in the CSF that track neurological severity; it does not identify an antigen or show that the response targets the cerebellum or brainstem. Replication-Stress Checkpoint Dependence
Mechanism confidence: Provisional
Neuroblastoma cells carry enough replication stress that they depend on the S and G2 checkpoint to survive it. CDK1 is held in check by CHK1 and WEE1, which buy time for repair before mitosis and let the cell tolerate stressed replication; removing either kinase collapses replication forks or forces an unprepared mitosis. A loss-of-function screen across the protein kinome found CHK1 the most potent of thirty cytotoxic hits in neuroblastoma, and the checkpoint is demonstrably running in patient material rather than only in culture: CHK1 was constitutively phosphorylated at Ser345 and Ser296 in six of eight high-risk primary tumours and in only one of eight low-risk ones. The dependence tracks N-Myc, since inhibitor sensitivity followed total MYC(N) protein and inducing MYCN in untransformed cells was by itself enough to phosphorylate CHK1. The node is marked PROVISIONAL because the disease-specific dependency rests largely on one screen and its follow-up assays, and because the clinical test of it has so far produced few responses in heavily pre-treated children.

Alternative Lengthening of Telomeres
Alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT), the recombination-based telomere maintenance mechanism that works without telomerase. Its measured frequency depends on cohort and assay: C-circle screening classified 9.2% of a 720-tumour screening cohort as ALT-positive, ALT-associated PML nuclear bodies marked 49 of 273 pretreatment neuroblastomas, and the C-circle assay marked 25 of 107 high-risk tumours from patients older than 18 months. In a registry cohort of 40 relapsed tumours, 47.5% were ALT-positive. ATRX alterations are found in only about half to 60% of ALT tumours. In primary tumours, ALT and the routes to telomerase activation occur almost mutually exclusively, and ATRX mutation and MYCN amplification co-occurred in only 1 of 819 tumours. ALT-positive neuroblastomas proliferate slowly, with a protracted clinical course, yet children with these tumours have a dismal outcome. About a third of ALT-positive tumours present with localized disease classified as low or intermediate risk, and in one cohort survival did not differ between ALT-positive tumours classified high risk and those classified low or intermediate risk.

Spontaneous Tumor Regression
Involution of a neuroblastoma, or its maturation toward ganglioneuroblastoma or ganglioneuroma, without cytotoxic treatment. It is seen mainly in infants whose tumours lack MYCN amplification, with localized disease or the 4S/MS pattern of metastasis: in the prospective NB95-S and NB97 trials, 44 of the 93 infants observed with gross residual localized tumour regressed spontaneously, with first signs 1 to 18 months after diagnosis and, in 15 of the 44, after the first year of life. Regression in this entry covers maturation as well as shrinkage, because among mass-screened localized adrenal tumours left in place, the six resected after one to four years of observation had all matured toward ganglioneuroblastoma, which the authors call a common phenomenon; 16 of 45 resected in infancy showed the same change. It is not universal in the 4S pattern: of 268 evaluable Italian infants with stage 4S disease, 29 progressed at 4S sites and 28 progressed to stage 4. Mass screening gives a figure for how much disease screening finds that never needed finding rather than a count of regressions: screening at about one year of age produced an estimated 7 overdiagnosed cases per 100,000 children, while stage 4 incidence and neuroblastoma mortality stayed similar to the unscreened control states. That estimate mixes tumours that would have regressed with tumours that would have stayed silent, and it cannot see tumours that regressed before the screening age or after clinical diagnosis, so it neither measures nor cleanly bounds regression. This node is the phenomenon rather than a mechanism; which mechanism produces it is unsettled, and the competing candidates are recorded as the entry's mechanistic hypothesis groups, two of which carry an edge into this node.

"For infants with localized neuroblastoma without MYCN amplification, chemotherapy was scheduled only in cases with threatening symptoms; otherwise, the tumor was either resected or observed by ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). ... Of 340 eligible participants, 190 underwent..."
In the prospective trials NB95-S and NB97, infants with localized neuroblastoma without MYCN amplification were given chemotherapy only for threatening symptoms; otherwise the tumour was resected or watched by ultrasound and MRI. Of 340 eligible participants, 190 underwent resection, 57 were given chemotherapy and 93 were observed with gross residual tumour. Of these 93, 44 showed spontaneous regression, with first signs 1 to 18 months after diagnosis and, in 15 of the 44, after the first year of life. This is direct human evidence that localized neuroblastoma can regress without resection or chemotherapy, and that regression can begin after the first year of life. The 44 of 93 figure describes this observed subgroup only and is not a population-wide regression rate; the abstract does not say whether the 39 infants whose tumours progressed were treated later. The ellipsis skips only the RESULTS section label.
PMID:29305654 SUPPORT DIRECT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Human Clinical
"Neuroblastomas are characterized by heterogeneous clinical behavior, from spontaneous regression or differentiation into a benign ganglioneuroma, to relentless progression despite aggressive, multimodality therapy. Indeed, neuroblastoma is unique among human cancers in terms of its propensity to..."
The opening of this single-author review's abstract states four things: neuroblastomas range in clinical behaviour from spontaneous regression or differentiation into a benign ganglioneuroma to relentless progression despite aggressive multimodality therapy; neuroblastoma is unique among human cancers in its propensity to undergo spontaneous regression; the strongest evidence for this comes from the mass screening studies conducted in Japan, North America and Europe; and it is most evident in infants with stage 4S disease. These statements are the review's synthesis of earlier screening programmes and stage 4S series, not data it generated. The quote presents differentiation into a benign ganglioneuroma as an alternative outcome to spontaneous regression rather than as a form of it. The body of the review qualifies two points. Spontaneous regression has also been observed in renal cell carcinoma, malignant melanoma, choriocarcinoma and lymphoid malignancies, so "unique" refers to how prevalent regression is in neuroblastoma. And regression is not restricted to stage 4S, because it can be seen in infants with virtually any stage of disease when the tumour is biologically favourable.
PMID:11685689 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"Fifty-one mass-screened adrenal neuroblastomas were divided into 2 groups. In infants less than 1 year of age (Group A), 45 neuroblastomas were resected, whereas 6 neuroblastomas were resected after observation in 1- to 4-year-old children (group B). ... Maturation toward ganglioneuroblastoma..."
Iwanaka et al. compared the histology of 51 mass-screened localized adrenal neuroblastomas: 45 resected in infancy (group A) and 6 resected after a period of observation, in children aged 1 to 4 years (group B). Maturation toward ganglioneuroblastoma was present in 16 of the 45 infant resections (36%) and in all six tumours resected after observation, so the 100% is 6 of 6. From this the authors conclude that, left untreated, maturation of mass-screened localized adrenal neuroblastoma is common. The finding is histological maturation rather than shrinkage or disappearance of the tumour, which is why this node counts maturation as one course of spontaneous regression. The study compares two different groups of tumours rather than repeated samples of the same tumour, and the abstract gives neither the length of observation nor how the six observed children came to resection, so group B may not represent every tumour that was observed. The ellipses skip the comparison and statistics sentences, the International Neuroblastoma Pathological Classification counts and the mitosis karyorrhexis index result.

NGF-TRKA Trophic Signaling Withdrawal
Mechanism confidence: Provisional
Loss of NGF-dependent TrkA signalling in the neuroblasts of a TRKA-expressing tumour, the cellular state on which the neurotrophin-deprivation account of spontaneous regression rests. Many more sympathetic neuronal precursors are produced during normal development than are needed, and those that fail to reach a target undergo developmentally programmed cell death, a process set primarily by the TrkA neurotrophin receptor and the limiting availability of its ligand NGF at the target site. Tumours from infants, especially with low-stage or 4S disease, generally express high levels of TrkA, and in patient tumours high TRK expression goes with favourable stage, age under one year and normal MYCN copy number. Cells cultured from TRK-expressing tumours survive and differentiate when NGF is supplied and die when it is withheld. Why TrkA-expressing favourable tumours survive at all despite a lack of available NGF is unresolved: a developmentally programmed switch from the ligand-independent TrkAIII isoform to TrkAI has been proposed as the step that makes such a tumour NGF-dependent. The node commits to no mode of death; that step is carried by the downstream edge, whose intermediate mechanisms state what has been measured and where.

Absence of a Telomere Maintenance Mechanism
Mechanism confidence: Provisional
Neuroblastomas in which neither route to telomere maintenance is present: no TERT rearrangement, no MYCN amplification, no elevated TERT expression in the absence of those alterations, and no ALT-associated PML nuclear bodies. Of 208 pretreatment neuroblastomas assessed for both telomerase activation and ALT, 99 met none of these criteria; they came mainly from young patients (mean age at diagnosis 378 days), and 96 of the 99 were from patients classified clinical low or intermediate risk, the other three from young stage 4 patients. This node is the mirror image of the entry's Telomerase Activation and Alternative Lengthening of Telomeres nodes, and carries the same two process terms with the modifier ABSENT. Whether the absence produces regression is unsettled, and the downstream edge records it as a hypothesis group of its own.

Unlimited Replicative Potential
The ability of tumour cells to keep dividing indefinitely, which a telomere maintenance mechanism (telomerase activation or ALT) provides. Its binding, increased cell population proliferation, follows the module node it conforms to and means expansion continuing past the limit that telomere shortening sets on normal cells, not a faster division rate: ALT-positive neuroblastomas proliferate more slowly than telomerase-activated ones. Aggressive neuroblastomas show a prolonged evolution during which they acquire telomere maintenance mechanisms, whereas tumours with a favourable prognosis expand clonally after a short evolution. In pretreatment neuroblastomas, patients whose tumours lacked a telomere maintenance mechanism had an excellent prognosis and those whose tumours had one did substantially worse. Within high-risk disease the picture is less clear: in one cohort the telomere maintenance groups differed in overall but not in event-free survival, and a subset of high-risk tumours lacks significant telomere lengthening activity, with cells derived from them proliferating for more than 200 population doublings while their telomeres shortened.

Limitations are a single cohort not uniformly treated on current protocols and a median TERT cutoff that may not be optimal.

Primary Tumor Growth and Local Mass Effect
Growth of the primary tumor at its site of origin along the sympathetic nervous system, and the pressure it exerts on, or its growth into, neighboring structures. About three-quarters of primary tumors arise in the abdomen or pelvis, half of these in the adrenal medulla, about a fifth in the posterior mediastinum and about a twentieth in the neck, and the local signs follow from the site. An abdominal primary can present as a palpable abdominal mass, abdominal distension or abdominal pain. A paravertebral tumor can grow through the neural foramina into the spinal canal and compress the spinal cord or nerve roots. Horner syndrome is seen mostly with localized disease, often with cervical or thoracic tumors, and is attributed to mass effect of the tumor on the sympathetic innervation of the eye. Compression of the renal artery or renal parenchyma is the usual explanation offered for hypertension at diagnosis, but a registry survey of hypertensive children could not demonstrate a correlation between hypertension and compression of the renal vascular pedicle. Cells leaving the primary tumor give rise to metastases at distant sites.

Horner Syndrome Horner syndrome arises mostly with localized disease, often with cervical or thoracic tumors, and can be the presenting sign. It is attributed to mass effect of the tumor on the sympathetic innervation of the eye; the cited series show its association with tumor site and localized disease rather than the nerve involvement itself. Horner syndrome can also follow surgical resection of the tumor, a complication of treatment that this edge does not cover.
Spinal Cord Compression A paravertebral tumor can extend through the neural foramina into the spinal canal and compress the spinal cord and/or nerve roots, causing radicular pain, motor deficit up to paraplegia, and sphincter dysfunction. Extension into the spinal canal does not always cause symptoms: in a prospective cohort selected for it, a third of the children were asymptomatic at enrollment.
Hypertension Compression of the renal artery or renal parenchyma by the tumor, with a renin-mediated rise in blood pressure, is the usual explanation offered for hypertension at diagnosis, and such hypertension frequently resolves after resection. The cited sources state this explanation rather than demonstrate it, and the link is contested. A registry survey of hypertensive children could not demonstrate a correlation between hypertension and compression of the renal vascular pedicle, although it found involvement of the renal pedicle to be the only risk factor consistently associated with hypertension persisting after surgery. In a single-center series of children with at least stage II hypertension, four had radiologic evidence of renal compression, but renin was normal in all four children in whom it was measured.
Metastatic Dissemination Tumor cells spread from the primary tumor through the lymphatic and hematogenous systems and establish metastases at distant sites. Tumors with unfavorable clinical behavior combine locally invasive growth with widespread metastatic dissemination, and orbital metastases mostly arise from an abdominal primary.

This supports the node's account of where primary tumors grow, which decides the local signs each can produce. It is a review summary rather than a cohort reported by the paper, and it does not itself describe mass effect.
Metastatic Dissemination
Spread of neuroblastoma cells from the primary tumor to distant sites, where they establish metastases. In 648 children with stage IV or IVS disease on two Children's Cancer Group protocols, metastases at diagnosis were in bone marrow (70.5%), bone (55.7%), lymph nodes (30.9%), liver (29.6%), and intracranial and orbital sites (18.2%), and rarely in lung or the central nervous system. Skeletal and marrow metastases account for bone pain, and orbital metastases for proptosis. Marrow infiltration has been associated with anemia and thrombocytopenia, but not in every series, and two series found anemia common with or without infiltration. In the metastatic pattern of INRGSS stage MS, in children younger than 18 months, metastases are confined to skin, liver and/or bone marrow; the liver is the main site and can enlarge enough to compress vital structures, and skin metastases present as subcutaneous nodules.

Downstream
Bone Pain Skeletal and bone marrow metastases cause bone pain, which can be diffuse and intense enough to stop a child moving freely.
Proptosis Orbital metastases infiltrating the periorbital bones cause proptosis and periorbital ecchymosis, often on both sides.
Anemia Infiltration of the bone marrow by tumor cells has been associated with anemia at diagnosis, in one series with infiltration by more than 10% malignant cells. The link is contested: two other series found anemia common in children with and without marrow infiltration and attributed it to iron or nutritional deficiency. The cited series report associations and do not measure how infiltration would lower red cell production.
Thrombocytopenia Infiltration of the bone marrow by tumor cells has been associated with thrombocytopenia at diagnosis in two series, in one of them with infiltration by more than 10% malignant cells, although a third series found it no more frequent with marrow involvement than without. The cited series report associations and do not measure how infiltration lowers the platelet count.
Hepatomegaly In the INRGSS stage MS pattern the liver is the main metastatic site, and extensive liver involvement enlarges the liver, which in young infants can compress vital structures, with signs of pulmonary, renal or hepatic compromise.
Subcutaneous Nodules Skin metastases can present as noncompressible, blue-purple subcutaneous nodules, part of the INRGSS stage MS pattern in young children.

Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide Hypersecretion
Secretion of vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) by tumor cells, the cause of a rare watery-diarrhea syndrome. In a French series of 22 patients with neuroblastic tumors and watery diarrhea, VIP secretion was confirmed by serum assay and/or immunohistochemistry. In 91 children with resected neuroblastic tumors, of which about a third were ganglioneuroblastomas, VIP was detected in the tumor by immunohistochemistry in 27.5%, and its staining intensity was higher in children with diarrhea and in those with hypokalemia and was associated with histopathological classification.

Adrenergic and Mesenchymal Cell-State Plasticity
Neuroblastoma tumour cells occupy two transcriptionally divergent identity states, and the field names them twice over. van Groningen and colleagues name them adrenergic and mesenchymal, defined by a super-enhancer contrast between isogenic cell-line pairs. Boeva and colleagues, profiling the super-enhancer landscape of neuroblastoma cell lines, name a sympathetic noradrenergic identity whose core regulatory circuitry module includes PHOX2B, HAND2 and GATA3, an NCC-like identity driven by a circuitry module containing AP-1 transcription factors, and a mixed type. Mesenchymal and NCC-like are close but not identical concepts: the first is defined by an isogenic-pair super-enhancer contrast, the second by membership of a core regulatory circuitry. In cell lines and xenografts the switch between the two identities arises spontaneously, runs in both directions and is accompanied by epigenetic reprogramming. The noradrenergic-to-mesenchymal shift occurs in culture; the reverse shift was documented after engraftment in mice. Enforced expression of a NOTCH3 intracellular domain drives the adrenergic-to-mesenchymal direction with genome-wide remodelling of the H3K27ac landscape, and a NOTCH feed-forward loop then maintains the induced state. SWI/SNF chromatin-remodelling ATPases are required to establish the mesenchymal gene-permissive chromatin state that facilitates this plasticity. In patient tumours the dominant identity is noradrenergic. Gene-expression signatures derived from established cell lines fail to identify mesenchymal tumour cells in patient tumours, whereas signatures developed from early-passage orthotopic patient-derived xenografts enable their identification. A minority subpopulation of noradrenergic tumour cells co-expresses mesenchymal features, found in a subset of tumours rather than in all of them, and the mesenchymal-like programme detectable in some pre-treated high-risk patient tumours is weakly expressed, sits inside cancer cells that remain otherwise adrenergic, and appears distinct from the presumptive drug-resistance mesenchymal programmes of cell lines. Whether patient tumours also carry a discrete, purely mesenchymal tumour-cell population of the kind cultured cells show is unsettled; the evidence collected here establishes neither its presence nor its exclusion. Microenvironmental influence is not one-directional, and the two documented cues were measured in different systems. In mouse xenografts, cells of either starting identity gave rise to tumours with a noradrenergic phenotype, which the authors read as microenvironmental pressure towards that state. In cultured cell panels, hypoxia shifted adrenergic cells towards mesenchymal gene expression. The mesenchymal state is not the less malignant of the two: in vivo reprogramming of adrenergic cells found mesenchymal and adrenergic cells equally oncogenic.

Downstream
Mesenchymal-State Chemotherapy Resistance The state switch is what produces the resistant fraction: cells at or moving towards the mesenchymal pole survive induction chemotherapy, so the mesenchymal proportion rises after treatment. The patient data behind this edge are observational and do not separate therapy-induced switching into the mesenchymal state from survival of mesenchymal cells already present.
ALK-Inhibitor Escape by Loss of Target Expression Occupying the mesenchymal pole leaves the cells without ALK expression, and so without the drug target, which is why the escape follows from the cell state rather than from any change in ALK itself. Demonstrated in cell lines and in xenografts of those cells.
Mesenchymal-State Immune Activation The state that confers chemotherapy resistance and ALK-inhibitor escape carries the opposite immune phenotype: the immune-enriched subset of neuroblastomas is the one characterised by mesenchymal lineage signatures, and mesenchymal-state cells are the ones cytotoxic lymphocytes recruit to and kill.

Mesenchymal-State Chemotherapy Resistance
Mechanism confidence: Provisional
Mesenchymal-state cells survive cytotoxic chemotherapy that kills adrenergic cells, and mesenchymal features have been reported to become enriched after chemotherapy and at relapse while adrenergic traits predominate in untreated tumours. What makes this a consequence of plasticity rather than an independent resistance mechanism is that blocking the switch itself prevents the resistance: degrading the SWI/SNF ATPases that hold mesenchymal genes in a permissive chromatin state inhibits plasticity and, with it, the outgrowth of the resistant fraction. The post-treatment enrichment reports are associations and do not separate selection of already resistant cells from therapy-induced switching, and the identity of the mesenchymal programme detectable in patients is not settled, which is why the node is held provisional.

ALK-Inhibitor Escape by Loss of Target Expression
Mechanism confidence: Provisional
Mesenchymal-type neuroblastoma cells express neither mutant nor wild-type ALK, so ALK inhibition has no target in them and the escape is absence of the drug target rather than an alteration in it. The mesenchymal cells resemble immature precursor cells, which also lack ALK expression, so the absence tracks the identity state the cells occupy. This is a cell-line and xenograft result: the cells were resistant to ALK inhibitors in culture, and tumours formed from them progressed under ALK inhibitor given to the xenografted animals. No patient-level evidence is curated here.

Mesenchymal-State Immune Activation
Mechanism confidence: Provisional
The subset of neuroblastomas enriched for immune-related transcripts is predominantly characterised by mesenchymal lineage gene-expression signatures, while tumours expressing adrenergic lineage signatures are less immunogenic by the same measures. The enrichment covers transcripts of immune activation and of immune inhibition together, so this is not a claim of net anti-tumour immunity: the same tumours carry higher immune-evasion scores. Functionally, mesenchymal lineage cells secrete inflammatory cytokines that recruit T cells and are efficiently killed by cytotoxic T and natural killer cells in culture, and in an immunocompetent mouse model the mesenchymal-marker-enriched, MHC class I-high tumours responded better to combined PD-1 and CTLA-4 blockade than their counterparts. The patient-level half is correlative transcriptomics; the killing and checkpoint results are functional and come from cultured cells and from mice.

Histopathology

7
Schwannian Stroma-Poor Neuroblastic Histology
The defining histology of this entry under the International Neuroblastoma Pathology Classification (INPC), which the International Neuroblastoma Pathology Committee proposed in 1999 on the framework of the Shimada classification with minor modifications. INPC is an age-linked classification that depends on the differentiation grade of the neuroblasts, their cellular turnover index and the presence or absence of Schwannian stromal development. It places peripheral neuroblastic tumors in four categories: neuroblastoma (Schwannian stroma-poor), subtyped as undifferentiated, poorly differentiated or differentiating; ganglioneuroblastoma, intermixed (Schwannian stroma-rich); ganglioneuroma (Schwannian stroma-dominant); and ganglioneuroblastoma, nodular. Only the stroma-poor neuroblastoma category belongs to this entry. INPC was designed for prognostic distinction among pediatric peripheral neuroblastic tumors and is not applicable to adult ones, although there is no clear consensus on the age that separates the two groups.

Undifferentiated Neuroblastoma Subtype VERY_RARE
INPC subtype of the neuroblastoma category composed of tumor cells without clearly recognizable neurite production. Accordingly, in routine practice the diagnosis is confirmed by immunohistochemistry, in which positive nuclear staining for PHOX2B is critical. INPC classifies every neuroblastoma of the undifferentiated subtype as unfavorable histology, regardless of the patient's age. It is the rarest subtype: 177 of 4,680 Schwannian stroma-poor tumors (3.8%) classified at central review in the Children's Oncology Group Neuroblastoma Pathology Reference Laboratory between August 2001 and March 2012, on specimens obtained before chemotherapy or irradiation.

Poorly Differentiated Neuroblastoma Subtype VERY_FREQUENT
INPC subtype in which the tumor cells produce neurites, with or without Homer Wright rosette formation, detectable on H&E staining; neuropil is present, but fewer than 5% of tumor cells show ganglionic differentiation. By differentiation grade, INPC places it in favorable histology when the patient is diagnosed younger than 18 months (up to 547 days) and in unfavorable histology from 18 months (548 days); a favorable assignment also requires a low or intermediate mitosis-karyorrhexis index (see INPC Favorable Histology). It is the commonest subtype: 4,081 of 4,680 Schwannian stroma-poor tumors (87.2%) classified at central review in the Children's Oncology Group Neuroblastoma Pathology Reference Laboratory between August 2001 and March 2012.

Differentiating Neuroblastoma Subtype OCCASIONAL
INPC subtype in which more than 5% of tumor cells have the appearance of differentiating neuroblasts, defined by synchronous nuclear and cytoplasmic differentiation: cytoplasmic and nuclear enlargement, a cytoplasmic diameter at least twice the nuclear diameter, and an eccentrically located nucleus with vesicular chromatin and a single prominent nucleolus. By differentiation grade, INPC places it in favorable histology when the patient is diagnosed younger than 5 years (up to 1824 days), provided the mitosis-karyorrhexis index also qualifies (see INPC Favorable Histology); from 5 years (1825 days) a favorable assignment requires further maturation beyond the neuroblastoma category. 422 of 4,680 Schwannian stroma-poor tumors (9.0%) classified at central review in the Children's Oncology Group Neuroblastoma Pathology Reference Laboratory between August 2001 and March 2012 were of this subtype.

Mitosis-Karyorrhexis Index
An INPC morphologic indicator for tumors in the neuroblastoma category: the number of mitotic and karyorrhectic cells per 5,000 neuroblastoma cells, classed as low (under 100), intermediate (100 to 200) or high (over 200). At the Children's Oncology Group Neuroblastoma Pathology Reference Laboratory it is determined on primary or metastatic tumor samples submitted before chemotherapy or irradiation, excluding bone-marrow metastases. The prognostic meaning of low and intermediate MKI depends on age at diagnosis: among 4,282 neuroblastomas reviewed at that laboratory between August 2001 and March 2012, the INPC age cut-offs of 60 months for low MKI and 18 months for intermediate MKI were independently prognostic in multivariable analysis, whereas a 4-month cut-off within high MKI was not significant after adjustment, consistent with the INPC applying no age cut-off to high MKI. In a Children's Cancer Group series reported in 2001, MYCN-amplified neuroblastomas lacked neuroblastic differentiation regardless of patient age and were generally linked to increased mitotic and karyorrhectic activity, with higher MKI classes in younger patients.

INPC Favorable Histology
The INPC favorable-histology group as defined for the neuroblastoma category: poorly differentiated or differentiating tumors with a low or intermediate mitosis-karyorrhexis index in patients younger than 18 months, and differentiating tumors with a low index in patients aged 18 months to 5 years. Among 630 neuroblastoma-category tumors in a Children's Cancer Group pathology review reported in 2001, this subgroup had 90.4% 5-year event-free survival. Under the INPC the grouping is to be determined only from primary or metastatic tumor tissue obtained before chemotherapy or irradiation, and once assigned it is not to be changed during the clinical course, because therapy-associated histologic changes may not have proven prognostic significance. The Children's Oncology Group and International Neuroblastoma Risk Group (INRG) classifications use INPC histology differently: the Children's Oncology Group stratifies treatment using age together with histology classified by the age-linked INPC criteria, which by definition duplicates the prognostic contribution of age, whereas the INRG classification incorporates individual histologic features underlying INPC. A 2020 analysis of the INRG Data Commons recommended replacing INPC with those individual features in the Children's Oncology Group classification as well; that was a proposal, and when it was published the Children's Oncology Group classification still combined INPC histology with age.

INPC Unfavorable Histology
The INPC unfavorable-histology group as defined for the neuroblastoma category: undifferentiated tumors and tumors with a high mitosis-karyorrhexis index at any age; poorly differentiated tumors, and tumors with an intermediate index, in patients aged 18 months to 5 years; and any neuroblastoma-category tumor in patients aged 5 years or older. The pre-treatment tissue rule and the differing use of the grouping by the Children's Oncology Group and INRG risk classifications apply as for favorable histology (see INPC Favorable Histology). In a Children's Cancer Group pathology review of tumors from the CCG-3881 and CCG-3891 studies, reported in 2001, this subgroup had 26.9% event-free survival. That figure belongs to its cohort and era: a 2022 review gives 5-year event-free survival of 54.6% for unfavorable and 88.1% for favorable histology (5-year overall survival 65.6% and 96.4%), citing the cohort analyzed for the 2021 revised Children's Oncology Group risk classification. In high-risk disease, histology after induction chemotherapy differs from the diagnostic histology, but the difference has not been shown to be prognostic: in paired diagnostic and post-induction resection samples from 94 high-risk patients on Children's Oncology Group trials (2001-2013), tumors resected after induction chemotherapy had shifted toward a more differentiated, less mitotically active histology, and neither histologic features at resection nor their change from diagnosis was significantly associated with progression-free or overall survival.

Here, not prognostic means no statistically significant association with progression-free or overall survival in a cohort of this size: the shift from intermediate or high MKI at diagnosis to low MKI at resection had hazard ratios of 2.1 for progression-free survival (p = 0.0908) and 2.3 for overall survival (p = 0.0773). The series is not restricted by stage or presentation (it spans every INSS stage), so it sets the phenotype's band: 15% falls in OCCASIONAL. The same weight-loss figure appears in the paper's results table. The authors' word 'frequently' is their own prose, not a frequency band. Limitations: a single center, data taken from a retrospective review of medical records, a case mix weighted toward advanced disease (the authors report a predominance of advanced INSS stages and note that several epidemiological studies show similar results), ages that run from the neonatal period into young adulthood, and no breakdown by histological subtype.

Retrospective single-center review of children with neuroblastoma seen at the Hospital for Sick Children, published in 1984. The first quoted sentence supplies the denominator, 405 children reviewed, 80 of whom had ophthalmic involvement; the second names opsoclonus as one of the three major eye signs the study examined, with proptosis and Horner syndrome; and the third says opsoclonus-myoclonus occurred in 9 children and in all 9 was the presenting sign of an occult, localized tumor. The abstract calls the syndrome opsoclonus-myoclonus and does not mention ataxia, and it reports survival only, not neurological outcome. A single-institution study from Campinas, Brazil, which screened 83 of the 178 children diagnosed with neuroblastoma there between 2000 and July 2014, chosen only by sample availability, for TP53 p.R337H. It was prompted by carriers at the same institution with both neuroblastoma and an adrenocortical tumour, two of the seven had both, and three of the seven were tested in tumour tissue only, so their germline status rests on the tumour genotype. Platform: Small molecule
Chemotherapy intensity varies by risk group. Most low-risk patients may need no immediate chemotherapy. In the Children's Oncology Group low-risk trial P9641, chemotherapy was reserved for patients with, or at risk for, symptomatic disease, with less than half of the tumor resected at diagnosis, or with unresectable progression after surgery alone. Infants with localized neuroblastoma without MYCN amplification and without threatening symptoms may be observed first instead of treated: in the NB95-S and NB97 trials, those whose tumors were left unresected and observed had excellent 3-year overall and metastasis-free survival, not different from that of infants treated with surgery or chemotherapy. In the Children's Oncology Group trial A3961, intermediate-risk patients were assigned four or eight cycles of carboplatin, etoposide, cyclophosphamide and doxorubicin by tumor biology and response, with a substantially shorter duration and lower doses than in earlier trials, and very high survival was still achieved, although 3-year overall survival was lower with unfavorable than with favorable tumor biology (93% vs 98%). In the single-arm Children's Oncology Group trial ANBL0531, subsets of intermediate-risk patients received less treatment than in legacy Children's Oncology Group trials, and 3-year event-free and overall survival among its 404 evaluable patients were 83.2% and 94.9%; infants with stage 4 tumors and one or more unfavorable biologic features had lower 3-year event-free survival than those with favorable biology (66.8% vs 86.9%), and the investigators conclude that more effective treatment is still needed for them. High-risk patients receive intensive multi-agent induction chemotherapy; one six-cycle regimen, based on the induction of the Children's Oncology Group trial ANBL0532, gives cisplatin, etoposide, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and topotecan.

PMID:22529259 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"Chemotherapy was reserved for patients with, or at risk for, symptomatic disease, with less than 50% tumor resection at diagnosis, or with unresectable progressive disease after surgery alone."
COG P9641's rule for who received chemotherapy. The abstract gives the protocol: patients underwent maximally safe resection of tumor, and chemotherapy was reserved for the three situations quoted. The full text defines them more narrowly. Immediate chemotherapy was offered for protocol-defined symptoms that compromised organ function or were life threatening and could not be relieved by surgery, for less than partial resection, and, at the investigator's discretion, for symptomatic spinal cord compression or the risk of it; at progression, surgery was repeated and patients with less than 90% resection were offered chemotherapy. The sentence states the design, not its outcome. The paper calls P9641 a phase III nonrandomized prospective study, so it does not compare observation with chemotherapy head to head. Abstract methods sentence.
PMID:22529259 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"Immediate use of chemotherapy may be restricted to a minority of patients with low-risk NBL."
The trialists' own conclusion from COG P9641, and the source for the statement that most low-risk patients may need no immediate chemotherapy. The full text gives the denominators behind 'minority': of the 915 eligible patients, 115 received chemotherapy at diagnosis, and 800 were asymptomatic and observed after their initial operation, 89 of whom (11.1%) later had recurrence or progression. Five-year overall survival was 97% for the patients treated with surgery alone and 98% for those given immediate chemotherapy. The word 'immediate' matters, because chemotherapy could still be given at progression. Outcomes were not equally good in every subgroup. The abstract notes that stage 2b patients who are older or have diploid or unfavorable-histology tumors fare less well, and in the full text the 41 asymptomatic stage 4S patients treated with surgery alone had lower 5-year event-free survival than the 39 stage 4S patients given surgery and chemotherapy (63% vs 92%, P = .0016), although overall survival did not differ significantly (84% vs 97%, P = .1302); the authors call that overall-survival difference surprising and say its reason is not yet evident. P9641 was nonrandomized, so this is a conclusion about withholding chemotherapy, not a head-to-head comparison with it. Abstract conclusion sentence.
PMID:18349403 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"Overall survival (OS; 3-year OS, 0.99 +/- 0.01) and metastases-free survival (rate at 3 years, 0.94 +/- 0.03) for patients with unresected tumors was excellent and was not different from patients treated with surgery or chemotherapy."
In the prospective multicenter trials NB95-S and NB97, the protocol for infants with localized neuroblastoma without MYCN amplification scheduled chemotherapy only for threatening symptoms; otherwise the tumor was either resected or observed by ultrasound and MRI. Of 340 eligible participants, 190 underwent resection, 57 received chemotherapy and 93 were observed with gross residual tumor. For the 93 observed infants, 3-year overall survival was 0.99 and 3-year metastases-free survival 0.94, which the authors report as excellent and not different from the infants treated with surgery or chemotherapy. This supports observing these infants first instead of treating them. Observation was not uneventful: of the 93, 28 had local progression, 7 progressed to stage 4S and 4 to stage 4, and the abstract neither says how they were then treated nor reports event-free survival, so the survival figures describe the observe-first strategy as a whole, not observation alone in every infant. Allocation among resection, chemotherapy and observation was not randomized: chemotherapy was reserved for threatening symptoms, and the abstract does not say how resection or observation was chosen for the others, so the three groups were selected differently. 'Not different' means no difference was detected, not that equivalence was shown, and the figures are 3-year only. The result is confined to infants and does not test observation in older children with low-risk disease. Abstract results sentence.

Surgical Resection
Action: Definitive Surgical ResectionNCI Thesaurus (NCIT) Relation: this treatment is this clinical intervention This treatment is Definitive Surgical Resection (NCIT:C154430). NCIT:C154430 is a clinical intervention from the NCI Thesaurus. NCIT:C154430
Platform: Surgery
Resection of the primary tumor has a role that differs by risk group. In low-risk disease surgery can be the only treatment: in the Children's Oncology Group trial P9641, asymptomatic patients with low-risk INSS stage 2a or 2b disease who were observed after their initial operation, without upfront chemotherapy, had excellent survival. Most infants younger than six months with a small adrenal mass suspected to be neuroblastoma, and confined to the adrenal gland on imaging, can be spared surgery by expectant observation with serial ultrasound and urine catecholamine monitoring: in the Children's Oncology Group study ANBL00P2, 81% of the 83 infants managed by expectant observation were spared resection. On long-term follow-up, 10-year event-free and overall survival for all 87 eligible infants, including the 4 who had immediate surgery, were 93.7% and 98.0%. In high-risk disease the primary tumor is resected after induction chemotherapy. More complete resection has been associated with better event-free survival and local control in two cooperative-group analyses, which disagree on overall survival. In the SIOPEN HR-NBL1 trial, complete macroscopic excision was associated with higher 5-year event-free and overall survival and a lower cumulative incidence of local progression than incomplete resection; severe operative complications occurred in 9.7% of patients and surgical mortality was 0.46%. In the Children's Oncology Group trial A3973, resection of 90% or more was associated with longer event-free survival and less local progression, but on multivariable analysis it had no significant effect on overall survival. Neither comparison was randomized, and the A3973 investigators described the role of primary tumor resection in high-risk disease as controversial.

PMID:22529259 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"Excellent survival rates can be achieved in asymptomatic low-risk patients with stages 2a and 2b NBL after surgery alone."
Abstract conclusion of COG P9641, stated for the trial's primary cohort, asymptomatic INSS stage 2a and 2b disease. In this phase III nonrandomized prospective study, patients underwent maximally safe resection, and asymptomatic low-risk patients with at least partial (more than 50%) resection were eligible for observation without chemotherapy. The 306 asymptomatic stage 2a/2b patients observed after their initial operation had 5-year event-free survival of 87% +/- 2% and overall survival of 96% +/- 1%, and the primary objective, 3-year overall survival of 95% in this cohort, was met (95% CI on 3-year overall survival, 96% to 100%). 'Surgery alone' names the initial strategy, analyzed by intent to treat, not the whole course of treatment: event-free survival counted relapse and progression as events, per protocol recurrent or progressive disease was treated with surgery again, with chemotherapy offered when less than 90% could be resected, and 42 of the 89 observed patients (all stages) whose disease recurred or progressed received off-protocol therapy that is not recorded. Within stage 2b, event-free and overall survival were significantly lower for unfavorable-histology or diploid tumors, and overall survival was significantly lower for patients 18 months or older. There was no randomized chemotherapy comparator: overall survival was similar to earlier POG studies that gave these patients multiagent chemotherapy for up to 8 months. Abstract conclusion sentence.
PMID:22964741 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"Eighty-one percent of patients on the observation arm were spared resection."
Primary result of COG ANBL00P2, a prospective multicenter study of infants younger than 6 months with a small adrenal mass confined to the gland on imaging. Parents chose the arm, so it was not randomized: of 87 eligible infants, 83 were managed by expectant observation with serial ultrasound and urine VMA/HVA monitoring, and 4 had immediate surgery. Sixteen of the 83 observed infants eventually had surgery, so 67 of 83 (81%) were spared resection. Three-year overall survival across all 87 infants was 100%, with a median follow-up of 3.2 years among infants without an event. Eligibility did not require a tissue diagnosis, so this is a cohort of suspected neuroblastoma. Of the 16 observed infants who went to surgery, 10 had neuroblastoma (8 INSS stage 1, one stage 2B, one stage 4S) and 6 had other lesions (2 low-grade adrenocortical neoplasms, 2 adrenal hemorrhages, 2 extralobar pulmonary sequestrations). The 81% is a crude proportion: the 67 spared include the 12 infants lost to follow-up before any known resection. The paper also gives a 3-year resection-free survival estimate for the observation arm, with resection as the only event counted, of 79.8% (standard error 6.0%). Abstract results sentence.
PMID:40452136 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"Among 87 eligible patients, the 10-year event-free survival (EFS) was 93.7%, and overall survival (OS) was 98.0%."
Long-term follow-up of COG ANBL00P2, in which the parents of infants aged 6 months or younger with small localized adrenal masses (suspected perinatal neuroblastoma, in the paper's own term) chose expectant observation or immediate surgery. These are whole-cohort figures: the 87 include 4 infants who had immediate surgery (original ANBL00P2 report, PMID:22964741), and the full text gives 10-year event-free and overall survival of 93.3% and 97.9% for the 83 on the observation arm alone, an estimated 79.9% of whom were still resection-free. Event-free survival here counts any malignant event as well as a neuroblastoma event or death, so it is not the same measure as the 3-year neuroblastoma-event figure of the original report. The 10-year estimates rest on few patients: median follow-up for the 82 observed children still alive was 4.7 years, 13 of the 27 who stopped observation early were lost to follow-up, and the authors note that relatively few completed 10 years, although the survival curves were flat between 5 and 10 years. One observed infant was found to have INSS stage 4 disease after 4.5 years and was treated for high-risk disease; that child was censored at 5.7 years with vital status unavailable, so the overall-survival figure cannot include that outcome. One observed child died of causes unrelated to neuroblastoma. Abstract results sentence.

Autologous Stem Cell Transplant
Action: hematopoietic stem cell transplantationNCI Thesaurus (NCIT) Relation: this treatment is this clinical intervention This treatment is hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, annotated with Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation (NCIT:C15431). NCIT:C15431 is a clinical intervention from the NCI Thesaurus. Ontology label: Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation NCIT:C15431
Platform: Cell therapy
High-dose, myeloablative chemotherapy with autologous stem-cell rescue, as consolidation after induction chemotherapy and surgery. Two randomized phase 3 trials set the current standard, and each changed a different part of it. The Children's Oncology Group's ANBL0532 compared tandem transplant, thiotepa and cyclophosphamide followed by dose-reduced carboplatin, etoposide and melphalan, with a single carboplatin-etoposide-melphalan transplant, and found three-year event-free survival from randomization of 61.6% against 48.4%. SIOPEN's HR-NBL1 compared two single regimens, busulfan with melphalan against carboplatin, etoposide and melphalan, and found three-year event-free survival of 50% against 38%, with fewer severe adverse events on busulfan-melphalan but more veno-occlusive disease. That high-dose therapy with autologous rescue is worth giving at all comes from CCG-3891, where it beat non-myeloablative chemotherapy on five-year event-free survival, 30% against 19%. The two newer results are not additive, because ANBL0532's tandem arm is itself carboplatin-etoposide-melphalan-based: tandem transplant and busulfan-melphalan have not been compared with each other. That gap is recorded as a knowledge gap attached to this record.

Platform: Radiotherapy
Radiation to the primary tumor site is used in high-risk disease after induction chemotherapy, surgical resection and consolidation with stem cell transplant. In the Children's Oncology Group phase III trial ANBL0532, patients were prescribed 21.6 Gy to the preoperative primary tumor volume, starting no sooner than 28 days after transplantation, with a boost to 36 Gy for gross residual tumor after incomplete resection; the boost did not significantly improve the 5-year cumulative incidence of local progression compared with historical controls. Primary-site relapse still occurs after radiotherapy.

For patients with an incomplete resection of the primary tumor (defined as > 1 cm3 residual soft tissue density on end-induction scans), a boost of 14.4 Gy in 1.8 Gy..."
Radiotherapy protocol of the Children's Oncology Group phase III trial ANBL0532 in newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma, from the full-text methods. Patients were prescribed 21.6 Gy to the primary tumor volume as it was before surgery, and those with gross residual tumor after incomplete resection received a further 14.4 Gy boost to it, 36 Gy in total. Radiotherapy began no sooner than 28 days after transplantation, and the full text places the assessment of incomplete resection after the fifth induction cycle and before transplantation, so radiotherapy followed induction chemotherapy, resection and consolidation with stem cell transplant. The trial compared radiation doses, not radiotherapy with no radiotherapy, so it is not evidence that radiotherapy itself improves outcome. Full-text methods sentences.
PMID:32530765 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"Boost radiotherapy to gross residual tumor present at the end of induction did not significantly improve 5-year CILP."
Abstract conclusion of COG ANBL0532. The boost was compared with a historical cohort from the preceding trial COG A3973, in which irradiated patients received 21.6 Gy without a boost; among patients with residual tumor, the difference in 5-year cumulative incidence of local progression (CILP) was not significant (P = .4126). Across all irradiated patients, 5-year CILP was 11.2% in ANBL0532 (323 patients) and 7.1% in A3973 (328 patients), so primary-site relapse still occurred after radiotherapy in both trials. The comparison is historical rather than randomized, and the authors conclude that new strategies are needed to lower the risk of locoregional failure. Abstract conclusion sentence.
PMID:22010014 SUPPORT INDIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"External beam radiotherapy (21.6 Gy in 1.8 Gy fractions) beginning ≥ 28 days following PBSC infusion was administered to the presurgical gross tumor volume and sites of residual disease"
Methods of the Children's Oncology Group pilot ANBL02P1, which enrolled 31 patients with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma. Residual primary tumor was resected after the fifth of six induction cycles. Patients with at least a partial response at the end of induction, an adequate stem cell product without detectable tumor contamination, and adequate cardiac and renal function then received consolidation with carboplatin, etoposide and melphalan, followed by stem cell infusion. The quoted sentence places radiotherapy after the transplant, beginning at least 28 days after that infusion, and gives the field: the presurgical gross tumor volume, the tumor as it was before resection, plus any sites of residual disease. That resection came before radiotherapy is not in this sentence; it follows from the word 'presurgical' and from the protocol's surgery step, which is a separate methods sentence. This is the planned treatment sequence of one feasibility pilot whose primary end point was induction feasibility; the paper reports no radiotherapy-specific results, so it is not evidence that radiotherapy improves outcome. Full-text methods sentence.

Platform: Monoclonal antibody
An anti-GD2 monoclonal antibody added to post-consolidation therapy is standard of care in high-risk neuroblastoma. In the randomized COG trial ANBL0032 the comparator arm was isotretinoin, which both arms received, and adding the antibody with alternating GM-CSF and interleukin-2 improved both event-free and overall survival; the five-year follow-up kept both differences. Dinutuximab is the licensed agent in the United States and dinutuximab beta in Europe. The contribution of the two cytokines is not settled in the way the antibody's is: in the European HR-NBL1/SIOPEN randomization, adding subcutaneous interleukin-2 to dinutuximab beta gave no event-free survival benefit and added toxicity, and the trialists recommended the regimen without it as the standard of care, while the United States label still lists interleukin-2. No trial has ever isolated GM-CSF's own contribution. The benefit is therefore recorded here as a regimen-level effect of anti-GD2-based immunotherapy rather than as an effect of any one component. Grade 3 to 5 pain occurred in about half the immunotherapy arm of ANBL0032, an on-target toxicity of GD2 on peripheral nerves.
Mechanism Target:
ACTIVATES Anti-GD2 Antibody-Mediated Tumor Cell Killing — The antibody supplies the opsonizing arm this node needs: bound to surface GD2 it recruits Fc-receptor-bearing innate effector cells and activates complement, so the treatment creates the killing rather than inhibiting an existing disease process. This is why the link is ACTIVATES and not INHIBITS.

Crizotinib
Action: Targeted TherapyNCI Thesaurus (NCIT) Relation: this treatment is this clinical intervention This treatment is Targeted Therapy (NCIT:C93352). NCIT:C93352 is a clinical intervention from the NCI Thesaurus. NCIT:C93352
Agent: crizotinib CHEBI:64310 Chemical Entities of Biological Interest (CHEBI) Relation: this treatment uses this therapeutic agent This treatment uses crizotinib (CHEBI:64310). CHEBI:64310 is a therapeutic agent from Chemical Entities of Biological Interest.
Platform: Small molecule
First-generation ATP-competitive ALK/MET inhibitor, and the first ALK inhibitor tested in neuroblastoma. Its activity in this disease is poor and variant-dependent: in the Children's Oncology Group ADVL0912 trial the objective response rate in 20 children with relapsed or refractory ALK-aberrant neuroblastoma was 15%, all three responders carried the R1275Q hotspot mutation, and patients with F1174L or F1174V progressed within one to three cycles. The failure has a specific mechanistic reading rather than being a general lack of target engagement: the F1174 mutants raise ALK's affinity for ATP, which blunts an ATP-competitive inhibitor at achievable exposures. This is what motivated the move to third-generation inhibitors. The ALK-altered subset this applies to includes amplification as well as point mutation, and there the preclinical and clinical results diverge: crizotinib inhibited cell lines carrying amplified wild-type ALK and produced complete regression of an ALK-amplified xenograft, but both amplified patients in ADVL0912 had no response and each received a single cycle before progression, and the trial concludes it has no objective single-agent activity in amplified disease. Two patients is a small denominator, but it is a reported negative rather than an absence of data.
Mechanism Target:
INHIBITS ALK Signaling Activation — ATP-competitive inhibition of the ALK tyrosine kinase domain removes the constitutive receptor autophosphorylation produced by activating ALK mutations, and with it the downstream proliferative signal. Target engagement is variant-dependent, because the F1174 substitutions raise the kinase's ATP affinity and so compete directly with the inhibitor.

Platform: Radiotherapy
A radiopharmaceutical given for MIBG-avid relapsed or refractory disease, in which the norepinephrine analogue carries iodine-131 into the tumor cell through the norepinephrine transporter. Eligibility turns on avidity: the randomized NANT phase II required at least one MIBG-avid site, and absence of avidity on a properly performed diagnostic scan is in principle a contraindication. Response figures from different designs are not comparable and are given separately. In that randomized trial the response rate after one course was 14% for MIBG alone, 14% with vincristine and irinotecan, and 32% with vorinostat; the trial used a pick-the-winner design, so the vorinostat arm is the one its design selected rather than one shown superior. Outside randomized comparison, a 164-patient phase II reported a 36% complete plus partial response rate, and a systematic review that identified no randomized controlled trials found objective response across 25 studies ranging from 0% to 75%, mean 32%. The frontline role is unproven: a Cochrane review found no randomized or controlled clinical trial comparing newly diagnosed high-risk regimens with and without the therapy, and could not make recommendations for its frontline use. One cohort of 106 relapsed or refractory patients found that markers of lower NET and VMAT2 protein expression were associated with a higher likelihood of response, while the NET H-score itself was not significantly associated with it.
Mechanism Target:
Norepinephrine Transporter (NET/SLC6A2) Expression — MIBG is a norepinephrine analogue actively transported into the tumor cell by NET and retained in neurosecretory granules through VMAT; iodine 131 then decays locally, inside the cell the transporter admitted it to. The transporter is the drug's route in rather than a target it acts on, which is why no treatment_effect is set. Avidity on a diagnostic scan is the clinical readout of that route being open, and is the eligibility criterion.

Diagnosis

3
123I-MIBG Scintigraphy
Whole-body scintigraphy with iodine-123-labelled metaiodobenzylguanidine (123I-MIBG), the functional imaging test for staging and response assessment. In its 2010 guideline on MIBG scans, the INRG Task Force called 123I-MIBG the radiopharmaceutical of choice in children, and MIBG scans, particularly with a semi-quantitative score, the most sensitive and specific method of staging and response evaluation. The INRG staging system makes 123I-MIBG scintigraphy mandatory, preferably before tumor excision. Under the 2017 revised International Neuroblastoma Response Criteria (INRC), response is assessed with anatomic imaging, 123I-MIBG or FDG-PET, and bilateral bone marrow aspirates and trephine biopsies; 123I-MIBG replaces technetium-99m bone scintigraphy at osteomedullary lesions, and skeletal uptake is scored relative to baseline with the same scoring method (for example Curie or SIOPEN) at each time point. In a prospective multicenter trial of patients with known or suspected neuroblastoma, 123I-MIBG scintigraphy had a sensitivity of 88% and a specificity of 83%. A 2024 systematic review of ten head-to-head studies found that PET/CT with catecholaminergic tracers (11C-HED, 18F-DOPA, 124I-MIBG or 18F-mFBG) detected significantly more lesions than MIBG scintigraphy in seven of them but was superior per patient in only two; the authors judged PET diagnostically superior but said its effect on clinical decisions was unknown, and noted that these tracers were rarely used in clinical practice and not included in new high-risk treatment protocols. Drugs can interfere with MIBG uptake: labetalol, which is usually effective for neuroblastoma-associated hypertension, must be stopped for several days before MIBG is given, and a tumor without MIBG uptake should raise the question of interfering medication, although complete blockade of uptake is rare.
123I-MIBG whole-body scintigraphy NCIT:C219704 NCI Thesaurus (NCIT)

Results: In the INRG staging system, one unequivocal MIBG-positive lesion at a distant site is sufficient to define metastatic disease, and a single equivocal lesion requires confirmation by another imaging modality (plain radiographs and, if they are negative, MRI) and/or biopsy. 18F-FDG PET/CT for MIBG-Nonavid Disease
18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET/CT, which the 2017 revised INRC use in place of 123I-MIBG when the tumor does not concentrate MIBG: FDG-PET or PET/CT for tumor detection in bone, and FDG-PET as an alternative modality for assessing primary or metastatic soft tissue and bony sites. FDG is less specific than MIBG, because inflammatory lesions and normal or cytokine-stimulated bone marrow also take it up, so the INRC add that a biopsy of at least one FDG-avid, MIBG-nonavid lesion may be required to confirm neuroblastoma or ganglioneuroblastoma. The earlier INRG documents named bone scintigraphy, not FDG-PET, for skeletal assessment in these patients: the 2009 INRG staging system requires technetium-99m bone scintigraphy, at any age, when MIBG positivity of the primary tumor cannot be confirmed because the primary has been removed or is not MIBG-avid, and the 2010 INRG Task Force MIBG guideline called the technetium-99m MDP bone scan the standard test for skeletal metastases in tumors negative for MIBG at diagnosis. That guideline considered investigating alternatives preferable, because the bone scan has low specificity and is hard to interpret in young children with growing bones, but judged the clinical value of FDG-PET not yet well defined and its routine use, especially as a substitute for 123I-MIBG scintigraphy, not justified. A 2015 Cochrane review advised an additional test, such as FDG-PET(-CT), for staging and response assessment in patients whose tumor does not accumulate 123I-MIBG, while noting that more evidence of its clinical value was needed. The 2018 EANM guideline covers PET/CT with 18F-FDG, 18F-DOPA and 68Ga-DOTA peptides and describes these studies as increasingly used in clinical practice.

Urinary Catecholamine Metabolites
Measurement of catecholamine metabolites in urine, chiefly vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) and homovanillic acid (HVA). Under the INSS diagnostic criteria used by the INRG classification system, neuroblastoma can be diagnosed from unequivocal tumor cells in bone marrow together with increased urine or serum catecholamines or metabolites, as an alternative to a diagnosis from tumor tissue. The 2017 revised INRC do not use urine catecholamine levels to evaluate response, because specimen collection and analysis are not standardized and diet influences the results; the same consensus statement names catecholamine levels, with bone scintigraphy, as examples of tumor-assessment modalities less sensitive and/or specific for neuroblastoma, which the revision set out to replace with 123I-MIBG and FDG-PET imaging. Studies comparing urinary catecholamines with bone marrow studies and MIBG scans have found HVA and VMA to have low sensitivity as markers for monitoring disease activity. In a retrospective high-risk cohort, however, positive status on an extended panel of eight urinary catecholamine metabolites at complete remission was associated with poorer event-free and overall survival. The frequency of raised VMA and HVA at diagnosis is recorded under the biochemical record Catecholamine Metabolites.

Imaging Findings

2
MIBG-Avid Disease VERY_FREQUENT
Uptake of MIBG at the sites of disease, primary and metastatic, on 123I-MIBG scintigraphy. Neuroblastoma cells typically express the norepinephrine transporter (NET), which mediates active MIBG uptake in about 90% of patients; in a Cochrane review, about 10% of histologically proven neuroblastomas did not accumulate 123I-MIBG (recorded separately as MIBG-Nonavid Disease). In a small COG series of high-risk patients, the percentage of tumor cells expressing NET protein was higher in avid than nonavid tumors (P = 0.027), but the groups overlapped widely, including an avid tumor with no NET-expressing cells; NET mRNA measured by quantitative PCR did not differ significantly (P = 0.31), and neither did VMAT1 or VMAT2 mRNA. In a later COG immunohistochemistry study of tumors from 76 patients with high-risk metastatic disease, avid tumors had higher composite VMAT2 protein scores than nonavid tumors (median 216 vs 45, P = 0.04), with substantial overlap between the groups, while VMAT1 protein showed no association. In a 23-patient expression-array subset of a 343-patient COG cohort, NET mRNA was lower in nonavid tumors at borderline significance (P = 0.052) while VMAT2 mRNA did not differ; the authors note that this NET result is contrary to their earlier PCR result and may reflect differences in methodology or tumor material.

modality is OTHER because the whole-body survey in 123I-MIBG imaging is planar scintigraphy, which ImagingModalityEnum does not list. SPECT or SPECT/CT, which the enum does list, is often added over selected regions, such as the chest and abdomen or sites where tumor must be told apart from physiological uptake, and does not replace the whole-body images. NCIT:C79553 is specific to 123I-MIBG, the INRG Task Force's radiopharmaceutical of choice in children; two of the COG transporter studies cited here (PMID:23050139, PMID:26338179) read avidity from diagnostic 123I- or 131I-MIBG scans obtained by local institutional practice, and the third (PMID:28383813) does not state the isotope. MIBG-Nonavid Disease OCCASIONAL
Tumor that does not take up MIBG on diagnostic scintigraphy, so that the MIBG scan is falsely negative. In a Cochrane review, about 10% of histologically proven neuroblastomas did not accumulate 123I-MIBG. The INRG Task Force attributes such false-negative scans to low norepinephrine transporter expression, the blood-brain barrier, or large areas of scar or necrosis, while the Cochrane authors judged the reasons not entirely clear, suggesting that altered uptake mechanisms or interfering medication may contribute. In a COG cohort of 343 patients with metastatic high- or intermediate-risk disease, 30 (8.7%) were MIBG-nonavid at diagnosis. Compared with patients with avid disease, they less often had adrenal primary tumors or bone metastases, less often had positive urine catecholamines (compared in the high-risk patients only), more often had MYCN-amplified tumors (a difference significant in the pooled cohort but not among the high-risk patients alone), and had better 5-year event-free survival. On multivariable analysis among the high-risk patients, avidity was the only adverse prognostic factor for event-free survival identified (hazard ratio 1.77 for avid versus nonavid disease; P = 0.034); in the pooled cohort the adjusted hazard ratio was not significant (P = 0.059).

Progression

1
Relapsed or Refractory Disease
Most patients with high-risk neuroblastoma respond to initial treatment and many then relapse with chemoresistant disease. Relapse tumours are enriched for RAS-MAPK-activating and p53-pathway lesions, which are often already detectable at diagnosis, though the two classes differ: RAS-MAPK mutations found at diagnosis are mostly subclonal, MDM2 amplification and p14ARF inactivation are usually present from diagnosis, and TP53 mutations are mostly first detected after chemotherapy. RAS-MAPK and p53 lesions are not the only alterations selected at relapse: in a pan-paediatric paired cohort, pooled across tumour types with neuroblastoma about a fifth of the pairs, mutations in epigenetic-modifier genes were also highly enriched at relapse. In one paired series, 7 of the 18 RAS-MAPK-activating aberrations found at relapse had not been detected in the matched diagnostic tumour by whole-genome sequencing, although the authors' deeper testing of those primaries then recovered two of the seven; they read this as an argument for sequencing a relapse biopsy rather than relying on the diagnostic tumour.

INRGSS Stage MS
Metastatic disease in a child younger than 18 months (547 days) with metastases confined to skin, liver and/or bone marrow, bone marrow involvement below 10% of nucleated cells, and meta-iodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scintigraphy negative in bone and bone marrow; the primary tumor may be L1 or L2, with no restriction on crossing or infiltrating the midline. INSS stage 4S is the narrower INSS counterpart, limited to infants younger than 12 months with an INSS stage 1 or 2 primary tumor and dissemination to liver, skin and/or bone marrow (under 10% involvement); the INRGSS extended the age limit to 18 months and admitted primaries infiltrating the midline (INSS stage 3). In an Italian series of 30 infants with stage IV-S disease treated in 1970-1981, the liver was the most frequent site of spread (87%), and subcutaneous nodules were recorded. In infants with stage IV-S or 4S disease the pattern is associated with spontaneous regression and good survival. In two infant cohorts, one limited to symptomatic or biologically unfavorable cases, most deaths occurred in infants younger than 2 months at diagnosis, most often from complications of hepatomegaly or extensive abdominal involvement. In the selected cohort, enrolled on the COG trial ANBL0531, no further deaths from hepatomegaly occurred after the protocol was amended to require immediate chemotherapy for infants younger than 2 months with evolving hepatomegaly. In a Children's Oncology Group cohort staged by the INRGSS, stage MS outcome was excellent except for MYCN-amplified tumors, which have a poor outcome. Whether toddlers aged 12 to 18 months with a 4S pattern of metastasis share the favorable outcome of infants is contested. In the INRG database, toddlers grouped by metastatic sites alone, without the marrow limit of stage MS, had worse event-free survival than infants with the 4S pattern and outcomes similar to stage 4 disease at the same age, and the authors concluded that tumor biology matters more than age or metastatic pattern. Registry data from two Japanese pediatric societies showed an excellent prognosis for stage 4s disease at 12 to 17 months.
INSS stage 4S is recorded within this stage, not as a has_subtypes row, because the cancer granularity ladder (design decisions §3a) records stage under stages. The 4S category descends from the IV-S category of the 1971 Evans staging system, recognizing patients with metastatic disease limited to skin, liver and bone marrow who have superior outcomes, and the 1993 revision of the INSS added restrictions on age and bone marrow involvement for stage 4S. When the INRG Task Force extended the age limit to 18 months, it described the group aged 12 to 18 months as small, with an unclear outcome.

Epidemiology

2
Proportion of childhood cancers
Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood, accounting for about 8-10% of childhood cancers and about 15% of childhood cancer deaths. In Canadian incidence data for 1982-1986 and 1987-1991 it accounted for a larger share of cancers in the first year of life than any other cancer.

Age at diagnosis
Neuroblastoma is diagnosed mainly in infancy and early childhood. In the Netherlands Cancer Registry (patients under 18 years diagnosed 1990-2014), 45% of 593 patients were younger than 18 months at diagnosis. In the German national trial cohort the median age at diagnosis fell from 23 months in 1980-1984 to 15 months in 2010-2014, and StatPearls gives a median of 17 months.
