Differential Diagnoses

13

Conditions with similar clinical presentations that must be differentiated from Neuroblastoma:

Wilms tumor MONDO:0006058
Overlapping Features An abdominal neuroblastoma can be mistaken for Wilms tumor at presentation, and the mistake can lead to a nephrectomy: in one single-institution retrospective review, nine children with neuroblastoma had an exploratory laparotomy with a preoperative diagnosis of Wilms tumor, and eight of them underwent nephrectomy at that operation. On tissue, nuclear PHOX2B staining favors neuroblastoma.
Distinguishing Features
  • Intratumoral calcification, vascular encasement, or both on preoperative CT point to neuroblastoma; in that review they were present in 78% of the nine misdiagnosed children with neuroblastoma and were never seen in the Wilms tumor comparison group.
  • Symptoms such as fever and weight loss at presentation were more frequent in the misdiagnosed children with neuroblastoma than in the Wilms tumor comparison group of the same review (67% versus 20%).
  • Raised urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) or homovanillic acid (HVA) points to neuroblastoma, and the authors of the same review say a raised result should prompt staging before an operation; all five of its children with neuroblastoma whose urine was collected before surgery had raised VMA and/or HVA, although each result came back only after the operation, while both Wilms tumor comparison patients who were tested were negative.
  • Nuclear PHOX2B staining favors neuroblastoma; in one immunohistochemistry study PHOX2B immunostaining was negative in every Wilms tumor tested, and its authors call PHOX2B specific for neuroblastoma in its differential diagnosis with other small round cell tumors. A second series found all 44 Wilms tumors among its comparison tumors negative, with positivity defined as nuclear staining in at least 5% of cells, and its authors conclude that PHOX2B reliably distinguishes neuroblastoma from mimics such as Wilms tumor. PHOX2B is not fully sensitive, though; that series found it in 70 of 76 peripheral neuroblastic tumors (68 of 72 pediatric cases), so a negative stain does not exclude a peripheral neuroblastic tumor.

Neonatal adrenal hemorrhage
Overlapping Features In the newborn most suprarenal masses prove to be either a congenital neuroblastoma or an adrenal hemorrhage. An adrenal hemorrhage can appear as a cystic suprarenal mass as it liquefies, and a high incidence of cystic tumors has been noted among prenatally diagnosed neuroblastomas. Cystic neuroblastoma and cystic adrenal hemorrhage are frequently difficult to tell apart, and the distinction is made harder still because neuroblastomas can be complicated by hemorrhage and prenatally detected neuroblastomas are frequently associated with normal urinary catecholamine metabolites. In one series an adrenal hemorrhage was resected on suspicion of neuroblastoma because it had been detected prenatally and looked like a cystic mass with wall enhancement; pathology showed an adrenal pseudocyst without neuroblastoma. In a Children's Oncology Group study of expectant observation of small adrenal masses in infants younger than 6 months, two of the 16 observed infants who went on to surgery had an adrenal hemorrhage.
Distinguishing Features
  • In a retrospective series that compared 16 congenital cystic neuroblastomas with 14 neonatal adrenal hemorrhagic pseudocysts, from which solid adrenal masses were excluded, size, solid portion, septation, enhancement and turbidity did not differ significantly; the authors concluded that prenatal detection (all of the neuroblastomas against three of the 14 pseudocysts), calcification on the initial images, vascular flow on color Doppler ultrasound and evolution to a more complex mass may all favor neuroblastoma. Calcification on the initial images and Doppler flow were each seen in three neuroblastomas and in none of the pseudocysts examined, but color Doppler was done in only nine neuroblastomas and two hemorrhages; most neuroblastomas in the series had no calcification on the initial images, and most of those examined by Doppler showed no flow.
  • On follow-up imaging the three cystic neuroblastomas that were followed became more complex solid and cystic masses and did not disappear for up to 90 days, whereas most hemorrhagic pseudocysts resolved completely or evolved to calcification only. Apart from the one that was resected, the pseudocysts were diagnosed by that resolution or calcification, so the contrast in evolution is partly built into how the series defined its cases, and calcification favors neuroblastoma only on the initial images.
  • In a small Doppler series, color-coded and power Doppler sonography showed vessels within the one congenital neuroblastoma studied and no flow in any of ten adrenal hemorrhages in eight neonates, whether the hemorrhage looked cystic or solid.

Wolman disease MONDO:0019148
Overlapping Features Bilateral adrenal enlargement with calcification and preserved adreniform shape is a hallmark radiologic feature of Wolman disease, present in approximately half of reported cases, and neuroblastoma is among the differential diagnoses of adrenal calcification, with adrenal hemorrhage, infections such as tuberculosis, congenital adrenal hyperplasia and other storage disorders such as Niemann-Pick disease.
Distinguishing Features

  • The work-up differs: neuroblastoma diagnosis depends largely on biopsy-dependent histopathology, whereas percutaneous biopsy of a PPGL is potentially dangerous and contraindicated, and PPGL is diagnosed by biochemical tests of catecholamine excess, with urinary or plasma metanephrines the recommended tests; the homovanillic acid (HVA) and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) measurements on which biochemical testing for neuroblastoma still largely relies are no longer recommended for PPGL.
  • Plasma dopamine and norepinephrine metabolite measurements alone may not separate the two in every child, because both tumors show overlapping increases in these metabolites. On imaging, calcification and encasement, invasion or infiltration are relatively common in neuroblastoma and far less so in PPGL, so they offer clues favoring neuroblastoma, although calcification can occasionally occur in PPGL and there can be exceptions.

"We herein report data on 10 children and adolescents with ACT and five with PCC/PGL, previously mistaken as NBL. ... Four (4/5) patients with a final diagnosis of PCC/PGL presented with clinical signs and symptoms of catecholamine excess. Urine tests indicated possible catecholamine excess in..."
In a retrospective analysis of the GPOH-MET registry of malignant endocrine tumors in children (the full text expands the name as the German Pediatric Oncology Hematology-Malignant Endocrine Tumor database), five children and adolescents with a final diagnosis of pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma (PCC/PGL) had first been taken for neuroblastoma. The full-text results add that the five tumors were three paragangliomas, one pheochromocytoma with paraganglioma, and one composite pheochromocytoma and neuroblastoma, so one of the five did contain neuroblastoma. Four of the five presented with clinical signs and symptoms of catecholamine excess. Urine tests, done in two, indicated possible catecholamine excess; no testing was done in the other three, and plasma metanephrines were measured in none. This supports the description's statements that PCC/PGL can be mistaken for neuroblastoma even when catecholamine excess is clinically evident, and that the biochemical work-up in these cases was incomplete. It is a five-patient registry subset, so it documents a diagnostic pitfall, not a misdiagnosis rate.
PMID:35957826 SUPPORT DIRECT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Human Clinical
"Catecholamine-producing tumors of childhood include most notably neuroblastoma, but also pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PPGL). Diagnosis of the former depends largely on biopsy-dependent histopathology, but this is contraindicated in PPGL where diagnosis depends crucially on biochemical..."
This review of the biochemical diagnosis of childhood catecholamine-producing tumors names neuroblastoma and PPGL as such tumors and says neuroblastoma diagnosis depends largely on biopsy-dependent histopathology, which is contraindicated in PPGL, where diagnosis depends on biochemical tests of catecholamine excess: urinary or plasma metanephrines are the recommended tests, and HVA and VMA are no longer recommended for PPGL. The full text adds that neuroblastoma is more common in children than PPGL, and that percutaneous biopsy, though commonly employed for neuroblastoma, is potentially dangerous in PPGL and therefore contraindicated. It also says that because both tumors show overlapping rises in plasma dopamine and norepinephrine metabolites, these measurements alone are unlikely to separate them in every child, and that on imaging calcification and encasement, invasion or infiltration are clues favoring neuroblastoma, though calcification occasionally occurs in PPGL and there can be exceptions. These are the authors' synthesis of published work, with no patient series of their own, and they do not say that biochemistry as a whole cannot separate the two tumors.

In this pediatric immunohistochemistry series, Phox2b was diffusely expressed in all 65 peripheral neuroblastic tumors (neuroblastoma subtypes, ganglioneuroblastoma and ganglioneuroma) and in all 23 pheochromocytomas/paragangliomas, and the authors conclude that it is a specific and sensitive marker for both groups. By 'specific' the authors mean specific for neural crest tumors with neuronal or neuroendocrine differentiation, a category that contains both groups, not that the stain tells them apart. Because every tumor in both groups was positive, a positive PHOX2B stain did not by itself separate neuroblastoma from PPGL in this series. The authors do not state this; it follows from the two staining results, so the item is graded INDIRECT. The abstract pools pheochromocytoma with paraganglioma, does not say whether the paragangliomas were sympathetic or head-and-neck tumors, and reports staining intensity only for the neuroblastic tumors, so it does not compare intensity between the two groups. All tumors were from children, so the result does not show how uniformly adult PPGL stain.

Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy MONDO:0002072
Overlapping Features Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy (MNTI) contains nests of neuroblastic cells, and the authors of one series distinguish it from metastatic neuroblastoma, as well as from melanoma, by its morphology and immunophenotype. In that series of 20 cases the patients were 1 to 9 months old and typically presented with a rapidly growing mass, 13 tumors arose in the maxilla, and the tumors were made up of tubular or alveolar formations of large melanin-containing cells around nests of smaller neuroblastic cells with scant or fibrillar cytoplasm.
Distinguishing Features
  • The authors of the series conclude that its distinctive morphology, with tubular or alveolar formations of large melanin-containing cells around nests of smaller neuroblastic cells, and its multiphenotypic epithelial, neural and melanocytic expression distinguish it from metastatic neuroblastoma. All 12 tumors studied immunohistochemically were positive for cytokeratin and for HMB 45, and no staining was found for chromogranin; neural markers were also expressed (neuron-specific enolase in seven of 12 tumors, Leu 7 in nine of 12, synaptophysin in four of 12). The series included no neuroblastomas, so it does not report how neuroblastoma itself stains.

PMID:8392815 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"Twenty cases of melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy (MNTI) are reported. The patients (13 females, seven males), whose ages ranged from 1 to 9 months (mean, 5 months), typically presented with a rapidly growing mass. Tumor sites included the maxilla (13 cases), mandible (three cases),..."
Kapadia and colleagues report a clinicopathological and immunohistochemical series of 20 MNTI cases. The patients were infants aged 1 to 9 months, and 13 of the 20 tumors arose in the maxilla. Histology showed large melanin-containing cells around nests of smaller neuroblastic cells. All 12 tumors studied immunohistochemically were positive for cytokeratin and HMB 45. Neuron-specific enolase (seven of 12), Leu 7 (nine of 12) and, in some tumors, synaptophysin (four of 12) were also expressed. No staining was found for chromogranin; the abstract does not say how many tumors were tested for it. The authors conclude that this distinctive morphology and multiphenotypic (epithelial, neural, melanocytic) expression distinguish MNTI from melanoma and metastatic neuroblastoma. The series contains no neuroblastoma cases, so it supports the MNTI features the authors use to separate the two, not any statement about how neuroblastoma itself stains.

Animal Models

2
Xenopus anteroventral noradrenergic (AVNA) cell differentiation model Developmental model of the presumed cell of origin
Rather than growing a tumour, this model reconstructs the normal differentiation of the neural-crest-derived sympathoadrenal cell that neuroblastoma is thought to arise from, and asks what stops it. Frog AVNA cells differentiate under transient Ascl1 expression; in neuroblastoma cells Ascl1 is instead persistently expressed and multiply phosphorylated. Introducing that phospho-state into the frog cells blocks their differentiation, and CDK or MYCN overexpression blocks it too — but not when Ascl1 cannot be phosphorylated, which places phosphorylation downstream of both. The model tests the differentiation-arrest hypothesis in a normal developmental context; it does not produce tumours and so says nothing about transformation, growth, or metastasis.

Xenopus laevis
Genotype
Embryos expressing wild-type Ascl1, a phospho-mutant Ascl1 that cannot be phosphorylated at serine-proline motifs, CDKs, or MYCN, with Ascl1 morpholino knockdown

Neural Crest Developmental Arrest recapitulates fidelity: moderate Supplies a molecular switch for the arrest this node asserts: multi-site phosphorylation of Ascl1 converts it from a driver of sympathoadrenal differentiation into an inert factor, matching the phospho-state Ascl1 is held in within neuroblastoma cells.
Limitations: Frog AVNA cells are a developmental counterpart of the presumed cell of origin, not tumour cells, and the model contains no transformed tissue — arrest is scored as failure to differentiate on schedule rather than as tumour formation. The link to human disease rests on the observed phospho-state of ASCL1 in neuroblastoma lines, so the model shows the state is sufficient to block differentiation, not that it is what maintains any patient's tumour.

Lin28B sympathetic-adrenergic lineage transgenic mouse Transgenic tumour-initiation model
Forced LIN28B expression in the sympathetic adrenergic lineage induces neuroblastomas in mice, and the tumours carry low let-7 and high MYCN protein, which is the chain this entry models run forwards in an animal. It shows that LIN28B overexpression is sufficient for tumour formation in that lineage; it says nothing about how often that route operates in human disease.

name: Neuroblastoma
creation_date: '2026-01-26T02:55:13Z'
description: >-
  Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood,
  arising from neural crest-derived sympathetic nervous system precursors.
  It demonstrates remarkable clinical heterogeneity, ranging from spontaneous
  regression in infants to highly aggressive metastatic disease in older
  children. MYCN amplification, present in approximately 20% of cases, is
  among the most powerful adverse genomic prognostic markers and drives
  aggressive tumor behavior. Risk stratification in the INRG system combines
  stage, age, histologic category and grade of differentiation, MYCN status,
  chromosome 11q status, and DNA ploidy to guide treatment intensity. A
  distinct axis of neuroblastoma biology is the mechanism of telomere
  maintenance: telomerase is activated through TERT rearrangement, MYCN
  amplification or high TERT expression without either alteration, while
  alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT), often with ATRX alteration,
  maintains telomeres without telomerase. The two mechanisms are almost mutually
  exclusive. ATRX-altered disease is enriched in older children, adolescents and
  young adults and often runs a slow but progressive course, with poor response
  to induction chemotherapy reported for large ATRX deletions and truncating
  mutations.
  Low-risk neuroblastoma may require only observation, while high-risk
  disease requires intensive multimodal therapy with immunotherapy.
categories:
- Pediatric Cancer
- Neural Tumor
- Solid Tumor
parents:
- neuroblastic tumor
synonyms:
- neuroblastoma, malignant
- neuroblastoma (Schwannian stroma-poor)
- NB
notes: >-
  This entry covers neuroblastoma of the sympathoadrenal lineage of the neural
  crest, arising in the adrenal medulla or elsewhere along the sympathetic
  nervous system, which is the Schwannian stroma-poor category of the
  International Neuroblastoma Pathology Classification. The entry's MONDO and
  NCIT classes (MONDO:0005072, NCIT:C3270; see mappings) also contain tumors it
  does not cover: olfactory neuroblastoma, cerebral neuroblastoma (including
  CNS neuroblastoma with FOXR2 activation) and retinal neuroblastoma.
  Site-specific subclasses of peripheral disease are within scope, and the
  adrenal gland subclass is recorded as a subtype; the adrenal gland and
  mediastinum ganglioneuroblastoma classes that MONDO files beneath two of
  them are not. Ganglioneuroblastoma (MONDO:0005035) and ganglioneuroma
  (MONDO:0005033) are separate diseases. MONDO's seven numbered neuroblastoma
  susceptibility classes are also outside this entry; MONDO files them under
  hereditary neoplastic syndrome, not under MONDO:0005072. Registry incidence
  figures under prevalence may count ganglioneuroblastoma together with
  neuroblastoma; each record says what its source states.

    explanation: >-
      This Netherlands Cancer Registry analysis took data on all patients aged
      under 18 years diagnosed with neuroblastoma from 1990 to 2014. Its own
      result is that 45% of the 593 newly diagnosed cases were younger than 18
      months at diagnosis, a share of the whole cohort across all stages. The
      abstract gives only this 18-month split, not a fuller age distribution,
      and does not say whether ganglioneuroblastoma was counted.
  - reference: PMID:28786082
    reference_title: "Incidence, Survival, and Treatment of Localized and Metastatic Neuroblastoma in Germany 1979-2015."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "The median age at diagnosis decreased from 23 months during 1980-1984 to 15 months during 2010-2014."
    explanation: >-
      Result of the nationwide analysis of the German GPOH neuroblastoma trials
      NB79 to NB2004, whose patients were 96.6% of those known to the German
      Childhood Cancer Registry. Table 2 gives the all-stage median age at
      diagnosis as 22.7 months in 1980-84 and 15.1 months in 2010-14; the median
      had already reached 15.1 months by 1995-99. The authors attribute the fall
      mainly to earlier diagnosis of low- and intermediate-risk patients; the
      median for stage 4 patients aged 18 months or more stayed near 40 months.
      Trial coverage of registered patients was lower in the early 1980s, above
      90% from 1985 and at least 98% from 1995.
  - reference: PMID:28846355
    reference_title: "Neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "The median age at diagnosis is 17 months"
    explanation: >-
      The StatPearls chapter states that the median age at diagnosis is 17
      months. It is a point-of-care review and the abstract does not name the
      cohort behind the median, so the figure is a synthesis rather than a
      primary measurement.
prevalence:
- population: "Europe, children aged 0-14 years (ACCIS registries, 1988-1997)"
  measure_type: ANNUAL_INCIDENCE
  prevalence_class: BAND_1_9_PER_100000
  rate_per_100000: 1.09
  rate_denominator: POPULATION_PER_YEAR
  notes: >-
    Age-standardised incidence rate of 10.9 cases per million children in
    1988-1997, highest in infants (52.6 per million). The authors suggest that
    some overdiagnosis in children under 2 years may explain the rise in
    incidence over 1978-1997. The abstract states the rate per million children
    without a time unit, recorded here as annual, the usual convention for
    registry age-standardised rates, and does not say whether
    ganglioneuroblastoma is counted.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:16919772
    reference_title: "Neuroblastoma incidence and survival in European children (1978-1997): report from the Automated Childhood Cancer Information System project."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "The age-standardised incidence rate (ASR) of neuroblastoma in Europe in 1988-1997 was 10.9 cases per million children, being highest in infants (52.6)."
    explanation: >-
      The ACCIS report, which pools European population-based childhood cancer
      registry data, gives the 1988-1997 age-standardised incidence rate of
      neuroblastoma in Europe as 10.9 cases per million children (1.09 per
      100,000), highest in infants at 52.6 per million. The abstract states the
      rate per million children without a time unit, and gives the 0-14 year age
      span only indirectly, by describing older children as aged 2-14 years. It
      does not say whether ganglioneuroblastoma is counted with neuroblastoma.
  - reference: PMID:16919772
    reference_title: "Neuroblastoma incidence and survival in European children (1978-1997): report from the Automated Childhood Cancer Information System project."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "A certain amount of overdiagnosis in children under 2 years of age may explain the increased incidence rates and partially the increase in survival."
    explanation: >-
      In the same registry analysis (6202 children with neuroblastoma from 59
      registries in 19 countries, 1978-1997), the authors suggest that some
      overdiagnosis in children under 2 years of age may explain the increased
      incidence rates, so the European rate may be inflated in the youngest
      children. They hedge (may explain) and do not estimate how much of the
      rise overdiagnosis accounts for.
- population: "Quebec and the Greater Delaware Valley, children under 15 years"
  measure_type: ANNUAL_INCIDENCE
  prevalence_class: BAND_1_9_PER_100000
  rate_per_100000: 1.095
  rate_denominator: POPULATION_PER_YEAR
  notes: >-
    Population-based series pooling Quebec (Canada) and the area covered by the
    Greater Delaware Valley Pediatric Tumor Registry (United States): 295
    children with neuroblastoma in a combined population of 3,178,736 children.
    Annual incidence was 10.95 per million under 15 years and 27.75 per million
    at ages 0-4 years. The Quebec data were collected shortly before
    province-wide screening began. The abstract gives no years of diagnosis and
    does not say whether ganglioneuroblastoma is counted.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:1732433
    reference_title: "A population-based study of neuroblastoma incidence, survival, and mortality in North America."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "One hundred thirty children with neuroblastoma were identified in Quebec and 165 in the GDV, in a combined population of 3,178,736 children. The annual incidence of neuroblastoma was 10.95/10(6) under the age of 15 years and 27.75/10(6) between the ages of 0 and 4 years."
    explanation: >-
      Primary result of this population-based study. The first quoted sentence
      gives the study population: 130 children with neuroblastoma in Quebec and
      165 in the Greater Delaware Valley (GDV), whose pediatric tumor registry
      covers all of Delaware and parts of New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Maryland,
      in a combined population of 3,178,736 children. The second gives the
      annual incidence in that population: 10.95 per million children under 15
      years (1.095 per 100,000) and 27.75 per million at ages 0-4. The Quebec
      data come from shortly before province-wide screening began. The abstract
      gives no years of diagnosis and does not say whether ganglioneuroblastoma
      was counted.
- population: "Australia, children aged 0-14 years (Australian Childhood Cancer Registry, 1983-2015)"
  measure_type: ANNUAL_INCIDENCE
  prevalence_class: BAND_1_9_PER_1000000
  rate_per_100000: 0.95
  rate_denominator: POPULATION_PER_YEAR
  notes: >-
    Age-standardised incidence of about 9.5 per million children per year,
    steady across 1983-2015. The study counted neuroblastoma and
    ganglioneuroblastoma together, so the rate covers a broader group of tumors
    than this entry; the abstract does not say how many of the 1269 patients had
    ganglioneuroblastoma.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:32068329
    reference_title: "Incidence and outcomes of neuroblastoma in Australian children: A population-based study (1983-2015)."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Age-standardised incidence rates remained steady across the study period at approximately 9.5 per million children per year."
    explanation: >-
      National population-based study of Australian Childhood Cancer Registry
      data for children aged 0-14 years diagnosed from 1983 to 2015:
      age-standardised incidence remained steady across the period at
      approximately 9.5 per million children per year (0.95 per 100,000). The
      registry extract covered neuroblastoma and ganglioneuroblastoma together
      and the abstract gives no separate rate for either, so the figure applies
      to the combined group. The abstract does not name the standard population
      used for age-standardisation.
  - reference: PMID:32068329
    reference_title: "Incidence and outcomes of neuroblastoma in Australian children: A population-based study (1983-2015)."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Deidentified data for all children (0-14 years) diagnosed with neuroblastoma and ganglioneuroblastoma from 1983 to 2015 were extracted."
    explanation: >-
      The abstract's methods define the study cohort as all children aged 0-14
      years diagnosed with neuroblastoma and ganglioneuroblastoma from 1983 to
      2015, and its results report that cohort's incidence of about 9.5 per
      million children per year without restating the case definition, so
      reading the rate as covering both tumor types is an inference from the
      abstract's structure. Ganglioneuroblastoma is outside this entry, so it
      widens the rate's numerator, the cases counted; the denominator,
      Australian children aged 0-14 years, is unchanged.
- population: "Germany, children aged 0-14 years (German Childhood Cancer Registry, 1980-2015)"
  measure_type: ANNUAL_INCIDENCE
  prevalence_class: BAND_1_9_PER_100000
  rate_per_100000: 1.32
  rate_denominator: POPULATION_PER_YEAR
  notes: >-
    Median of the annual age-standardised incidence rates (Segi world standard)
    over 1980-2015: 13.2 per million children per year, ranging from 8.7 in 1981
    (incomplete registration) to 17.8 in 2000 (the last year of the screening
    trial). Urine screening for catecholamine metabolites was offered at about 1
    year of age in 6 of 16 German states from 1995 to 2000, and incidence in
    those years ran above the long-term trend (rate ratio 1.26). The paper does
    not say whether ganglioneuroblastoma is counted with neuroblastoma.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:28786082
    reference_title: "Incidence, Survival, and Treatment of Localized and Metastatic Neuroblastoma in Germany 1979-2015."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "The population-based median annual age standardized incidence rate (ASR) of neuroblastoma per million children per year in Germany between the periods 1980 and 2015 was 13.2"
    explanation: >-
      The authors' population-based analysis of German Childhood Cancer Registry
      data gives the median of the annual age-standardised incidence rates (Segi
      world standard) for 1980-2015 as 13.2 neuroblastoma cases per million
      children per year, which is 1.32 per 100,000. It is a median of annual
      rates, not a pooled rate for the period, and the paper's Figure 1 gives
      the age band as 0-14 years. The same sentence goes on to give the
      extremes, 8.7 per million in 1981 (incomplete registration) and 17.8 in
      2000 (the last year of the screening trial); the Methods add that case
      numbers before 1986 were not complete enough for epidemiological analysis,
      although the median spans 1980-2015. The paper does not say whether
      ganglioneuroblastoma is counted with neuroblastoma.
  - reference: PMID:28786082
    reference_title: "Incidence, Survival, and Treatment of Localized and Metastatic Neuroblastoma in Germany 1979-2015."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "The age-adjusted regression curve (Fig. 1) shows an increase in crude neuroblastoma incidence rates during the period of neuroblastoma screening (RR 1.26; 95% CI 1.17-1.36)"
    explanation: >-
      The authors' age-adjusted trend analysis of German registry incidence in
      children aged 0-14 (trend fitted to 1986-2014 and adjusted for age
      distribution, German reunification and the screening trial) found crude
      incidence during the screening period raised by a rate ratio of 1.26 (95%
      CI 1.17-1.36) relative to the fitted trend. A median taken over 1980-2015
      therefore includes these raised years. The rate ratio is a deviation from
      the fitted trend, not a comparison with a fixed pre-screening baseline,
      and it is a national estimate although screening was offered in only some
      states.
  - reference: PMID:28786082
    reference_title: "Incidence, Survival, and Treatment of Localized and Metastatic Neuroblastoma in Germany 1979-2015."
    supports: SUPPORT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Urine screening for catecholamine metabolites to detect early neuroblastoma was offered to children at approximately 1 year of age in 6 of 16 German States from 1995 to 2000"
    explanation: >-
      Gives the dates and scope of the screening period: urine screening for
      catecholamine metabolites was offered at about 1 year of age in 6 of 16
      German states from 1995 to 2000. This Methods sentence describes a
      programme reported separately (the paper's reference 11) and says nothing
      about incidence; the rate ratio comes from the Results sentence above.
- population: "Europe"
  measure_type: POINT_PREVALENCE
  prevalence_class: BAND_1_5_PER_10000
  rate_low: 10.0
  rate_high: 50.0
  notes: >-
    Orphanet point-prevalence class for Europe, 1-5 per 10,000, which Orphadata
    attributes to a 2018 European Medicines Agency document. A point prevalence
    counts everyone living with the disease at one time, so it is not comparable
    with the childhood incidence records above.
  evidence:
  - reference: ORPHA:635
    reference_title: "Neuroblastoma"
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: "1-5 / 10 000 | Europe | Point prevalence"
    explanation: >-
      Orphanet's epidemiology table for ORPHA:635 gives a point-prevalence class
      of 1-5 per 10,000 for Europe. It is a coarse class for the whole
      population, not a rate measured in a defined cohort. The quote stops
      before the row's source column; Orphadata gives the source as a 2018
      European Medicines Agency document rather than a journal article.
inheritance:
- name: Sporadic occurrence in most cases
  inheritance_term:
    preferred_term: Sporadic
    term:
      id: HP:0003745
      label: Sporadic
  description: >-
    Most neuroblastoma arises sporadically, with no family history and no
    identified germline predisposing variant. About 1% of cases have a
    positive family history, so the heritable forms below describe a small
    minority of the disease even though they are what the genetic section
    characterises in most detail. A sporadic presentation is the default and
    is not a statement that no germline contribution exists: common
    susceptibility variants and de novo events are not excluded by an absent
    family history.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:21734404
    reference_title: "Genome-wide linkage analysis to identify genetic modifiers of ALK mutation penetrance in familial neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Most NBs arise sporadically, but approximately 1% of all cases have a positive family history"
    explanation: >-
      Gives both halves of this block: sporadic occurrence is the usual case,
      and the familial share is about 1%. The sentence is the introduction of
      a study about penetrance modifiers rather than that study's own result,
      so it restates the established epidemiology and is graded BACKGROUND.
- name: Autosomal dominant familial neuroblastoma with incomplete penetrance
  inheritance_term:
    preferred_term: Autosomal dominant inheritance
    term:
      id: HP:0000006
      label: Autosomal dominant inheritance
  penetrance: INCOMPLETE
  description: >-
    The familial form is transmitted as a dominant trait with markedly
    incomplete penetrance. Germline activating ALK variants account for the
    majority of familial cases and germline PHOX2B variants for a smaller
    share; both are detailed in the genetic section rather than here. The
    penetrance figure is what makes this block worth stating separately from
    the gene records: in the pedigrees used to map ALK, only about half of
    mutation carriers developed neuroblastoma, so carrier status is not a
    prediction of disease and a transmission probability is not a risk of
    illness. Reduced penetrance is itself under genetic investigation, with
    modifier variants proposed at or near the ALK locus.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:21734404
    reference_title: "Genome-wide linkage analysis to identify genetic modifiers of ALK mutation penetrance in familial neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Dominant mutations in ALK are found in more than 50% of familial NB cases. However, in the families used for the linkage study, only about 50% of carriers of ALK mutations are affected by NB."
    explanation: >-
      Both claims this block makes: the mode of transmission is dominant and
      accounts for more than half of familial cases, and penetrance is about
      50% in the mapping pedigrees. Graded BACKGROUND because the sentences
      introduce a penetrance-modifier study by restating its predecessor's
      findings rather than reporting this study's own linkage result. The
      penetrance figure is from the specific families used for linkage, so it
      is not a population estimate.
  - reference: PMID:18724359
    reference_title: "Identification of ALK as a major familial neuroblastoma predisposition gene."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Resequencing of regional candidate genes identified three separate germline missense mutations in the tyrosine kinase domain of ALK that segregated with the disease in eight separate families."
    explanation: >-
      The segregation observation the dominant model rests on: three germline
      ALK missense variants tracking the disease through eight pedigrees.
      Segregation in families is what establishes heritable transmission here,
      and the dominant mode is read from it together with the carrier
      frequencies above rather than from this sentence alone. Graded
      HUMAN_CLINICAL to match this sentence's grading in
      ALK-Related_Neuroblastic_Tumor_Susceptibility, which cites it for the
      same families.
progression:
- phase: Relapsed or Refractory Disease
  notes: >-
    Most patients with high-risk neuroblastoma respond to initial treatment
    and many then relapse with chemoresistant disease. Relapse tumours are
    enriched for RAS-MAPK-activating and p53-pathway lesions, which are
    often already detectable at diagnosis, though the two classes differ:
    RAS-MAPK mutations found at diagnosis are mostly subclonal, MDM2
    amplification and p14ARF inactivation are usually present from
    diagnosis, and TP53 mutations are mostly first detected after
    chemotherapy. RAS-MAPK and p53 lesions are not the only alterations
    selected at relapse: in a pan-paediatric paired cohort, pooled across
    tumour types with neuroblastoma about a fifth of the pairs, mutations in
    epigenetic-modifier genes were also highly enriched at relapse. In one paired
    series, 7 of the 18 RAS-MAPK-activating aberrations found at relapse had
    not been detected in the matched diagnostic tumour by whole-genome
    sequencing, although the authors' deeper testing of those primaries then
    recovered two of the seven; they read this as an argument for sequencing
    a relapse biopsy rather than relying on the diagnostic tumour.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:26121087
    reference_title: "Relapsed neuroblastomas show frequent RAS-MAPK pathway mutations."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Patients with high-risk neuroblastoma have a survival rate of less than 50% ... despite extensive treatment involving chemotherapy, surgery, radiation therapy and immunotherapy. In a majority of patients an initial response is observed, however, up to 60% of these patients subsequently relapse with therapy resistant tumors"
    explanation: >-
      States the course this phase describes: initial response in most
      patients, then relapse with therapy-resistant tumours in up to 60% of
      them. The Therapy-Resistant Relapse pathophysiology node carries the
      same quote with the full reading of what it does and does not
      establish.
  - reference: PMID:26121087
    reference_title: "Relapsed neuroblastomas show frequent RAS-MAPK pathway mutations."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "In 7/18 cases these mutations were observed only in the relapse tumor, which indicates that analysis on primary tumor samples is not sufficient to guide the choice of treatment for neuroblastoma relapses."
    explanation: >-
      In this paired diagnosis-relapse sequencing series, 7 of the 18
      relapses carrying a RAS-MAPK pathway mutation carried it only in the
      relapse tumour as far as whole-genome sequencing could tell, and the
      authors conclude that analysis of primary tumour samples is not
      sufficient to guide treatment at relapse, which is the basis for this
      phase's re-biopsy note. The paper's own follow-up testing of the
      matched primaries found two of those seven events there, both ALK, so
      the seven are events not detected at diagnosis rather than events
      shown to be absent.
  - reference: PMID:39693475
    reference_title: "Stratified Medicine Pediatrics: Cell-Free DNA and Serial Tumor Sequencing Identifies Subtype-Specific Cancer Evolution and Epigenetic States."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Across the cohort, there was a strong positive selection at relapse for missense and truncating mutations in CHEK2 (Fig. 3G). Mutations in genes responsible for epigenetic modification of DNA were also highly enriched at relapse including ATRX, SETD2, ARID1B, and CREBBP"
    explanation: >-
      In the Stratified Medicine Paediatrics paired diagnosis-relapse panel
      sequencing, a dN/dS selection analysis pooled across all tumour types
      found strong positive selection at relapse for CHEK2 mutations and, as
      the quote's also records, mutations in the epigenetic-modifier genes
      ATRX, SETD2, ARID1B and CREBBP highly enriched at relapse. The
      epigenetic-modifier genes are what support this phase's statement that
      RAS-MAPK and p53 lesions are not the only alterations selected at
      relapse. The item corroborates neither of those lesion classes: the paper's
      account of this analysis names no RAS-MAPK gene and reports TP53 and
      truncating CDKN2A mutations as positively selected at both diagnosis
      and relapse rather than at relapse only. Indirect because the analysis
      pools every paediatric tumour type in the study. Neuroblastoma was the
      largest single type but made up about a fifth of the pairs, and the
      main text gives no per-type breakdown, so this is not a
      neuroblastoma-specific figure. Highly enriched describes a selection
      signal rather than a frequency, and the authors note that only a
      limited number of tumours acquired additional driver mutations at
      relapse. ATRX in the quoted list is already modelled on this entry's
      Reduced ATRX/DAXX Complex Abundance node, so this item adds no new
      ATRX claim.
has_subtypes:
- name: MYCN-Amplified Neuroblastoma
  classification: molecular
  description: >-
    Approximately 20% of neuroblastomas harbor MYCN gene amplification,
    associated with rapid tumor progression and poor prognosis. MYCN
    amplification is one of the earliest oncogene amplifications discovered.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:41560679
    reference_title: "Coexpression of MYCN and ALK Induces Neuroblastoma-Like Tumors From Human iPS Cell-Derived Cranial Neural Crest Cells."
    supports: SUPPORT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "MYCN amplification is a key factor contributing to the poor prognosis of NB."
    explanation: >-
      States the adverse prognostic association of MYCN amplification. The
      sentence is background in the abstract of an iPSC-derived neural crest
      model study, restating the clinical picture; it is not something that
      study measured. The patient-derived support is the Brodeur and INRG
      evidence below.
  - reference: PMID:6719137
    reference_title: "Amplification of N-myc in untreated human neuroblastomas correlates with advanced disease stage."
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Furthermore, N-myc amplification is highly correlated with advanced stages of disease (P less than 0.001) and with the ability to grow in vitro as an established cell line, both of which are associated with a poor prognosis."
    explanation: >-
      Human clinical support for the rapid-progression and poor-prognosis
      claim, from untreated primary neuroblastoma tissue.
  - reference: PMID:19047291
    reference_title: "The International Neuroblastoma Risk Group (INRG) classification system: an INRG Task Force report."
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Stage, age, histologic category, grade of tumor differentiation, the status of the MYCN oncogene, chromosome 11q status, and DNA ploidy were the most highly statistically significant and clinically relevant factors."
    explanation: >-
      Confirms MYCN status as a statistically significant, clinically relevant
      prognostic factor in the 8,800-patient INRG cohort.
  - reference: PMID:22936790
    reference_title: "N-myc and noncoding RNAs in neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Amplification and overexpression of the MYCN proto-oncogene occurs in approximately 20% of neuroblastomas and is associated with advanced stage disease, rapid tumor progression, and poor prognosis."
    explanation: >-
      A review statement that amplification and overexpression of MYCN occur
      in approximately 20% of neuroblastomas and are associated with advanced
      stage disease, rapid tumor progression and poor prognosis, matching this
      subtype's description. The sentence pairs amplification with
      overexpression; it is read here as a statement about amplification.
- name: High-Risk Neuroblastoma
  classification: risk_group
  subtype_term:
    preferred_term: high-risk neuroblastoma
    term:
      id: NCIT:C150281
      label: High Risk Neuroblastoma
  description: >-
    A pretreatment risk group that sets treatment intensity, not a histologic or
    molecular entity; which tumors it contains depends on the classification
    system. In the International Neuroblastoma Risk Group (INRG) classification
    (2009), which defines 16 pretreatment groups, high risk denotes the groups
    with 5-year event-free survival below 50%, and 18 months was selected as the
    age cutoff. The Children's Oncology Group (COG) classifier version 2 (2021)
    uses the INRG Staging System (INRGSS) and adds segmental chromosome
    aberrations. Among stage L1, L2 and M tumors, it classifies as high risk
    stage M at 18 months or older, MYCN-amplified stage M at any age and stage M
    in toddlers aged 12 to under 18 months with any unfavorable biomarker, as
    well as MYCN-amplified L2 tumors, L2 tumors without MYCN amplification but
    with unfavorable International Neuroblastoma Pathology Classification (INPC)
    histology at 18 months or older, and incompletely resected MYCN-amplified L1
    tumors. Its rules for stage MS are set out separately; for stages M and MS
    together, MYCN status affected risk group assignment in children younger
    than 12 months, and MYCN status, histology, ploidy and segmental chromosome
    aberrations did so at 12 to 18 months. The International Society of
    Pediatric Oncology European Neuroblastoma Group (SIOPEN) high-risk trial
    HR-NBL1 took patients older than 12 months with International Neuroblastoma
    Staging System (INSS) stage 4 disease and patients with MYCN-amplified stage
    2, 3 or 4 disease. In the SIOPEN HR-NBL1.5 study, random assignment between
    two induction regimens used a 1-year age threshold: it was open to patients
    aged 1 to 20 years with stage 4 disease and to infants younger than 1 year
    with MYCN-amplified stage 4 or 4S disease. High-risk treatment typically
    includes myeloablative therapy and immunotherapy.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:19047291
    reference_title: "The International Neuroblastoma Risk Group (INRG) classification system: an INRG Task Force report."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "The optimal age cutoff was determined to be between 15 and 19 months, and 18 months was selected for the classification system. Sixteen pretreatment groups were defined on the basis of clinical criteria and statistically significantly different EFS of the cohort stratified by the INRG criteria. Patients with 5-year EFS more than 85%, more than 75% to < or = 85%, > or = 50% to < or = 75%, or less than 50% were classified as very low risk, low risk, intermediate risk, or high risk, respectively."
    explanation: >-
      The INRG Task Force report found the optimal age cutoff to lie between 15
      and 19 months, and the Task Force selected 18 months for the
      classification system. In its cohort of 8,800 children diagnosed in
      1990-2002, sixteen pretreatment groups were defined, and groups with
      5-year event-free survival below 50% were classified as high risk. The
      risk categories are survival bands from this pooled cohort.
  - reference: PMID:34319759
    reference_title: "Revised Neuroblastoma Risk Classification System: A Report From the Children's Oncology Group."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "A revised 2021 COG neuroblastoma risk classifier (version 2) that uses the INRGSS and incorporates SCAs has been adopted to prospectively define COG clinical trial eligibility and treatment assignment."
    explanation: >-
      The conclusion of this COG analysis of 4,832 patients on the ANBL00B1
      biology study states that the revised 2021 COG classifier (version 2) uses
      the INRGSS, incorporates segmental chromosome aberrations and has been
      adopted to define COG trial eligibility and treatment assignment. High
      risk is one of the groups this classifier assigns; the paper notes that
      risk schemas differ across cooperative groups.
  - reference: PMID:34319759
    reference_title: "Revised Neuroblastoma Risk Classification System: A Report From the Children's Oncology Group."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Thus, L1 tumors are classified in v2 as LR except rare MYCN-A tumors (4%) that are incompletely resected (macroscopic residual tumor), which are considered HR. ... INPC was prognostic for most L2 subsets, with the largest impact in patients age >= 18 months with MYCN-NA tumors ... In this group, those with unfavorable INPC tumors had outcomes inferior to those with favorable or unknown INPC ... Thus, these patients, in addition to L2 patients with MYCN-A, are classified HR in v2."
    explanation: >-
      The results of the COG ANBL00B1 analysis state the three locoregional
      groups that COG version 2 classifies as high risk: incompletely resected
      MYCN-amplified L1 tumors, MYCN-amplified L2 tumors, and MYCN-non-amplified
      L2 tumors with unfavorable INPC histology in patients aged 18 months or
      older ("these patients" refers back to that subset). These are
      COG-specific rules.
  - reference: PMID:34319759
    reference_title: "Revised Neuroblastoma Risk Classification System: A Report From the Children's Oncology Group."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "The majority of patients with stage M disease are >= 18 months at diagnosis and their outcome remains poor (EFS and OS: 46.1% +/- 1.6% and 59.4% +/- 1.5%). ... Similarly, patients with stage M disease of any age with MYCN-A tumors have poor outcomes (EFS and OS: 44.5% +/- 2.3% and 51.0% +/- 2.3%). Both groups receive treatment that typically includes one or more myeloablative therapies10,26 and immunotherapy12,13 and remain HR in v2. ... Patients age 12 to < 18 months with INRGSS M disease had outcomes intermediate to those of patients age < 12 and >= 18 months. ... Thus, toddlers with stage M disease with any unfavorable biomarker are classified as HR in v2."
    explanation: >-
      In the COG ANBL00B1 cohort used to build the 2021 version 2 classifier,
      stage M disease at 18 months or older and MYCN-amplified stage M disease
      at any age had poor outcomes and remain high risk. The quote also gives
      the stage M group aged 12 to under 18 months, the source's toddlers, whose
      outcomes were intermediate, and states that toddlers with stage M disease
      and any unfavorable biomarker are classified high risk. The treatment
      clause describes standard high-risk therapy cited to earlier COG trials,
      not a finding of this analysis.
  - reference: PMID:34319759
    reference_title: "Revised Neuroblastoma Risk Classification System: A Report From the Children's Oncology Group."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "For patients with stage M (metastatic) and MS (metastatic, special) disease, genomic biomarkers affected risk group assignment for those < 12 months (MYCN) or 12-18 months (MYCN, histology, ploidy, and SCA) of age. ... Risk classification for MS in v2 is discussed in the Data Supplement."
    explanation: >-
      The abstract of this COG ANBL00B1 analysis states that, for stages M and
      MS together, MYCN status affected risk group assignment under the revised
      classifier in children younger than 12 months, and MYCN status, histology,
      ploidy and segmental chromosome aberrations did so at 12 to 18 months. The
      sentence pools the two stages and does not say which stage MS groups are
      high risk; the results section refers stage MS risk classification under
      version 2 to the Data Supplement.
  - reference: PMID:30754710
    reference_title: "The Evolution of Risk Classification for Neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Finally, SIOPEN completed a SIOPEN HR-NBL1 evaluating patients over 12 months with INSS stage 4 disease and patients with stage 2, 3, or 4 disease with MYCN amplification"
    explanation: >-
      This review of cooperative-group risk classification describes the SIOPEN
      high-risk trial HR-NBL1 as taking patients older than 12 months with INSS
      stage 4 disease and patients with MYCN-amplified stage 2, 3 or 4 disease,
      so its high-risk population included locoregional MYCN-amplified disease
      as well as metastatic disease. The review restates the trial's criteria
      and reports no patient data.
  - reference: PMID:34152804
    reference_title: "Randomized Trial of Two Induction Therapy Regimens for High-Risk Neuroblastoma: HR-NBL1.5 International Society of Pediatric Oncology European Neuroblastoma Group Study."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Patients (age 1-20 years) with stage 4 neuroblastoma or stage 4/4s aged < 1 year with MYCN amplification were eligible for random assignment to rCOJEC or MSKCC-N5."
    explanation: >-
      States who was eligible for the HR-NBL1.5 randomization between two
      induction regimens: patients aged 1 to 20 years with stage 4
      neuroblastoma, or infants younger than 1 year with MYCN-amplified stage 4
      or 4S disease. The age threshold for stage 4 disease was therefore 1 year.
      This is eligibility for one randomization within a SIOPEN high-risk study,
      not the study's whole population or a SIOPEN definition of high risk.
- name: Adrenal Gland Neuroblastoma
  classification: anatomic
  subtype_term:
    preferred_term: adrenal gland neuroblastoma
    term:
      id: MONDO:0006076
      label: adrenal gland neuroblastoma
  locations:
  - preferred_term: adrenal gland
    term:
      id: UBERON:0002369
      label: adrenal gland
  description: >-
    Neuroblastoma whose primary tumor arises in the adrenal gland. In the INRG
    database, 47% of 8,369 children with neuroblastoma or ganglioneuroblastoma
    and a known primary site had adrenal tumors. After adjustment for age, stage
    and histologic grade, adrenal primaries had about twice the odds of MYCN
    amplification of non-adrenal primaries (adjusted odds ratio 2.09), and after
    adjustment for age, MYCN status and stage they carried a modestly higher
    risk of events (hazard ratio 1.13).
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:25154816
    reference_title: "Clinical, biologic, and prognostic differences on the basis of primary tumor site in neuroblastoma: a report from the international neuroblastoma risk group project."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Among 8,369 children, 47% had adrenal tumors. ... Adrenal tumors were more likely than nonadrenal tumors (adjusted odds ratio, 2.09; 95% CI, 1.67 to 2.63; P < .001) and thoracic tumors were less likely than nonthoracic tumors (adjusted odds ratio, 0.20; 95% CI, 0.11 to 0.39; P < .001) to have MYCN amplification after controlling for age, stage, and histologic grade. ... After controlling for age, MYCN status, and stage, patients with adrenal tumors had higher risk for events (hazard ratio, 1.13 compared with nonadrenal tumors; 95% CI, 1.03 to 1.23; P = .008)"
    explanation: >-
      In the INRG database cohort of children younger than 21 years diagnosed
      with neuroblastoma or ganglioneuroblastoma in 1990-2002 with a known
      primary site, 47% of the 8,369 children had adrenal primary tumors.
      Compared with non-adrenal primaries, adrenal tumors had about twice the
      odds of MYCN amplification after adjustment for age, stage and histologic
      grade (adjusted odds ratio 2.09), and a higher risk of an event after
      adjustment for age, MYCN status and stage (hazard ratio 1.13). Because the
      cohort includes ganglioneuroblastoma, the 47% is a share of this cohort,
      not a frequency among neuroblastoma alone.
mechanistic_hypotheses:
- hypothesis_group_id: regression_trka_ngf_deprivation
  hypothesis_label: >-
    Withdrawal of NGF-dependent TrkA signalling triggers developmentally
    programmed cell death in TRKA-expressing tumours
  status: ALTERNATIVE
  description: >-
    Spontaneous regression is the delayed activation of developmentally
    programmed cell death in a tumour whose cells have become dependent on NGF
    through the TrkA receptor, occurring where NGF is not available in the
    tumour's microenvironment. Of the candidate mechanisms the reviews name,
    this is the one a 2014 review judged the available data most consistent
    with, and the 2018 review by its first author says a switch in TrkA
    dependence could explain regression while adding that further mechanisms
    explain the phenomenon as well. Both reviews also state that the exact
    mechanisms of regression are uncertain, which is why this group is recorded
    as an alternative rather than a canonical model. Edges belonging to it opt
    in via hypothesis_groups: [regression_trka_ngf_deprivation]; in this entry
    that is the edge from NGF-TRKA Trophic Signaling Withdrawal to Spontaneous
    Tumor Regression, whose intermediate mechanisms state what has been
    measured and where.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:25331179
    reference_title: Mechanisms of neuroblastoma regression.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: "However, the available data regarding the possible mechanisms of neuroblastoma regression are most consistent with a TrkA dependence mechanism."
    explanation: >-
      Closing its discussion of the Trk receptors, Brodeur and Bagatell's 2014
      review states that the available data on the possible mechanisms of
      neuroblastoma regression are most consistent with a TrkA dependence
      mechanism. This is the sentence that ranks the TrkA mechanism as an
      explanation; both reviews' abstracts rank the same mechanism first as a
      drug target, which is a different claim. It is a 2014 judgement, and in
      the matching paragraph of the 2018 review the first author instead says
      that a switch in TrkA dependence could explain regression but that
      additional mechanisms do as well. Graded OTHER because the sentence is
      the authors' synthesis across cultured tumour cells, developmental
      biology and clinical associations rather than a report of any one study
      type.
  - reference: PMID:29305654
    reference_title: Spontaneous regression of neuroblastoma.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: "Thus, a switch in TrkA dependence could explain spontaneous regression of neuroblastomas but there are additional mechanisms to explain this phenomenon as well."
    explanation: >-
      Brodeur's 2018 review closes its TrkA section by saying that a switch in
      TrkA dependence could explain spontaneous regression of neuroblastoma,
      but that additional mechanisms explain the phenomenon as well. It
      supports this hypothesis as a candidate explanation while stating that it
      is not the only one, which fits a status of ALTERNATIVE, a plausible
      competing or superimposed hypothesis with supporting evidence, rather
      than CANONICAL. Graded OTHER because the sentence is the review's own
      assessment, drawn from developmental work in animals, primary culture of
      tumour cells and the association of high TrkA expression with favourable
      tumours, and reports no single study type.
  - reference: PMID:25331179
    reference_title: Mechanisms of neuroblastoma regression.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: "This evidence also suggests several possible mechanisms to explain the phenomena of spontaneous regression in neuroblastomas, including neurotrophin deprivation, humoral or cellular immunity, loss of telomerase activity and alterations in epigenetic regulation."
    explanation: >-
      The abstract of the same 2014 review names neurotrophin deprivation first
      among several possible mechanisms of spontaneous regression, alongside
      humoral or cellular immunity, loss of telomerase activity and altered
      epigenetic regulation. In the body of the review, neurotrophin
      deprivation is the death of TrkA-expressing tumour cells when NGF is
      absent from their microenvironment, which is the mechanism this group
      records. The sentence supports the group as one candidate among several,
      which is its ALTERNATIVE status, and not as an established mechanism.
      Graded OTHER because it is the review's synthesis of earlier work rather
      than a report of any one study type.
- hypothesis_group_id: regression_absent_telomere_maintenance
  hypothesis_label: >-
    Absence of a telomere maintenance mechanism is a prerequisite for
    spontaneous regression
  status: ALTERNATIVE
  description: >-
    Tumour cells with neither telomerase activation nor ALT have a finite
    telomere reserve, and this absence is proposed as a precondition for
    spontaneous regression or differentiation, because telomere maintenance is
    essential for cancer cells to achieve immortal proliferation capacity. The
    claim the source makes is that the absence is likely a prerequisite, a
    necessary condition, so it is equally consistent with the absence
    permitting a regression that one of the other mechanisms drives. Absence of
    a detectable mechanism is not sufficient for regression: this entry's
    Unlimited Replicative Potential node records high-risk tumours lacking
    significant telomere lengthening activity whose cells kept proliferating
    for more than 200 population doublings while their telomeres shortened
    (PMID:28636942). The observational basis is that 99 of 208 assessed
    pretreatment tumours lacked any maintenance mechanism, 57 of those patients
    were never given cytotoxic treatment, and 18 had documented spontaneous
    regression. Edges belonging to this group opt in via hypothesis_groups:
    [regression_absent_telomere_maintenance].
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:30523111
    reference_title: A mechanistic classification of clinical phenotypes in neuroblastoma.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Because telomere maintenance is essential for cancer cells to achieve immortal proliferation capacity (8, 28), its absence is likely a prerequisite for spontaneous regression and differentiation in neuroblastoma."
    explanation: >-
      Ackermann et al. assessed telomerase activation and ALT in 208
      pretreatment neuroblastomas; the 99 patients whose tumours lacked a
      telomere maintenance mechanism had an excellent outcome, and 18 of them
      had documented spontaneous regression. In the concluding paragraph the
      authors state this claim: because telomere maintenance is essential for
      cancer cells to achieve immortal proliferation capacity, its absence is
      likely a prerequisite for spontaneous regression and differentiation. The
      premise is cited to earlier work and the conclusion is the authors' own
      hedged inference rather than a measured result, since the study recorded
      telomere maintenance status and patient outcome rather than how tumours
      regress. A prerequisite is a necessary condition and not a cause, so the
      sentence is equally consistent with the absence permitting a regression
      that another mechanism drives.
  - reference: PMID:36030273
    reference_title: Connecting telomere maintenance and regulation to the developmental origin and differentiation states of neuroblastoma tumor cells.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "In short, the critical importance of telomeres in NB malignancy is underscored by (i) the poor prognosis of tumors that harbor telomerase or ALT and (ii) the spontaneous regression and/or maturation of low stage tumors that harbor no TMM."
    explanation: >-
      A 2022 review of telomere biology in neuroblastoma sums up the clinical
      picture: tumours with telomerase or ALT have a poor prognosis, while
      low-stage tumours with no telomere maintenance mechanism undergo
      spontaneous regression or maturation. That places both regression and
      maturation on the telomere-maintenance-negative side, which is the
      pairing this hypothesis rests on. Indirect because the quoted sentence
      records which tumours regress or mature rather than that the absence is
      required for regression, and it covers low-stage tumours only. Elsewhere
      the review proposes that such tumours regress once their telomere
      reserves are exhausted, but it presents that as a model rather than a
      measured result. The review reports no new data and the cohort studies it
      draws on include Ackermann et al. 2018, cited above, so it is not
      independent replication.
- hypothesis_group_id: regression_immune_mediated
  hypothesis_label: >-
    An anti-tumour immune response destroys the tumour
  status: EMERGING
  description: >-
    Spontaneous regression is tumour destruction mediated by a humoral or
    cellular anti-tumour immune response. The human evidence is associational:
    in 107 untreated tumours, expression of the iNKT-cell-specific T-cell
    receptor was higher in the lower-stage and lower-risk group, in tumours
    with high TrkA expression and favourable histology, and in younger
    patients, and overall survival was higher where iNKT cells had infiltrated.
    No study cited here observes an immune effector producing a regression. In
    the TH-MYCN transgenic mouse model of aggressive disease the natural
    antitumour antibody did not correlate with spontaneous regression and
    B-cell depletion left tumour incidence unchanged, which bears against the
    antibody-mediated arm in that model while leaving cellular immunity
    untested. The group carries no causal edge in this entry, because no
    pathophysiology node is annotated for an immune effector here.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:29018959
    reference_title: Invariant natural killer T infiltration in neuroblastoma with favorable outcome.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Vα24-Jα18 receptor was detected in 62 untreated cases (57.9%). The expression was significantly higher in stages 1, 2, 3, or 4S (P = 0.0099), in tumors with low or intermediate risk (P = 0.0050), with high TrkA expression (P = 0.0229), with favorable histology (P = 0.0026) ... and in younger patients (P = 0.0036). The overall survival rate was significantly higher in patients with iNKT-cell infiltration (log-rank; P = 0.0089)."
    explanation: >-
      Hishiki et al. used real-time quantitative PCR to quantify expression of
      the iNKT-cell-specific T-cell receptor in untreated tumour samples from
      107 neuroblastoma patients and detected it in 62 (57.9%). Expression was
      significantly higher in tumours of stage 1, 2, 3 or 4S, reported as one
      pooled group, in low- or intermediate-risk tumours, in tumours with high
      TrkA expression, in tumours with favourable histology and in younger
      patients, and overall survival was significantly higher in patients whose
      tumours showed iNKT-cell infiltration. This is evidence from human
      tumours that an innate-like T-cell population is more abundant in the
      favourable-biology group that contains stage 4S. It supports
      immune-mediated regression only indirectly: the abstract reports no
      regression outcome, it does not report stage 4S separately from stages 1
      to 3, and it gives each association on its own, so infiltration may mark
      lower stage, lower risk, younger age or high TrkA expression rather than
      act independently of them. The ellipsis skips the association with
      aneuploidy.
  - reference: PMID:30054041
    reference_title: Natural antibody against neuroblastoma of TH-MYCN transgenic mice does not correlate with spontaneous regression.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    snippet: "Mice with no or small (<5 mm) tumors showed higher antibody titers in plasma than mice with large (>5 mm) tumors. A significant negative correlation was observed between the tumor diameter and the titer of antitumor antibody. This antibody had complement-dependent cytotoxicity but not antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity against neuroblastoma cells."
    explanation: >-
      The half of Kawakubo et al.'s result that is consistent with an antibody
      arm, quoted separately from the half that is not. In homozygous and
      heterozygous TH-MYCN mice the natural antitumour antibody titre was
      higher in animals with no or small tumours than in those with large ones,
      with a significant negative correlation between tumour diameter and
      titre, and the antibody killed neuroblastoma cells through complement but
      not through antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity. Indirect because an
      inverse correlation with tumour size is not an observation of regression,
      the direction of the association is not established, and the cytotoxicity
      was measured in cultured cells. The companion item below carries the
      result that cuts the other way.
  - reference: PMID:30054041
    reference_title: Natural antibody against neuroblastoma of TH-MYCN transgenic mice does not correlate with spontaneous regression.
    supports: REFUTE
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    snippet: "Moreover, B-cell depletion had no effect on the tumor incidence in vivo. We revealed that TH-MYCN transgenic mice have a natural antibody against neuroblastoma that correlate with tumor size. However, this antibody does not correlate with the spontaneous regression of neuroblastoma."
    explanation: >-
      The authors' own negative result, split from the supporting half above
      because one evidence item cannot carry both directions: depleting B cells
      left tumour incidence unchanged, and the natural antibody tracked tumour
      size without tracking spontaneous regression. This contradicts the
      antibody-mediated arm of the immune hypothesis in this model. It does not
      refute the hypothesis as a whole: only natural antibody was tested, so
      cellular immunity is untested, and the model is MYCN-driven aggressive
      disease rather than the favourable-biology tumours that regress in
      patients, which is why the item is graded indirect.
- hypothesis_group_id: regression_epigenetic
  hypothesis_label: >-
    Altered epigenetic regulation, including subtelomeric promoter
    hypermethylation, contributes to regression
  status: EMERGING
  description: >-
    Spontaneous regression follows from altered epigenetic regulation of gene
    expression rather than from a genomic change. The specific finding recorded
    here is that stage 4S tumours carry a characteristic DNA methylation
    portrait, with hypermethylation of specific subtelomeric promoters, which
    the authors suggest may be an additional mechanism by which telomere length
    and spontaneous regression are controlled; that suggestion connects this
    group to the telomere group above rather than standing apart from it. Stage
    4S is used as a surrogate for tumours likely to regress, so the comparison
    is by stage rather than by observed regression, and the subtelomeric result
    rests on 14 stage 4S tumours. The group carries no causal edge in this
    entry, because no pathophysiology node is annotated for a methylation state
    here.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:27599161
    reference_title: Stage 4S neuroblastoma tumors show a characteristic DNA methylation portrait.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "In this study, we have shown that specific subtelomeric promoters are hypermethylated in stage 4S tumors compared to stage 1/2 and stage 4 tumors, which suggests that subtelomeric DNA methylation may represent an additional mechanism by which telomere length and spontaneous regression are controlled in NB."
    explanation: >-
      A re-analysis of methyl-CpG-binding domain sequencing data from 41
      MYCN-non-amplified primary neuroblastomas (14 stage 4S, 14 stage 4 and 13
      stage 1/2) found specific subtelomeric promoters hypermethylated in stage
      4S tumours compared with both other groups. From this the authors suggest
      that subtelomeric DNA methylation may be an additional mechanism by which
      telomere length and spontaneous regression are controlled. Indirect for
      this hypothesis on three counts: tumours were grouped by stage, used as a
      surrogate for regression, rather than by whether they regressed; telomere
      length was not measured in these tumours, and the authors note that this
      route of telomere-length regulation is unexplored in neuroblastoma; and
      the stage 4S group is small, at 14 tumours.
stages:
- name: INRGSS Stage L1
  description: >-
    Locoregional tumor with none of the 20 image-defined risk factors (IDRFs).
    The International Neuroblastoma Risk Group Staging System (INRGSS) stages
    patients before any treatment, from clinical criteria and IDRFs, because the
    International Neuroblastoma Staging System (INSS) is a postsurgical staging
    system.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:19047290
    reference_title: "The International Neuroblastoma Risk Group (INRG) staging system: an INRG Task Force report."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: "Because the International Neuroblastoma Staging System (INSS) is a postsurgical staging system, a new clinical staging system was required for the INRG pretreatment risk classification system. ... To stage patients before any treatment, the INRG Task Force, consisting of neuroblastoma experts from Australia/New Zealand, China, Europe, Japan, and North America, developed a new INRG staging system (INRGSS) based on clinical criteria and image-defined risk factors (IDRFs). ... In the INGRSS, locoregional tumors are staged L1 or L2 based on the absence or presence of one or more of 20 IDRFs, respectively."
    explanation: >-
      The INRG Task Force report states that a new clinical staging system was
      required for the INRG pretreatment risk classification because the INSS is
      a postsurgical staging system. To stage patients before any treatment, the
      Task Force based the INRGSS on clinical criteria and image-defined risk
      factors (IDRFs), and it stages locoregional tumors L1 or L2 by the absence
      or presence of one or more of 20 IDRFs. These sentences give the Task
      Force's consensus definition and rationale, not patient data; INGRSS is
      the source's own misspelling, kept verbatim.
- name: INRGSS Stage L2
  description: >-
    Locoregional tumor with one or more of the 20 IDRFs. In the INRG Task
    Force's analysis of European patients with locoregional disease, 5-year
    event-free survival was lower for L2 than for L1 tumors (78% versus 90%).
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:19047290
    reference_title: "The International Neuroblastoma Risk Group (INRG) staging system: an INRG Task Force report."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: "In the INGRSS, locoregional tumors are staged L1 or L2 based on the absence or presence of one or more of 20 IDRFs, respectively."
    explanation: >-
      The INRG Task Force report stages locoregional tumors L1 or L2 by the
      absence or presence of one or more of 20 image-defined risk factors, so a
      locoregional tumor with at least one of them is stage L2. This is the Task
      Force's consensus staging rule rather than a patient observation; INGRSS
      is the source's own misspelling of INRGSS.
  - reference: PMID:19047290
    reference_title: "The International Neuroblastoma Risk Group (INRG) staging system: an INRG Task Force report."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Patients with INRGSS stage L2 disease had significantly lower 5-year event-free survival than those with INRGSS stage L1 disease (78% +/- 4% v 90% +/- 3%; P = .0010)."
    explanation: >-
      The Task Force's post hoc analysis of European (SIOPEN) patients with
      locoregional (INSS stage 1 to 3) tumors reports 5-year event-free survival
      of 78% for INRGSS L2 against 90% for L1 (P = .0010). Per the full text,
      474 of the 661 patients analysed had outcome data, 213 with L1 and 261
      with L2 disease. The comparison covers locoregional tumors only.
- name: INRGSS Stage M
  description: >-
    Distant metastatic disease, except the restricted metastatic pattern in
    children younger than 18 months that is staged MS.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:19047290
    reference_title: "The International Neuroblastoma Risk Group (INRG) staging system: an INRG Task Force report."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: "Metastatic tumors are defined as stage M, except for stage MS, in which metastases are confined to the skin, liver, and/or bone marrow in children younger than 18 months of age."
    explanation: >-
      The INRG Task Force report defines metastatic tumors as INRGSS stage M,
      with one exception: stage MS, in which metastases are confined to skin,
