  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:26121087
    reference_title: "Relapsed neuroblastomas show frequent RAS-MAPK pathway mutations."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Eighteen of the 23 relapse tumors (78%) showed mutations predicted to activate the RAS-MAPK pathway. Seven of these events were detected only in the relapse tumor, whereas the others showed clonal enrichment."
    explanation: >-
      Whole-genome sequencing of matched lymphocyte, diagnostic-tumour and
      relapse DNA from 23 patients; the abstract gives the 18 of 23 (78%)
      figure and the seven events detected only at relapse. Indirect for
      this node because the study shows the alterations are present while
      pathway activity was not measured in the patient tumours, and because
      predicted to activate is the authors' own hedge: the point mutations
      were selected as COSMIC-annotated hotspots. Three qualifications come
      from the results and Table 2. The 18 include 10 ALK aberrations, which
      this entry models on its ALK Signaling Activation node, leaving 8
      non-ALK lesions (NF1 in two tumours; NRAS, KRAS, HRAS, BRAF, PTPN11
      and FGFR1 in one each), and no tumour carried two such events.
      Detected only in the relapse tumor means not detected at diagnosis by
      whole-genome sequencing: re-testing the matched primaries found two of
      the seven, an ALK point mutation by ultra-deep sequencing and an ALK
      rearrangement by PCR, so 13 of the 18 were detectable at diagnosis,
      and the authors leave open whether the other five arose after
      diagnosis, sat below detection limits or were missed through spatial
      heterogeneity of the primary. The closing clause, that the others
      showed clonal enrichment, is looser than the paper's own clonality
      analysis of the 15 relapses with point mutations: the relapse
      cancer-cell fraction exceeded the diagnostic fraction with over 90%
      probability in 7 pairs, while the other 8 showed retention without
      clear enrichment. The series was selected only on the availability of
      matched samples, spans low-, intermediate- and high-risk cases roughly
      equally, and the authors report that the RAS-MAPK frequency did not
      differ between risk groups.
  - reference: PMID:26121087
    reference_title: "Relapsed neuroblastomas show frequent RAS-MAPK pathway mutations."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "We also detect mutations in NF1, BRAF, PTPN11, FGFR1 and the three RAS genes, and all lesions in the RAS-MAPK pathway were mutually exclusive."
    explanation: >-
      The authors' summary of their Table 2, the RAS-MAPK lesions in the
      relapse tumours of 23 patients sequenced as matched germline,
      diagnostic and relapse samples; the sentence's also follows the
      paragraph reporting ALK in 10 relapse tumours. Table 2 lists PTPN11
      A72T, FGFR1 N546K, NRAS Q61K, HRAS Q61K, KRAS G12D, a BRAF
      catalytic-domain tandem duplication and two inactivating NF1 lesions
      (a homozygous deletion; a splice-donor mutation with a hemizygous
      deletion), so mutations here includes structural lesions, and these
      are the seven genes this node binds besides ALK. Table 2 carries one
      row per patient and no row holds two pathway lesions, so mutual
      exclusivity means no tumour carried more than one: 18 of the 23
      relapse tumours carried one and 5 carried none. The list covers
      lesions present in the relapse tumour rather than lesions acquired
      there, since the PTPN11, FGFR1, NRAS and KRAS events were already
      detected in the matched diagnostic tumour while the two NF1 lesions,
      HRAS Q61K and the BRAF duplication were not.
  - reference: PMID:40036726
    reference_title: "Frequency and Clinical Significance of Clonal and Subclonal Driver Mutations in High-Risk Neuroblastoma at Diagnosis: A Children's Oncology Group Study."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "RAS pathway mutations occurred in 7.9% of tumors (n = 19; four clonal, 15 subclonal), with EFS and OS for those with VAF ≥5% inferior to RAS-WT patients (5-year OS 19.1% v 60.0%; HR, 3.021; P = .0168)."
    explanation: >-
      Children's Oncology Group study that ultra-deep sequenced 242
      pretherapy tumours from patients on the phase III high-risk trial
      ANBL0532. RAS pathway mutations were present in 19 tumours (7.9%), 15
      of them subclonal, where clonal means a variant allele frequency of
      20% or more and is not corrected for tumour cell content. Patients
      whose tumours carried such a mutation at a variant allele frequency of
      5% or more had worse event-free and overall survival than
      RAS-wild-type patients; that contrast rests on seven patients, four at
      20% or more and three at 5-20%. Comparing all 19 RAS-mutant tumours
      with wild-type showed no outcome difference, and the authors say finer
      strata were too small for robust analysis. The panel's RAS pathway
      calls cover targeted regions of NRAS, KRAS, HRAS, BRAF and PTPN11,
      limited to mutations reported more than once in COSMIC, so the 7.9%
      excludes ALK, which the paper counts separately, and says nothing
      about NF1 or FGFR1 alterations, which the panel does not cover. The
      study does not measure MAPK pathway activity.
  - reference: PMID:26121087
    reference_title: "Relapsed neuroblastomas show frequent RAS-MAPK pathway mutations."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: IN_VITRO
    snippet: "Expression of this tandem duplication in the BRAF gene in a neuroblastoma cell line induced activation of the RAS-MAPK pathway"
    explanation: >-
      The one experiment among this node's sources that measures pathway
      activity rather than counting lesions: expressing the BRAF tandem
      duplication found in one of the relapse tumours in a neuroblastoma
      cell line induced activation of the RAS-MAPK pathway. It covers one of
      the seven lesion classes bound on this node, in a cell line rather
      than in a patient tumour, so the step from it to ligand-independent
      cascade flux across the other six lesions is an inference, which is
      why the item is graded indirect. The node's other items report
      lesions, frequencies or selection and measure no pathway activity;
      this one is what grounds the INCREASED modifiers.
  downstream:
  - target: Therapy-Resistant Relapse
    description: >-
      RAS-MAPK-activating mutations are selected over the interval between
      diagnosis and relapse, in which most patients receive chemotherapy,
      and a paired series reads clonal selection for NF1 mutations as a
      candidate driver of therapy resistance. Neither series tests whether
      the pathway state confers resistance: neither relates RAS-MAPK status
      to treatment response or survival, so the intervening mechanism is
      undemonstrated and the edge is an association between a selected
      lesion class and relapse rather than a mechanism of resistance.
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:26121087
      reference_title: "Relapsed neuroblastomas show frequent RAS-MAPK pathway mutations."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: "Collectively, these results support RAS-MAPK mutations as somatic drivers that undergo positive selection over the course of neuroblastoma treatment."
      explanation: >-
        Whole-genome sequencing of 23 paired diagnostic and relapse
        neuroblastomas, from low-, intermediate- and high-risk patients in
        roughly equal numbers. In the 15 pairs carrying a RAS-MAPK point
        mutation, a Bayesian cancer-cell-fraction comparison placed the
        mutation in a major subclonal population at relapse in 14 and found
        strong relapse-specific enrichment in 7, while the other 8 retained
        a mutation already present at diagnosis; the quoted sentence is the
        authors' conclusion from that analysis. The paper counts activating
        ALK mutations as RAS-MAPK lesions, and ALK accounted for 4 of the 7
        enriched pairs, with HRAS, KRAS and NF1 one each. Twenty-one of the
        23 patients received chemotherapy before relapse and none a targeted
        inhibitor, but the only KRAS-mutant pair, one of the 7 enriched, had
        no radiotherapy, chemotherapy or surgery between diagnosis and
        relapse, and the authors place the expansion only possibly under the
        selective pressure of chemotherapy. Indirect for this edge: pathway
        activity was inferred from the mutations rather than measured, the
        paper does not relate RAS-MAPK status to patient outcome or
        response, and its discussion says an association with resistance to
        conventional cytotoxic therapies still needs research. The quote
        supports selection and retention of these mutations from diagnosis
        to relapse, not a demonstrated contribution to therapy resistance.
    - reference: PMID:39693475
      reference_title: "Stratified Medicine Pediatrics: Cell-Free DNA and Serial Tumor Sequencing Identifies Subtype-Specific Cancer Evolution and Epigenetic States."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: "Taken together, this identifies clonal selection for NF1 mutations as a potential driver of therapy resistance in neuroblastoma."
      explanation: >-
        Paired sequencing from the Stratified Medicine Paediatrics
        programme, comparing archival diagnostic tumour with relapse tumour
        and plasma cell-free DNA taken at relapse. Neuroblastoma was the largest
        single tumour type, and NF1 was among the genes most often mutated
        only at relapse in the tissue comparison of 58 neuroblastoma pairs,
        which the discussion puts at 4 of 59, so the paper's own
        denominators differ by one. Relapse cell-free DNA carried NF1
        variants absent from the matched tissue in 5 of 72 patients; with no
        plasma from diagnosis, these show NF1 variants present at relapse
        rather than when they arose. From these counts, and an earlier
        paired series reporting NF1 acquired in 2 of 23 relapses, the
        authors conclude only that clonal selection for NF1 mutations is a
        potential driver of therapy resistance. The main text reports no
        statistical test of NF1 enrichment and no functional test of
        resistance, and across the whole cohort the authors stress that
        relapse tumours stayed genetically close to diagnosis and argue that
        epigenetic change is the more parsimonious explanation for relapse.
        Indirect for this edge: the quote is about NF1 mutations rather than
        RAS-MAPK pathway activity, and the paper neither characterises the
        variants' function nor shows the step from NF1 mutation to pathway
        hyperactivation.
- name: p53 Pathway Inactivation
  biological_scale: MOLECULAR
  conforms_to: "evading_growth_suppressors#Tumor Suppressor Inactivation"
  description: >-
    Loss of p53-axis control, through an inactivating TP53 mutation, MDM2
    amplification (in the SIOPEN cohort cited here as CDK4/MDM2
    co-amplification, the two genes lying at 12q14.1 and 12q15; in the
    relapse series cited here as MDM2 amplification alone at 12q15), or
    homozygous CDKN2A deletion removing p14ARF. In 84 tumours from 41
    patients with relapsed neuroblastoma, a p53-pathway abnormality was
    detected in 20 of 41 (49%) cases. That is a share of patients who
    relapsed rather than of relapse tumours, and it is a floor, because MDM2
    amplification was assessed in only 23 of the roughly 35 patients whose
    relapse tumour was p53-wild-type and TP53 sequencing covered exons
    4-9. The parts of the pathway differ in timing: TP53
    mutations were first detected after chemotherapy in all but one of the
    six mutated cases, whereas MDM2 amplification and p14ARF inactivation
    were present at both diagnosis and relapse in most cases, so this is not
    a uniformly therapy-era lesion. The p14ARF readout in that series was
    specific to CDKN2A exon 1-beta, the p53-arm product, whereas p16INK4a
    from the same locus acts in the RB arm. The pathway is not confined to
    MYCN-amplified disease: in a SIOPEN series of 98 non-MYCN-amplified,
    localized unresectable or stage 3 tumours of unfavourable histology,
    classed as intermediate risk under the European criteria used there and,
    in the paper's own words, as high risk in most of North America, 10 tumours
    carried a p53-pathway abnormality and those patients had inferior
    event-free and overall survival. That study's definition of the
    abnormality also admits a pathogenic ATM mutation, which this node does
    not bind.
  notes: >-
    The node binds one molecular function although it carries three genes,
    and the three do not share one: p53 is a transcription factor, MDM2 an
    E3 ubiquitin ligase and p16INK4a a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor.
    The function bound is the one all three routes converge on losing. An
    inactivating TP53 mutation removes it directly; MDM2 amplification
    degrades the protein that carries it; CDKN2A loss releases MDM2 to do
    so. So DECREASED here describes the state of the pathway's output, not
    the activity of whichever gene is altered in a given tumour, and the
    ligase and kinase-inhibitor activities are deliberately not bound on
    this node.

  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:20145180
    reference_title: "High Frequency of p53/MDM2/p14ARF Pathway Abnormalities in Relapsed Neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Abnormalities in the p53 pathway were identified in 20 of 41 (49%) cases."
    explanation: >-
      Abstract result. The cohort is 84 tumours from 41 patients with
      relapsed neuroblastoma, 38 of them with paired tumours from different
      stages of therapy and 3 with a relapse tumour only, so the 49% is a
      share of patients rather than of relapse tumours: a patient counts if
      any tumour studied carried an inactivating TP53 mutation, MDM2
      amplification, or p14ARF methylation or homozygous deletion. It counts
      abnormalities detected rather than a complete census, since TP53 was
      sequenced over exons 4-9 only and MDM2 amplification was assessed in
      only 23 of the roughly 35 patients whose relapse tumour was
      p53-wild-type, so 20 of 41 is a floor. It is also not a rate of
      abnormalities acquired at relapse: in the paper's case table the
      abnormality is already present in the diagnostic tumour in 12 of the
      20 cases, is absent at diagnosis and found later in 6, and 2 cases
      have no diagnostic tumour, while the results text gives the split as
      13 at presentation and 8 post-chemotherapy or at relapse, figures that
      sum to 21. The series was assembled for relapse across risk groups
      with no non-relapsing comparison group, and 3 of the 41 patients
      progressed during initial therapy rather than relapsing after a
      response.
  - reference: PMID:20145180
    reference_title: "High Frequency of p53/MDM2/p14ARF Pathway Abnormalities in Relapsed Neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "p53 mutations were detected following chemotherapy in all but one case, whereas MDM2 amplification and p14ARF inactivation were present at both diagnosis and relapse in the majority of cases"
    explanation: >-
      Results sentence from the same paired-sample series, giving the timing
      of each arm of the pathway. Inactivating TP53 mutations were first
      detected after chemotherapy in 5 of the 6 mutated cases; the
      exception, a patient aged 15 at diagnosis, carried the mutation from
      diagnosis. MDM2 amplification in all 3 cases and, by the authors'
      count, p14ARF inactivation in 9 of 12 were present at diagnosis and
      persisted to relapse, although the case table shows that one of those
      p14ARF cases had no diagnostic sample, its earliest sample taken after
      induction chemotherapy. The remaining p14ARF lesions, 2 of the 3
      promoter methylations and 1 of the 9 homozygous deletions, were found
      only after treatment, so the node is not uniformly therapy-acquired:
      the upstream result runs against the paper's own hypothesis that the
      pathway is inactivated during treatment, while the TP53 arm fits it.
      The ARF assays were specific to p14ARF, methylation-specific PCR of
      its promoter and duplex PCR for exon 1-beta, the ARF-only first exon
      of the INK4a/ARF locus; no p16INK4a assay is described, and the
      authors place p16INK4a in the RB pathway rather than the p53 pathway.
      Even for TP53 the data give detection timing rather than proven
      acquisition, because one mutated case had no diagnostic tumour and
      only in one case did mutation-specific PCR exclude a mutant clone
      above about 1 in 2000 cells at diagnosis.
  - reference: PMID:42385103
    reference_title: "Frequency and Prognostic Significance of Genetic Abnormalities in a Subgroup of Patients With Intermediate-Risk Neuroblastoma: A SIOPEN Study."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Patients with tumors with p53 pathway abnormalities defined as TP53 inactivating mutations, MDM2 amplification, homozygous CDKN2A deletion, or pathogenic ATM mutations (n = 10) had inferior 5-year EFS and OS compared with patients with tumors without p53 pathway abnormalities"
    explanation: >-
      SIOPEN study of 98 patients older than 18 months with
      non-MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma that was localized and unresectable
      (INRGSS L2) or INSS stage 3, with unfavourable histology, diagnosed
      2007-2021 and treated without upfront myeloablative therapy; most
      tumour DNA was taken at diagnosis. The survival comparison covered 76
      patients, ten of whose tumours carried a p53-pathway abnormality (5
      CDK4/MDM2 co-amplifications, 3 pathogenic loss-of-function TP53
      mutations, 1 homozygous CDKN2A loss and 1 ATM), with 5-year event-free
      survival of 0% against 61.1% and overall survival of 26.7% against
      80.9%. Because the groups overlap, the multivariable Cox model entered
      p53-pathway abnormality and oncogene amplification as one combined
      variable, so it does not separate the two; after the authors excluded
      the cases with oncogene amplification, p53-pathway alterations
      remained associated with inferior event-free and overall survival, a
      comparison resting on about five patients. The paper classes this
      subgroup as intermediate risk and notes that in most of North America
      these patients are classified as high risk and receive myeloablative
      therapy; it names no risk classifier, and none is asserted here, so the
      finding places the abnormality and its poor prognosis outside
      MYCN-amplified disease rather than outside high-risk disease on every
      classification. ATM is part of the source's definition of a
      p53-pathway abnormality but is not bound on this node.
  - reference: PMID:42385103
    reference_title: "Frequency and Prognostic Significance of Genetic Abnormalities in a Subgroup of Patients With Intermediate-Risk Neuroblastoma: A SIOPEN Study."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "p53 pathway alterations include CDK4/MDM2 coamplification (n = 5), TP53 mutations (n = 3), CDKN2A homozygous loss (n = 1), and ATM (n = 1)."
    explanation: >-
      Figure legend from the same SIOPEN cohort, breaking the ten
      p53-pathway-altered tumours down as CDK4/MDM2 co-amplification in
      five, TP53 mutation in three, homozygous CDKN2A loss in one and ATM in
      one, so co-amplification was the commonest and the four categories
      account for all ten. The co-amplified tumours count towards the
      pathway through MDM2: the study defines a p53-pathway abnormality as a
      TP53 inactivating mutation, MDM2 amplification, homozygous CDKN2A
      deletion or a pathogenic ATM mutation, its sequencing panel groups
      CDK4 with the ALK and RAS-MAPK genes, and CDK4 amplification alone,
      found in two tumours, does not meet that definition. CDK4 is therefore
      not bound on this node: it is co-amplified with MDM2 at 12q14.1 and
      12q15 but acts in the RB arm rather than the p53 arm. Tumour DNA
      came from diagnosis in 93 of the 98 patients, so this shows which
      p53-pathway lesions occur in the subgroup rather than that they are
      enriched at relapse.
  downstream:
  - target: Therapy-Resistant Relapse
    description: >-
      Among patients who relapsed, an inactivating TP53 mutation was
      independently prognostic for overall survival, and abolishing p53
      function in p53-intact neuroblastoma cell lines is enough on its own
      to confer high-level resistance to several cytotoxic drugs. The
      patient evidence is a prognostic association rather than a
      demonstrated mechanism, and it is specific to the downstream limb of
      this node: in the same series the upstream MDM2 amplification and
      p14ARF inactivation were not associated with survival.
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:20145180
      reference_title: "High Frequency of p53/MDM2/p14ARF Pathway Abnormalities in Relapsed Neuroblastoma."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: "The presence of a p53 mutation was independently prognostic for overall survival (hazard ratio, 3.4; 95% confidence interval, 1.2-9.9; P = 0.02)."
      explanation: >-
        In a series of 84 tumours from 41 patients with relapsed
        neuroblastoma, a TP53 mutation was independently prognostic for
        overall survival in a forward stepwise Cox model; this is the
        outcome association the edge rests on. Indirect because a survival
        association is an inference step away from a mechanism of
        resistance. It covers only the downstream limb of this node, the
        TP53 mutation found in 6 of the 41 patients: the same study found
        p14ARF inactivation associated with stage 4 disease but not with
        survival, and no relationship between MDM2 amplification and
        survival, and those upstream defects account for 15 of the 41 cases.
        The estimate is imprecise, its confidence interval nearly including
        1, and it comes from stepwise selection over six candidate
        covariates; in the same model stage 4 disease and MYCN amplification
        were also independent factors for overall survival, MYCN with the
        larger hazard ratio, and MYCN amplification was the only independent
        factor for progression-free survival.
    - reference: PMID:11507071
      reference_title: "Loss of p53 function confers high-level multidrug resistance in neuroblastoma cell lines."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: IN_VITRO
      snippet: "Loss of p53 function was selectively achieved by transduction of human papillomavirus 16 E6 (which degrades p53) into two drug-sensitive neuroblastoma cell lines with intact p53, causing high-level drug resistance to L-PAM, carboplatin, and etoposide."
      explanation: >-
        Interventional cell-line support for this edge: degrading p53 with
        human papillomavirus 16 E6 in two drug-sensitive neuroblastoma cell
        lines with intact p53 produced high-level resistance to melphalan,
        carboplatin and etoposide, so losing p53 function can by itself
        confer multidrug resistance in neuroblastoma cells. Three limits.
        The loss of function was engineered with a viral oncoprotein that
        degrades p53, not by any of the lesions this node curates, so the
        functional end state is shared but the route is not. The result is
        in cultured cell lines rather than patient tumours, and the authors
        put the step to patients conditionally, as needing confirmation in
        patient tumour samples. The resistance shown is to three cytotoxic
        drugs and should not be read as resistance to therapy in general.
- name: Therapy-Resistant Relapse
  biological_scale: ORGANISM
  description: >-
    The clinical state the relapse-enriched lesion classes converge on:
    disease that responds to initial treatment and returns resistant to it.
    Most patients with high-risk neuroblastoma respond initially, yet up to
    60% of them relapse with therapy-resistant tumours despite chemotherapy,
    surgery, radiotherapy and immunotherapy, and over half of high-risk
    neuroblastomas relapse with chemoresistant disease. Relapse can be the
    outgrowth of clones established early: genomic profiling of 470
    sequential and spatially separated samples from 283 patients found
    metastatic clones already at distant sites by diagnosis that could stay
    dormant and cause relapse years later, although the authors describe
    years-long dormancy as rare and most relapses in that cohort also
    carried additional genomic changes.
  notes: >-
    This node carries no biological-process binding, because GO covers
    molecular and cellular processes and this node is an organism-level
    clinical outcome. The two GO terms closest to the subject are rejected
    on the same positive ground rather than on absence: GO:0009410 response
    to xenobiotic stimulus, the term conventionally bound on drug-resistance
    nodes, and GO:0097327 response to antineoplastic agent both assert a
    response induced by the agent, whereas the lesions upstream of this node
    are selected rather than induced.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:26121087
    reference_title: "Relapsed neuroblastomas show frequent RAS-MAPK pathway mutations."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Patients with high-risk neuroblastoma have a survival rate of less than 50% ... despite extensive treatment involving chemotherapy, surgery, radiation therapy and immunotherapy. In a majority of patients an initial response is observed, however, up to 60% of these patients subsequently relapse with therapy resistant tumors"
    explanation: >-
      States that patients with high-risk neuroblastoma have a survival rate
      below 50% despite chemotherapy, surgery, radiotherapy and
      immunotherapy, and that although most respond initially, up to 60% of
      them then relapse with therapy-resistant tumours, which is the
      clinical course this node describes. The passage opens the
      introduction of a whole-genome sequencing study of paired diagnostic
      and relapse neuroblastomas and cites earlier clinical reports for
      these figures, so it restates the established course rather than
      reporting the study's own measurement; the ellipsis omits only
      citation numbers. The abstract of the same paper makes the statement
      for neuroblastoma as a whole, without the high-risk qualifier, and
      many low-risk tumours never receive chemotherapy.
  - reference: PMID:20145180
    reference_title: "High Frequency of p53/MDM2/p14ARF Pathway Abnormalities in Relapsed Neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Most high risk neuroblastomas do initially respond to cytotoxic therapy, however over half relapse with chemoresistant disease"
    explanation: >-
      A second group's statement of the same course: most high-risk
      neuroblastomas initially respond to cytotoxic therapy, but over half
      relapse with chemoresistant disease. The sentence opens the
      introduction of a study of p53-pathway abnormalities in neuroblastomas
      sampled at diagnosis and at relapse, and cites earlier work for it, so
      it restates the established clinical picture rather than reporting
      that study's own result; every patient in that cohort had relapsed or
      progressed, so the study could not measure how often relapse occurs.
      Its abstract makes the same statement for all neuroblastomas, without
      the high-risk qualifier.
  - reference: PMID:37169874
    reference_title: "Clonal evolution during metastatic spread in high-risk neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "At diagnosis metastatic clones were already established at distant sites where they could stay dormant, only to cause relapses years later and spread via metastasis-to-metastasis and polyclonal seeding after therapy."
    explanation: >-
      The study profiled 470 sequential and spatially separated tumour
      samples from 283 patients, predominantly with stage 4 disease, and
      reconstructed clonal phylogenies for the patients with two or more
      tumours. The quoted closing sentence of the abstract joins two of its
      findings. In 13 evaluable patients, 18 of 21 metastasising subclones
      carried no therapy-related mutational signature, which the authors
      read as spread before treatment, including to the central nervous
      system; and in two patients followed through several relapses the
      relapsing clone was already present at diagnosis, driving relapses 2.7
      to 3.4 years and 8 years later, both in stage I tumours with
      locoregional relapses. This is one route to relapse rather than the
      rule, since the authors describe years-long dormancy as occurring in rare
      cases, and of 114 clonal transitions 72% came with additional
      copy-number changes, mutations or structural variants at recurrent
      loci.
- name: Reduced ATRX/DAXX Complex Abundance
  description: >-
    Reduced abundance of the ATRX/DAXX chromatin remodelling complex, a
    recurrent molecular feature of alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) in
    neuroblastoma. ATRX encodes an ATP-dependent helicase of the SWI/SNF family
    of chromatin remodellers and, with DAXX, deposits the histone variant H3.3
    at telomeric regions. ALT-positive neuroblastomas show reduced ATRX/DAXX
    complex abundance, due either to ATRX mutation (55% of them in one cohort)
    or to low protein expression, while mutations in the complex members DAXX
    and H3F3A were extremely rare. In a pooled analysis of published
    ATRX-altered neuroblastomas, 68% of ATRX aberrations were multi-exon
    deletions, and 75% of these were predicted to be in-frame. ATRX mutation is
    strongly age-dependent: in 104 patients with metastatic disease, sampled to
    represent each age group, it was found in tumours from 14 of 32 adolescents
    and young adults, 9 of 54 children and none of 18 infants, although infant
    cases are reported. In the pooled analysis, each of the three types of ATRX
    aberration was more frequent in patients diagnosed at an older age, yet
    about 40% of the ATRX-aberrant patients were five years or younger at
    diagnosis.

ATRX forms a chromatin remodeling complex with DAXX, which performs the replication-independent deposition of the histone variant H3.3 at pericentromeric and telomeric regions."

      The introduction of this pooled analysis of published ATRX-altered

    supports: SUPPORT

    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "We subdivide the ATRX aberrations into nonsense, missense, and multiexon deletions (MEDs) and show that 68% of them are MEDs. Of these MEDs, 75% are predicted to be in-frame."
    explanation: >-
      This meta-analysis pooled 127 neuroblastoma patients and three cell lines
      with ATRX aberrations from 20 published papers; all but two tumours were

    explanation: >-

      patient tumours, 60 of them ALT-positive, mutations in the ATRX complex

    snippet: "In 81 infant cases, MYCN amplification, TERT rearrangements and ATRX mutations were detected in 3, 4, and 3 cases, respectively."
    explanation: >-
      In this cohort of 121 neuroblastomas, ATRX mutations were found in 3 of 81
      infant cases, so in infancy the lesion is present but rare. The cohort's
      ATRX status was already known and its 11 ATRX/DAXX-mutated ALT cases match
      those of PMID:25487495, so these are almost certainly the same three
      infants, not an independent finding. The abstract does not define 'infant'
      or say how many of its 67 mass-screening cases were infants, so the rate
      may not hold for clinically detected infant tumours.
  downstream:
  - target: Alternative Lengthening of Telomeres
    description: >-
      Loss of ATRX/DAXX complex function permits alternative lengthening of
      telomeres. ATRX mutation is associated with loss of nuclear ATRX protein
      and with ALT, and in one series every ALT tumour carried an ATRX or DAXX
      alteration. Without ATRX, histone H3.3 is not efficiently deposited at
      telomeric repeats, replication forks stall there, and the telomeres
      undergo the homologous recombination that leads to ALT.
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_KNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    intermediate_mechanisms:
    - "Loss of ATRX/DAXX-dependent deposition of histone H3.3 at telomeric repeats"
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:22416102
      reference_title: "Association of age at diagnosis and genetic mutations in patients with neuroblastoma."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: "ATRX mutations were associated with loss of nuclear ATRX protein, longer telomeres and ALT."
      explanation: >-
        In patients' stage 4 neuroblastomas, all 8 ATRX-mutant tumours with
        tissue had complete or mosaic loss of nuclear ATRX protein and the
        ultrabright telomeric FISH signal that is a hallmark of ALT, while only
        1 of 20 ATRX wild-type tumours had ALT. One wild-type tumour with mosaic
        nuclear ATRX loss had no ALT. Longer telomeres by sequencing did not
        separate the groups significantly (8 of 10 mutant, 12 of 30 wild-type).
        These are co-occurrences, not a causal test, and the paper reports ATRX
        immunostaining, not DAXX protein or complex levels.

      reference_title: "Clinical features of ATRX or DAXX mutated neuroblastoma."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: "In NBLs, ALT was caused by ATRX or DAXX alterations."
      explanation: >-
        In a separate clinical series of 121 neuroblastomas, 10 of the 11
        tumours with ALT carried ATRX alterations and 1 a DAXX mutation, while
        only 1 of the 110 tumours with normal or shortened telomeres carried
        either. The causal wording is the authors' reading of this co-occurrence
        in 11 ALT cases, and the DAXX evidence is a single tumour. The abstract
        reports gene alterations found by sequencing, not ATRX or DAXX protein
        levels, so reading them as reduced complex abundance is an inference.
    - reference: PMID:32060267
      reference_title: "MYCN amplification and ATRX mutations are incompatible in neuroblastoma."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: BACKGROUND
      evidence_source: IN_VITRO
      snippet: "In cells lacking ATRX, H3.3 is not efficiently deposited at the telomeric G-rich regions, G4 structures form, and replication forks stall ... Consequently, telomeres undergo homologous recombination leading to alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT)"
      explanation: >-
        The introduction of this neuroblastoma study, citing earlier work,
        states the step named as this edge's intermediate: in cells lacking
        ATRX, histone H3.3 is not efficiently deposited at telomeric G-rich
        regions, G4 structures form and replication forks stall, and the
        telomeres then undergo homologous recombination, leading to ALT. Support
        is indirect because this restates cell biology from earlier work rather
        than a measurement in neuroblastoma tumours, and it concerns loss of
        ATRX, not of DAXX. In the paper's own experiments, ATRX knockdown
        changed neither telomere content nor ALT status in any cell line tested
        after two weeks.
- name: Intratumoral Lymphoid Infiltration with Lymphoid Follicles
  description: >-
    Most neuroblastic tumors from children with opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia
    syndrome (OMAS) carry a heavier lymphoid infiltrate than other neuroblastic
    tumors. In a blinded review of 13 such tumors against 41 age- and
    stage-matched controls, 12 had diffuse and extensive lymphocytic
    infiltration with lymphoid follicles, a pattern the authors call
    characteristic; no control had diffuse or extensive infiltration, although
    18 had focal infiltrates and 6 had lymphoid follicles. In a comparison of
    OMAS-associated neuroblastomas with neuroblastomas from children without
    OMAS (38 against 26 tumors by RNA sequencing, fewer for repertoire
    sequencing and histology), B- and T-cell infiltration was greater and
    polyclonal; B cells were more numerous and, in the authors' summary,
    activated, and lay in tertiary lymphoid structures rich in T cells; and
    tertiary lymphoid structures were more frequent (10 of 14 OMAS-associated
    tumors against 2 of 6 low-risk and 1 of 5 high-risk controls), though not
    confined to OMAS. The infiltrate is not uniform: on clustering by immune
    gene signatures, several OMAS-associated tumors grouped with high-risk
    tumors from children without OMAS that had low immune-marker scores.
  biological_scale: TISSUE
  cell_types:
  - preferred_term: B cell
    term:
      id: CL:0000236
      label: B cell
  - preferred_term: T cell
    term:
      id: CL:0000084
      label: T cell
  biological_processes:
  - preferred_term: B cell activation
    modifier: INCREASED
    term:
      id: GO:0042113
      label: B cell activation
  notes: >-
    No anatomical-entity class for a tertiary lymphoid structure is available,
    so the follicles are described in prose and no location is bound. On
    2026-10-22, OLS4 searches of UBERON for "tertiary lymphoid structure",
    "tertiary lymphoid organ", "tertiary lymphoid" and "ectopic lymphoid", and
    of GO for "tertiary lymphoid structure", "tertiary lymphoid" and "ectopic
    lymphoid", returned nothing. NCIT:C176410 Tertiary Lymphoid Structure is an
    NCIT finding (under Immune System Finding), not an anatomical entity.
    UBERON:0000444 lymphoid follicle was considered and not bound, because these
    follicles form ectopically inside the tumor: UBERON places lymphoid follicle
    under lymphoid tissue, and its five subclasses are the follicles of the
    spleen, lymph nodes and Peyer's patches and the generic primary and
    secondary nodular lymphoid tissue, none of them a follicle formed in a
    tumor. The node has no upstream edge: the cited studies compare tumors from
    children with and without OMAS and do not attribute the infiltrate to any
    tumor mechanism modeled in this entry.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:11344493
    reference_title: "Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome in neuroblastoma: histopathologic features-a report from the Children's Cancer Group."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Pathology slides from a total of 54 neuroblastoma tumors were reviewed blindly. They included 13 tumors associated with opsoclonus-myoclonus and 41 age- and stage-matched controls. ... Twelve of 13 cases had diffuse (found in every section prepared from the multiple portions of the primary tumor) and extensive (occupying more than 50% of a single of multiple microscopic fields with x 100 magnification) lymphocytic infiltration with lymphoid follicles. Of the 41 control cases (27 FH and 14 UH tumors), 18 had focal areas of lymphocytic infiltration and six showed lymphoid follicles, but none had diffuse or extensive infiltration in their primary tumors."
    explanation: >-
      In a blinded Children's Cancer Group review of pathology slides from 54
      neuroblastoma tumors (13 from patients with opsoclonus-myoclonus and 41
      age- and stage-matched controls), 12 of the 13 opsoclonus-myoclonus tumors
      had lymphocytic infiltration that was both diffuse (found in every section
      prepared from multiple portions of the primary tumor) and extensive
      (occupying more than half of one or more microscopic fields at x100), with
      lymphoid follicles. Of the 41 controls, 18 had focal infiltration and 6
      had lymphoid follicles, but none had diffuse or extensive infiltration;
      the absence in controls applies to the diffuse or extensive pattern, not
      to follicles. It is a single 13-case series, and the abstract does not say
      how the cases were selected.

  - reference: PMID:37537844
    reference_title: "Polyclonal lymphoid expansion drives paraneoplastic autoimmunity in neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "We compared tumor transcriptomes and tumor-infiltrating T and B cell repertoires from 38 OMAS subjects with neuroblastoma to 26 non-OMAS-associated neuroblastomas. We found greater B and T cell infiltration in OMAS-associated tumors compared to controls and showed that both were polyclonal expansions. Tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) were enriched in OMAS-associated tumors. ... We identify four conspicuous differences between OMAS- and non-OMAS-associated neuroblastomas ... These are (1) increased numbers and activation of B cells in tumor infiltrate, rich in memory B cells; (2) localization of B cell infiltrate to TLSs rich in T cells; (3) polyclonality of lymphocytic infiltrate; and (4) differential expression of TCF7, CXCR5, and CXCL13."
    explanation: >-
      A study of archival primary tumors from patients, using RNA sequencing,
      TCR-beta and IgH repertoire sequencing of tumor DNA, and histology with
      CD20 and CD3 immunofluorescence. The abstract reports greater, polyclonal
      B- and T-cell infiltration in OMAS-associated tumors than in controls, and
      more tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs). Among four defining differences,
      the discussion lists B cells that were more numerous and activated and lay
      in T-cell-rich TLSs; the fourth item (TCF7, CXCR5 and CXCL13 expression)
      is quoted only to complete the sentence. This is the basis for binding B
      cell activation (GO:0042113), but activation is the authors' summary: the
      paper reports no functional assay of the B cells, and its B-cell results
      are transcript-level (a higher B-cell score, memory B-cell enrichment, and
      CD22 and BANK1, which the authors say modulate B-cell activity, among the
      most differentially expressed genes against low-risk tumors), alongside
      repertoire and histology data on B-cell numbers. All 38 OMAS tumors are
      the primary tumors available from Children's Oncology Group trial
      ANBL00P3, the OMAS trial of intravenous immunoglobulin, so the cohort is
      not independent of that trial. The 26 controls were 13 low-risk and 13
      high-risk tumors (7 of the high-risk ones MYCN-amplified) from age-matched
      patients without OMAS. Only the RNA sequencing covers the full
      38-versus-26 comparison: TCR-beta repertoires came from 31 OMAS tumors and
      the 26 controls, IgH repertoires from 37 OMAS tumors and the 26 controls
      (29 OMAS, 8 low-risk and 5 high-risk after subsampling), and TLSs were
      scored by histology in 14 OMAS, 6 low-risk and 5 high-risk tumors (the
      counts are quoted in the separate results-section item). Several
      repertoire differences were significant against the high-risk controls
      but not against the low-risk ones. Ki67 was largely absent from the TLSs,
      so no proliferation process is bound.

    reference_title: "Polyclonal lymphoid expansion drives paraneoplastic autoimmunity in neuroblastoma."

However, OMAS samples did not segregate into a single cluster among all neuroblastoma samples in the study but rather into several clusters bearing differing levels of expression of immune gene features, including several OMAS samples clustered with HR non-OMAS neuroblastoma samples exhibiting low immune-marker scores"
    explanation: >-
      The results section of the same study gives the histology counts behind
      the abstract's statement that tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) were
      enriched in OMAS-associated tumors: TLSs were found in 10 of the 14
      OMAS-associated tumors that could be scored (71%), against 2 of 6 low-risk
      (LR, 33%) and 1 of 5 high-risk (HR, 20%) tumors from children without
      OMAS. The groups are small and the paper gives no significance test for
      these counts, and the TLSs in low-risk controls show that they are not
      confined to OMAS. The last part shows that the infiltrate is not uniform:
      on clustering by immune gene signatures, the OMAS-associated tumors fell
      into several clusters with differing immune-marker expression, and several
      grouped with high-risk tumors from children without OMAS that had low
      immune-marker scores, so the heavier infiltrate describes most of these
      tumors rather than all of them.
  downstream:
  - target: Cerebellar and Brainstem-Directed B- and T-Cell Autoimmunity
    description: >-
      This entry reads the tumor's lymphoid response as feeding the
      autoimmunity. In a model drawn from tumor studies, polyclonal autoreactive
      B cells act as antigen-presenting cells and drive tertiary lymphoid
      structure formation, thereby supporting the paraneoplastic neuropathology;
      the authors present tumor and nervous-system involvement as parts of one
      systemic autoimmune process, the step from the tumor to the brain was not
      tested, and whether the tumor infiltrate arises from lymphocytes entering
      from the circulation is unsettled. A pathology review read the tumors'
      lymphoid infiltrate as suggesting an immune-mediated mechanism for the
      syndrome, and in one child the same B-cell clone was dominant in both the
      cerebrospinal fluid and the tumor. The intermediate steps are unknown.
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:37537844
      reference_title: "Polyclonal lymphoid expansion drives paraneoplastic autoimmunity in neuroblastoma."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: "We propose a model in which polyclonal auto-reactive B lymphocytes act as antigen-presenting cells and drive TLS formation, thereby supporting both sustained polyclonal T cell-mediated anti-tumor immunity and paraneoplastic OMAS neuropathology. ... Combining these observed differences with insights from both cancer and autoimmunity, we propose a framework to explain how systemic autoimmunity drives superior tumor outcomes and neurological damage in OMAS."
      explanation: >-
        Rosenberg et al. studied archival primary tumors from children with OMAS
        treated on Children's Oncology Group trial ANBL00P3, against age-matched
        neuroblastomas without OMAS, and found greater, polyclonal B- and T-cell
        infiltration and more tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) in the
        OMAS-associated tumors. The first quoted part, from the abstract, is the
        model the authors draw from these data: polyclonal autoreactive B cells
        act as antigen-presenting cells and drive TLS formation, thereby
        supporting OMAS neuropathology. This edge uses only the neuropathology
        half of that model; the anti-tumor-immunity half is a separate claim.
        The antigen-presenting role is the authors' inference and was not
        measured in these tumors. The second quoted part, from the discussion,
        frames the model as systemic autoimmunity driving both the tumor
        outcomes and the neurological damage, so the authors present the tumor
        and the nervous system as two sites of one process rather than the
        tumor as the source of the brain disease. In the same discussion they
        link B-cell trafficking to both tumor and CNS, note that it is still
        unclear whether the tumor infiltrate arises from lymphocyte influx from
        the periphery, and list the putative role of autoreactive T cells in
        brain neuropathology among predictions for future work. The
        tumor-to-brain direction of this edge is therefore a reading of their
        model, and the step to cerebellar and brainstem autoimmunity was not
        tested. Graded indirect because the quoted text asserts a proposed model
        rather than the causal step this edge draws.

      reference_title: "Presence of identical B-cell clone in both cerebrospinal fluid and tumor tissue in a patient with opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome associated with neuroblastoma."

      explanation: >-
        Report of a single patient. A child with neuroblastoma-associated OMS,
        treated with immunosuppressive therapy, had increased B cells in the CSF
        and multiple lymphoid follicles containing abundant B cells in the
        tumor. Unbiased B-cell receptor repertoire analysis found that the same
        B-cell clone was the dominant clone in both the CSF and the tumor
        tissue. A dominant clone shared between tumor and CSF, in a tumor with
        B-cell-rich follicles, fits the tumor's B-cell response reaching the
        CNS, which is what this edge proposes; the authors say only that the
        clone may contribute to the pathogenesis of OMS with neuroblastoma. The
        abstract leaves several things open: it does not place the clone in the
        follicles, show which way the cells moved, show what the clone
        recognizes or that it causes the neurological disease, or say when the

        receptor delta2 antibody is a single-patient finding and is not part of

- name: Cerebellar and Brainstem-Directed B- and T-Cell Autoimmunity
  description: >-
    Autoimmunity held to be directed at the cerebellum and brainstem and to
    involve B and T lymphocytes. Children with opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome
    (OMS), most with normal cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cell counts, have expanded
    B-cell and gamma-delta T-cell subsets and a higher percentage of activated T
    cells in the CSF. In a cross-sectional cohort the subset expansion was found
    even years after onset and conventional treatment, the abnormalities
    correlated with neurological severity and disease duration, they did not
    differ significantly between children with and without a tumor, and, in
    children with neuroblastoma, tumor resection or chemotherapy did not alter
    them. In a larger cohort of 389 children from the same investigators,
    commercial serum paraneoplastic antibody panels were negative apart from
    subclinical titers in four children, whereas in untreated children CSF
    oligoclonal bands (58%) and a raised CSF B-cell percentage (93%) were
    common. No specific antibody is associated with neuroblastoma-associated
    OMS, and a study of OMAS-associated tumors identified no unifying single
    antigen behind their lymphoid infiltrate. Most of the CSF findings come from
    cohorts of children with and without a detected tumor.

    The locations record the structures the autoimmunity is described as
    directed at; the immune cells themselves were sampled in the cerebrospinal
    fluid. B cell activation is bound for the expanded CSF B cells and the CSF
    oligoclonal bands, and T cell activation for the higher percentage of
    activated CSF T cells; for B cells the cited passages report frequencies
    and oligoclonal bands rather than activation markers.

    reference_title: "B- and T-cell markers in opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome: immunophenotyping of CSF lymphocytes."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Although most children with OMS had normal CSF cell counts, they exhibited expansion of CD19+ B-cell (up to 29%) and gammadelta T-cell (up to 26%) subsets and a lower percentage of CD4+ T-cells and CD4/CD8 ratio, which persisted even years after disease onset and conventional treatments. The percentage of activated CSF T-cells was also higher. Abnormalities correlated with neurologic severity, as scored blinded from videotapes using a 12-item motor scale, and disease duration. No significant differences were found between tumor and no-tumor groups. In children with neuroblastoma, tumor resection or cancer chemotherapy did not alter immunologic abnormalities."
    explanation: >-
      Flow cytometry of CSF and blood lymphocytes from 36 children with OMS and
      18 control subjects, in a cross-sectional study. These are OMS-wide data:
      the cohort includes children with and without a tumor, not only
      neuroblastoma-associated OMS. The expanded B-cell and gamma-delta T-cell
      subsets are given as subset percentages, and most children had normal CSF
      cell counts. The abstract reports no significant differences between the
      tumor and no-tumor groups, which is what lets OMS-wide data stand for the
      paraneoplastic autoimmunity node, but it does not give the size of the
      tumor subgroup or say which measures were compared, and a non-significant
      difference in 36 children does not show that the groups are the same.
      Because the design is cross-sectional, the persistence of the
      abnormalities and their being unaltered by resection or chemotherapy most
      likely come from comparing children sampled at different disease durations
      and treatment states, not from following the same children over time. The
      quote shows B- and T-cell changes in the CSF that track neurological
      severity; it does not identify an antigen or show that the response
      targets the cerebellum or brainstem. The data come from the same
      investigators as PMID:28959231 (Pranzatelli and Tate, of the National
      Pediatric Myoclonus Center), whose CSF B-cell method cites this study and
      which describes itself as confirming and updating these B-cell data, so
      the two are not independent evidence.

    explanation: >-
      Cross-sectional study of 389 children with OMS at one US specialty center;
      a neuroblastic tumor was found in about half (50%). In the results, serum
      screened on commercial paraneoplastic antibody panels was negative apart
      from subclinical titers of one of two antibodies in four children (three
      anti-GAD or anti-GAD65, one anti-neuronal voltage-gated potassium
      channel); the elided text lists the paraneoplastic antibodies that were
      not found. In untreated children, CSF oligoclonal bands (OCB) were
      positive in 58% and the CSF B-cell percentage was pathologically raised
      in 93%, while OCB positivity was 27% in children already on treatment.

      untreated children. The CSF and serum results are not reported separately
      for children with and without a tumor, so they describe pediatric OMS as
      a whole. A negative commercial panel shows that none of the antibodies on
      the panel marks pediatric OMS; it does not show that no specific antibody
      exists.

    explanation: >-
      International expert-consensus criteria for paraneoplastic neurologic
      syndromes (PNS). Definite PNS normally requires a high- or
      intermediate-risk antibody, but the panel makes an exception for OMS with
      neuroblastoma or small-cell lung cancer, because no specific antibody is
      associated with it, so such cases count as definite PNS without one. The

      and unpublished data from its members' laboratories, and the quoted
      statement summarizes patient serology, hence the human clinical grade.

      neuroblastoma-associated OMS. It does not extend to all OMS, since the
      same paper notes that adults with breast cancer and paraneoplastic OMS
      usually carry a specific antineuronal antibody, and it says nothing about
      CSF oligoclonal bands or B cells. The sentence is in the full text, not
      the abstract.
