  - reference: PMID:37142597
    reference_title: "Reversible transitions between noradrenergic and mesenchymal tumor identities define cell plasticity in neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    snippet: "xenografts with cells from each identity eventually harbor a noradrenergic phenotype suggesting that the microenvironment provides a powerful pressure towards this phenotype"
    explanation: >-
      Mouse xenografts seeded with FACS-sorted cells of either identity,
      CD44-negative noradrenergic and CD44-positive mesenchymal, all
      developed tumours with a noradrenergic phenotype, which the authors
      read as microenvironmental pressure towards that state. Three
      limits travel with it: the system is subcutaneous mouse xenografts
      of human cell lines; the causal attribution is the source's own
      hedge, "suggesting"; and only the mesenchymal arm is a shift, the
      noradrenergic arm having remained noradrenergic. Cells recovered
      from the mesenchymal-seeded xenografts still regenerated
      mesenchymal cells more readily in culture, so the convergence is at
      the tumour phenotype rather than a loss of the starting identity.
  - reference: PMID:41724733
    reference_title: "Hypoxia Promotes an Adrenergic to Mesenchymal Transcriptional Program Transition in Neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: IN_VITRO
    snippet: "Our results suggest that hypoxia changes expression of genes in ADRN cells towards MES cells."
    explanation: >-
      The opposite-direction environmental cue, and the reason this node
      records no single net microenvironmental direction. In a panel of
      adrenergic and mesenchymal cells cultured under normoxic or hypoxic
      conditions, only the adrenergic cells increased expression of
      mesenchymal signature genes under hypoxia, while the mesenchymal
      cells showed only modestly elevated hypoxia signalling and no
      phenotypic change. Graded IN_VITRO because the measurement is in
      cultured cell panels, which is a different system from the mouse
      xenografts behind the convergence towards the noradrenergic state.
  - reference: PMID:30948783
    reference_title: "A NOTCH feed-forward loop drives reprogramming from adrenergic to mesenchymal state in neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: IN_VITRO
    snippet: "Here, we unravel how a NOTCH3 intracellular domain reprogrammed the ADRN transcriptional landscape towards a MES state."
    explanation: >-
      A NOTCH3 intracellular domain reprogrammed the adrenergic
      transcriptional landscape towards a mesenchymal state. The
      reprogramming was driven by a doxycycline-inducible NOTCH3
      intracellular-domain transgene in SH-SY5Y and confirmed in two
      further adrenergic neuroblastoma cell lines, so the quote
      establishes that the switch can be forced in culture rather than
      that it proceeds this way in patient tumours.
  - reference: PMID:30948783
    reference_title: "A NOTCH feed-forward loop drives reprogramming from adrenergic to mesenchymal state in neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: IN_VITRO
    snippet: "This transition induces genome-wide remodeling of the H3K27ac landscape and a switch from ADRN SEs to MES SEs. Once established, the NOTCH feed-forward loop maintains the induced MES state."
    explanation: >-
      The adrenergic-to-mesenchymal transition remodels the H3K27ac
      landscape genome-wide and exchanges adrenergic for mesenchymal
      super-enhancers, and the NOTCH feed-forward loop then holds the
      induced mesenchymal state. The chromatin evidence comes from a
      single line: H3K27ac ChIP-sequencing of SH-SY5Y cells carrying the
      inducible NOTCH3 intracellular-domain transgene after seven days of
      induction, with the maintenance result from blocking NOTCH with a
      gamma-secretase inhibitor in the same line. The two further
      adrenergic lines confirmed only a mesenchymal marker profile and a
      migratory phenotype. The paper's full text records the enhancer
      change as asymmetric, repression of adrenergic super-enhancers
      being stronger than induction of mesenchymal ones. No patient
      material bears on either result.
  - reference: PMID:39174852
    reference_title: "Targeting SWI/SNF ATPases reduces neuroblastoma cell plasticity."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: IN_VITRO
    snippet: "SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex ATPases are essential in establishing an mesenchymal gene-permissive chromatin state in adrenergic-type NB, facilitating lineage plasticity."
    explanation: >-
      The paper's own statement of what it demonstrates: SWI/SNF
      chromatin-remodelling ATPases are essential for establishing a
      mesenchymal gene-permissive chromatin state in adrenergic-type
      neuroblastoma, which facilitates lineage plasticity. The verb is
      the source's, and the claim here is no stronger than it. Shown
      entirely in culture: SMARCA2/4 dual degraders and SMARCA4 siRNA in
      the adrenergic lines IMR5, IMR32, BE(2)C and KELLY read out by
      ATAC-seq, H3K27ac ChIP-seq and RNA-seq, with the plasticity and
      heterogeneity result from the patient-derived SJNBL012407_X1 cell
      model by single-cell RNA-seq. The study performed no animal
      experiment, so this is not an observation in patient tumours, and
      the authors state in their Discussion that direct evidence for an
      effect of the ATPases on trans-differentiation itself is lacking
      and call that link a hypothesis awaiting single-cell lineage
      tracing. The source's own wording "an mesenchymal" is reproduced
      uncorrected.
  - reference: PMID:30948783
    reference_title: "A NOTCH feed-forward loop drives reprogramming from adrenergic to mesenchymal state in neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    snippet: "In vivo reprogramming of ADRN cells shows that MES and ADRN cells are equally oncogenic."
    explanation: >-
      The guard against reading an undifferentiated mesenchymal state as
      the more benign one: the authors' own in vivo result is that
      mesenchymal and adrenergic cells are equally oncogenic. The
      experiment is a subcutaneous xenograft of the adrenergic human line
      SH-SY5Y carrying doxycycline-inducible NOTCH3-IC, with growth
      kinetics compared against uninduced controls at three mice per
      group, and the transgene was induced only once tumours had reached
      about 200 cubic millimetres, so what was measured is whether an
      established tumour keeps growing after the state switch rather than
      whether mesenchymal cells initiate tumours as efficiently. The
      comparison is between a reprogrammed tumour and its own isogenic
      control rather than between independently arising mesenchymal and
      adrenergic tumours. Nothing in the quoted sentence bears on how
      differentiated either state is.
  notes: >-
    Assigning a mesenchymal signal to tumour cells is the standing
    difficulty in this literature, and it is a sampling problem rather
    than a measurement one. The tumour microenvironment contains
    endothelial cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts and Schwann cells
    that are themselves mesenchymal, so mesenchymal signal in bulk tissue,
    or in immunohistochemistry without a mesenchymal marker specific to
    tumour cells, cannot be attributed to tumour cells. Single-cell work
    resolves this by inferring each cell's copy-number profile and
    checking that the candidate cells carry the tumour's own alterations
    while the stromal clusters do not. Read the post-treatment and relapse
    enrichment reports with that in mind.

    Neuroblastoma has no epithelial compartment, so the mesenchymal pole
    of this axis is not an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and no
    epithelial-to-mesenchymal process term is bound here; the two poles
    are states of one neural crest-derived lineage. AP-1 is a
    transcription-factor family rather than a single gene, which is why
    the core regulatory circuitry factors are named in this node's
    description and in its quoted evidence rather than bound as gene
    descriptors.
  downstream:
  - target: Mesenchymal-State Chemotherapy Resistance
    description: >-
      The state switch is what produces the resistant fraction: cells at
      or moving towards the mesenchymal pole survive induction
      chemotherapy, so the mesenchymal proportion rises after treatment.
      The patient data behind this edge are observational and do not
      separate therapy-induced switching into the mesenchymal state from
      survival of mesenchymal cells already present.
    causal_link_type: DIRECT
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:40229600
      reference_title: "Longitudinal single-cell multiomic atlas of high-risk neuroblastoma reveals chemotherapy-induced tumor microenvironment rewiring."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: "Mesenchymal neoplastic cells, resembling mixed developmental lineages, showed a slight increase after therapy. A higher mesenchymal state at diagnosis did not predict worse survival, but correlated with poorer chemotherapy response."
      explanation: >-
        The only patient-level therapy consequence curated on this axis,
        in 22 patients with high-risk neuroblastoma each sampled by
        diagnostic biopsy and again at resection after three to four
        cycles of induction chemotherapy. Across the paired
        single-nucleus profiles the mesenchymal fraction rose only
        slightly, and the larger shifts were from proliferating towards
        more differentiated neuronal-like adrenergic states. The response
        association is a baseline one: a higher mesenchymal proportion in
        the diagnostic samples went with a poorer response to induction
        chemotherapy (one-sided t-test, P = 0.02). The survival clause
        comes from separate bulk data, where in a 498-patient cohort the
        mesenchymal signature was not significantly associated with
        prognosis; neither bulk cohort was analysed for chemotherapy
        response. Graded INDIRECT because the study calls the shifts
        therapy-induced without testing whether the extra mesenchymal
        cells arise by switching or by survival of cells already present,
        so these observational data reach this edge through an inference
        step.
  - target: ALK-Inhibitor Escape by Loss of Target Expression
    description: >-
      Occupying the mesenchymal pole leaves the cells without ALK
      expression, and so without the drug target, which is why the escape
      follows from the cell state rather than from any change in ALK
      itself. Demonstrated in cell lines and in xenografts of those
      cells.
    causal_link_type: DIRECT
  - target: Mesenchymal-State Immune Activation
    description: >-
      The state that confers chemotherapy resistance and ALK-inhibitor
      escape carries the opposite immune phenotype: the immune-enriched
      subset of neuroblastomas is the one characterised by mesenchymal
      lineage signatures, and mesenchymal-state cells are the ones
      cytotoxic lymphocytes recruit to and kill.
    causal_link_type: DIRECT
- name: Mesenchymal-State Chemotherapy Resistance
  description: >-
    Mesenchymal-state cells survive cytotoxic chemotherapy that kills
    adrenergic cells, and mesenchymal features have been reported to
    become enriched after chemotherapy and at relapse while adrenergic
    traits predominate in untreated tumours. What makes this a
    consequence of plasticity rather than an independent resistance
    mechanism is that blocking the switch itself prevents the resistance:
    degrading the SWI/SNF ATPases that hold mesenchymal genes in a
    permissive chromatin state inhibits plasticity and, with it, the
    outgrowth of the resistant fraction. The post-treatment enrichment
    reports are associations and do not separate selection of already
    resistant cells from therapy-induced switching, and the identity of
    the mesenchymal programme detectable in patients is not settled,
    which is why the node is held provisional.
  biological_scale: CELLULAR
  mechanism_confidence: PROVISIONAL
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:28650485
    reference_title: "Neuroblastoma is composed of two super-enhancer-associated differentiation states."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: IN_VITRO
    snippet: "Mesenchymal cells were more chemoresistant in vitro and were enriched in post-therapy and relapse tumors."
    explanation: >-
      The in vitro half of this sentence is what the item is cited for:
      mesenchymal cells were the more chemoresistant, which is the
      cell-level basis for treating the mesenchymal state as a resistance
      mechanism. The same sentence also reports enrichment in
      post-therapy and relapse tumours, a tumour-material observation
      that the IN_VITRO grading does not cover; the cached record is
      abstract-only and names no assay for either half. Thirant et al.
      (PMID:37142597) note that immunohistochemistry on diagnosis and
      relapse cases only suggested such enrichment, because without a
      mesenchymal marker specific to tumour cells the tumour identity of
      the stained cells is hard to establish, so the enrichment half
      should be read as suggestive.
  - reference: PMID:39174852
    reference_title: "Targeting SWI/SNF ATPases reduces neuroblastoma cell plasticity."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: IN_VITRO
    snippet: "Targeting SWI/SNF ATPases with SMARCA2/4 dual degraders effectively inhibits NB cell proliferation, invasion, and notably, cellular plasticity, thereby preventing chemotherapy resistance."
    explanation: >-
      This is the item that makes the resistance a consequence of
      plasticity: degrading the SWI/SNF ATPases inhibits cellular
      plasticity and, by that route, prevents chemotherapy resistance.
      The measured basis is pharmacological and entirely in culture.
      Pre-treatment with the SMARCA2/4 degrader ACBI1 lowered the
      mesenchymal-type fraction of the patient-derived SJNBL012407_X1
      line, and ACBI1 with etoposide was synergistic in that line and in
      a five-line neuroblastoma panel, depleting cells of
      mesenchymal-type morphology. No resistance-emergence or
      dose-response-shift assay was run, the effect is dose-dependent
      (40 nM ACBI1 did not prevent mesenchymal-type expansion), and the
      quoted sentence lists three inhibited properties before "thereby",
      so it does not isolate plasticity as the route. Nothing here bears
      on the clinical status of any SWI/SNF-directed agent.
  - reference: PMID:39174852
    reference_title: "Targeting SWI/SNF ATPases reduces neuroblastoma cell plasticity."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Adrenergic traits predominate in NB tumors, while mesenchymal features becomes enriched post-chemotherapy or after relapse."
    explanation: >-
      The clinical picture this node sits in: adrenergic traits
      predominate in neuroblastoma tumours, while mesenchymal features
      become enriched after chemotherapy or after relapse. Graded
      HUMAN_CLINICAL for the tumour observation the sentence describes
      and BACKGROUND because it is an opening framing statement
      attributed in the paper's introduction to earlier work rather than
      a result of this study, whose own experiments are all in cultured
      cells, spheroids and cultured patient-derived cells. Where the
      paper restates the point in its Discussion it places the
      post-chemotherapy enrichment in neuroblastoma cells treated with
      chemotherapy and the relapse enrichment in tumours from relapsed
      patients. Enrichment after therapy is an association and does not
      separate selection of resistant cells from therapy-induced
      switching. The source's own wording "features becomes" is
      reproduced uncorrected.
- name: ALK-Inhibitor Escape by Loss of Target Expression
  description: >-
    Mesenchymal-type neuroblastoma cells express neither mutant nor
    wild-type ALK, so ALK inhibition has no target in them and the escape
    is absence of the drug target rather than an alteration in it. The
    mesenchymal cells resemble immature precursor cells, which also lack
    ALK expression, so the absence tracks the identity state the cells
    occupy. This is a cell-line and xenograft result: the cells were
    resistant to ALK inhibitors in culture, and tumours formed from them
    progressed under ALK inhibitor given to the xenografted animals. No
    patient-level evidence is curated here.
  biological_scale: CELLULAR
  mechanism_confidence: PROVISIONAL
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:34853072
    reference_title: "Mesenchymal-Type Neuroblastoma Cells Escape ALK Inhibitors."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: IN_VITRO
    snippet: "MES cells did not express either mutant or wild-type ALK and were resistant to ALKi"
    explanation: >-
      States both halves of the mechanism in one clause: mesenchymal-type
      neuroblastoma cells express neither the mutant nor the wild-type
      ALK allele, and they are resistant to ALK inhibitors. Because the
      mutant allele is named as unexpressed, the resistance sits with
      absence of the target rather than with an altered target. The
      measurements are in cultured neuroblastoma cells, so the escape
      route is demonstrated in culture; no patient data bear on it. The
      cached record is abstract-only.
  - reference: PMID:34853072
    reference_title: "Mesenchymal-Type Neuroblastoma Cells Escape ALK Inhibitors."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    snippet: "MES cells formed tumors that progressed under ALKi therapy"
    explanation: >-
      The in vivo arm of the same result: tumours grown from
      mesenchymal-type neuroblastoma cells continued to progress while
      ALK inhibitor was being given. Tumour formation under an
      administered drug is necessarily an animal experiment, and the
      paper's companion in vivo result names the system as neuroblastoma
      xenografts treated in the animals, so this is preclinical xenograft
      evidence and carries no claim about ALK-inhibitor response in
      patients.
- name: Mesenchymal-State Immune Activation
  description: >-
    The subset of neuroblastomas enriched for immune-related transcripts
    is predominantly characterised by mesenchymal lineage gene-expression
    signatures, while tumours expressing adrenergic lineage signatures
    are less immunogenic by the same measures. The enrichment covers
    transcripts of immune activation and of immune inhibition together,
    so this is not a claim of net anti-tumour immunity: the same tumours
    carry higher immune-evasion scores. Functionally, mesenchymal lineage
    cells secrete inflammatory cytokines that recruit T cells and are
    efficiently killed by cytotoxic T and natural killer cells in
    culture, and in an immunocompetent mouse model the
    mesenchymal-marker-enriched, MHC class I-high tumours responded
    better to combined PD-1 and CTLA-4 blockade than their counterparts.
    The patient-level half is correlative transcriptomics; the killing
    and checkpoint results are functional and come from cultured cells
    and from mice.
  biological_scale: TISSUE
  mechanism_confidence: PROVISIONAL
  biological_processes:
  - preferred_term: immune response to tumour cells of the mesenchymal state
    modifier: INCREASED
    term:
      id: GO:0002418
      label: immune response to tumor cell
  - preferred_term: T cell recruitment into mesenchymal-state tumour tissue
    modifier: INCREASED
    term:
      id: GO:0072678
      label: T cell migration
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:36138189
    reference_title: "Mesenchymal and adrenergic cell lineage states in neuroblastoma possess distinct immunogenic phenotypes."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Here, from bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analyses, we identify a subset of neuroblastomas enriched for transcripts associated with immune activation and inhibition and show that these are predominantly characterized by gene expression signatures of the mesenchymal lineage state. By contrast, tumors expressing adrenergic lineage signatures are less immunogenic."
    explanation: >-
      In the authors' bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analyses of
      primary neuroblastomas, the tumour subset enriched for transcripts
      of both immune activation and immune inhibition was predominantly
      characterised by mesenchymal lineage gene-expression signatures,
      whereas tumours expressing adrenergic lineage signatures were less
      immunogenic. Both halves of the enrichment matter: the same subset
      carried higher immune-evasion scores and more regulatory T cell and
      M2 macrophage signatures, so the finding is not one of net
      anti-tumour immunity. "Immunogenic" here means immune-related gene
      expression scored in tumour samples, not a measured immune response
      in patients, and the association is correlative, so on its own it
      does not show that the mesenchymal state causes immune activation.
  - reference: PMID:36138189
    reference_title: "Mesenchymal and adrenergic cell lineage states in neuroblastoma possess distinct immunogenic phenotypes."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: IN_VITRO
    snippet: "Mesenchymal lineage cells promote T cell infiltration by secreting inflammatory cytokines, are efficiently targeted by cytotoxic T and natural killer cells"
    explanation: >-
      The functional half, and the grounding for the T cell migration
      binding on this node. Conditioned media from all five mesenchymal
      neuroblastoma cell lines upregulated CXCL10, which the authors
      identify as a major driver of T cell infiltration in solid tumours,
      against one of five adrenergic lines, with CCL5, CCL2, CCL11 and
      IL4 showing the same differential; CXCR3-bearing Jurkat cells and
      primary CD8-positive T cells were recruited into mesenchymal
      tumour spheroids; natural killer degranulation and killing were
      NKG2D-dependent; and PRAME-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes killed
      mesenchymal cells more efficiently. All of these are cell line,
      conditioned-media and spheroid experiments, hence IN_VITRO. The
      checkpoint-blockade response reported in the same abstract sentence
      is a mouse in vivo result and is cited as a separate
      MODEL_ORGANISM item on this node rather than folded in here.
  - reference: PMID:36138189
    reference_title: "Mesenchymal and adrenergic cell lineage states in neuroblastoma possess distinct immunogenic phenotypes."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    snippet: "Treatment with anti-PD1 and anti-CTLA4 antibodies resulted in more pronounced reductions in tumor growth and prolongation of survival in H-2Kbhi compared with H-2Kblo models"
    explanation: >-
      The checkpoint-blockade arm, in immunocompetent mice bearing
      tumours sorted on MHC class I surface expression: combined anti-PD1
      and anti-CTLA4 antibodies reduced tumour growth and prolonged
      survival more in the MHC class I-high than in the MHC class I-low
      model. Graded MODEL_ORGANISM, and INDIRECT on two counts. The arms
      were defined by MHC class I level rather than directly by cell
      state, with the high arm described as enriched for mesenchymal
      markers, so the mesenchymal attribution is a step away from what
      was sorted; and the result is a comparative growth and survival
      difference in mice, not a response rate, so nothing here concerns
      checkpoint blockade in patients. The authors state that their
      findings need validation in further immunocompetent neuroblastoma
      models.
histopathology:
- name: Schwannian Stroma-Poor Neuroblastic Histology
  diagnostic: true
  finding_term:
    preferred_term: Schwannian stroma-poor neuroblastic tumor
  context: Peripheral neuroblastic tumors classified by the INPC, whose prognostic grouping is designed for pediatric tumors
  description: >-
    The defining histology of this entry under the International Neuroblastoma
    Pathology Classification (INPC), which the International Neuroblastoma
    Pathology Committee proposed in 1999 on the framework of the Shimada
    classification with minor modifications. INPC is an age-linked
    classification that depends on the differentiation grade of the
    neuroblasts, their cellular turnover index and the presence or absence of
    Schwannian stromal development. It places peripheral neuroblastic tumors
    in four categories: neuroblastoma (Schwannian stroma-poor), subtyped as
    undifferentiated, poorly differentiated or differentiating;
    ganglioneuroblastoma, intermixed (Schwannian stroma-rich); ganglioneuroma
    (Schwannian stroma-dominant); and ganglioneuroblastoma, nodular. Only the
    stroma-poor neuroblastoma category belongs to this entry. INPC was designed
    for prognostic distinction among pediatric peripheral neuroblastic tumors
    and is not applicable to adult ones, although there is no clear consensus
    on the age that separates the two groups.
  notes: >-
    Left unbound. OLS searches of NCIT on 2026-10-20 for "stroma-poor" and
    "Schwannian stroma" (up to 15 results each) returned NCIT:C3270
    Neuroblastoma, the Shimada classification terms NCIT:C85414 and
    NCIT:C85415, the composite tumor concepts NCIT:C42059 and NCIT:C42060,
    other neuroblastic tumor concepts, findings for other histologies (among
    them NCIT:C42049, NCIT:C42062, NCIT:C42063, NCIT:C42066, NCIT:C42068 and
    NCIT:C42071) and unrelated tumors and drug regimens, but no finding term
    for stroma-poor histology; searches for "Schwannian stroma absent" and
    "limited Schwannian stroma" returned no results. NCIT:C3270, whose
    definition includes the absence of a prominent Schwannian stroma, is this
    entry's own disease concept, and a bound histopathology term is exported
    as a has_phenotype edge from the disease.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:10421272
    reference_title: "Terminology and morphologic criteria of neuroblastic tumors: recommendations by the International Neuroblastoma Pathology Committee."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Based on morphologic criteria defined in this article, NTs were classified into four categories and their subtypes: 1) neuroblastoma (Schwannian stroma-poor), undifferentiated, poorly differentiated, and differentiating; 2) ganglioneuroblastoma, intermixed (Schwannian stroma-rich); 3) ganglioneuroma (Schwannian stroma-dominant), maturing and mature; and 4) ganglioneuroblastoma, nodular"
    explanation: >-
      The 1999 terminology paper of the International Neuroblastoma Pathology
      Committee, whose six member pathologists defined the morphologic criteria
      from a review of 227 cases. It classifies neuroblastic tumors into four
      categories, with neuroblastoma (Schwannian stroma-poor) and its
      undifferentiated, poorly differentiated and differentiating subtypes as
      the first; the quote ends before the stromal label of the fourth. The
      abstract names the neuroblastoma subtypes but gives no criteria for them,
      so this item supports the category scheme, not the subtype definitions.
      In this abstract INPC abbreviates the Committee; the Classification
      itself is reported in a companion article in the same issue
      (PMID:10421273).
  - reference: PMID:10421272
    reference_title: "Terminology and morphologic criteria of neuroblastic tumors: recommendations by the International Neuroblastoma Pathology Committee."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "It is an age-linked classification dependent on the differentiation grade of the neuroblasts, their cellular turnover index, and the presence or absence of Schwannian stromal development."
    explanation: >-
      In the results of its abstract, the International Neuroblastoma
      Pathology Committee describes the prognostic system it adopted, which
      the preceding sentence says is modeled on the one proposed by Shimada
      et al., as an age-linked classification dependent on the differentiation
      grade of the neuroblasts, their cellular turnover index, and the
      presence or absence of Schwannian stromal development. The abstract's
      conclusion names the Committee's proposal the International
      Neuroblastoma Pathology Classification. The abstract gives no survival
      figures, and the quote does not say how the cellular turnover index is
      measured.
  - reference: PMID:10421273
    reference_title: "The International Neuroblastoma Pathology Classification (the Shimada system)."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "The International Neuroblastoma Pathology Classification, a system based on a framework of the Shimada classification with minor modifications, is proposed for international use in assessing NTs."
    explanation: >-
      In its conclusion, the 1999 paper that proposed the classification
      describes it as a system based on a framework of the Shimada
      classification with minor modifications. This supports describing INPC
      as built on the Shimada framework but not identical to it. The authors
      call the changes minor, the paper's own title calls INPC "the Shimada
      system", and the abstract does not say which modifications were made.
      The classification was evaluated on 227 reviewed cases with survival
      analysis.
  - reference: PMID:41612478
    reference_title: "Pathology of peripheral neuroblastic tumors."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: 'It should be noted that since INPC is designed for prognostic distinction among "pediatric" pNTs, it is not applicable to "adult" pNTs even though no clear consensus for separating these two age groups.'
    explanation: >-
      The review states that, since INPC was designed for prognostic
      distinction among pediatric peripheral neuroblastic tumors, it is not
      applicable to adult ones. The same paragraph says adult tumors are still
      histologically diagnosed in the same categories, so the stated limit
      concerns INPC's prognostic grouping, not the diagnosis of these tumors.
      The authors add that there is no clear consensus on the age that
      separates pediatric from adult tumors, so the source does not say where
      the boundary falls. The sentence is the review authors' own statement of
      the classification's scope, with no data or citation attached, so it is
      graded OTHER as an expert statement rather than a study of INPC in
      adults.
- name: Undifferentiated Neuroblastoma Subtype
  finding_term:
    preferred_term: undifferentiated neuroblastoma (INPC subtype)
    term:
      id: NCIT:C42046
      label: Undifferentiated Neuroblastoma
  frequency: VERY_RARE
  context: Diagnostic tumor tissue obtained before chemotherapy or irradiation
  description: >-
    INPC subtype of the neuroblastoma category composed of tumor cells without
    clearly recognizable neurite production. Accordingly, in routine practice
    the diagnosis is confirmed by immunohistochemistry, in which positive
    nuclear staining for PHOX2B is critical. INPC classifies every
    neuroblastoma of the undifferentiated subtype as unfavorable histology,
    regardless of the patient's age. It is the rarest subtype: 177 of 4,680
    Schwannian stroma-poor tumors (3.8%) classified at central review in the
    Children's Oncology Group Neuroblastoma Pathology Reference Laboratory
    between August 2001 and March 2012, on specimens obtained before
    chemotherapy or irradiation.
  notes: >-
    NCIT:C42046 defines this subtype by the absence of differentiating
    neuroblasts, a criterion a poorly differentiated tumor can also meet
    (NCIT:C42047 defines that subtype by differentiating neuroblasts making up
    less than five percent of the tumor cells). INPC separates the two
    subtypes by neurite production, and the description follows the INPC
    wording.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:41612478
    reference_title: "Pathology of peripheral neuroblastic tumors."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: "Undifferentiated subtype: Tumors in this subtype are composed of cells without clearly recognizable neurite production (Fig. 1B). Accordingly, positive nuclear immunostaining for PHOX2B is critical for confirming the diagnosis in routine practice. The tumor cells seem to have little to no potential for neuroblastic differentiation, and the cases are always classified into the UH group regardless of age of the patients."
    explanation: >-
      In its account of the INPC, the review defines the undifferentiated
      subtype as tumors composed of cells without clearly recognizable neurite
      production, states that positive nuclear PHOX2B immunostaining is
      critical for confirming the diagnosis in routine practice, and states
      that these cases are always classified into the unfavorable histology
      (UH) group regardless of the patient's age. The passage restates the
      classification and a practice recommendation and reports no patient
      data, so it is graded OTHER.
  - reference: PMID:25207821
    reference_title: "Age-dependent prognostic effect by Mitosis-Karyorrhexis Index in neuroblastoma: a report from the Children's Oncology Group."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "A total of 5,929 cases of pNTs were reviewed at the COG Neuroblastoma Pathology Reference Laboratory, Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, Children's Hospital Los Angeles, Los Angeles, California, between August 1, 2001, and March 31, 2012, and 4680 of them were classified as neuroblastoma (Schwannian stroma-poor) tumors including undifferentiated subtype (177 cases), poorly differentiated subtype (4081 cases), and differentiated subtype (422 cases) based on the review of pathology specimens obtained before starting chemotherapy/irradiation therapy."
    explanation: >-
      Of 4,680 Schwannian stroma-poor neuroblastomas classified at central
      review in the COG Neuroblastoma Pathology Reference Laboratory
      (Children's Hospital Los Angeles, August 2001 to March 2012), on
      pathology specimens obtained before chemotherapy or irradiation, 177
      were the undifferentiated subtype: 177/4,680 = 3.8%, within the
      VERY_RARE band (under 5%). This is a single reference-laboratory
      central-review series, not a population-based sample.
- name: Poorly Differentiated Neuroblastoma Subtype
  finding_term:
    preferred_term: poorly differentiated neuroblastoma (INPC subtype)
    term:
      id: NCIT:C42047
      label: Poorly Differentiated Neuroblastoma
  frequency: VERY_FREQUENT
  context: Diagnostic tumor tissue obtained before chemotherapy or irradiation
  description: >-
    INPC subtype in which the tumor cells produce neurites, with or without
    Homer Wright rosette formation, detectable on H&E staining; neuropil is
    present, but fewer than 5% of tumor cells show ganglionic differentiation.
    By differentiation grade, INPC places it in favorable histology when the
    patient is diagnosed younger than 18 months (up to 547 days) and in
    unfavorable histology from 18 months (548 days); a favorable assignment
    also requires a low or intermediate mitosis-karyorrhexis index (see INPC
    Favorable Histology). It is the commonest subtype: 4,081 of 4,680
    Schwannian stroma-poor tumors (87.2%) classified at central review in the
    Children's Oncology Group Neuroblastoma Pathology Reference Laboratory
    between August 2001 and March 2012.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:41612478
    reference_title: "Pathology of peripheral neuroblastic tumors."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: "Poorly differentiated subtype: Tumor cells in this subtype are characterized by their neurite production, with or without Homer Wright rosette formation, detectable by H&E staining (Fig. 1C)."
    explanation: >-
      In its account of the INPC, the review characterizes the poorly
      differentiated subtype by tumor-cell neurite production, with or without
      Homer Wright rosette formation, detectable by H&E staining. The passage
      restates an INPC criterion and reports no patient data, so it is graded
      OTHER. It gives no percentage threshold for differentiating neuroblasts.
  - reference: PMID:41294259
    reference_title: "Histologic Response to Induction Chemotherapy in High-Risk Neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Tumor differentiation was scored based on the proportion of differentiating neuroblasts and presence of neuropil as undifferentiated (no signs of maturation, no differentiated neuroblasts, or neuropil), poorly differentiated (neuropil present but < 5% ganglionic differentiation), or differentiating (> 5% ganglionic differentiation)"
    explanation: >-
      The methods of a study of paired diagnostic and resection specimens
      from 94 patients with high-risk neuroblastoma enrolled in Children's
      Oncology Group trials give the INPC differentiation grades the authors
      scored, following the INPC publications they cite: poorly differentiated
      tumors have neuropil but under 5% ganglionic differentiation, scored as
      the proportion of differentiating neuroblasts, and differentiating
      tumors have over 5%. The sentence restates the INPC criteria; the study
      applies the threshold and does not derive it.
  - reference: PMID:41612478
    reference_title: "Pathology of peripheral neuroblastic tumors."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: "When the patient with a tumor in this subtype is diagnosed less than 18 months (547 days) of age, the case is classified into the FH group. While the patient with tumor having the same histology of NB, poorly differentiated subtype but diagnosed over 18 months (548 days) of age is considered to have no potential of neuroblastic differentiation and tumor maturation, and the case is classified into UH group."
    explanation: >-
      The review states the INPC age rule for the poorly differentiated
      subtype: a case diagnosed at less than 18 months (547 days) is classified
      into the favorable histology (FH) group, and one diagnosed over 18 months
      (548 days) into the unfavorable histology (UH) group. Elsewhere the
      review pairs 548 days with 18 months or more, so 547 days is the last
      day under 18 months. This passage gives the grade criterion only; the
      review's separate MKI paragraph adds that high-MKI tumors indicate a poor
      prognosis at any age, so a poorly differentiated tumor diagnosed under 18
      months is favorable histology only with a low or intermediate MKI. The
      passage states a classification rule and reports no patient data, so it
      is graded OTHER.
  - reference: PMID:25207821
    reference_title: "Age-dependent prognostic effect by Mitosis-Karyorrhexis Index in neuroblastoma: a report from the Children's Oncology Group."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "A total of 5,929 cases of pNTs were reviewed at the COG Neuroblastoma Pathology Reference Laboratory, Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, Children's Hospital Los Angeles, Los Angeles, California, between August 1, 2001, and March 31, 2012, and 4680 of them were classified as neuroblastoma (Schwannian stroma-poor) tumors including undifferentiated subtype (177 cases), poorly differentiated subtype (4081 cases), and differentiated subtype (422 cases) based on the review of pathology specimens obtained before starting chemotherapy/irradiation therapy."
    explanation: >-
      Of 4,680 Schwannian stroma-poor neuroblastomas classified at central
      review in the COG Neuroblastoma Pathology Reference Laboratory
      (Children's Hospital Los Angeles, August 2001 to March 2012), on

      were the poorly differentiated subtype: 4,081/4,680 = 87.2%, within the
      VERY_FREQUENT band (80-99%). The stroma-poor category is the denominator
