    snippet: "As described both in the literature and in this review, in about 10% of the patients with histologically proven neuroblastoma the tumour does not accumulate ¹²³I-MIBG (false negative results). For these patients, it is advisable to perform an additional test for staging and assess response to therapy. Additional tests might for example be (18)F-FDG-PET(-CT), but to be certain of its clinical value, more evidence is needed."
    explanation: >-
      This Cochrane diagnostic-accuracy review of 11 studies in children
      (searched to September 2012) concludes that in about 10% of patients with
      histologically proven neuroblastoma the tumour does not take up 123I-MIBG.
      For these patients it advises an additional test for staging and response
      assessment, names 18F-FDG-PET(-CT) only as a possible example, and says
      more evidence of its clinical value is needed. This is a recommendation,
      not a measured result: only one included study reported FDG-PET as an
      add-on test, with 2 of 24 eligible patients MIBG-negative and
      FDG-PET-positive.
  - reference: PMID:29938300
    reference_title: "Guidelines on nuclear medicine imaging in neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: "These EANM guidelines include updated information on 123I-mIBG, the most common study in nuclear medicine for the evaluation of neuroblastoma, and on PET/CT imaging with 18F-FDG, 18F-DOPA and 68Ga-DOTA peptides. These PET/CT studies are increasingly employed in clinical practice."
    explanation: >-
      This 2018 EANM guideline states that it covers 123I-mIBG, which it calls
      the most common nuclear-medicine study for evaluating neuroblastoma, and
      PET/CT with 18F-FDG, 18F-DOPA and 68Ga-DOTA peptides, and says these
      PET/CT studies are increasingly employed in clinical practice. The quoted
      text reports no patient data, so the usage trend is the guideline's own
      2018 assessment rather than a measured figure. The abstract does not
      mention MIBG-nonavid disease, so on its own it does not support using
      18F-FDG PET/CT specifically for MIBG-nonavid tumours.
- name: Urinary Catecholamine Metabolites
  description: >-
    Measurement of catecholamine metabolites in urine, chiefly vanillylmandelic
    acid (VMA) and homovanillic acid (HVA). Under the INSS diagnostic criteria
    used by the INRG classification system, neuroblastoma can be diagnosed from
    unequivocal tumor cells in bone marrow together with increased urine or
    serum catecholamines or metabolites, as an alternative to a diagnosis from
    tumor tissue. The 2017 revised INRC do not use urine catecholamine levels to
    evaluate response, because specimen collection and analysis are not
    standardized and diet influences the results; the same consensus statement
    names catecholamine levels, with bone scintigraphy, as examples of
    tumor-assessment modalities less sensitive and/or specific for
    neuroblastoma, which the revision set out to replace with 123I-MIBG and
    FDG-PET imaging. Studies comparing urinary catecholamines with bone marrow
    studies and MIBG scans have found HVA and VMA to have low sensitivity as
    markers for monitoring disease activity. In a retrospective high-risk
    cohort, however, positive status on an extended panel of eight urinary
    catecholamine metabolites at complete remission was associated with poorer
    event-free and overall survival. The frequency of raised VMA and HVA at
    diagnosis is recorded under the biochemical record Catecholamine
    Metabolites.
  diagnosis_term:
    preferred_term: urinary catecholamine metabolite measurement
    term:
      id: NCIT:C61044
      label: Urine Chemistry Measurement
  measurements:
  - preferred_term: urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA)
    term:
      id: LOINC:LP15947-2
      label: Vanillylmandelate
  - preferred_term: urinary homovanillic acid (HVA)
    term:
      id: LOINC:LP15096-8
      label: Homovanillate
  notes: >-
    VMA and HVA are bound at the LOINC Part level (Vanillylmandelate,
    Homovanillate), which names the analyte rather than one specimen- or
    method-specific code. NCIT also has procedure terms for one analyte each,
    such as NCIT:C74875 Vanillyl Mandelic Acid Measurement and NCIT:C74863
    Homovanillic Acid Measurement; diagnosis_term takes one term and this row
    covers both analytes, so the procedure is bound to Urine Chemistry
    Measurement and the analytes are named in measurements.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:19047290
    reference_title: "The International Neuroblastoma Risk Group (INRG) staging system: an INRG Task Force report."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: "In the INRG classification system, the diagnosis of neuroblastoma will be made using INSS criteria. ... A diagnosis can also be made if unequivocal tumor cells are seen in bone marrow samples and increased urine or serum catecholamines or metabolites are present."
    explanation: >-
      This INRG Task Force report states that, in the INRG classification
      system, neuroblastoma is diagnosed using the INSS criteria; the same
      paragraph then allows a diagnosis from unequivocal tumour cells in bone
      marrow together with increased urine or serum catecholamines or
      metabolites. The quote skips the paragraph's middle sentence, on diagnosis
      by tissue histology. This route requires both findings and names
      catecholamines or metabolites in general, not VMA or HVA. The criterion is
      restated expert consensus, not a result of the paper's 661-patient
      survival analysis.
  - reference: PMID:28471719
    reference_title: "Revisions to the International Neuroblastoma Response Criteria: A Consensus Statement From the National Cancer Institute Clinical Trials Planning Meeting."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: "Urine catecholamine levels will not be used to evaluate response because of a lack of standardization in specimen collection and analysis and the influence of diet on results."
    explanation: >-
      The 2017 consensus statement revising the International Neuroblastoma
      Response Criteria (INRC), from a panel of 52 investigators in 13
      countries, says that urine catecholamine levels will not be used to
      evaluate response, because specimen collection and analysis lack
      standardization and diet influences results. The sentence records the
      panel's decision and stated reasons and reports no data. It covers urine
      catecholamines in general, not VMA and HVA by name, and does not say the
      levels carry no information about response.
  - reference: PMID:28471719
    reference_title: "Revisions to the International Neuroblastoma Response Criteria: A Consensus Statement From the National Cancer Institute Clinical Trials Planning Meeting."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: "The goal of the current INRC revision is to eliminate modalities for tumor assessment that are less sensitive and/or specific for neuroblastoma (eg, bone scintigraphy and catecholamine levels) and replace these with nuclear imaging modalities (123I-MIBG and FDG-PET imaging)"
    explanation: >-
      In its discussion, the same consensus statement gives the broader aim of
      the revision: to remove tumor-assessment modalities that are less
      sensitive and/or specific for neuroblastoma, naming bone scintigraphy and
      catecholamine levels as examples, and to replace them with 123I-MIBG and
      FDG-PET imaging. The sentence concerns tumor assessment within the
      response criteria rather than diagnosis, does not say whether sensitivity,
      specificity or both is the shortfall for catecholamine levels, and cites
      no data for it.
  - reference: PMID:39983076
    reference_title: "Urinary Catecholamines Predict Relapse During Complete Remission in High-Risk Neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Several studies compared urinary catecholamines with other modalities, including bone marrow studies and MIBG scans, and showed that HVA and VMA have low sensitivity as markers for monitoring disease activity in patients with neuroblastoma."
    explanation: >-
      In the discussion of this retrospective cohort study, the authors
      summarise earlier studies that compared urinary catecholamines with bone
      marrow studies and MIBG scans and found HVA and VMA to have low
      sensitivity as markers for monitoring disease activity. This restates
      other studies rather than reporting this cohort's own data, which concern
      an extended eight-metabolite panel.
  - reference: PMID:39983076
    reference_title: "Urinary Catecholamines Predict Relapse During Complete Remission in High-Risk Neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "However, in patients who achieved CR, those with a positive catecholamine status had poor EFS (38% v 80%, respectively; P < .01) and OS (52% v 86%, respectively; P = .01) compared with those with a negative catecholamine status."
    explanation: >-
      Retrospective Dutch cohort of 153 high-risk patients, in which urinary
      catecholamine status was positive if any of eight metabolites exceeded its
      age-related upper reference limit. Among 69 patients with urine tested at
      complete remission, positive status was associated with lower 5-year
      event-free survival (38% versus 80%) and overall survival (52% versus 86%)
      from remission. This finding rests on the eight-metabolite panel: a
      two-marker HVA/VMA panel did not predict event-free survival at remission
      (P = .08), and status at diagnosis or during treatment was not
      significantly associated with survival.
differential_diagnoses:
- name: Wilms tumor
  description: >-
    An abdominal neuroblastoma can be mistaken for Wilms tumor at presentation, and
    the mistake can lead to a nephrectomy: in one single-institution retrospective
    review, nine children with neuroblastoma had an exploratory laparotomy with a
    preoperative diagnosis of Wilms tumor, and eight of them underwent nephrectomy
    at that operation. On tissue, nuclear PHOX2B staining favors neuroblastoma.
  disease_term:
    preferred_term: Wilms tumor
    term:
      id: MONDO:0006058
      label: Wilms tumor
  distinguishing_features:
  - Intratumoral calcification, vascular encasement, or both on preoperative CT point to neuroblastoma; in that review they were present in 78% of the nine misdiagnosed children with neuroblastoma and were never seen in the Wilms tumor comparison group.
  - Symptoms such as fever and weight loss at presentation were more frequent in the misdiagnosed children with neuroblastoma than in the Wilms tumor comparison group of the same review (67% versus 20%).
  - Raised urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) or homovanillic acid (HVA) points to neuroblastoma, and the authors of the same review say a raised result should prompt staging before an operation; all five of its children with neuroblastoma whose urine was collected before surgery had raised VMA and/or HVA, although each result came back only after the operation, while both Wilms tumor comparison patients who were tested were negative.
  - Nuclear PHOX2B staining favors neuroblastoma; in one immunohistochemistry study PHOX2B immunostaining was negative in every Wilms tumor tested, and its authors call PHOX2B specific for neuroblastoma in its differential diagnosis with other small round cell tumors. A second series found all 44 Wilms tumors among its comparison tumors negative, with positivity defined as nuclear staining in at least 5% of cells, and its authors conclude that PHOX2B reliably distinguishes neuroblastoma from mimics such as Wilms tumor. PHOX2B is not fully sensitive, though; that series found it in 70 of 76 peripheral neuroblastic tumors (68 of 72 pediatric cases), so a negative stain does not exclude a peripheral neuroblastic tumor.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:18558200
    reference_title: "Avoiding misdiagnosing neuroblastoma as Wilms tumor."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Nine patients with NBL were identified as those who had an exploratory laparotomy with a preoperative diagnosis of WT; 8 underwent nephrectomy at exploration. Children with NBL had symptoms such as fever and weight loss at presentation (67%) more often than patients with WT (20%). Preoperative computed tomography demonstrated intratumoral calcifications, vascular encasement, or both in 78% of patients with NBL but were never seen in WT patients."
    explanation: >-
      Retrospective case cohort study (chart and imaging review) at St. Jude
      Children's Research Hospital. Nine children later shown to have neuroblastoma
      had an exploratory laparotomy with a preoperative diagnosis of Wilms tumor,
      and eight had a nephrectomy at that operation. Compared with the Wilms tumor
      patients most recently treated at the same institution, they more often had
      symptoms such as fever and weight loss at presentation (67% against 20%; the
      full text specifies fever and/or weight loss), and in 78% of them preoperative
      CT showed intratumoral calcification, vascular encasement or both, which was
      never seen in the Wilms tumor group. The neuroblastoma group was selected
      because it had been misdiagnosed, so these percentages describe misdiagnosed
      cases, not abdominal neuroblastoma in general.
  - reference: PMID:18558200
    reference_title: "Avoiding misdiagnosing neuroblastoma as Wilms tumor."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Although NBL can be mistaken for WT at presentation, the presence of constitutional symptoms, or intratumoral calcification or vascular encasement on preoperative imaging should heighten suspicion for NBL."
    explanation: >-
      The authors' conclusion from the same series: neuroblastoma can be mistaken
      for Wilms tumor at presentation, and constitutional symptoms, or intratumoral
      calcification or vascular encasement on preoperative imaging, should raise
      suspicion of neuroblastoma. It supports the statement that the two tumors can
      be confused and names the features used to tell them apart. It is a
      recommendation drawn from a small series of misdiagnosed cases, not a measured
      sensitivity or specificity; the frequencies behind it are in the results
      sentences of the same abstract.
  - reference: PMID:18558200
    reference_title: "Avoiding misdiagnosing neuroblastoma as Wilms tumor."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "One clear difference in patients with NBL versus WT was the presence of elevated urinary catecholamines or metanephrines. Review of the pre-operative laboratory work up revealed that 5 patients in the NBL group actually had urinary vanillylmendalic acid (VMA) and/or homovanillic acid (HVA) evaluated; in each case these were subsequently found to be elevated. ... Surprisingly, however, in each case, surgery preceded the availability of these results. Of the 20 patients treated for WT, only 2 underwent pre-operative urinary catecholamine analysis, and each was negative. The finding of elevated urinary catecholamines clearly suggests a diagnosis of neuroblastoma and should prompt the surgical and medical teams to complete the staging evaluation prior to proceeding with an operation."
    explanation: >-
      Retrospective review, at one referral center, of nine children with
      neuroblastoma who had been operated on at referring institutions as presumed
      Wilms tumor, compared with the 20 Wilms tumor patients most recently treated
      at that center. The authors name raised urinary catecholamines as one clear
      difference between the groups. All five neuroblastoma children whose urine was
      collected before surgery had raised VMA and/or HVA, although in each case the
      result came back only after the operation, and both Wilms tumor comparison
      patients who were tested were negative. The authors conclude that a raised
      result should prompt staging before any operation. Testing was not systematic
      in either group (5 of 9 and 2 of 20), so the counts show which way the
      difference runs; they are not a sensitivity or specificity.
  - reference: PMID:25822764
    reference_title: "Diagnostic utility of PHOX2B in primary and treated neuroblastoma and in neuroblastoma metastatic to the bone marrow."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "PHOX2B staining was absent in all cases of rhabdomyosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, and Wilms tumor, and in the negative bone marrow. ... PHOX2B is specific for NB in its differential diagnosis with other small round cell tumors, and its nuclear staining may be helpful for accurate bone marrow tumor quantification."
    explanation: >-
      Immunohistochemical study of patient tumor tissue microarrays. PHOX2B staining
      was absent in every rhabdomyosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma and Wilms tumor on the
      comparison arrays, and the authors conclude that PHOX2B is specific for
      neuroblastoma in its differential diagnosis with other small round cell
      tumors. The nuclear staining the abstract describes is that of neuroblastoma
      cells; the comparison tumors showed no staining. The abstract gives no case
      counts for the comparison tumors and does not name the rhabdomyosarcoma
      subtypes tested.
  - reference: PMID:28640941
    reference_title: "PHOX2B reliably distinguishes neuroblastoma among small round blue cell tumours."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "We evaluated 240 cases (133 in whole-tissue sections; 107 in tissue microarrays), including 76 peripheral neuroblastic tumours (median age 2 years; including four adults) and 164 other tumours: 44 Wilms tumours; 20 Ewing sarcomas; 10 each of CIC-rearranged round cell sarcomas, poorly differentiated synovial sarcomas, lymphoblastic lymphomas, alveolar rhabdomyosarcomas, embryonal rhabdomyosarcomas, mesenchymal chondrosarcomas, Merkel cell carcinomas, olfactory neuroblastomas, and melanomas; and five each of NUT midline carcinomas and desmoplastic small round cell tumours. ... PHOX2B positivity was defined as the presence of nuclear immunoreactivity in ≥5% of cells. PHOX2B was positive in 70 (92%) peripheral neuroblastic tumours, including 68 of 72 (94%) paediatric and two of four (50%) adult cases. Furthermore, PHOX2B was consistently negative in all non-peripheral neuroblastic tumours, with staining being absent in 160 cases and limited in four cases. ... PHOX2B is a highly sensitive and specific immunohistochemical marker for peripheral neuroblastic tumours, including neuroblastoma. PHOX2B reliably distinguishes neuroblastoma from histological mimics such as Wilms tumour, Ewing sarcoma, and CIC-rearranged round cell sarcoma."
    explanation: >-
      Immunohistochemical series whose 164 comparison tumors included 44 Wilms
      tumors, alongside 20 Ewing sarcomas and ten each of alveolar and embryonal
      rhabdomyosarcomas. With positivity defined as nuclear immunoreactivity in at
      least 5% of cells, PHOX2B was negative in all of them, and the authors conclude
      that it is a highly sensitive and specific marker for peripheral neuroblastic
      tumors, including neuroblastoma, and that it reliably distinguishes
      neuroblastoma from histological mimics such as Wilms tumor. Staining was absent
      in 160 comparison cases and limited in four, and the abstract does not say
      which tumor types the four were, so the series shows the Wilms tumors were
      PHOX2B-negative by that threshold, not that staining was absent in every one.
      PHOX2B was positive in 70 of the 76 peripheral neuroblastic tumors, 68 of 72
      pediatric and two of four adult cases, so a negative stain does not exclude a
      peripheral neuroblastic tumor; the abstract does not say which tumor types the
      four negative pediatric cases were.
- name: Neonatal adrenal hemorrhage
  description: >-
    In the newborn most suprarenal masses prove to be either a congenital
    neuroblastoma or an adrenal hemorrhage. An adrenal hemorrhage can appear as a
    cystic suprarenal mass as it liquefies, and a high incidence of cystic tumors
    has been noted among prenatally diagnosed neuroblastomas. Cystic neuroblastoma
    and cystic adrenal hemorrhage are frequently difficult to tell apart, and the
    distinction is made harder still because neuroblastomas can be complicated by
    hemorrhage and prenatally detected neuroblastomas are frequently associated with
    normal urinary catecholamine metabolites. In one series an adrenal hemorrhage
    was resected on suspicion of neuroblastoma because it had been detected
    prenatally and looked like a cystic mass with wall enhancement; pathology showed
    an adrenal pseudocyst without neuroblastoma. In a Children's Oncology Group
    study of expectant observation of small adrenal masses in infants younger than 6
    months, two of the 16 observed infants who went on to surgery had an adrenal
    hemorrhage.
  distinguishing_features:
  - "In a retrospective series that compared 16 congenital cystic neuroblastomas with 14 neonatal adrenal hemorrhagic pseudocysts, from which solid adrenal masses were excluded, size, solid portion, septation, enhancement and turbidity did not differ significantly; the authors concluded that prenatal detection (all of the neuroblastomas against three of the 14 pseudocysts), calcification on the initial images, vascular flow on color Doppler ultrasound and evolution to a more complex mass may all favor neuroblastoma. Calcification on the initial images and Doppler flow were each seen in three neuroblastomas and in none of the pseudocysts examined, but color Doppler was done in only nine neuroblastomas and two hemorrhages; most neuroblastomas in the series had no calcification on the initial images, and most of those examined by Doppler showed no flow."
  - "On follow-up imaging the three cystic neuroblastomas that were followed became more complex solid and cystic masses and did not disappear for up to 90 days, whereas most hemorrhagic pseudocysts resolved completely or evolved to calcification only. Apart from the one that was resected, the pseudocysts were diagnosed by that resolution or calcification, so the contrast in evolution is partly built into how the series defined its cases, and calcification favors neuroblastoma only on the initial images."
  - "In a small Doppler series, color-coded and power Doppler sonography showed vessels within the one congenital neuroblastoma studied and no flow in any of ten adrenal hemorrhages in eight neonates, whether the hemorrhage looked cystic or solid."
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:21228940
    reference_title: "Comparison of clinico-radiological features between congenital cystic neuroblastoma and neonatal adrenal hemorrhagic pseudocyst."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "All (100%) neuroblastomas and three (21%) of the 14 hemorrhagic pseudocysts were detected prenatally. Both groups of cystic lesions occurred more frequently on the right side; 11 of 16 (69%) for neuroblastomas and 11 of 14 (79%) for hemorrhagic pseudocysts. The size, presence of solid portion, septum, enhancement, and turbidity did not differ significantly (p > 0.05) between the two groups of cystic lesions. However, tiny calcifications (n = 3) and vascular flow on color Doppler US (n = 3) were noted in only neuroblastomas. The cystic neuroblastomas became complex solid and cystic masses, and did not disappear for up to 90 days in the three following cases, whereas 11 of the 14 (79%) hemorrhagic pseudocysts disappeared completely and the three remaining (27%) evolved to calcifications only. ... Although the imaging findings of two groups of cystic lesions were similar, prenatal detection, the presence of calcification on initial images, vascularity on color Doppler US, and evolution to a more complex mass may all favor neuroblastomas. ... Although solid adrenal masses were excluded, cysts with solid portions were included in the analysis. ... All of the neuroblastomas were surgically resected and pathologically confirmed. One adrenal hemorrhage was surgically removed due to the suspicion of neuroblastoma on the basis of the prenatal detection and the imaging appearance of a cystic mass with wall enhancement. A pathological examination revealed an adrenal pseudocyst without evidence of neuroblastoma. The remaining 13 adrenal hemorrhagic pseudocysts detected in the 12 patients were diagnosed by complete resolution (n = 11) or evolution to only calcifications (n = 2) on follow-up images. ... Color Doppler US was performed on 11 patients (nine cystic neuroblastomas and two adrenal hemorrhages) and three (33%) patients with cystic neuroblastomas showed evidence of vascular flow signals in the outer wall or internal septum (Fig. 1)."
    explanation: >-
      Retrospective series comparing congenital cystic neuroblastomas with neonatal
      adrenal hemorrhagic pseudocysts. Solid adrenal masses were excluded, so the
      comparison covers the cystic presentation only. The imaging overlapped: both
      lesions were mostly right-sided, and size, solid portion, septation,
      enhancement and turbidity did not differ significantly. The authors concluded
      that four features may favor neuroblastoma: prenatal detection (every
      neuroblastoma, against a minority of pseudocysts), calcification on initial
      images and color Doppler flow (each seen only in neuroblastomas), and
      evolution on follow-up to a more complex solid and cystic mass. That
      conclusion is hedged ('may all favor'). Apart from prenatal detection, the
      features rest on small numbers: calcification and Doppler flow were each seen
      in three neuroblastomas, color Doppler was done in only nine neuroblastomas
      and two hemorrhages, and the follow-up comparison rests on three
      neuroblastomas. The contrast in evolution is partly built into the case
      definitions: every neuroblastoma was confirmed by resection, while 13 of the
      14 pseudocysts were diagnosed by complete resolution or calcification on
      follow-up imaging. Because pseudocysts can end as calcification, calcification
      separates the two only on initial images. The overlap had a cost: one
      prenatally detected hemorrhage that looked like a cystic mass with wall
      enhancement was resected as a suspected neuroblastoma, and pathology showed an
      adrenal pseudocyst. The abstract says three pseudocysts evolved to
      calcification; the methods count two, with 11 resolved and one resected.
  - reference: PMID:21228940
    reference_title: "Comparison of clinico-radiological features between congenital cystic neuroblastoma and neonatal adrenal hemorrhagic pseudocyst."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "There are diverse cystic lesions of the gastrointestinal tract (1), but the majority of neonatal suprarenal masses are ultimately identified as congenital neuroblastomas or adrenal hemorrhages. ... An adrenal hemorrhage may be observed as a cystic suprarenal mass in the process of liquefaction, and a high incidence (44%) of cystic tumors has been previously noted among prenatally diagnosed neuroblastomas (3). The differentiation of those two groups of neonatal adrenal cystic lesions frequently proves to be difficult. Moreover, neuroblastomas can be complicated by hemorrhaging (5), and prenatally detected neuroblastomas are frequently associated with normal levels of the urinary catecholamine metabolites (3), which render such differentiations even more difficult."
    explanation: >-
      Introduction of a multicenter retrospective clinical and imaging comparison of
      congenital cystic neuroblastoma with neonatal adrenal hemorrhagic pseudocyst.
      The authors state that most neonatal suprarenal masses prove to be congenital
      neuroblastoma or adrenal hemorrhage, that an adrenal hemorrhage can appear as
      a cystic suprarenal mass as it liquefies, and that a high incidence of cystic
      tumors had previously been noted among prenatally diagnosed neuroblastomas.
      They state that these two groups of neonatal adrenal cystic lesions are
      frequently difficult to differentiate, and that the distinction is made harder
      still because neuroblastomas can be complicated by hemorrhage and prenatally
      detected neuroblastomas are frequently associated with normal urinary
      catecholamine metabolites. These are Introduction sentences framing the study,
      not its results: the suprarenal-mass and difficulty statements are the
      authors' own uncited framing, and the cystic-tumor, hemorrhage and
      catecholamine points restate earlier work they cite. The incidence figure in
      the quote is the authors' restatement of an earlier report (their reference
      3), so the row does not repeat it.
  - reference: PMID:9578964
    reference_title: "Differential diagnosis of neonatal adrenal haemorrhage and congenital neuroblastoma by colour coded Doppler sonography and power Doppler sonography."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "We investigated eight neonates with adrenal haemorrhage and one patient with congenital neuroblastoma by colour coded Doppler sonography and power Doppler sonography. Six haemorrhages were cystic, whereas the neuroblastoma and four adrenal haemorrhages had a solid appearance. Colour coded Doppler sonography and power Doppler demonstrated vessels within the neuroblastoma. In none of the ten adrenal haemorrhages could flow be shown either with conventional colour coded Doppler sonography or power Doppler sonography."
    explanation: >-
      Small Doppler series of eight neonates with ten adrenal hemorrhages and one
      patient with congenital neuroblastoma. Color-coded and power Doppler
      sonography showed vessels within the neuroblastoma and no flow in any of the
      ten hemorrhages, whether the hemorrhage looked cystic or solid; the
      neuroblastoma itself looked solid. This supports only the Doppler-flow
      distinguishing feature, in a patient series separate from PMID:21228940, and
      adds solid-appearing hemorrhages to the comparison; it says nothing about
      prenatal detection, calcification or evolution. The series has a single
      neuroblastoma, so it shows that flow inside the lesion can separate the two
      but not how often neuroblastomas show flow, and it cannot show that absent
      flow argues against neuroblastoma. The abstract does not say how either
      diagnosis was confirmed.
  - reference: PMID:22964741
    reference_title: "A prospective study of expectant observation as primary therapy for neuroblastoma in young infants: a Children's Oncology Group study."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "A prospective study of infants younger than 6 months with small adrenal masses and no evidence of spreading beyond the primary tumor was performed at participating Children's Oncology Group institutions. ... Sixteen observational patients ultimately had surgery; 8 had International Neuroblastoma Staging System stage 1 neuroblastoma, 2 had higher staged neuroblastoma (2B and 4S), 2 had low-grade adrenocortical neoplasm, 2 had adrenal hemorrhage, and 2 had extralobar pulmonary sequestration."
    explanation: >-
      COG ANBL00P2 was a prospective study of expectant observation as primary
      therapy for neuroblastoma in infants younger than 6 months who had a small
      adrenal mass with no evidence of spread beyond it. Entry rested on a small
      adrenal mass, not on a tissue diagnosis, and parents chose either observation,
      with serial ultrasound and urine VMA/HVA measurements, or immediate surgery.
      Of the 16 infants on the observation arm who eventually had surgery, 2 had
      adrenal hemorrhage and 2 had extralobar pulmonary sequestration; the others
      were 8 with stage 1 neuroblastoma, 2 with higher-stage neuroblastoma and 2
      with a low-grade adrenocortical neoplasm. Both lesions were therefore found at
      surgery in masses that had met the study's entry criteria for a small adrenal
      mass and had been managed within a neuroblastoma-observation study. The cohort
      was infants younger than 6 months, not newborns only, and the quote does not
      give the age of the two infants with hemorrhage. These are counts within one
      cohort, not rates of misdiagnosis: most observed infants were spared surgery,
      so what their masses were was never established at operation. Abstract methods
      and results sentences.
  notes: >-
    No MONDO class fits neonatal adrenal hemorrhage, so the row is left unbound. OLS
    searches of MONDO on 28 October 2026 for 'adrenal hemorrhage', 'adrenal
    haemorrhage', 'adrenal gland hemorrhage' and 'hemorrhage adrenal' returned,
    between them, only bilateral massive adrenal hemorrhage (MONDO:0017871),
    Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (MONDO:0006015) and Sheehan syndrome
    (MONDO:0019618), and searches for 'neonatal adrenal hemorrhage', 'adrenal
    hematoma' and 'adrenal pseudocyst' returned no term. MONDO defines MONDO:0017871
    as acute bleeding into both adrenal glands associated with illnesses such as
    severe sepsis, congestive heart failure, antiphospholipid syndrome,
    anticoagulant use or severe physical stress such as trauma and surgery, which
    does not describe perinatal adrenal hemorrhage.
- name: Extralobar pulmonary sequestration
  description: >-
    A subdiaphragmatic (intra-abdominal) extralobar pulmonary sequestration can
    present as a suprarenal mass on prenatal ultrasound. A literature review of
    prenatally diagnosed suprarenal masses that proved to be either subdiaphragmatic
    extralobar pulmonary sequestration or neuroblastoma found one sequestration
    reported for every 2.5 neuroblastomas, and its authors conclude that
    subdiaphragmatic extralobar pulmonary sequestration must be considered in the
    differential diagnosis of a suprarenal mass identified on prenatal ultrasound.
    In a Children's Oncology Group study of expectant observation of small adrenal
    masses in infants younger than 6 months, two of the 16 observed infants who went
    on to surgery had an extralobar pulmonary sequestration.
  disease_term:
    preferred_term: extralobar pulmonary sequestration
    term:
      id: MONDO:0017246
      label: extralobar congenital pulmonary sequestration
  distinguishing_features:
  - "On prenatal ultrasound a subdiaphragmatic extralobar pulmonary sequestration is usually echogenic, left-sided and can be identified in the second trimester, whereas a prenatally detected neuroblastoma is most often cystic, right-sided and identified in the third trimester. The review's authors state that with the algorithm they propose, built on these differences, the correct diagnosis can be determined prenatally in 95% of patients; the abstract reports no separate validation of the algorithm."
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:9166798
    reference_title: "Prenatal ultrasound characterization of the suprarenal mass: distinction between neuroblastoma and subdiaphragmatic extralobar pulmonary sequestration."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "The literature was reviewed for cases of prenatally diagnosed suprarenal masses that proved ultimately to be either subdiaphragmatic extralobar pulmonary sequestration or neuroblastoma. The distinguishing features of the two lesions were identified and an algorithm was created on the basis of these distinctions. Prenatally diagnosed subdiaphragmatic extralobar pulmonary sequestration is no longer rare, with one case being reported for every 2.5 cases of neuroblastoma. On prenatal ultrasonography subdiaphragmatic extralobar pulmonary sequestration usually is echogenic, is left-sided, and can be identified in the second trimester. Neuroblastoma is most often cystic, right-sided, and identified in the third trimester. In summary, subdiaphragmatic extralobar pulmonary sequestration must be considered in the differential diagnosis of the suprarenal mass identified on prenatal ultrasonography. Using the algorithm which we propose, the correct diagnosis can be determined prenatally in 95% of patients."
    explanation: >-
      Curtis et al. reviewed published cases of prenatally detected suprarenal
      masses that proved to be either subdiaphragmatic extralobar pulmonary
      sequestration or neuroblastoma, and derived prenatal ultrasound features that
      separate the two. Among the published cases, one sequestration was reported
      for every 2.5 neuroblastomas. This is a ratio of reported cases, not an
      incidence ratio. Sequestration was usually echogenic, left-sided and
      identifiable in the second trimester, whereas prenatally detected
      neuroblastoma was most often cystic, right-sided and identified in the third
      trimester. The authors conclude that sequestration must be considered in the
      differential diagnosis of a suprarenal mass seen on prenatal ultrasound. The
      95% is the authors' own estimate for the algorithm they built from these
      features: the abstract reports no independent validation set and does not give
      the number of cases reviewed. Abstract sentences 4 to 10.
  - reference: PMID:22964741
    reference_title: "A prospective study of expectant observation as primary therapy for neuroblastoma in young infants: a Children's Oncology Group study."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "A prospective study of infants younger than 6 months with small adrenal masses and no evidence of spreading beyond the primary tumor was performed at participating Children's Oncology Group institutions. ... Sixteen observational patients ultimately had surgery; 8 had International Neuroblastoma Staging System stage 1 neuroblastoma, 2 had higher staged neuroblastoma (2B and 4S), 2 had low-grade adrenocortical neoplasm, 2 had adrenal hemorrhage, and 2 had extralobar pulmonary sequestration."
    explanation: >-
      COG ANBL00P2 was a prospective study of expectant observation as primary
      therapy for neuroblastoma in infants younger than 6 months who had a small
      adrenal mass with no evidence of spread beyond it. Entry rested on a small
      adrenal mass, not on a tissue diagnosis, and parents chose either observation,
      with serial ultrasound and urine VMA/HVA measurements, or immediate surgery.
      Of the 16 infants on the observation arm who eventually had surgery, 2 had
      adrenal hemorrhage and 2 had extralobar pulmonary sequestration; the others
      were 8 with stage 1 neuroblastoma, 2 with higher-stage neuroblastoma and 2
      with a low-grade adrenocortical neoplasm. Both lesions were therefore found at
      surgery in masses that had met the study's entry criteria for a small adrenal
      mass and had been managed within a neuroblastoma-observation study. These are
      counts within one cohort, not rates of misdiagnosis: most observed infants
      were spared surgery, so what their masses were was never established at
      operation. Abstract methods and results sentences.
  notes: >-
    MONDO has no class for the subdiaphragmatic form. OLS searches of MONDO on 28
    October 2026 for 'extralobar pulmonary sequestration' and 'pulmonary
    sequestration' returned extralobar congenital pulmonary sequestration
    (MONDO:0017246), intralobar congenital pulmonary sequestration (MONDO:0017245)
    and congenital pulmonary sequestration (MONDO:0017843); searches for
    'subdiaphragmatic pulmonary sequestration', 'intra-abdominal pulmonary
    sequestration' and 'subdiaphragmatic sequestration' returned no term, and
    MONDO:0017246 has no subclasses. The row therefore uses MONDO:0017246.
- name: Wolman disease
  description: >-
    Bilateral adrenal enlargement with calcification and preserved adreniform shape
    is a hallmark radiologic feature of Wolman disease, present in approximately
    half of reported cases, and neuroblastoma is among the differential diagnoses of
    adrenal calcification, with adrenal hemorrhage, infections such as tuberculosis,
    congenital adrenal hyperplasia and other storage disorders such as Niemann-Pick
    disease.
  disease_term:
    preferred_term: Wolman disease
    term:
      id: MONDO:0019148
      label: Wolman disease
  distinguishing_features:
  - "When the adrenal glands are calcified, both glands in Wolman disease are uniformly enlarged, with calcification within the adrenal cortex, and keep their adreniform shape, whereas a neuroblastoma arising in the adrenal gland is a neoplastic growth of the gland with internal specks of calcification."
  - "Definitive diagnosis of Wolman disease is confirmed by identifying pathogenic variants in LIPA and measuring lysosomal acid lipase (LAL) activity."
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:34401013
    reference_title: "CT features of Wolman disease (lysosomal acid lipase enzyme deficiency) - A case report."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "There is a broad differential in adrenal calcification, but in Wolman disease, adrenal glands are uniformly enlarged with calcifications within the adrenal cortex on both sides, with preserved adreniform shape. ... In neuroblastoma, neoplastic growth of the adrenal gland is seen, with internal specks of calcification."
    explanation: >-
      In its Discussion, this Wolman disease CT case report sets out the
      differential of adrenal calcification. In Wolman disease both adrenal glands
      are uniformly enlarged, with calcification in the adrenal cortex, and keep
      their adreniform shape; in neuroblastoma there is neoplastic growth of the
      adrenal gland with internal specks of calcification. The two quoted sentences
      are the authors' general statements, not findings in the reported infant, and
      carry no citation of their own. They describe calcified glands and a tumor of
      the adrenal gland and give no frequencies, so they do not show that every case
      of Wolman disease has adrenal calcification or that every neuroblastoma arises
      in the adrenal gland. This supports listing Wolman disease in the differential
      of an adrenal neuroblastoma with calcification, and the adrenal-pattern
      contrast in this row's distinguishing features.
  - reference: PMID:41869254
    reference_title: "Bilateral Adrenal Calcifications as an Imaging Clue to Wolman Disease in Early Infancy: A Case Report."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "A hallmark radiologic feature of Wolman disease is bilateral adrenal enlargement with parenchymal calcifications while preserving the adreniform morphology, a finding present in approximately half of reported cases. ... Definitive diagnosis is confirmed by identification of pathogenic mutations in the LIPA gene and measurement of LAL activity in lymphocytes or fibroblasts. Differential diagnoses associated with adrenal calcifications include adrenal hemorrhage, infections such as tuberculosis, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, neuroblastoma, and other storage disorders such as Niemann-Pick disease."
    explanation: >-
      In the Introduction and Discussion of this Wolman disease case report, the
      authors make three general statements, as background rather than findings from
      their own case. Bilateral adrenal enlargement with calcification and preserved
      adreniform shape is a hallmark radiologic feature of Wolman disease, present
      in approximately half of reported cases. Definitive diagnosis is confirmed by
      finding pathogenic LIPA mutations and measuring LAL activity. Neuroblastoma is
      among the differential diagnoses of adrenal calcification. Together these
      support listing Wolman disease as a condition to tell apart from neuroblastoma
      when the adrenal glands are calcified, with LIPA testing and LAL activity as
      the confirmatory tests. The paper does not compare the two diseases directly.
      It names lymphocytes or fibroblasts as the specimens for the enzyme assay;
      the row does not name a specimen.
- name: Infantile hepatic hemangioma
  description: >-
    Hepatic infantile hemangioma and metastatic neuroblastoma can present similarly:
    in one reported 4-month-old girl with a known superficial and deep infantile
    hemangioma, new axillary nodules and hepatosplenomegaly were initially suspected
    to reflect infantile hemangioma and were later determined to be widely
    metastatic neuroblastoma. A review of infantile hepatic hemangioma states that
    the differential diagnosis of a liver mass found in an infant includes
    metastatic neuroblastoma, lists metastatic neuroblastoma among the primary
    differential diagnoses of a lesion that may be a focal infantile hepatic
    hemangioma, and notes that when multiple well-demarcated liver lesions are
    present, particularly ones that enhance avidly on MRI and look alike on every
    sequence, multifocal infantile hemangioma is the most likely diagnosis, although
    an atypical presentation of neuroblastoma is still possible.
  disease_term:
    preferred_term: infantile hepatic hemangioma
    term:
      id: MONDO:0002404
      label: liver hemangioma
  distinguishing_features:
  - "Before a focal liver lesion in an infant is diagnosed as a presumptive focal infantile hepatic hemangioma, a review recommends evaluating the neuroblastoma primary sites (the adrenal glands, the organ of Zuckerkandl and the paraspinal chain) and screening the urine for catecholamines; it allows the presumptive diagnosis only if those results are unremarkable, the lesion hyperenhances on multiphase CT or MRI and no other structure is invaded, and says the lesion should still be monitored for further growth."
  - "New findings in an infant with a known infantile hemangioma are not necessarily more hemangioma: in a reported 4-month-old with a known superficial and deep hemangioma, new axillary nodules and hepatosplenomegaly proved to be widely metastatic neuroblastoma, and the authors advise keeping a broad differential when evaluating new findings in a patient with a previously diagnosed infantile hemangioma."
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:27610342
    reference_title: "History of the infantile hepatic hemangioma: From imaging to generating a differential diagnosis."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: "The primary differential diagnoses include metastatic neuroblastoma, hepatoblastoma (Figure 5) and mesenchymal hamartoma (Figure 6). Primary sites of neuroblastoma (adrenal glands, organ of Zuckerkandel and paraspinal chain) should be evaluated and the urine samples should be screened for the presence of catecholamines. If the above results are unremarkable, the lesion demonstrates hyper enhancement (either on multiphase CT with iodinated contrast or MRI with gadolinium based contrast material) and there is no invasion of other structures, then a presumptive focal IHHs may be diagnosed but should still be monitored to ensure there is no further growth."
    explanation: >-
      This review of infantile hepatic hemangioma lists metastatic neuroblastoma,
      hepatoblastoma and mesenchymal hamartoma as the primary differential diagnoses
      of a focal liver lesion in an infant that may be a focal infantile hepatic
      hemangioma, so it names metastatic neuroblastoma as a differential of focal
      infantile hepatic hemangioma directly. It then recommends evaluating the
      neuroblastoma primary sites (adrenal glands, organ of Zuckerkandl, paraspinal
      chain) and screening urine for catecholamines, which is the work-up that tests
      for neuroblastoma; if those results are unremarkable, the lesion hyperenhances
      on multiphase CT or MRI and no other structure is invaded, a presumptive focal
      hemangioma may then be diagnosed and monitored for further growth. The advice
      is scoped to that presumptive diagnosis, not to every infant liver lesion. The
      passage is the review's own diagnostic recommendation and reports no data; the
      quote keeps the source's spelling 'Zuckerkandel'.
  - reference: PMID:27610342
    reference_title: "History of the infantile hepatic hemangioma: From imaging to generating a differential diagnosis."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: OTHER

      differential diagnosis of a liver mass found in an infant includes metastatic
      neuroblastoma. It also states that when multiple well-demarcated hepatic
      lesions are present, particularly ones that enhance avidly on MRI and look
      alike on every sequence, multifocal infantile hemangioma is the most likely
      diagnosis, although an atypical presentation of neuroblastoma is still
      possible. Both sentences are the review authors' diagnostic guidance: the
      second cites no study, and neither reports observations from a patient series.
      The quote keeps the source's spelling 'well-demarked'.

      hepatic infantile hemangioma and metastatic neuroblastoma can present
      similarly, and that new findings in a patient with a previously diagnosed
      infantile hemangioma call for a broad differential. Direct: the abstract
      states both the case and the general conclusion. A single case, abstract only:

    hemangioma', 'hepatic infantile hemangioma' and 'infantile hepatic haemangioma'
    returned no term; 'hepatic hemangioma' returned liver hemangioma and hepatic
    vascular disorder (MONDO:0002405); 'liver hemangioma' also returned liver
    cavernous hemangioma (MONDO:0006267), the only subclass of liver hemangioma, and
    diffuse neonatal hemangiomatosis (MONDO:0016237), which MONDO defines by

    'infantile hemangioma' returned capillary infantile hemangioma (MONDO:0011191),
    infantile hemangioma of rare localization (MONDO:0016223) and other classes not
    specific to the liver.
- name: Sacrococcygeal teratoma
  description: >-
    A congenital presacral or sacrococcygeal neuroblastoma can present as a mass in
    the newborn and be taken for a sacrococcygeal teratoma. Neuroblastoma can arise
    from extra-adrenal sites in the paraspinal sympathetic chain, including the
    presacral region, where it must be differentiated from an immature or malignant
    neural lesion arising from a teratoma. In a report of two congenital presacral
    neuroblastomas the main clinical differential diagnoses were sacrococcygeal
    teratoma and meningomyelocele, and in a newborn with an extremely large
    sacrococcygeal mass, imaging strongly suggested an Altman type III
    sacrococcygeal teratoma until histopathology of the incompletely resected tumor
    showed neuroblastoma. These are a single-patient and a two-patient report, so
    they show that the pitfall exists, not how often it occurs.
  disease_term:
    preferred_term: sacrococcygeal teratoma
    term:
      id: MONDO:0042727
      label: sacrococcygeal teratoma
  distinguishing_features:
  - "In the reported cases the diagnosis rested on tissue: the two congenital presacral neuroblastomas showed no teratomatous tissue on pathology and lacked germ cell serum markers, and their authors conclude that congenital presacral neuroblastoma should be differentiated from teratomatous lesions; in the newborn whose imaging suggested an Altman type III teratoma, histopathologic examination of the tumor showed neuroblastoma. The report of the two cases names no germ cell marker and does not test how well serum markers separate the lesions."
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:33307929
    reference_title: "Congenital Sacrococcygeal Neuroblastoma: A Report of Two Cases with Summary of Prior Published Cases."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "We describe two congenital presacral neuroblastomas. The main clinical differential diagnoses were sacrococcygeal teratoma and meningomyelocele. Pathologically, they lacked teratomatous tissues, lacked germ cell serum markers, were localized without metastases, and were MYCN non-amplified. ... Congenital presacral neuroblastoma should be differentiated from teratomatous lesions, and in general have a good prognosis."
    explanation: >-
      A case report of two congenital presacral neuroblastomas states that their
      main clinical differential diagnoses were sacrococcygeal teratoma and
      meningomyelocele. It reports that the tumors lacked teratomatous tissues on
      pathology and lacked germ cell serum markers, and it concludes that congenital
      presacral neuroblastoma should be differentiated from teratomatous lesions.
      This directly supports listing sacrococcygeal teratoma as a differential
      diagnosis of congenital presacral neuroblastoma. It rests on two cases, so it
      shows that the diagnostic pitfall exists, not how often it occurs, and it does
      not test how well germ cell serum markers tell the two apart. The staging,
      MYCN and prognosis clauses in the quote are not used for this item.

      This is the background statement of the same two-patient case report, not a

      sites in the paraspinal sympathetic chain, including the presacral region, and
      that there it must be differentiated from an immature or malignant neural

      differential applies and names the teratoma-derived lesion that presacral

Imaging studies strongly suggested Altman type III sacrococcygeal teratoma. On the 10th day after the birth, the tumor was incompletely removed at surgery. Histopathologic examination of the tumor showed neuroblastoma."
    explanation: >-
      In a single neonatal case report, imaging of an extremely large sacrococcygeal
      mass strongly suggested an Altman type III sacrococcygeal teratoma, but
      histopathology of the incompletely removed tumor showed neuroblastoma. This
      shows that in this case imaging did not tell sacrococcygeal teratoma apart

- name: Langerhans cell histiocytosis
  description: >-
    Langerhans cell histiocytosis and metastatic neuroblastoma can both produce bone
    lesions of the orbit in children. LCH tends to involve the skull bones,
    especially the lateral orbital roof, and the orbit is a common site of
    neuroblastoma bone metastases. At imaging, osseous orbital lesions may appear
    similar to each other, and LCH, granulocytic sarcoma and neuroblastoma
    metastases to the orbit are often bilateral. The Euro Histio Net guideline for
    patients up to 18 years lists neuroblastoma among the possible other conditions
    in its differential-diagnosis table for LCH involving the orbit.
    The same table also lists neuroblastoma among the possible other conditions for
    LCH skin nodules, with mastocytosis, juvenile xanthogranuloma and infant leukemia.
  disease_term:
    preferred_term: Langerhans cell histiocytosis
    term:
      id: MONDO:0018310
      label: Langerhans cell histiocytosis
  distinguishing_features:
  - LCH tends to involve the skull bones, especially the lateral orbital roof, and produces lytic bone destruction with a sclerotic rim and a large intraorbital soft-tissue mass, whereas neuroblastoma metastases to the orbit cause an aggressive periosteal reaction in the orbital roof or lateral wall.
  - A definitive diagnosis of LCH requires positive immunostaining of the lesional cells for CD1a and/or CD207 (langerin).
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:18635637
    reference_title: "From the Archives of the AFIP. Pediatric orbit tumors and tumorlike lesions: osseous lesions of the orbit."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Langerhans cell histiocytosis, an idiopathic reticuloendothelial proliferative disorder, tends to involve the bones of the skull, especially the lateral orbital roof; it produces lytic destruction of bone with a sclerotic rim and a large intraorbital soft-tissue mass. Granulocytic sarcoma is a solid tumor that may occur in children with myelogenous leukemia. These tumors tend to arise in the subperiosteum of the lateral orbital wall, although they usually do not disrupt the bone. Finally, the orbit is a common site for bone metastases from neuroblastoma, which cause aggressive periosteal reaction in the orbital roof or lateral wall. The last three conditions are often bilateral. At imaging evaluation, osseous lesions may appear similar to each other and to nonosseous masses of the orbit. Knowledge of the pathologic features of these tumors and how these features are reflected in their imaging appearances may help radiologists differentiate them."
    explanation: >-
      This AFIP radiologic-pathologic review of osseous lesions of the pediatric
      orbit says Langerhans cell histiocytosis tends to involve the skull bones,
      especially the lateral orbital roof, producing lytic bone destruction with a
      sclerotic rim and a large intraorbital soft-tissue mass. It calls the orbit a
      common site for neuroblastoma bone metastases, which cause aggressive
      periosteal reaction in the orbital roof or lateral wall. It then says LCH,
      granulocytic sarcoma and neuroblastoma metastases ('the last three
      conditions') are often bilateral, that at imaging these osseous lesions may
      look alike, and that knowing how their pathologic features show on imaging may
      help radiologists tell them apart. So orbital neuroblastoma metastasis is an
      imaging differential for orbital LCH in a child, and the sclerotic rim with a
      soft-tissue mass in LCH, against aggressive periosteal reaction with
      neuroblastoma, are the descriptions the review offers for separating them. For
      the LCH and neuroblastoma statements, the pediatric scope comes from the
      review's title and opening sentence; within the quoted passage only the
      granulocytic sarcoma sentence names children.

    reference_title: "Langerhans cell histiocytosis in children: Diagnosis, differential diagnosis, treatment, sequelae, and standardized follow-up."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Positive immunohistochemistry staining for CD1a and CD207 (langerin) are required for a definitive diagnosis."
    explanation: >-
      Krooks, Minkov and Weatherall's 2018 review of childhood LCH states that
      positive immunohistochemical staining for CD1a and CD207 (langerin) is
      required for a definitive diagnosis, after stating that a definitive diagnosis
      combines clinical presentation, histology and immunohistochemistry. The review
      names both markers, which is stricter than the CD1a and/or CD207 wording of
      the 2013 Euro Histio Net guideline; a requirement for both markers implies the
      requirement for at least one that this row states. The sentence states a
      diagnostic requirement and reports no patient data.

    explanation: >-
      The Euro Histio Net guideline for patients up to 18 years (Haupt, Minkov and
      colleagues, 2013) states that LCH lesions have a well-defined characteristic
      appearance on hematoxylin and eosin sections, but that positive CD1a and/or
      CD207 (Langerin) staining of the lesional cells is required for a definitive

      agreement between all experts or between available studies. Staining for

      that confirms LCH on biopsy and says nothing about neuroblastoma's own
      markers; the guideline's differential-diagnosis table is quoted in the next
      item.
