- name: Acute megakaryoblastic leukemia
  description: >-
    In a series of six infants with acute megakaryoblastic leukemia and
    t(1;22)(p13;q13), aged 0.8 to 6.5 months at initial examination, all had
    hepatosplenomegaly and the marrow showed fibrosis at presentation. The series'
    liver and lymph-node biopsy specimens were suggestive of a nonhematopoietic
    malignant condition because of the cohesiveness of the tumor cells, stromal
    fibrosis and a prominent sinusoidal and vascular pattern of infiltration, and
    the authors single out neuroblastoma among the childhood small round cell tumors
    the infiltrates had to be told apart from.
  disease_term:
    preferred_term: acute megakaryoblastic leukemia with t(1;22)
    term:
      id: MONDO:0018436
      label: megakaryoblastic acute myeloid leukemia with t(1;22)(p13;q13)
  distinguishing_features:
  - "On paraffin sections a panel of monoclonal antibodies confirmed the nature of the infiltrates and differentiated them from other childhood small round cell tumors, especially neuroblastoma; the typical staining pattern the series reports is negative for CD45, CD20, CD45RO, synaptophysin, chromogranin, cytokeratin and desmin and positive for CD43 and Ulex europaeus I, with von Willebrand factor listed without a sign."
  - "Immunophenotyping of peripheral blood mononuclear cells helped identify the blasts as belonging to the megakaryoblastic lineage, and the authors conclude that this leukemia can be recognized with confidence from its clinical features, its pathologic characteristics, the morphology and immunophenotype of the megakaryoblasts, and the t(1;22) cytogenetic abnormality."
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:1510033
    reference_title: "Acute megakaryoblastic leukemia in infants with t(1;22)(p13;q13) abnormality."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Six infants with acute megakaryoblastic leukemia and a translocation (1;22)(p13;q13) were studied. There were five female infants and one male infant, and the age at initial examination varied from 0.8 to 6.5 months (median, 2.3 months). All the patients had hepatosplenomegaly and anemia (6 to 8.3 g/dL), and four patients had thrombocytopenia (9,000 to 63,000/mm3). The bone marrow showed prominent fibrosis in five cases and reticulin fibrosis in one patient at presentation. ... Biopsy specimens of the liver and lymph node were suggestive of a nonhematopoietic malignant condition because of the cohesiveness of the tumor cells, stromal fibrosis, and the prominent sinusoidal and vascular pattern of infiltration. Immunophenotyping of peripheral blood mononuclear cells was helpful in identifying the blasts as belonging to the megakaryoblastic lineage. Using a panel of mononclonal antibodies, it was also possible to confirm the nature of the infiltration in paraffin sections and to differentiate it from other childhood small round cell tumors, especially neuroblastoma in paraffin sections (typical staining pattern: CD45-, CD43+, vW Factor, Ulex europeus I+, CD20-, CD45RO-, synaptophysin-, chromogranin-, cytokeratin-, desmin-). This special type of infantile acute leukemia can be recognized with confidence if one is aware of its clinical features, peculiar pathologic characteristics, the morphologic features and immunophenotype of the megakaryoblasts, and the unique cytogenetic abnormality."
    explanation: >-
      Primary series of six infants with acute megakaryoblastic leukemia and
      t(1;22)(p13;q13), aged 0.8 to 6.5 months at initial examination. All had
      hepatosplenomegaly, and the marrow showed prominent fibrosis in five and
      reticulin fibrosis in one. Liver and lymph-node biopsy specimens suggested a
      nonhematopoietic malignancy (cohesive tumor cells, stromal fibrosis, a
      sinusoidal and vascular infiltration pattern), and a monoclonal antibody panel
      on paraffin sections confirmed the nature of the infiltrate and differentiated
      it from other childhood small round cell tumors, especially neuroblastoma.
      Because the authors single out neuroblastoma as the tumor the infiltrate had
      to be told apart from, the series supports listing this leukemia among the
      conditions to tell apart from neuroblastoma; the abstract does not report that
      any of the six infants was suspected of having neuroblastoma, and does not say
      how many of them were biopsied. Immunophenotyping of peripheral blood
      mononuclear cells helped assign the blasts to the megakaryoblastic lineage,
      and the authors name the clinical and pathologic features, the megakaryoblast
      morphology and immunophenotype, and the unique cytogenetic abnormality as what
      allows confident recognition. In the quoted staining pattern the infiltrate is
      CD45-negative, and von Willebrand factor is listed without a sign; the quote
      keeps the source's spellings 'mononclonal' and 'europeus'.
  notes: >-
    Bound to MONDO:0018436 because the cited series covers only infants with
    t(1;22)(p13;q13). This knowledge base curates that leukemia as the
    RBM15::MRTFA-Rearranged AMKL subtype of its Acute Megakaryoblastic Leukemia
    entry, which is bound to the broader acute megakaryoblastic leukemia class
    (MONDO:0018872). The row is named after that entry so that it links to it,
    while its preferred term, description and binding keep the narrower t(1;22)
    scope of the evidence.
- name: Alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma
  description: >-
    Rhabdomyosarcoma and neuroblastoma are both small blue round cell tumors of
    childhood and are separated on tissue by lineage markers. Alveolar
    rhabdomyosarcoma involving the bone marrow at presentation may not be
    distinguishable from metastatic neuroblastoma by marrow immunophenotyping: in
    one reported child the marrow held a CD45-negative population positive for CD56,
    a profile reported in both rhabdomyosarcoma and neuroblastoma, and
    immunophenotyping could not rule out neuroblastoma; contrast-enhanced MRI,
    PET-CT and biopsy subsequently established alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma. The marrow
    evidence is a single pediatric case and establishes a diagnostic pitfall rather
    than its frequency in an ARMS population.
  disease_term:
    preferred_term: alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma
    term:
      id: MONDO:0009994
      label: alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma
  distinguishing_features:
  - Nuclear myogenin and MyoD1 staining supports rhabdomyosarcoma; in one series of 72 small blue round cell tumors each was found in 30 of 33 rhabdomyosarcomas, with no significant difference in sensitivity between histological subtypes, and neither showed nuclear staining in any of 12 neuroblastomas. Most neuroblastomas did show fibrillary cytoplasmic staining with the MyoD1 antibody, which the authors suggest may be cross-reaction, so MyoD1 separates the two tumors only when its staining is nuclear.
  - Nuclear PHOX2B staining favors neuroblastoma; PHOX2B immunostaining was negative in every rhabdomyosarcoma tested in one immunohistochemistry study, and a second series, which included ten alveolar rhabdomyosarcomas among its 164 non-neuroblastic tumors, found all 164 negative, with positivity defined as nuclear staining in at least 5% of cells. PHOX2B is not fully sensitive, though; the second series found it in 70 of 76 peripheral neuroblastic tumors (68 of 72 pediatric cases), so a negative stain does not exclude a peripheral neuroblastic tumor.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:41225378
    reference_title: "A case report: pediatric rhabdomyosarcoma presenting with bone marrow metastasis."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Early bone marrow cytology was suggestive of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Further immunophenotyping could not rule out neuroblastoma (NB). Subsequent contrast-enhanced MRI, PET-CT scans, and pathological biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (ARMS). ... Further immunophenotyping revealed that this CD45-negative population was positive for CD9, CD56, and CD81(Fig. 2), a profile that is highly atypical for leukemia but has been reported in certain solid tumors, notably NB and RMS."
    explanation: >-
      Single case report. Early bone marrow cytology suggested AML. Flow-cytometric
      immunophenotyping then found a CD45-negative marrow population positive for
      CD9, CD56 and CD81, a profile the authors note has been reported in both
      neuroblastoma and rhabdomyosarcoma, and it could not rule out neuroblastoma.
      Contrast-enhanced MRI, PET-CT and biopsy subsequently confirmed ARMS. This
      shows that marrow involvement by ARMS may not be distinguishable from
      metastatic neuroblastoma by marrow immunophenotyping. The authors describe the
      case overall as mimicking AML and Henoch-Schönlein purpura; neuroblastoma was
      the differential that immunophenotyping left open. It records a diagnostic
      pitfall in one patient, not how often it happens, and the authors say a single
      case report is limited in how far it generalizes.
  - reference: PMID:41225378
    reference_title: "A case report: pediatric rhabdomyosarcoma presenting with bone marrow metastasis."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "While RMS cells can express the immunophenotype CD45-/CD56+, this pattern alone is insufficient to identify RMS cells as it is present in many types of non-hematopoietic small blue round cell tumors, including NB, among others [18]."
    explanation: >-
      In their discussion, citing earlier work (their reference 18), the authors
      state that the CD45-negative, CD56-positive immunophenotype that RMS cells can
      show is also present in other non-hematopoietic small blue round cell tumors,
      including neuroblastoma, so this pattern alone cannot identify RMS. This
      supports the description's point that the marrow profile is shared, and
      explains why marrow flow cytometry could not separate the two tumors in this
      case. It restates prior literature rather than the case's own result, and it
      is stated for RMS in general rather than ARMS specifically, so the mimicry
      itself follows from it by inference.
  - reference: PMID:7495304
    reference_title: "Expression of myogenic regulatory proteins (myogenin and MyoD1) in small blue round cell tumors of childhood."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "We performed a retrospective immunohistochemical analysis on 72 cases of small blue round cell tumors, including 33 RMSs, 1 metastatic myogenous Wilms' tumor, 26 Ewing's sarcomas/pPNETs, and 12 neuroblastomas. Nuclear expression of myogenin and MyoD1 were both found in 30/33 non-overlapping cases of RMS, with no significant differences in the sensitivity with respect to histological subtypes, and in 1/1 case of myogenous Wilms' tumor. None of the neuroblastomas or Ewing's sarcomas/pPNETs demonstrated positive nuclear staining with either antibody. However, most of the neuroblastomas, and occasional Ewing's sarcomas/pPNETs, showed variable fibrillary, cytoplasmic immunoreactivity with antibody to MyoD1. We conclude that, with the use of microwave-based epitope retrieval, antibodies to myogenin and MyoD1 are both useful markers for the identification of RMS among other small blue round cell tumors of childhood, but antibodies to myogenin have technical advantages over those to MyoD1, as the latter may cross-react with an unknown cytoplasmic antigen in non-muscle cells and tumors."
    explanation: >-
      Retrospective immunohistochemistry, with microwave-based epitope retrieval, on
      72 small blue round cell tumors of childhood. Nuclear myogenin and nuclear
      MyoD1 were each found in 30 of 33 rhabdomyosarcomas, with no significant
      difference in sensitivity between histological subtypes, and none of the 12
      neuroblastomas showed nuclear staining with either antibody. Most
      neuroblastomas showed variable fibrillary cytoplasmic staining with the MyoD1
      antibody, which the authors suggest may be cross-reaction of MyoD1 antibodies
      with an unknown cytoplasmic antigen in non-muscle cells and tumors, so MyoD1
      separates the two tumors only when its staining is nuclear; the authors judge
      that myogenin antibodies have technical advantages over MyoD1 antibodies. The
      33 rhabdomyosarcomas are pooled: the abstract names neither the histological
      subtypes included nor their counts, so applying the result to alveolar
      rhabdomyosarcoma is an inference from the pooled result and the
      no-significant-difference clause, which is why the item is graded INDIRECT.
      The abstract does not define 'non-overlapping', so this item does not claim
      that the same 30 cases were positive for both markers. 'Ewing's sarcoma/pPNET'
      is the paper's older name for Ewing sarcoma.
  - reference: PMID:25822764
    reference_title: "Diagnostic utility of PHOX2B in primary and treated neuroblastoma and in neuroblastoma metastatic to the bone marrow."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "PHOX2B staining was absent in all cases of rhabdomyosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, and Wilms tumor, and in the negative bone marrow. ... PHOX2B is specific for NB in its differential diagnosis with other small round cell tumors, and its nuclear staining may be helpful for accurate bone marrow tumor quantification."
    explanation: >-
      Immunohistochemical study of patient tumor tissue microarrays. PHOX2B staining
      was absent in every rhabdomyosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma and Wilms tumor on the
      comparison arrays, and the authors conclude that PHOX2B is specific for
      neuroblastoma in its differential diagnosis with other small round cell
      tumors. The nuclear staining the abstract describes is that of neuroblastoma
      cells; the comparison tumors showed no staining. The abstract gives no case
      counts for the comparison tumors and does not name the rhabdomyosarcoma
      subtypes tested. It therefore does not show that any alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma
      was among the cases, so applying the result to this subtype is an inference.
  - reference: PMID:28640941
    reference_title: "PHOX2B reliably distinguishes neuroblastoma among small round blue cell tumours."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "We evaluated 240 cases (133 in whole-tissue sections; 107 in tissue microarrays), including 76 peripheral neuroblastic tumours (median age 2 years; including four adults) and 164 other tumours: 44 Wilms tumours; 20 Ewing sarcomas; 10 each of CIC-rearranged round cell sarcomas, poorly differentiated synovial sarcomas, lymphoblastic lymphomas, alveolar rhabdomyosarcomas, embryonal rhabdomyosarcomas, mesenchymal chondrosarcomas, Merkel cell carcinomas, olfactory neuroblastomas, and melanomas; and five each of NUT midline carcinomas and desmoplastic small round cell tumours. ... PHOX2B positivity was defined as the presence of nuclear immunoreactivity in ≥5% of cells. PHOX2B was positive in 70 (92%) peripheral neuroblastic tumours, including 68 of 72 (94%) paediatric and two of four (50%) adult cases. Furthermore, PHOX2B was consistently negative in all non-peripheral neuroblastic tumours, with staining being absent in 160 cases and limited in four cases. ... PHOX2B is a highly sensitive and specific immunohistochemical marker for peripheral neuroblastic tumours, including neuroblastoma. PHOX2B reliably distinguishes neuroblastoma from histological mimics such as Wilms tumour, Ewing sarcoma, and CIC-rearranged round cell sarcoma."
    explanation: >-
      Immunohistochemical series whose 164 comparison tumors included ten alveolar
      and ten embryonal rhabdomyosarcomas, alongside 44 Wilms tumors and 20 Ewing
      sarcomas. With positivity defined as nuclear immunoreactivity in at least 5%
      of cells, PHOX2B was negative in all of them, and the authors conclude that it
      is a highly sensitive and specific marker for peripheral neuroblastic tumors,
      including neuroblastoma; the mimics their final sentence names are Wilms
      tumor, Ewing sarcoma and CIC-rearranged round cell sarcoma, not
      rhabdomyosarcoma. Staining was absent in 160 comparison cases and limited in
      four, and the abstract does not say which tumor types the four were, so the
      series shows these tumors were PHOX2B-negative by that threshold, not that
      staining was absent in every one. Because the comparison set names both
      rhabdomyosarcoma subtypes, the result applies to alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma
      directly, on ten cases. PHOX2B was positive in 70 of the 76 peripheral
      neuroblastic tumors, 68 of 72 pediatric and two of four adult cases, so a
      negative stain does not exclude a peripheral neuroblastic tumor; the abstract
      does not say which tumor types the four negative pediatric cases were.
- name: Ewing sarcoma
  description: >-
    In its section on clinical and radiological diagnosis, the GEIS clinical
    practice guideline lists metastatic neuroblastoma among the differential
    diagnoses of Ewing sarcoma, with osteomyelitis, osteosarcoma, lymphoma, leukemia
    and Langerhans cell histiocytosis. On tissue both are small round cell tumors,
    and Ewing sarcoma is a differential diagnosis of poorly differentiated
    neuroblastoma.
  disease_term:
    preferred_term: Ewing sarcoma
    term:
      id: MONDO:0012817
      label: Ewing sarcoma
  distinguishing_features:
  - Nuclear PHOX2B staining favors neuroblastoma; in one immunohistochemistry study PHOX2B immunostaining was negative in every Ewing sarcoma tested, and its authors call PHOX2B specific for neuroblastoma in its differential diagnosis with other small round cell tumors. A second series found all 20 Ewing sarcomas among its comparison tumors negative, with positivity defined as nuclear staining in at least 5% of cells, and its authors conclude that PHOX2B reliably distinguishes neuroblastoma from mimics such as Ewing sarcoma. PHOX2B is not fully sensitive, though; that series found it in 70 of 76 peripheral neuroblastic tumors (68 of 72 pediatric cases), so a negative stain does not exclude a peripheral neuroblastic tumor.
  - CD99 immunonegativity is one of the features that help distinguish neuroblastoma from other small round cell tumors, and NKX2.2 is described as a marker of Ewing sarcoma, a differential of poorly differentiated neuroblastoma; one metastatic neuroblastoma has nonetheless been reported as immunoreactive for both on cytology of the metastatic site, and its authors stress evaluating the primary site because cytology has limits.
  - Ewing sarcoma cells show intense, diffuse membranous CD99 and nuclear NKX2.2 immunoreactivity, but the GEIS guideline notes that neither marker is entirely specific for Ewing sarcoma and that genetic confirmation is required for the diagnosis; every Ewing sarcoma harbors a FET-ETS fusion.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:39158802
    reference_title: "Clinical practice guidelines for the treatment of Ewing sarcoma (Spanish Sarcoma Research Group-GEIS)."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: "Differential diagnosis should include osteomyelitis, osteosarcoma, lymphoma, leukemia, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, and metastatic neuroblastoma."
    explanation: >-
      The Spanish Sarcoma Research Group (GEIS) clinical practice guideline,
      developed by a multidisciplinary panel, says the differential diagnosis of
      Ewing sarcoma should include metastatic neuroblastoma, along with
      osteomyelitis, osteosarcoma, lymphoma, leukemia and Langerhans cell
      histiocytosis. The sentence is in the guideline's section headed Clinical and
      radiological diagnosis, after its description of how Ewing sarcoma looks on
      radiography, CT and MRI and before its biopsy recommendations. It carries no
      citation or evidence grade, so it is the panel's own recommendation rather
      than reported patient data. Neuroblastoma is mentioned nowhere else in the
      guideline's text: its separate pathology differential, for tumors with small
      round-cell morphology, names round cell sarcoma with EWSR1 non-ETS fusion,
      CIC-rearranged sarcoma and sarcoma with a BCOR genetic alteration, and the
      guideline does not say which findings separate metastatic neuroblastoma from
      Ewing sarcoma. Its immunohistochemical and genetic criteria for Ewing sarcoma
      itself are quoted in the next item.
  - reference: PMID:39158802
    reference_title: "Clinical practice guidelines for the treatment of Ewing sarcoma (Spanish Sarcoma Research Group-GEIS)."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: "Immunohistochemically, neoplastic cells show a membranous pattern of intense and diffuse CD99 expression (Fig. 1B) and NKX2.2 nuclear immunoreactivity (Fig. 1C). However, it is important to note that CD99 and NKX2.2 are not entirely specific for ES ... Genetic confirmation is required for ES diagnosis. ... All cases of ES harbor a FET-ETS fusion."
    explanation: >-
      In its account of Ewing sarcoma pathology, the GEIS guideline states that the
      tumor cells show intense, diffuse membranous CD99 and nuclear NKX2.2
      immunoreactivity, that
      neither marker is entirely specific for Ewing sarcoma, that genetic
      confirmation is required for the diagnosis, and that every Ewing sarcoma
      harbors a FET-ETS fusion. These are the guideline's criteria for Ewing
      sarcoma itself; its text does not set them against neuroblastoma. They bear on
      this differential because the case report cited in this row describes a
      metastatic neuroblastoma that was immunoreactive for both CD99 and NKX2.2.
      The sentences are the guideline's synthesis of published work, with no
      patient data of its own.

    reference_title: "CD99 and NKX2.2 positive neuroblastoma diagnosed on cytology: A potential diagnostic pitfall and necessity of pathological evaluation of the primary site."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "CD99 immunonegativity is one of the features, which helps in distinguishing neuroblastoma from other small round cell tumors. NKX2.2 is a specific marker of Ewing sarcoma, which is a differential for poorly differentiated neuroblastoma."
    explanation: >-
      The case report's framing sentences restate established immunohistochemistry

    reference_title: "CD99 and NKX2.2 positive neuroblastoma diagnosed on cytology: A potential diagnostic pitfall and necessity of pathological evaluation of the primary site."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Here, we present a case of metastatic neuroblastoma showing immunoreactivity for both CD99 and NKX2.2 on cytology of the metastatic site causing diagnostic dilemma. Biopsy study of the adrenal lesion revealed presence of differentiating cells and neuropil, highlighting the importance of evaluation of the primary site and limitation of cytology."
    explanation: >-
      A single case report: a metastatic neuroblastoma was immunoreactive for both
      CD99 and NKX2.2 on cytology of the metastatic site, which caused a diagnostic
      dilemma. On the report's own framing both results argue against neuroblastoma,
      because CD99 immunonegativity is listed as a neuroblastoma feature and NKX2.2
      is called a specific marker of Ewing sarcoma. Biopsy of the adrenal lesion
      showed differentiating cells and neuropil, and the authors stress the
      importance of evaluating the primary site given the limitation of cytology.
      One case shows that the pitfall exists, not how often it occurs.

- name: Hepatoblastoma
  description: >-
    A review of infantile hepatic hemangioma lists metastatic neuroblastoma,
    hepatoblastoma and mesenchymal hamartoma among the primary differential
    diagnoses of a focal liver lesion in an infant that may be a focal hemangioma,
    so both tumors are considered when an infant has a focal liver lesion. A
    pedunculated hepatoblastoma, attached to the liver by a vascular pedicle and
    presenting as a perihepatic mass, can also be taken for neuroblastoma: in one
    reported four-month-old infant, a hepatoblastoma in the left upper quadrant was
    first suspected to be neuroblastoma on abdominal ultrasound. That presentation
    rests on a single case and establishes a diagnostic pitfall rather than its
    frequency.
  disease_term:
    preferred_term: hepatoblastoma
    term:
      id: MONDO:0018666
      label: hepatoblastoma
  distinguishing_features:
  - In the reported four-month-old, bone marrow aspiration and 24-hour urinary VMA and HVA were negative for neuroblastoma; with CT showing nutrient vessels entering the mass from the left hepatic vein, coarse calcification and its enhancement pattern, pedunculated hepatoblastoma was suggested, serum AFP was above 100,000 ng/ml (the report's normal range is 5-109), and percutaneous biopsy confirmed hepatoblastoma.
  - The case report's authors conclude that pedunculated hepatoblastoma should be considered when a perihepatic mass in a child can be confused with other upper abdominal masses such as an adrenal mass, and that the vascular pedicle should then be looked for on imaging and the AFP check kept in mind.
  - A 2006 management review states that histology is essential for differential diagnosis and may be omitted only in some hepatoblastoma patients of the typical age (6 months to 3 years) with an excessively elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:27610342
    reference_title: "History of the infantile hepatic hemangioma: From imaging to generating a differential diagnosis."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: "The primary differential diagnoses include metastatic neuroblastoma, hepatoblastoma (Figure 5) and mesenchymal hamartoma (Figure 6). Primary sites of neuroblastoma (adrenal glands, organ of Zuckerkandel and paraspinal chain) should be evaluated and the urine samples should be screened for the presence of catecholamines. If the above results are unremarkable, the lesion demonstrates hyper enhancement (either on multiphase CT with iodinated contrast or MRI with gadolinium based contrast material) and there is no invasion of other structures, then a presumptive focal IHHs may be diagnosed but should still be monitored to ensure there is no further growth."
    explanation: >-
      This review of infantile hepatic hemangioma lists metastatic neuroblastoma,
      hepatoblastoma and mesenchymal hamartoma among the primary differential
      diagnoses of a focal liver lesion in an infant that may be a focal infantile
      hepatic hemangioma. Because metastatic neuroblastoma and hepatoblastoma appear
      in the same differential for that presentation, hepatoblastoma is a
      differential of neuroblastoma; the quote does not state that pairing itself,
      so the link is one inference step. The review then recommends evaluating the
      neuroblastoma primary sites (adrenal glands, organ of Zuckerkandl, paraspinal
      chain) and screening urine for catecholamines, which is the work-up that tests
      for neuroblastoma; if those results are unremarkable, the lesion hyperenhances
      on multiphase CT or MRI and no other structure is invaded, a presumptive focal
      hemangioma may then be diagnosed and monitored for further growth. The advice
      is scoped to that presumptive diagnosis, not to every infant liver lesion, so
      this row uses the item only for the shared differential of a focal liver
      lesion in an infant. The passage is the review's own diagnostic
      recommendation and reports no data; the quote keeps the source's spelling
      'Zuckerkandel'.
  - reference: PMID:36997898
    reference_title: "Giant pedunculated hepatoblastoma mimicking neuroblastoma in a 4-month-old infant: a case report."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Here, we report a case of asymptomatic giant palpable hepatoblastoma in the LUQ of a four-month-old male infant, initially suspected of neuroblastoma based on abdominal ultrasound findings. The final diagnosis of giant pedunculated hepatoblastoma was made based on the abdominal CT scan and the diagnosis was confirmed by percutaneous biopsy. ... To rule in or rule out the diagnosis of neuroblastoma, bone marrow aspiration and 24-hour urine collection (VMA and HVA) were performed, which were negative. ... According to the negative results for neuroblastoma and considering the entry of nutrient vessels into the mass from the left hepatic vein and the coarse calcification areas and the pattern of enhancement, pedunculated hepatoblastoma was suggested and AFP was measured which was more than 100,000 ng/ml (normal 5-109)."
    explanation: >-
      Single case report. A pedunculated hepatoblastoma in the left upper quadrant
      of a four-month-old infant was first suspected to be neuroblastoma on
      abdominal ultrasound. Bone marrow aspiration and 24-hour urinary VMA and HVA
      were negative for neuroblastoma. Given those results and the imaging, which
      showed nutrient vessels entering the mass from the left hepatic vein, coarse
      calcification and the mass's enhancement pattern, pedunculated hepatoblastoma
      was suggested; serum AFP was then above 100,000 ng/ml, and percutaneous biopsy
      confirmed hepatoblastoma. The abstract attributes the final diagnosis to the
      abdominal CT scan. It documents neuroblastoma as a real diagnostic pitfall
      when a pedunculated hepatoblastoma presents as a perihepatic upper abdominal
      mass in a young infant. It does not show how often the confusion occurs.
  - reference: PMID:36997898
    reference_title: "Giant pedunculated hepatoblastoma mimicking neuroblastoma in a 4-month-old infant: a case report."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Pedunculated hepatoblastoma is rare but should be considered as a possibility in the case of a perihepatic mass in a pediatric patient that can be confused with other upper abdominal masses such as an adrenal mass. Therefore, in such cases, we must look for the vascular pedicle in the imaging and keep the AFP check in mind."
    explanation: >-
      The case report's conclusion: pedunculated hepatoblastoma is rare but should
      be considered when a perihepatic mass in a pediatric patient can be confused
      with other upper abdominal masses such as an adrenal mass, and in such cases
      the vascular pedicle should be looked for on imaging and the AFP check kept in
      mind. In this report the mass was first taken for neuroblastoma; the nutrient
      vessels entering it from the left hepatic vein were among the findings that
      led to the suggestion of hepatoblastoma, and AFP, measured next, was above
      100,000 ng/ml. It is the authors' recommendation from a single case, not a
      measured diagnostic accuracy.
  - reference: PMID:16458842
    reference_title: "Management of liver tumors in childhood."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT

    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: "Histological diagnosis is essential for differential diagnosis and may only be omitted in some hepatoblastoma patients of the typical age (6 months to 3 years) with an excessively elevated serum-alpha-fetoprotein."
    explanation: >-
      A 2006 review of pediatric liver-tumor management states that histology is
      essential for differential diagnosis and may be omitted only in some
      hepatoblastoma patients of the typical age (6 months to 3 years) with an
      excessively elevated serum AFP. The review covers primary liver tumors and
      does not name neuroblastoma, so applying it here is an inference: outside that
      narrow exception, histology is what settles the differential diagnosis,
      including between hepatoblastoma and neuroblastoma.
- name: Pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma
  description: >-
    The catecholamine-producing tumors of childhood include most notably
    neuroblastoma, but also pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PPGL). Neuroblastoma
    is the more common of the two in children, and because the clinical presentations can
    overlap the two can be difficult to tell apart: in the German GPOH-MET registry,
    five children and adolescents with a final diagnosis of PPGL, one of them a
    composite pheochromocytoma and neuroblastoma, had first been mistaken for
    neuroblastoma. Four of the five presented with clinical signs and symptoms of
    catecholamine excess; urine tests, done in two, indicated possible catecholamine
    excess, and plasma metanephrines were measured in none. In one pediatric
    immunohistochemistry series PHOX2B was diffusely expressed in all 23
    pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas as well as in all 65 peripheral
    neuroblastic tumors, so in that series a positive PHOX2B stain did not by itself
    separate the two. Series disagree on how often PPGL stain for PHOX2B, though: in
    another immunohistochemistry series, whose abstract does not give the patients'
    ages, Phox2b was expressed in all neuroblastomas, ganglioneuroblastomas and
    ganglioneuromas and in 40% of its 35 paragangliomas, but in none of its 21
    pheochromocytomas, and a 2024 review describes the results of PHOX2B
    immunohistochemistry in pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma as conflicting.
  disease_term:
    preferred_term: pheochromocytoma-paraganglioma
    term:
      id: MONDO:0035540
      label: pheochromocytoma-paraganglioma
  distinguishing_features:
  - "The work-up differs: neuroblastoma diagnosis depends largely on biopsy-dependent histopathology, whereas percutaneous biopsy of a PPGL is potentially dangerous and contraindicated, and PPGL is diagnosed by biochemical tests of catecholamine excess, with urinary or plasma metanephrines the recommended tests; the homovanillic acid (HVA) and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) measurements on which biochemical testing for neuroblastoma still largely relies are no longer recommended for PPGL."
  - "Plasma dopamine and norepinephrine metabolite measurements alone may not separate the two in every child, because both tumors show overlapping increases in these metabolites. On imaging, calcification and encasement, invasion or infiltration are relatively common in neuroblastoma and far less so in PPGL, so they offer clues favoring neuroblastoma, although calcification can occasionally occur in PPGL and there can be exceptions."
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:35784570
    reference_title: "Adrenocortical Tumors and Pheochromocytoma/Paraganglioma Initially Mistaken as Neuroblastoma-Experiences From the GPOH-MET Registry."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "We herein report data on 10 children and adolescents with ACT and five with PCC/PGL, previously mistaken as NBL. ... Four (4/5) patients with a final diagnosis of PCC/PGL presented with clinical signs and symptoms of catecholamine excess. Urine tests indicated possible catecholamine excess in two patients, while no testing was carried out in three patients. Measurements of plasma metanephrines were not performed in any patient. ... In five out of 15 patients suspected to have NBL, subsequent histological findings confirmed a PGL in three out of five cases, PCC and PGL in another, and a composite PCC and NBL in the fifth case (Table 2)."
    explanation: >-
      In a retrospective analysis of the GPOH-MET registry of malignant endocrine
      tumors in children (the full text expands the name as the German Pediatric
      Oncology Hematology-Malignant Endocrine Tumor database), five children and
      adolescents with a final diagnosis of pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma
      (PCC/PGL) had first been taken for neuroblastoma. The full-text results add
      that the five tumors were three paragangliomas, one pheochromocytoma with
      paraganglioma, and one composite pheochromocytoma and neuroblastoma, so one of
      the five did contain neuroblastoma. Four of the five presented with clinical
      signs and symptoms of catecholamine excess. Urine tests, done in two,
      indicated possible catecholamine excess; no testing was done in the other
      three, and plasma metanephrines were measured in none. This supports the
      description's statements that PCC/PGL can be mistaken for neuroblastoma even
      when catecholamine excess is clinically evident, and that the biochemical
      work-up in these cases was incomplete. It is a five-patient registry subset,
      so it documents a diagnostic pitfall, not a misdiagnosis rate.
  - reference: PMID:35957826
    reference_title: "Biochemical Diagnosis of Catecholamine-Producing Tumors of Childhood: Neuroblastoma, Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Catecholamine-producing tumors of childhood include most notably neuroblastoma, but also pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PPGL). Diagnosis of the former depends largely on biopsy-dependent histopathology, but this is contraindicated in PPGL where diagnosis depends crucially on biochemical tests of catecholamine excess. Such tests retain some importance in neuroblastoma though continue to largely rely on measurements of homovanillic acid (HVA) and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA), which are no longer recommended for PPGL. For PPGL, urinary or plasma metanephrines are the recommended most accurate tests. ... Neuroblastoma is more common in children than PPGL and since clinical presentations can overlap, there can be difficulties in the differential diagnosis of the two tumor entities (22). ... Though commonly employed for neuroblastoma, percutaneous biopsy of a PPGL is potentially dangerous and is therefore contraindicated for those tumors (82, 83). ... Since both PPGL and neuroblastoma show overlapping patterns of increases in plasma dopamine and norepinephrine metabolites, as well as in some cases the precursor catecholamines themselves, these measurements alone are unlikely to offer a solution for differential diagnosis in all pediatric cases of these tumors. ... Differences in imaging features between neuroblastoma and PPGL, such as presence of calcifications in the former, could also offer clues to help distinguish the two types of tumors (93). However, calcifications can occasionally occur in PPGL (94). Imaging characteristics of encasement, invasion and infiltration are relatively common in neuroblastoma (95), but far less so in PPGL and might thereby offer other clues to differentiate the two tumor types. Nevertheless, as indicated in the case series covered in this issue, there can be exceptions."
    explanation: >-
      This review of the biochemical diagnosis of childhood catecholamine-producing
      tumors names neuroblastoma and PPGL as such tumors and says neuroblastoma
      diagnosis depends largely on biopsy-dependent histopathology, which is
      contraindicated in PPGL, where diagnosis depends on biochemical tests of
      catecholamine excess: urinary or plasma metanephrines are the recommended
      tests, and HVA and VMA are no longer recommended for PPGL. The full text adds
      that neuroblastoma is more common in children than PPGL, and that percutaneous
      biopsy, though commonly employed for neuroblastoma, is potentially dangerous
      in PPGL and therefore contraindicated. It also says that because both tumors
      show overlapping rises in plasma dopamine and norepinephrine metabolites,
      these measurements alone are unlikely to separate them in every child, and
      that on imaging calcification and encasement, invasion or infiltration are
      clues favoring neuroblastoma, though calcification occasionally occurs in PPGL
      and there can be exceptions. These are the authors' synthesis of published
      work, with no patient series of their own, and they do not say that
      biochemistry as a whole cannot separate the two tumors.
  - reference: PMID:28986989
    reference_title: "Utility of Phox2b immunohistochemical stain in neural crest tumours and non-neural crest tumours in paediatric patients."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Phox2b was expressed diffusely in pNT (n = 65 of 65), strongly in NB-UD and NB-PD and with less intensity in NB-D, GNB and GN. ... PCC/PG expressed diffuse Phox2b (n = 23 of 23) and diffuse TH, except for one tumour (n = 22 of 23). ... Phox2b was a specific and sensitive marker for pNT and PCC/PG, especially useful for identifying NB-UD often lacking TH."
    explanation: >-
      In this pediatric immunohistochemistry series, Phox2b was diffusely expressed
      in all 65 peripheral neuroblastic tumors (neuroblastoma subtypes,
      ganglioneuroblastoma and ganglioneuroma) and in all 23
      pheochromocytomas/paragangliomas, and the authors conclude that it is a
      specific and sensitive marker for both groups. By 'specific' the authors mean
      specific for neural crest tumors with neuronal or neuroendocrine
      differentiation, a category that contains both groups, not that the stain
      tells them apart. Because every tumor in both groups was positive, a positive
      PHOX2B stain did not by itself separate neuroblastoma from PPGL in this
      series. The authors do not state this; it follows from the two staining
      results, so the item is graded INDIRECT. The abstract pools pheochromocytoma
      with paraganglioma, does not say whether the paragangliomas were sympathetic
      or head-and-neck tumors, and reports staining intensity only for the
      neuroblastic tumors, so it does not compare intensity between the two groups.
      All tumors were from children, so the result does not show how uniformly adult
      PPGL stain.
  - reference: PMID:23715162
    reference_title: "A study of gata3 and phox2b expression in tumors of the autonomic nervous system."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Anti-Phox2b and anti-Gata3 antibodies were applied to a total of 77 autonomic nervous system tumors, including 35 paragangliomas, 21 pheochromocytomas, 9 neuroblastomas, 4 ganglioneuroblastomas, and 8 ganglioneuromas, as well as their potential morphologic mimics, including tumors of the small round cell tumor group, neuroendocrine carcinomas of lung and gastrointestinal tract (carcinoid tumors/neuroendocrine tumors, large cell neuroendocrine carcinomas, and small cell carcinomas), Merkel cell carcinomas, benign and malignant tumors of thyroid, parathyroid, and adrenal cortex, and malignant melanomas. ... Phox2b expression was seen in all neuroblastomas, ganglioneuroblastomas, and ganglioneuromas and in 40% of paragangliomas, but pheochromocytomas and all other tumors were negative. ... Phox2b is also highly specific, but its low sensitivity to paragangliomas and pheochromocytomas would limit the utility only to neuroblastic tumors."
    explanation: >-
      Immunohistochemical study of 77 autonomic nervous system tumors, among them
      35 paragangliomas, 21 pheochromocytomas, 9 neuroblastomas, 4
      ganglioneuroblastomas and 8 ganglioneuromas, together with their morphologic
      mimics. Phox2b was expressed in every neuroblastoma, ganglioneuroblastoma and
      ganglioneuroma and in 40% of the paragangliomas, but in none of the
      pheochromocytomas, and the authors conclude that its low sensitivity for
      paragangliomas and pheochromocytomas limits its usefulness to neuroblastic
      tumors. This differs from the pediatric series cited above for this row, in
      which all 23 pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas stained, and supports the
      description's statement that series disagree. The abstract does not give the
      patients' ages, so the series cannot be taken to be pediatric, and it does not
      say where the paragangliomas arose or how strongly they stained.
  - reference: PMID:38458747
    reference_title: "PHOX2B: a diagnostic cornerstone in neurocristopathies and neuroblastomas."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "The utility of PHOX2B immunohistochemistry in pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma has also been studied but yields conflicting results."
    explanation: >-
      A 2024 review of PHOX2B in neurocristopathies and neuroblastic tumors states
      that PHOX2B immunohistochemistry in pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma has been
      studied but yields conflicting results. It supports the description's
      statement that series disagree on PHOX2B staining in PPGL. The abstract does
      not name the conflicting studies or say how often PPGL stain, and the sentence
      is the authors' summary of published work, with no patient series of their
      own.
  notes: >-
    Bound to MONDO:0035540, the disease term of this knowledge base's
    Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma entry; the row covers both tumors because
    each cited source discusses both.
- name: Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy
  description: >-
    Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy (MNTI) contains nests of
    neuroblastic cells, and the authors of one series distinguish it from metastatic
    neuroblastoma, as well as from melanoma, by its morphology and immunophenotype.
    In that series of 20 cases the patients were 1 to 9 months old and typically
    presented with a rapidly growing mass, 13 tumors arose in the maxilla, and the
    tumors were made up of tubular or alveolar formations of large
    melanin-containing cells around nests of smaller neuroblastic cells with scant
    or fibrillar cytoplasm.
  disease_term:
    preferred_term: melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy
    term:
      id: MONDO:0002072
      label: melanotic neuroectodermal tumor
  distinguishing_features:
  - "The authors of the series conclude that its distinctive morphology, with tubular or alveolar formations of large melanin-containing cells around nests of smaller neuroblastic cells, and its multiphenotypic epithelial, neural and melanocytic expression distinguish it from metastatic neuroblastoma. All 12 tumors studied immunohistochemically were positive for cytokeratin and for HMB 45, and no staining was found for chromogranin; neural markers were also expressed (neuron-specific enolase in seven of 12 tumors, Leu 7 in nine of 12, synaptophysin in four of 12). The series included no neuroblastomas, so it does not report how neuroblastoma itself stains."
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:8392815
    reference_title: "Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy. Clinicopathological, immunohistochemical, and flow cytometric study."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Twenty cases of melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy (MNTI) are reported. The patients (13 females, seven males), whose ages ranged from 1 to 9 months (mean, 5 months), typically presented with a rapidly growing mass. Tumor sites included the maxilla (13 cases), mandible (three cases), dura (two cases), brain (one case), and skull/orbit (one case). ... Histologic appearance was distinctive, with tubular or alveolar formations of large melanin-containing cells around nests of smaller neuroblastic cells possessing scant or fibrillar cytoplasm. Twelve tumors were studied immunohistochemically; tumor was positive for cytokeratin in 12 of 12, for HMB 45 in 12 of 12, for vimentin in seven of eight, and for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) in four of nine tumors, mainly in the large cells. Neuron-specific enolase (NSE) (seven of 12) and Leu 7 (nine of 12) were positive in small and large cells; some tumors also expressed synaptophysin (four of 12), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP, three of 12 tumors), or S-100 protein (two of 12 tumors). No staining was found for chromogranin, desmin, or carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA). ... Distinctive morphology and multiphenotypic (epithelial, neural, melanocytic) expression distinguish MNTI from melanoma and metastatic neuroblastoma."
    explanation: >-
      Kapadia and colleagues report a clinicopathological and immunohistochemical
      series of 20 MNTI cases. The patients were infants aged 1 to 9 months, and 13
      of the 20 tumors arose in the maxilla. Histology showed large
      melanin-containing cells around nests of smaller neuroblastic cells. All 12
      tumors studied immunohistochemically were positive for cytokeratin and HMB 45.
      Neuron-specific enolase (seven of 12), Leu 7 (nine of 12) and, in some tumors,
      synaptophysin (four of 12) were also expressed. No staining was found for
      chromogranin; the abstract does not say how many tumors were tested for it.
      The authors conclude that this distinctive morphology and multiphenotypic
      (epithelial, neural, melanocytic) expression distinguish MNTI from melanoma
      and metastatic neuroblastoma. The series contains no neuroblastoma cases, so
      it supports the MNTI features the authors use to separate the two, not any
      statement about how neuroblastoma itself stains.
imaging_findings:
- name: MIBG-Avid Disease
  modality: OTHER
  frequency: VERY_FREQUENT
  description: >-
    Uptake of MIBG at the sites of disease, primary and metastatic, on 123I-MIBG
    scintigraphy. Neuroblastoma cells typically express the norepinephrine
    transporter (NET), which mediates active MIBG uptake in about 90% of
    patients; in a Cochrane review, about 10% of histologically proven
    neuroblastomas did not accumulate 123I-MIBG (recorded separately as
    MIBG-Nonavid Disease). In a small COG series of high-risk patients, the
    percentage of tumor cells expressing NET protein was higher in avid than
    nonavid tumors (P = 0.027), but the groups overlapped widely, including an
    avid tumor with no NET-expressing cells; NET mRNA measured by quantitative
    PCR did not differ significantly (P = 0.31), and neither did VMAT1 or VMAT2
    mRNA. In a later COG immunohistochemistry study of tumors from 76 patients
    with high-risk metastatic disease, avid tumors had higher composite VMAT2
    protein scores than nonavid tumors (median 216 vs 45, P = 0.04), with
    substantial overlap between the groups, while VMAT1 protein showed no
    association. In a 23-patient expression-array subset of a 343-patient COG
    cohort, NET mRNA was lower in nonavid tumors at borderline significance (P =
    0.052) while VMAT2 mRNA did not differ; the authors note that this NET
    result is contrary to their earlier PCR result and may reflect differences
    in methodology or tumor material.
  imaging_finding_term:
    preferred_term: increased 123I-MIBG uptake (MIBG avidity)
    term:
      id: NCIT:C79553
      label: Increased Uptake by 123-Iodine-Meta-Iodobenzylguanidine Scintigraphy
  notes: >-
    modality is OTHER because the whole-body survey in 123I-MIBG imaging is
    planar scintigraphy, which ImagingModalityEnum does not list. SPECT or
    SPECT/CT, which the enum does list, is often added over selected regions,
    such as the chest and abdomen or sites where tumor must be told apart from
    physiological uptake, and does not replace the whole-body images.
    NCIT:C79553 is specific to 123I-MIBG, the INRG Task Force's
    radiopharmaceutical of choice in children; two of the COG transporter
    studies cited here (PMID:23050139, PMID:26338179) read avidity from
    diagnostic 123I- or 131I-MIBG scans obtained by local institutional
    practice, and the third (PMID:28383813) does not state the isotope. NCIT has
    no isotope-neutral or 131I uptake finding to bind instead: OLS NCIT searches
    on 2026-10-21 for "MIBG uptake" and "MIBG scintigraphy" returned NCIT:C79553
    as the only finding term, "131I-MIBG" returned only the tracer NCIT:C970
    Iobenguane I-131, and "MIBG avid" returned nothing.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:28471719
    reference_title: "Revisions to the International Neuroblastoma Response Criteria: A Consensus Statement From the National Cancer Institute Clinical Trials Planning Meeting."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Neuroblastoma is a tumor derived from the sympathetic nervous system, and neuroblastoma cells typically express the norepinephrine transporter, which mediates active intracellular uptake of radiolabeled MIBG in approximately 90% of patients"
    explanation: >-
      This 2017 National Cancer Institute consensus statement revising the
      International Neuroblastoma Response Criteria states that neuroblastoma
      cells typically express the norepinephrine transporter (NET), which
      mediates active MIBG uptake in approximately 90% of patients. That places
      MIBG avidity in the very frequent band (80-99% of patients) and names NET
      as the uptake route. The figure is restated from a cited earlier source,
      not measured by the consensus group, and it counts patients whose tumour
      takes up MIBG, not patients with metastases.
  - reference: PMID:26417712
    reference_title: "123I-MIBG scintigraphy and 18F-FDG-PET imaging for diagnosing neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "As described both in the literature and in this review, in about 10% of the patients with histologically proven neuroblastoma the tumour does not accumulate ¹²³I-MIBG (false negative results)."
    explanation: >-
      This Cochrane diagnostic test accuracy review of 11 studies in children
      concludes that in about 10% of patients with histologically proven
      neuroblastoma the tumour does not take up 123I-MIBG, giving a
      false-negative scan. The figure is approximate, combining earlier
      literature with the review's own crude total false-negative rate of 11% in
      608 patients (no pooled estimate was possible), and per-study sensitivity
      ranged from 67% to 100%. The review also notes that physiological uptake
      can make small lesions less visible, so some false-negative scans may
      reflect missed lesions.
  - reference: PMID:23050139
    reference_title: "Evaluation of Norepinephrine Transporter Expression and Metaiodobenzylguanidine Avidity in Neuroblastoma: A Report from the Children's Oncology Group."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Median NET mRNA expression level for the 19 MIBG avid patients was 12.9% (range 1.6-73.7%) versus 5.9% (range 0.6-110.0%) for the 8 nonavid patients (P = 0.31). Median percent NET protein expression was 50% (range 0-100%) in MIBG avid patients compared to 10% (range 0-80%) in nonavid patients (P = 0.027)."
    explanation: >-
      This Children's Oncology Group study compared NET expression in archived
      tumour samples with centrally reviewed diagnostic 123I- or 131I-MIBG
      scans. The percentage of tumour cells staining for NET protein was higher
      in MIBG-avid than nonavid tumours (median 50% vs 10%, P = 0.027), whereas
      NET mRNA did not differ significantly (P = 0.31). Numbers were small, and
      both comparisons used only high-risk patients: 27 for mRNA (19 avid, 8
      nonavid) and 23 for protein (15 avid, 8 nonavid). Protein values
      overlapped widely, so the difference holds only at group level.
  - reference: PMID:23050139
    reference_title: "Evaluation of Norepinephrine Transporter Expression and Metaiodobenzylguanidine Avidity in Neuroblastoma: A Report from the Children's Oncology Group."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "However, these two groups showed extensive overlap in the distribution of the percent of tumor cells expressing NET, including one MIBG-avid patient with 0% NET expression"
    explanation: >-
      In a Children's Oncology Group study, 23 high-risk patients from trial
      A3973 had NET immunohistochemistry and centrally reviewed diagnostic
      123I- or 131I-MIBG scans (15 avid, 8 nonavid). The percentage of tumour
      cells expressing NET overlapped extensively between avid and nonavid
      tumours, and one MIBG-avid patient's tumour had 0% NET-expressing cells;
      the authors say this raises the possibility that factors besides NET
      protein may influence MIBG uptake. Limitations: the subset is small, and
      avid tumours still had a higher median percentage of NET-expressing cells
      (50% vs 10%, P = 0.027).
  - reference: PMID:23050139
    reference_title: "Evaluation of Norepinephrine Transporter Expression and Metaiodobenzylguanidine Avidity in Neuroblastoma: A Report from the Children's Oncology Group."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "While the median VMAT1 and VMAT2 expression levels were higher in MIBG avid tumors, none of these differences were statistically significant (P > 0.10 for all comparisons; Table 4)."
    explanation: >-
      In 27 high-risk patients from COG A3973 with centrally reviewed diagnostic
      123I- or 131I-MIBG scans (19 avid, 8 nonavid), tumour VMAT1 and VMAT2 mRNA
      measured by quantitative PCR did not differ significantly by avidity,
      although median VMAT2 mRNA was higher in avid tumours (175% vs 27% of PGK1
      expression; Table 4). The comparison is small, and in the same study NET
      mRNA correlated poorly with NET protein (correlation coefficient 0.22), so
      this mRNA result does not test the later VMAT2 protein association.
  - reference: PMID:26338179
    reference_title: "Vesicular monoamine transporter protein expression correlates with clinical features, tumor biology, and MIBG avidity in neuroblastoma: a report from the Children's Oncology Group."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "VMAT1 expression intensity category, percent of cells positive for VMAT1, and VMAT1 composite expression score were not associated with MIBG avidity (Table 2 and Fig 2b). For VMAT2, expression intensity category was not statistically associated with MIBG avidity. However, MIBG avid tumors had significantly higher VMAT2 composite expression scores compared to MIBG non-avid tumors, though there was substantial overlap between groups (median 216 vs. 45; p = 0.04; Table 2 and Fig 2c)."
    explanation: >-
      In a retrospective immunohistochemistry study of tumours from 76 patients
      with high-risk metastatic neuroblastoma on COG A3973 (centrally reviewed
      diagnostic 123I- or 131I-MIBG scans; cohort enriched with 20 nonavid
      tumours), VMAT1 was not associated with avidity on any measure (assessed
      in 74), and neither was the VMAT2 intensity category (p = 0.26), but the
      VMAT2 composite expression score was higher in avid tumours, with
      substantial overlap between the groups (median 216 vs 45, p = 0.04). VMAT2
      also correlated with NET expression, so the association may not be
      independent of NET.
  - reference: PMID:28383813
    reference_title: "MIBG avidity correlates with clinical features, tumor biology, and outcomes in neuroblastoma: A report from the Children's Oncology Group."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Of the membrane transporters investigated, only expression for the gene encoding NET differed between MIBG avid versus. nonavid tumors (Fig. 3). The median NET mRNA expression was 9.1 (range 6.3-10.1) for MIBG avid tumors versus 7.6 (range 6.1-8.6) for MIBG non-avid tumors (P =0.052)."
    explanation: >-
      In the secondary gene-expression analysis of this retrospective Children's
      Oncology Group cohort (23 patients, 18 MIBG-avid and 5 nonavid, with
      TARGET Affymetrix HuEx array data), median NET mRNA was 7.6 in nonavid
      versus 9.1 in avid tumours; Welch t-tests on log2-transformed values gave
      P = 0.052. The authors call NET the only transporter gene whose expression
      differed, but the paper states no significance threshold, and this P value
      lies just above the conventional 0.05 level. NET, one of 16 genes
      compared, was measured as mRNA only.
  - reference: PMID:28383813
    reference_title: "MIBG avidity correlates with clinical features, tumor biology, and outcomes in neuroblastoma: A report from the Children's Oncology Group."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "We demonstrated that NET mRNA expression, but not VMAT2 mRNA expression, is lower in MIBG nonavid tumors. This finding is contrary to prior work by our group that relied on polymerase chain reaction assays for NET mRNA expression and failed to demonstrate a difference in NET gene expression between MIBG avid versus nonavid tumors ... This discrepancy may reflect differences in methodology and/or tumor material between studies."
    explanation: >-
      In the 23-patient expression-array subset of this retrospective Children's
      Oncology Group cohort (18 MIBG-avid, 5 nonavid), VMAT2 mRNA did not differ
      by avidity. The authors state that the lower NET mRNA they found in
      nonavid tumours (P = 0.052) is contrary to their group's earlier PCR study
      (PMID:23050139), which found no NET mRNA difference, and suggest that
      differences in methodology or tumour material may explain the discrepancy.
      With only five nonavid tumours the sample may have been too small to
      detect differences, so the VMAT2 mRNA result is weak evidence of no
      association.
- name: MIBG-Nonavid Disease
  modality: OTHER
  frequency: OCCASIONAL
  description: >-
    Tumor that does not take up MIBG on diagnostic scintigraphy, so that the
    MIBG scan is falsely negative. In a Cochrane review, about 10% of
    histologically proven neuroblastomas did not accumulate 123I-MIBG. The INRG
    Task Force attributes such false-negative scans to low norepinephrine
    transporter expression, the blood-brain barrier, or large areas of scar or
    necrosis, while the Cochrane authors judged the reasons not entirely clear,
    suggesting that altered uptake mechanisms or interfering medication may
    contribute. In a COG cohort of 343 patients with metastatic high- or
    intermediate-risk disease, 30 (8.7%) were MIBG-nonavid at diagnosis.
    Compared with patients with avid disease, they less often had adrenal
    primary tumors or bone metastases, less often had positive urine
    catecholamines (compared in the high-risk patients only), more often had
    MYCN-amplified tumors (a difference significant in the pooled cohort but not
    among the high-risk patients alone), and had better 5-year event-free
    survival. On multivariable analysis among the high-risk patients, avidity
    was the only adverse prognostic factor for event-free survival identified
    (hazard ratio 1.77 for avid versus nonavid disease; P = 0.034); in the
    pooled cohort the adjusted hazard ratio was not significant (P = 0.059).
  imaging_finding_term:
    preferred_term: absent MIBG uptake by tumor (MIBG nonavidity)
  notes: >-
    No imaging finding term is bound. NCIT has no finding term for absent or
    decreased MIBG uptake: OLS NCIT searches on 2026-10-21 for "decreased uptake
    MIBG", "absent MIBG uptake", "MIBG non-avid", "nonavid" and "MIBG avid"
    returned nothing, "MIBG negative" returned only the stage terms NCIT:C198075
    and NCIT:C9504, and "MIBG uptake" returned NCIT:C79553 (increased uptake,
    bound on MIBG-Avid Disease), NCIT:C133468 Curie Intensity Score and the
    tracer NCIT:C74049. OLS HP searches for "MIBG", "metaiodobenzylguanidine"
    and "iobenguane" on the same date returned nothing. modality is OTHER for
    the reason given on MIBG-Avid Disease. The 8.7% figure comes from a
    metastatic high- or intermediate-risk cohort.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:26417712
    reference_title: "123I-MIBG scintigraphy and 18F-FDG-PET imaging for diagnosing neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "As described both in the literature and in this review, in about 10% of the patients with histologically proven neuroblastoma the tumour does not accumulate ¹²³I-MIBG (false negative results)."
    explanation: >-
      This Cochrane diagnostic test accuracy review of 11 studies in children
      concludes that in about 10% of patients with histologically proven
      neuroblastoma the tumour does not take up 123I-MIBG, giving a
      false-negative scan. The figure is approximate, combining earlier
      literature with the review's own crude total false-negative rate of 11% in
      608 patients (no pooled estimate was possible), and per-study sensitivity
      ranged from 67% to 100%. The review also notes that physiological uptake
      can make small lesions less visible, so some false-negative scans may
      reflect missed lesions.
  - reference: PMID:20424613
    reference_title: "Criteria for evaluation of disease extent by (123)I-metaiodobenzylguanidine scans in neuroblastoma: a report for the International Neuroblastoma Risk Group (INRG) Task Force."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "False-negative scans may be observed in approximately 10% of neuroblastomas that do not concentrate mIBG, owing to low expression of the norepinephrine transporter (Carlin et al, 2003), or owing to blood-brain barrier or large areas of scar or necrosis (Matthay et al, 2003a)."
    explanation: >-
      This 2010 INRG Task Force consensus guideline on 123I-MIBG scans lists the
      reasons for a false-negative scan in the roughly 10% of neuroblastomas
      that do not concentrate MIBG: low norepinephrine transporter expression,
      lesions behind the blood-brain barrier, and large areas of scar or
      necrosis. It restates cited studies and does not say how often each cause
      applies.
  - reference: PMID:26417712
    reference_title: "123I-MIBG scintigraphy and 18F-FDG-PET imaging for diagnosing neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "The reasons for these MIBG-non-avid tumours are not entirely clear. Possible modifications in the uptake mechanism or interfering medication may play a role (Boubaker 2008), but most studies do not report on the reasons of MIBG-non-avid neuroblastoma lesions."
    explanation: >-
      In its discussion, this Cochrane diagnostic test accuracy review, which
      found MIBG-nonavid disease in 11% of 608 patients across 11 studies, says
      the reasons for nonavid tumours are not entirely clear and that changes in
      the uptake mechanism or interfering medication may play a role, citing an
      earlier review. Most included studies did not report why lesions were
      nonavid, so the review cannot divide the roughly 10% figure between tumour
      biology and drug interference.
  - reference: PMID:28383813
    reference_title: "MIBG avidity correlates with clinical features, tumor biology, and outcomes in neuroblastoma: A report from the Children's Oncology Group."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Thirty of 343 patients (8.7%) had MIBG nonavid disease."
    explanation: >-
      This retrospective Children's Oncology Group analysis of 343 patients with
      metastatic high- or intermediate-risk neuroblastoma reports that 30 (8.7%)
      had MIBG-nonavid disease at diagnosis; Table 1 lists the other 313 as MIBG
      avid. The 306 high-risk patients (protocol A3973) had centrally reviewed
      scans, while avidity for the 37 intermediate-risk patients (A3961, each
      with at least one bone metastasis) was recorded at enrollment without
      central review. The authors state that generalization to low-risk or
      localized disease is unknown, and the paper does not state which isotope
      the diagnostic scans used.
  - reference: PMID:28383813
    reference_title: "MIBG avidity correlates with clinical features, tumor biology, and outcomes in neuroblastoma: A report from the Children's Oncology Group."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Patients with nonavid tumors were less likely to have adrenal primary tumors (34.5 vs. 57.2%; P = 0.019), bone metastases (36.7 vs. 61.7%; P = 0.008), or positive urine catecholamines (66.7 vs. 91.0%; P < 0.001) compared with patients with MIBG avid tumors."
    explanation: >-
      This retrospective Children's Oncology Group analysis of 343 patients (30
      MIBG-nonavid) with metastatic high- or intermediate-risk neuroblastoma
      reports all three differences directly. Urine catecholamines were compared
      only in the high-risk cohort. Intermediate-risk patients had to have a
      bone metastasis and 36 of 37 were avid, inflating the avid group's pooled
      bone-metastasis rate, but the adrenal and bone differences persist in the
      high-risk cohort alone. No multiple-testing correction was made, and the
      authors say it is unclear whether the bone difference is real or reflects
      differing MIBG and bone-scan sensitivity.
  - reference: PMID:28383813
    reference_title: "MIBG avidity correlates with clinical features, tumor biology, and outcomes in neuroblastoma: A report from the Children's Oncology Group."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Nonavid tumors were more likely to be MYCN amplified (53.8 vs. 32.6%; P = 0.030) ... Patients with MIBG nonavid disease had a 5-year EFS of 50.0% compared with 38.7% for patients with MIBG avid disease (P = 0.028)."
    explanation: >-
      Retrospective Children's Oncology Group analysis of 343 patients with
      metastatic intermediate- or high-risk neuroblastoma, 30 of them
      MIBG-nonavid. The abstract reports both differences for this pooled
      cohort: MYCN amplification in 53.8% of nonavid versus 32.6% of avid
      tumours with known MYCN status, and 5-year event-free survival of 50.0%
      versus 38.7%. The MYCN comparison was made without correction for multiple
      testing and was not significant among the 306 high-risk patients alone (P
      = 0.078), and the authors state it is unknown whether the findings extend
      to localised or low-risk disease.
  - reference: PMID:28383813
    reference_title: "MIBG avidity correlates with clinical features, tumor biology, and outcomes in neuroblastoma: A report from the Children's Oncology Group."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "On multivariate testing, the hazard ratio for an event for patients with MIBG avid tumors was 1.77 (95% confidence interval 0.98-3.19; P = 0.059) after adjusting for significant variables (age and ploidy) following backward selection. ... On multivariate testing in high-risk patients, MIBG avidity was the sole adverse prognostic factor for EFS identified (hazard ratio 1.77; 95% confidence interval 1.04-2.99; P = 0.034)."
    explanation: >-
      In this retrospective Children's Oncology Group analysis, Cox models built
      by backward selection kept MIBG avidity as a fixed variable. In the pooled
      cohort of 343 patients with metastatic high- or intermediate-risk disease,
      the event hazard ratio for avid versus nonavid disease after adjustment
      for age and ploidy was 1.77 (95% CI 0.98-3.19; P = 0.059), short of
      significance. Among the high-risk patients (COG A3973, centrally reviewed
      scans), avidity was the only adverse prognostic factor for event-free
      survival the model identified (hazard ratio 1.77; 95% CI 1.04-2.99; P =
      0.034). Avidity did not predict overall survival on multivariate testing
      in either cohort.
treatments:
- name: Risk-Adapted Chemotherapy
  description: >-
    Chemotherapy intensity varies by risk group. Most low-risk patients may need
    no immediate chemotherapy. In the Children's Oncology Group low-risk trial
    P9641, chemotherapy was reserved for patients with, or at risk for,
    symptomatic disease, with less than half of the tumor resected at diagnosis,
    or with unresectable progression after surgery alone. Infants with localized
    neuroblastoma without MYCN amplification and without threatening symptoms
    may be observed first instead of treated: in the NB95-S and NB97 trials,
    those whose tumors were left unresected and observed had excellent 3-year
    overall and metastasis-free survival, not different from that of infants
    treated with surgery or chemotherapy. In the Children's Oncology Group trial
    A3961, intermediate-risk patients were assigned four or eight cycles of
    carboplatin, etoposide, cyclophosphamide and doxorubicin by tumor biology
    and response, with a substantially shorter duration and lower doses than in
    earlier trials, and very high survival was still achieved, although 3-year
    overall survival was lower with unfavorable than with favorable tumor
    biology (93% vs 98%). In the single-arm Children's Oncology Group trial
    ANBL0531, subsets of intermediate-risk patients received less treatment than
    in legacy Children's Oncology Group trials, and 3-year event-free and
    overall survival among its 404 evaluable patients were 83.2% and 94.9%;
    infants with stage 4 tumors and one or more unfavorable biologic features
    had lower 3-year event-free survival than those with favorable biology
    (66.8% vs 86.9%), and the investigators conclude that more effective
    treatment is still needed for them. High-risk patients receive intensive
    multi-agent induction chemotherapy; one six-cycle regimen, based on the
    induction of the Children's Oncology Group trial ANBL0532, gives cisplatin,
    etoposide, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and topotecan.
  therapeutic_modality: SMALL_MOLECULE
  treatment_term:
    preferred_term: chemotherapy
