discussions:
- discussion_id: mismatch_nb_aurora_a_mycn_amplified_benefit
  kind: HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH
  status: OPEN
  prompt: >-
    Why do MYCN-amplified neuroblastomas respond worse to Aurora A inhibition
    than non-amplified ones, when the preclinical mechanism makes them the
    tumours that depend on Aurora A most?
  attaches_to:
  - "pathophysiology#Aurora A-Mediated N-Myc Protein Stabilization"
  - "treatments#Alisertib (Aurora A Inhibition)"
  rationale: >-
    The preclinical case is specific about direction. An shRNA screen found
    AURKA required for the growth of MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma cells and
    largely dispensable for cells without amplification, and Aurora A
    stabilises N-Myc by binding it and the SCF(Fbxw7) ligase. The prediction
    that follows is that amplified tumours should be the ones Aurora A
    inhibition helps.

    The trial predicted exactly that, in its own words, and found the
    opposite: activity concentrated in MYCN non-amplified tumours, with MYCN
    amplification associated with inferior progression-free survival.

    Three readings are open and the entry does not choose between them.
    Alisertib inhibits the catalytic site, while the stabilisation is
    kinase-independent and is undone by compounds that distort Aurora A's
    conformation, so the drug may simply be the wrong tool for the mechanism.
    Or the clinical comparison may be confounded, since MYCN amplification
    predicts worse outcome whatever the treatment, and the association comes
    from an exploratory analysis pooling three cohorts rather than a
    randomized comparison. Or the dependency shown in cell lines may not hold
    in patient tumours.

    What would separate them is a conformation-disrupting Aurora A compound
    tested in MYCN-amplified disease with N-Myc protein measured on treatment,
    rather than a catalytic inhibitor assessed by response rate alone.
  posed_by: "dismech curation (issue #14976)"
  posed_date: '2026-10-27T00:00:00Z'
- discussion_id: controversy_nb_mesenchymal_state_prognosis
  kind: CONTROVERSY
  status: OPEN
  prompt: >-
    Does a high mesenchymal cell-state signature predict worse outcome in
    neuroblastoma, better outcome, or neither?
  attaches_to:
  - "pathophysiology#Adrenergic and Mesenchymal Cell-State Plasticity"
  - "pathophysiology#Mesenchymal-State Chemotherapy Resistance"
  rationale: >-
    Three patient-level studies published within two years point in three
    directions, which is why no node in this entry asserts a prognostic
    direction for the mesenchymal state.

    A spatial-omics study of 54 profiled tumours, using signatures built
    from early-passage orthotopic patient-derived xenografts because
    established cell line-derived signatures failed to identify
    mesenchymal tumour cells, reports that high mesenchymal gene
    expression correlates with worse event-free and overall survival.

    A longitudinal single-cell multiomic study reports a tested null in
    the other direction: in 498 diagnostic bulk transcriptomes the
    mesenchymal signature was not significantly associated with
    prognosis. Two things bound that null. It is adjusted for age, sex and
    MYCN amplification in a cohort spanning all stages, and the same paper
    finds the mesenchymal state enriched in patients with MYCN
    amplification, so it is a null conditional on those covariates rather
    than an absence of any association. In the paper's own high-risk
    cohort a higher mesenchymal proportion at diagnosis correlated with a
    poorer response to induction chemotherapy and with adverse clinical
    events. Those two findings come from different analyses on different
    cohorts: the post-therapy increase from 22 paired longitudinal
    patients, the survival null from the bulk transcriptome cohort.

    A hypoxia study reports the opposite direction again, with better
    three-year overall survival for high scores in both a discovery and a
    validation cohort. It scores a composite signature of 94 mesenchymal
    signature genes selected because they rose in adrenergic cells under
    hypoxia, and it scores it only within hypoxic tumours, where the same
    score was not prognostic in the low-hypoxia subsets. So it is not a
    head-to-head contradiction of a pure mesenchymal signature, but it is
    a published, two-cohort, patient-level result pointing the other way.

    The three studies also score different things under one word:
    established cell line-derived signatures, xenograft-derived
    signatures, a single-cell-defined state signature scored in bulk
    tissue, and a hypoxia-conditioned composite. None of them measures a
    mesenchymal cell fraction directly.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:42849441
    reference_title: "Spatial omics resolves adrenergic and mesenchymal cell states in neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "In patients, high MES gene expression correlates with worse event-free and overall survival."
    explanation: >-
      The adverse-prognosis position, stated directly: in patients, high
      mesenchymal gene expression correlates with worse event-free and
      overall survival. This is a prognostic correlation and not evidence
      that the mesenchymal state causes poor outcome. The abstract reports
      no effect size, does not identify the patient cohort or the
      signature used for the survival analysis, and does not say whether
      the association holds after adjustment for established risk factors;
      the 54 tumours it describes are its profiling cohort, which may or
      may not be the survival cohort. The finding follows the authors'
      development of mesenchymal and adrenergic signatures from
      early-passage orthotopic patient-derived xenografts, which they
      introduced because established cell line-derived signatures failed
      to identify mesenchymal neuroblastoma cells.
  - reference: PMID:40229600
    reference_title: "Longitudinal single-cell multiomic atlas of high-risk neuroblastoma reveals chemotherapy-induced tumor microenvironment rewiring."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "The MES signature was not significantly associated with prognosis in the diagnostic samples"
    explanation: >-
      The tested-null position, which is what stops a reader assuming the
      adverse one. In the authors' survival analysis of 498 diagnostic
      neuroblastoma bulk transcriptomes the mesenchymal state signature
      was not significantly associated with prognosis. Its scope: a
      signature score from bulk tumour RNA rather than a measured
      mesenchymal cell fraction, split at the median and modelled against
      overall and event-free survival with age, sex and MYCN
      amplification as covariates, in a cohort spanning all stages rather
      than the high-risk cohort the paper profiled by single-nucleus
      sequencing. The authors also report the mesenchymal state enriched
      in patients with MYCN amplification, so the null holds conditional
      on MYCN status. The same paper qualifies it twice: in its
      alternative stratification, patients assigned to the mesenchymal
      state had an intermediate prognosis, and in the diagnostic samples
      of its own high-risk cohort a higher mesenchymal proportion
      correlated with poorer response to induction chemotherapy and with
      adverse clinical events (one-sided t-tests, P = 0.02 and 0.05). The
      419-sample validation cohort is described only as largely
      replicating the survival findings, with nothing specific to the
      mesenchymal signature.
  - reference: PMID:41724733
    reference_title: "Hypoxia Promotes an Adrenergic to Mesenchymal Transcriptional Program Transition in Neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "High-risk patients with hypoxic tumors that had high MES/hypoxia scores had significantly improved 3-year OS compared to those with low MES/hypoxia scores (71% vs. 40%; p = 0.0054)"
    explanation: >-
      The opposite-direction position, in the discovery cohort: among
      high-risk patients whose diagnostic tumours scored high for
      hypoxia, a high composite mesenchymal and hypoxia score went with
      significantly better three-year overall survival than a low score.
      Two caveats must be read with it. The score is a composite of 94
      mesenchymal signature genes selected because they were upregulated
      in adrenergic cells exposed to hypoxia, so it is not a pure
      mesenchymal signature; and the comparison is made only within
      hypoxic tumours, where the same score was not prognostic in the
      low-hypoxia subset. The authors note that their cohorts are
      retrospective with treatment received unknown, and that the
      signature would need prospective confirmation before any use as a
      clinical prognostic biomarker.
  - reference: PMID:41724733
    reference_title: "Hypoxia Promotes an Adrenergic to Mesenchymal Transcriptional Program Transition in Neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Superior survival was also observed in high-risk patients with hypoxic tumors that had high MES/hypoxia scores in the validation cohort (GSE73517; n = 28; 3-year OS 78% vs. 26%, p = 0.0012)"
    explanation: >-
      An independent cohort reproduces the same direction of effect in
      high-risk patients, which is what makes the better-survival
      position a two-cohort patient-level result rather than a
      single-cohort signal. The same two caveats qualify it: the score is
      a 94-gene composite of mesenchymal signature genes selected because
      they were upregulated in adrenergic cells under hypoxia, and the
      comparison is made only within hypoxic tumours. The subgroup is
      small, 15 patients with high scores against 13 with low scores, and
      the quoted 28 is that hypoxic subset rather than the whole
      validation cohort. The authors name small sample size,
      retrospective cohorts and unknown treatment received among their
      stated limitations.
- discussion_id: controversy_nb_intermediate_adrenergic_mesenchymal_state
  kind: CONTROVERSY
  status: OPEN
  prompt: >-
    Which intermediate noradrenergic and mesenchymal population do patient
    tumours contain, and does it lie on a trajectory between the two
    states?
  attaches_to:
  - "pathophysiology#Adrenergic and Mesenchymal Cell-State Plasticity"
  rationale: >-
    The disagreement here is about definition, markers and trajectory, not
    about whether an intermediate population exists. Framing it as one
    study reporting an intermediate state and another denying it would
    misstate the dissenting source, which reports an intermediate
    population of its own.

    Trajectory modelling of single-cell data from peripheral neuroblastic
    tumours places malignant neuroblasts moving between the adrenergic and
    mesenchymal states via an intermediate state its authors term
    transitional, defined in part by MYCN, NEUROD6, EZH2 and SOX11.

    The dissenting study reports a bridge cluster of noradrenergic tumour
    cells co-expressing mesenchymal features, found in a subset of an
    18-biopsy series and running towards normal Schwann and mesenchymal
    cells, and marked by FOXC1, TIMP3, ETV1 and HGF. What it disputes is
    the other study's transitional state specifically: that those cells
    did not appear in a path or a cluster between the two identities, and
    that its own noradrenergic and mesenchymal signature does not include
    the genes defining that transitional state. Its own data place EZH2
    and SOX11 in cycling-cell clusters instead.

    A third patient dataset independently reports an intermediate cluster
    with moderate adrenergic and mesenchymal signatures, so the
    population is reported more than once; what differs between the
    studies is which cells are being named, which markers define them,
    and whether they sit on a trajectory.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:36198269
    reference_title: "Single-cell profiling of peripheral neuroblastic tumors identifies an aggressive transitional state that bridges an adrenergic-mesenchymal trajectory."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: COMPUTATIONAL
    snippet: 'Trajectory modeling suggests that malignant neuroblasts move between adrenergic and mesenchymal cell states via an intermediate state that we term "transitional."'
    explanation: >-
      The trajectory position. Yuan et al. profiled 10 peripheral
      neuroblastic tumours by single-cell RNA sequencing, and their
      trajectory modelling suggests that malignant neuroblasts move
      between adrenergic and mesenchymal states through an intermediate
      state they call transitional. Graded COMPUTATIONAL because the
      quoted statement is a trajectory-model inference from static
      single-cell transcriptomes rather than an observation of cells
      changing state, even though the transcriptomes themselves are the
      authors' own measurements on patient tumours. The source's hedge is
      kept: it suggests the movement rather than demonstrating it. The
      abstract defines peripheral neuroblastic tumours as a spectrum that
      includes ganglioneuroblastoma and ganglioneuroma as well as
      neuroblastoma, and it does not give the histology of the 10
      profiled tumours, so this is one position and not a settled result
      for neuroblastoma.
  - reference: PMID:37142597
    reference_title: "Reversible transitions between noradrenergic and mesenchymal tumor identities define cell plasticity in neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Yet, these transitional cells did not appear in a path or in a cluster in between noradrenergic and mesenchymal cells"
    explanation: >-
      The competing position, in its proponents' words. Thirant et al.
      record in their Discussion that a transitional state between the
      noradrenergic and mesenchymal states had been proposed from
      pseudotime trajectory analysis of single-cell data across a
      neuroblastoma, ganglioneuroblastoma and ganglioneuroma series, and
      then state that those transitional cells did not appear in a path
      or in a cluster between the noradrenergic and mesenchymal cells.
      The judgement is about patient tumour single-cell data, which is
      what evidence_source grades; it is the citing authors' reading of
      another group's published results rather than a measurement of
      their own, and the paper re-analyses a different published cohort
      without any sign of re-analysing the data it is commenting on. No
      quote_role value fits a critical re-reading of another group's
      published analysis inside a primary research article, so the slot
      is left absent.
  - reference: PMID:37142597
    reference_title: "Reversible transitions between noradrenergic and mesenchymal tumor identities define cell plasticity in neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "our present results suggest that cells in an intermediate noradrenergic/mesenchymal state are detected in a subset of patients"
    explanation: >-
      What keeps the disagreement from being misread as a denial that any
      intermediate population exists. The same paper that disputes the
      trajectory structure reports, from its own single-cell RNA
      sequencing of patient tumour biopsies, that cells in an
      intermediate noradrenergic and mesenchymal state are detected in a
      subset of patients. Its bridge population came from four of the 18
      biopsies, three at diagnosis and one at relapse, and ran towards
      normal Schwann and mesenchymal cells. The source's hedge is kept.
  - reference: PMID:37142597
    reference_title: "Reversible transitions between noradrenergic and mesenchymal tumor identities define cell plasticity in neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "This signature does not include the MYCN, NEUROD6, EZH2 and SOX11 genes that define the transitional state in the study by Yuan et al."
    explanation: >-
      What makes the disagreement one about markers rather than about
      existence: the dissenting study's own signature for noradrenergic
      tumour cells with mesenchymal features, built on FOXC1, TIMP3, ETV1
      and HGF, does not include the genes that define the other study's
      transitional state. The same paper places two of those genes, EZH2
      and SOX11, in cycling-cell clusters instead. So the two groups are
      naming different populations, which is why the question in the
      prompt is which population and which signature rather than whether
      an intermediate state exists.
- discussion_id: nb_myc_high_subset_proliferation_model_mismatch
  prompt: >-
    The zebrafish model attributes the c-MYC advantage to reduced apoptosis
    together with a higher proliferative fraction, and the patient series
    matches the apoptotic half while placing the mitotic half out of reach:
    is there a proliferative difference between MYC-driven and MYCN-driven
    human tumours at all?
  kind: HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH
  status: OPEN
  attaches_to:
  - pathophysiology#c-MYC Activation by Enhancer Hijacking or Enhancer Amplification
  rationale: >-
    The model makes a two-part claim and the patient data answer one part of
    it. In transgenic zebrafish the expansion driven by c-MYC was rapid and
    sustained where MYCN-driven lesions regressed after five weeks, which the
    authors attribute to reduced apoptosis together with a higher
    proliferative fraction; and disrupting c-MYC in SKNAS, a
    MYCN-non-amplified line with high c-MYC, costs viability and colony
    formation while leaving the MYCN-amplified line Kelly unaffected. In
    patient tumours the only index reported for this subset is the
    mitosis-karyorrhexis index, which counts mitotic and karyorrhectic figures
    together, and the MYC-protein-positive tumours tend to low or intermediate
    values where the MYCN-protein-positive ones are high. That series
    separates the two components rather than leaving them merged: it places
    the difference in karyorrhexis rather than in mitosis, and reads it as a
    functional difference between the two proteins in their apoptotic and
    karyorrhectic pathways. So the apoptotic half of the model's claim is
    matched in the patient tumours, and the proliferative half is left
    unmeasured rather than contradicted. A mitotic-figure count reported only
    as not being the driver of the index difference, with the data not shown,
    is not a proliferation fraction, and no Ki-67 or other labelling index
    stratified by MYC against MYCN protein appears in that work. The cohorts
    also differ: the index comes from a series restricted to undifferentiated
    and poorly differentiated tumours with the subset defined by
    immunohistochemistry, while the zebrafish and cell-line work follows a
    subset defined by expression rank. Until a proliferation fraction is
    measured in MYC-high patient tumours, a proliferation node for this subset
    would rest on the fish and the cell line alone, which is why this entry
    does not carry one.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:29284669
    reference_title: "MYC Drives a Subset of High-Risk Pediatric Neuroblastomas and Is Activated through Mechanisms Including Enhancer Hijacking and Focal Enhancer Amplification."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    snippet: "due to reduced apoptosis and a higher proliferative fraction of c-MYC compared with MYCN-transformed PSNS cells in this model"
    explanation: >-
      The model side of the mismatch. In transgenic zebrafish expressing human
      c-MYC in the developing peripheral sympathetic nervous system under a
      dopamine-beta-hydroxylase promoter, the authors attribute the rapid and
      sustained expansion of interrenal gland tissue, against MYCN-driven
      lesions that regressed after five weeks, to reduced apoptosis together
      with a higher proliferative fraction. Graded MODEL_ORGANISM because the
      measurement is in fish, and INDIRECT because whether that advantage
      describes human tumours is precisely what this discussion leaves open.
      The quote is the clause stating the attributed cause; the surrounding
      sentence carries figure references. Note that the comparison is c-MYC
      against MYCN within the fish, not against normal tissue, and that the
      two transgenes were expressed from the same promoter at similar levels.
  - reference: PMID:26035700
    reference_title: "Augmented expression of MYC and/or MYCN protein defines highly aggressive MYC-driven neuroblastoma: a Children's Oncology Group study."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "MYC(+) tumours were also frequently UH but not associated with MYCN amplification, and more likely to have low-/intermediate-MKI."
    explanation: >-
      The human side of the mismatch, and the reason this entry carries no
      proliferation node for the MYC-high subset. Among 357 undifferentiated
      or poorly differentiated neuroblastomas immunostained in this Children's
      Oncology Group series, the MYC-protein-positive tumours were usually
      MYCN-non-amplified and tended to a low or intermediate
      mitosis-karyorrhexis index while still being unfavourable histology.
      Table 2 gives 31 of 38 in the low or intermediate index classes and 30
      of 39 unfavourable histology, and the two denominators agree: 39 is the
      MYC-protein-positive total including the single tumour positive for both
      proteins, which the abstract counts separately as 38 MYC(+) plus one
      with both, and the index row drops to 38 because MKI was scored in 343
      of the 357 cases. Read the finding as a property of MYC-positive tumours within
      this histology rather than of neuroblastoma generally, since the series
      excludes differentiating tumours by design, and note that the index
      counts mitotic and karyorrhectic figures together so it does not isolate
      the mitotic rate.
  - reference: PMID:26035700
    reference_title: "Augmented expression of MYC and/or MYCN protein defines highly aggressive MYC-driven neuroblastoma: a Children's Oncology Group study."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "MYCN(+) tumours were associated with amplified MYCN, Unfavourable Histology (UH), and High-MKI (Mitosis-Karyorrhexis Index)."
    explanation: >-
      The comparator that makes the MYC-positive index finding a contrast
      rather than an isolated number. In the same series the
      MYCN-protein-positive tumours were amplified, unfavourable histology,
      and high mitosis-karyorrhexis index, Table 2 giving 53 of 65 in the high
      class and 68 of 68 unfavourable histology. Both groups are therefore
      aggressive on histology and on outcome while differing on the index, so
      the index difference is not a difference in how advanced the tumours
      are. The quoted sentence also spells the index out, which is what makes
      its composite nature readable from the evidence rather than only from
      the rationale.
  - reference: PMID:26035700
    reference_title: "Augmented expression of MYC and/or MYCN protein defines highly aggressive MYC-driven neuroblastoma: a Children's Oncology Group study."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "the major quantitative difference in MKI in these tumours was due to the difference in karyorrhexis rather than in mitosis (data not shown)"
    explanation: >-
      The sentence that decides what the index difference does and does not
      say about proliferation. The authors separate the two components of the
      mitosis-karyorrhexis index and place the between-group difference in the
      karyorrhectic one, so the lower index in MYC-protein-positive tumours is
      not a report of fewer mitoses and does not contradict the proliferative
      advantage the zebrafish work describes. INDIRECT because the supporting
      counts are not shown, and because a mitotic-figure count is in any case
      not a proliferation fraction: what the sentence establishes is that the
      published human index does not measure the quantity the model claims.
  - reference: PMID:26035700
    reference_title: "Augmented expression of MYC and/or MYCN protein defines highly aggressive MYC-driven neuroblastoma: a Children's Oncology Group study."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "The difference in karyorrhectic activities in MYCN protein(+) and MYC protein(+) tumours suggests that these two proteins could have some functional difference especially in their apoptotic/karyorrhectic pathways."
    explanation: >-
      The authors' own reading of that component difference, and the point at
      which the patient data meet the model rather than diverge from it: the
      zebrafish work attributes the c-MYC advantage partly to reduced
      apoptosis, and this series places the MYC-versus-MYCN difference in the
      apoptotic and karyorrhectic pathways. INDIRECT because the authors offer
      it as a suggestion rather than a measurement, and because reading
      karyorrhectic figures as apoptosis is their inference.
  proposed_experiments:
  - experiment_id: nb_myc_high_proliferation_fraction_vs_mycn
    name: Proliferation fraction in MYC-protein-positive versus MYCN-protein-positive primary neuroblastoma
    description: >-
      Measure a proliferation fraction separable from apoptosis in archival
      primary tumours stratified by MYC and MYCN protein immunohistochemistry:
      a Ki-67 or MIB-1 labelling index, and a mitotic count scored by
      phospho-histone H3 so that mitotic figures are read independently of
      karyorrhectic ones, with apoptosis recorded separately by cleaved
      caspase-3 or TUNEL. Draw the series without restricting it to
      undifferentiated and poorly differentiated histology, so that the result
      is not conditioned on the inclusion criterion behind the existing index
      comparison.
    decision_criterion: >-
      Whether MYC-protein-positive tumours differ from MYCN-protein-positive
      tumours in proliferation fraction once the mitotic and karyorrhectic
      components of the mitosis-karyorrhexis index are measured separately.
    supporting_outcome:
    - >-
        A proliferation fraction in MYC-protein-positive tumours at or above that
        of MYCN-protein-positive tumours, with the lower mitosis-karyorrhexis
        index accounted for by reduced karyorrhexis, would carry the zebrafish
        and cell-line result into human tumours and make a proliferation node for
        this subset curatable.
    refuting_outcome:
    - >-
        A proliferation fraction genuinely lower in MYC-protein-positive tumours,
        with the mitotic component itself reduced, would place this subset's
        aggressiveness somewhere other than proliferative rate and leave the
        zebrafish proliferative advantage as a property of that model.

- discussion_id: gap_nb_consolidation_tandem_versus_busulfan_melphalan
  kind: KNOWLEDGE_GAP
  status: OPEN
  prompt: >-
    Which consolidation gives better event-free survival in high-risk
    neuroblastoma, a tandem transplant built on carboplatin, etoposide and
    melphalan or a single busulfan-melphalan transplant?
  attaches_to:
  - "treatments#Autologous Stem Cell Transplant"
  rationale: >-
    Two randomized phase 3 trials each improved on a
    carboplatin-etoposide-melphalan comparator, and neither tested the other's
    winner.

    The Children's Oncology Group's ANBL0532 randomized tandem transplant,
    thiotepa and cyclophosphamide followed by dose-reduced carboplatin,
    etoposide and melphalan, against a single carboplatin-etoposide-melphalan
    transplant, and found three-year event-free survival from randomization of
    61.6% against 48.4%.

    SIOPEN's HR-NBL1 randomized busulfan with melphalan against carboplatin,
    etoposide and melphalan as single high-dose regimens, and found three-year
    event-free survival of 50% against 38%, with fewer severe adverse events
    on busulfan-melphalan but more veno-occlusive disease.

    So both beat the same regimen, and the arm that won each trial has never
    met the arm that won the other. The comparison is not recoverable from the
    two results: the trials differ in their induction regimens and their eras,
    and they randomize different populations. HR-NBL1 randomized only patients
    who had completed induction and achieved an adequate disease response,
    whereas ANBL0532 randomized 355 of its 652 enrolled patients, 207 of them
    withheld by physician or parent preference, and reports event-free survival
    from the time of randomization. The absolute percentages are therefore not
    comparable across them, and ANBL0532's authors say its result may not
    represent all patients with high-risk neuroblastoma.

    Resolving this needs a randomized comparison of tandem
    carboplatin-etoposide-melphalan consolidation against single
    busulfan-melphalan, in one induction backbone, with anti-GD2 maintenance
    in both arms.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:31454045
    reference_title: "Effect of Tandem Autologous Stem Cell Transplant vs Single Transplant on Event-Free Survival in Patients With High-Risk Neuroblastoma: A Randomized Clinical Trial."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Patients were randomized to receive tandem transplant with thiotepa/cyclophosphamide followed by dose-reduced carboplatin/etoposide/melphalan (n = 176) or single transplant with carboplatin/etoposide/melphalan (n = 179)."
    explanation: >-
      Establishes what ANBL0532's winning arm actually was: a tandem schedule
      whose second course is dose-reduced carboplatin, etoposide and melphalan.
      That is why its result does not speak to busulfan-melphalan, which the
      trial did not use in either arm.
  - reference: PMID:28259608
    reference_title: "Busulfan and melphalan versus carboplatin, etoposide, and melphalan as high-dose chemotherapy for high-risk neuroblastoma (HR-NBL1/SIOPEN): an international, randomised, multi-arm, open-label, phase 3 trial."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Busulfan and melphalan improved event-free survival in children with high-risk neuroblastoma with an adequate response to induction treatment and caused fewer severe adverse events than did carboplatin, etoposide, and melphalan. Busulfan and melphalan should thus be considered standard high-dose chemotherapy and ongoing randomised studies will continue to aim to optimise treatment for high-risk neuroblastoma."
    explanation: >-
      The other side of the gap: SIOPEN's conclusion that busulfan-melphalan
      should be considered the standard high-dose regimen, reached against the
      same comparator ANBL0532 improved on by giving two courses. The authors
      themselves close by saying further randomized studies are needed to
      optimise treatment.
  posed_by: "dismech curation (issue #14976)"
  posed_date: '2026-10-23T00:00:00Z'
- discussion_id: question_nb_alt_status_and_wee1_inhibitor_benefit
  kind: OPEN_QUESTION
  status: OPEN
  prompt: >-
    Does alternative lengthening of telomeres mark the neuroblastomas that
    benefit from WEE1 inhibition?
  attaches_to:
  - "pathophysiology#Replication-Stress Checkpoint Dependence"
  - "pathophysiology#Alternative Lengthening of Telomeres"
  - "treatments#Adavosertib (WEE1 Inhibition)"
  rationale: >-
    In the ADVL1312 neuroblastoma cohort, two of the three patients with an
    objective response had tumours with alternative lengthening of telomeres.
    The observation is worth recording because it joins two things this entry
    already models separately: ALT is a telomere-maintenance mechanism that
    runs on homologous recombination at telomeres, and the checkpoint
    dependence this treatment targets is a response to replication stress, so
    a tumour already carrying that burden is a plausible place for the drug to
    work.

    It is two patients. The trial analysed ALT and ATRX in tumour tissue but
    was not designed or powered to test ALT as a predictive marker, there is
    no comparison with the response rate in non-ALT tumours, and the second
    adavosertib trial reports its own candidate markers instead, finding
    clinical benefit in seven of eight patients with alterations in homologous
    recombination, replication-stress or RAS-pathway genes. Nothing here
    establishes ALT as a biomarker, and the entry does not claim it.

    What would settle it is a trial that stratifies on ALT status up front, or
    a pooled reanalysis across adavosertib studies with ALT called by a single
    assay.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:37081608
    reference_title: "Pediatric phase 2 trial of a WEE1 inhibitor, adavosertib (AZD1775), and irinotecan for relapsed neuroblastoma, medulloblastoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Two of the three patients with objective responses had tumors with alternative lengthening of telomeres."
    explanation: >-
      The whole of the observation, and the reason the question is recorded as
      open rather than as a finding: it is a count of two, reported alongside
      the trial's tissue analysis rather than as a tested association.
  posed_by: "dismech curation (issue #14976)"
  posed_date: '2026-10-27T00:00:00Z'

Edit: Neuroblastoma — evidence for four unquoted figures, retired PARTIAL prose, ALK/MYCN HGNC bindings · 2026-10-15T16:47:34Z · View source

Evidence repairs in an existing entry: four figures that were stated without a quote, two explanations that still argued for the retired PARTIAL grade, quote_role and grading of six background citations, two prose claims next to the rewritten text, and HGNC bindings for ALK and MYCN. No new mechanisms, phenotypes or treatments. Figures: - MYCN amplification "approximately 20%": kept. Sourced to the Children's Oncology Group biology-study cohort (PMID:28696504: 845 of 4,672 patients, 18.1%; 133 more with MYCN gain) and two review statements (PMID:25345447; PMID:22936790 on the MYCN-amplified subtype). The unsourced "historical series enriched for advanced-stage disease" was replaced by the stage split in the 1984 Brodeur abstract (PMID:6719137: 0 of 15 stage 1-2 vs 24 of 48 stage 3-4). - ALK point mutations "8-10%": kept, without "sporadic" (the 8% cohort counts germline carriers). Sourced to PMID:25517749 (8% of 1,596 diagnostic samples) and PMID:26059187 (10% at diagnosis with hotspot deep sequencing, more than half subclonal). The unsourced "F1174L and R1275Q are the most common mutations" was replaced by the per-residue counts in PMID:25517749 (R1275 43%, F1174 30%, F1245 12%) and the germline statement in PMID:28674118 (R1275Q most frequent). - Germline ALK in familial neuroblastoma "75-80%": restated as the range of published estimates, about 50% to 80%: more than 50% from the group that mapped ALK (PMID:21734404), 50% (PMID:25345447), 75% (PMID:29589100) and 80% (PMID:38791942). The 75% and 80% statements are in cached full texts, not abstracts. The PMID:18724359 explanation that argued "majority (not ~50%)" was rewritten. The combined ALK+PHOX2B clause cites PMID:28674118. - Urinary VMA/HVA ">90%": softened. Diagnostic series give 84% (PMID:28061374) and 82.2% (PMID:31724812) for the pair, 95% with an eight-metabolite panel; >90% and 92% are review statements (PMID:15235064, PMID:8790511), and a relapse-selected cohort found 92% at diagnosis (PMID:12932669, which also supports the added caveat that markers alone do not reliably detect relapse). First evidence block for this marker. Grading: the six PMID:41560679 items now carry quote_role (five introduction sentences BACKGROUND, the 17q result PRIMARY_RESULT). The five background items were regraded MODEL_ORGANISM -> HUMAN_CLINICAL because the quoted sentences describe the human disease, per the CLAUDE.md quote_role guidance (#10262); the 17q result stays MODEL_ORGANISM. directness: INDIRECT on the two former PARTIAL items, with explanations giving the inference step. Other: PHOX2B notes corrected (it was the first neuroblastoma predisposition gene identified, not the second after ALK; PMID:29589100). genetic[ALK Mutations].gene_term hgnc:427 and genetic[MYCN Amplification].gene_term hgnc:7559 (cached; HGNC REST confirmed). Node-level genes: wiring is left for a later change, because it also needs molecular_functions (check-gene-activity-grounding). Method: candidate quotes came from literature-search agents (PubMed E-utilities, two search angles per figure) and were checked by independent verifier agents for exact match, support for the claim, and grading; the curator selected from the verified set, and a three-lens red-team review of the diff preceded the commit. No deep-research report was generated; research/Neuroblastoma-deep-research-falcon.md predates this change and was not used. Falcon ▸
Pathophysiology description
Edison Scientific Literature 24 citations 2026-02-01T12:46:31.619413

Pathophysiology description Neuroblastoma (NB) arises from neural crest–derived sympathoadrenal lineage cells and exhibits marked inter- and intra-tumoral heterogeneity. Despite a low tumor mutational burden, disease biology is driven by a limited set of recurrent genomic and epigenomic programs that confer proliferative advantage, telomere immortality, lineage/cell-state plasticity, and an immunologically “cold” tumor microenvironment.

  • Genomic drivers and copy-number programs: High-risk NB is frequently defined by MYCN amplification, TERT activation (via rearrangements or copy-number mechanisms), and ATRX alterations, together with segmental chromosomal aberrations including 1p deletion, 11q deletion, and 17q gain; collectively these shape aggressive phenotypes despite overall few point mutations (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765, Aug 2024) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3). Telomere programs and copy-number dosage have pervasive effects on transcriptional control and disease pathways; recurrent 11q loss with 17q gain correlates with upregulation of histone variant genes and reduced PRC2 activity, providing a mechanistic route to ALT activation in a subset, while TERT overexpression can be driven by rearrangements and dosage in others (URL: https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.08.16.504100, Aug 2024) (burkert2024copynumberdosageregulates pages 18-24).

  • Telomere maintenance mechanisms (TMM): High-risk NB nearly always acquires a telomere maintenance mechanism. Two non-overlapping solutions dominate: telomerase activation (often via TERT rearrangement or MYCN-driven TERT transcription) and the alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT), frequently associated with ATRX dysfunction and chromatin changes at telomeres. Allele-specific dosage and copy-number imbalances further tune TERT levels and ALT-associated programs, linking segmental CNAs to TMM state and outcome (URL: https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.08.16.504100, Aug 2024) (burkert2024copynumberdosageregulates pages 18-24); overview also summarized in an immunotherapy-focused review (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765, Aug 2024) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3).

  • Lineage/cell-state plasticity: NB cells switch between two epigenetically-defined identities—noradrenergic (ADRN) and mesenchymal (MES)—with distinct core regulatory circuitries (ADRN: PHOX2A/PHOX2B, HAND1/2, GATA2/3; MES: AP-1–programs). Transitions are spontaneous and reversible and are shaped by tumor microenvironmental cues; MES-like states are enriched during or after therapy and confer chemoresistance, while in patient tumors the dominant phenotype is often ADRN with subclonal MES-like populations (URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-38239-5, May 2023) (thirant2023reversibletransitionsbetween pages 1-2). Targeted depletion of SWI/SNF ATPases (SMARCA2/4) compacts cis-regulatory elements, displaces ADRN core TFs (e.g., MYCN, HAND2, PHOX2B, GATA3), reduces enhancer activity, inhibits invasion, and—critically—reduces cellular plasticity, positioning SWI/SNF as a mechanistic driver of lineage flexibility and a therapeutic node (URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s44318-024-00206-1, Aug 2024) (xu2024targetingswisnfatpases pages 1-2). Additional reviews integrating single-cell multi-omics emphasize ADRN↔MES plasticity, persister states at relapse, and the developmental origin of state diversity (URL: https://doi.org/10.3389/fimmu.2025.1637626, Jul 2025; URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41388-025-03635-2, Nov 2025) (wang2025emergingfrontiersin pages 6-7, he2025dissectingneuroblastomaheterogeneity pages 6-7).

  • Tumor microenvironment (TME) and immune evasion: NB is typically immunologically “cold,” with low neoantigen load, downregulated MHC class I and antigen processing, and abundant immunosuppressive myeloid populations (TAMs, MDSCs) and Tregs. Additional barriers include CD47-mediated phagocytosis inhibition, inhibitory checkpoints (e.g., B7-H3, PD-L1), and metabolic constraints. These features limit T cell infiltration and efficacy of checkpoint inhibition and shape responses to GD2-directed therapies (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765, Aug 2024) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3). Combining chemotherapy and immunotherapy to deliberately exploit ADRN–MES plasticity (e.g., inducing more immunogenic MES features or immunogenic cell death) is a proposed strategy to overcome immune evasion and resistance (URL: https://doi.org/10.3389/fimmu.2023.1268645, Oct 2023) (d’amico2023twobulletsin pages 6-7). Broader pediatric-oncology reviews concur that epigenetic dysregulation (PRC2 imbalance, DNA hypomethylation) intersects with immune coldness, suggesting epigenetic modulators may prime NB for immunotherapy (URL: https://doi.org/10.3389/fimmu.2025.1637626, Jul 2025) (wang2025emergingfrontiersin pages 1-2).

Key concepts and definitions with current understanding - Segmental chromosomal aberrations (SCA): Partial arm gains/losses (e.g., 17q gain, 1p and 11q loss) that correlate with high-risk disease, telomere program activation, and poor outcome (URL: https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.08.16.504100, Aug 2024) (burkert2024copynumberdosageregulates pages 18-24). - Telomere maintenance mechanisms: Mutually exclusive telomerase activation vs ALT in most tumors; in NB, TERT activation (via rearrangements/MYCN) or ALT (often ATRX-linked) is a hallmark of high-risk biology (URL: https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.08.16.504100, Aug 2024) (burkert2024copynumberdosageregulates pages 18-24). - Core regulatory circuitry (CRC): Super-enhancer–anchored TF networks defining cell identity; ADRN CRC includes PHOX2B/HAND2/GATA3 and is displaced by mSWI/SNF ATPase degradation (URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s44318-024-00206-1, Aug 2024) (xu2024targetingswisnfatpases pages 1-2); ADRN↔MES circuits are epigenetically rewired during plasticity (URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-38239-5, May 2023) (thirant2023reversibletransitionsbetween pages 1-2). - Immunologically “cold” tumor: Low T-cell infiltration/activation with innate suppressive myeloid dominance; characteristic of NB and a barrier to ICI efficacy (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765, Aug 2024) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3).

Recent developments and latest research (2023–2024 priority) - Telomere dosage–ALT axis: Integrative genome/transcriptome analysis links 11q loss/17q gain to histone variant upregulation, PRC2 attenuation, and ALT predisposition, while TERT dosage and rearrangements drive telomerase activation—offering pathway-level biomarkers and vulnerabilities (URL: https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.08.16.504100, Aug 2024) (burkert2024copynumberdosageregulates pages 18-24). - Epigenetic control of plasticity: Dual degradation of SMARCA2/4 collapses enhancer landscapes and reduces ADRN–MES interconversion and invasion, nominating mSWI/SNF ATPases as targets to suppress therapy-evasive states (URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s44318-024-00206-1, Aug 2024) (xu2024targetingswisnfatpases pages 1-2). Foundational plasticity evidence in vivo/in patients was consolidated with single-cell profiling and xenografts (URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-38239-5, May 2023) (thirant2023reversibletransitionsbetween pages 1-2). - Immune microenvironment–informed therapy: Consensus descriptions of NB immune evasion—including MHC downregulation, suppressive myeloid infiltration, CD47 signaling, and checkpoint expression—explain limited ICI activity and motivate combinatorial strategies with cytotoxics/epigenetic modulators to increase tumor immunogenicity (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765, Aug 2024; URL: https://doi.org/10.3389/fimmu.2023.1268645, Oct 2023) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3, d’amico2023twobulletsin pages 6-7).

Current applications and real-world implementations - GD2-directed immunotherapy: Anti-GD2 monoclonal antibodies are standard in high-risk consolidation/maintenance; their efficacy is impacted by the cold TME and immune-evasion circuitry summarized above, leading to active development of combination immunotherapy approaches (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765, Aug 2024) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3). - Epigenetic and plasticity-directed strategies: Preclinical mSWI/SNF ATPase degraders reduce plasticity and invasion, supporting exploration as partners with cytotoxic or immune therapies to prevent emergence of MES-like resistant states (URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s44318-024-00206-1, Aug 2024) (xu2024targetingswisnfatpases pages 1-2). Epigenetic agents proposed to reprogram immunogenicity are reviewed (URL: https://doi.org/10.3389/fimmu.2025.1637626, Jul 2025) (wang2025emergingfrontiersin pages 1-2).

Expert opinions and analysis from authoritative sources - Authoritative clinical-immunology perspective: “Immune-evasion features include central tolerance to oncofetal antigens, downregulation of MHC class I, defective antigen processing, low NK-activating ligands… abundant TAMs, MDSCs and Tregs… resulting in immunologically ‘cold’ tumors.” This synthesis explains the limited efficacy of ICIs and informs rational combination strategies with GD2 antibodies and adoptive cellular therapy (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765, Aug 2024) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3). - Fundamental cell-state paradigm: NB plasticity is an epigenetically governed, microenvironment-influenced spectrum between ADRN and MES states; suppressing plasticity or redirecting state can modulate therapy response (URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-38239-5, May 2023; URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s44318-024-00206-1, Aug 2024) (thirant2023reversibletransitionsbetween pages 1-2, xu2024targetingswisnfatpases pages 1-2). - Multi-omics viewpoint: Developmental lineage programs and persister states underlie relapse and resistance; multi-omic single-cell atlases are needed to map vulnerability (URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41388-025-03635-2, Nov 2025; URL: https://doi.org/10.3389/fimmu.2025.1637626, Jul 2025) (he2025dissectingneuroblastomaheterogeneity pages 6-7, wang2025emergingfrontiersin pages 1-2).

Relevant statistics and data from recent studies - While NB as a whole has seen survival gains, high-risk cohorts continue to have 5-year overall survival below 50% in many contemporary series, consistent with the immunotherapy-focused clinical review summarizing outcomes and obstacles (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765, Aug 2024) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3).

Required Information 1) Core Pathophysiology - Primary mechanisms: Oncogene activation (MYCN amplification), telomere maintenance acquisition (TERT activation or ALT), segmental chromosomal instability (1p/11q loss, 17q gain), epigenetic remodeling of lineage programs (CRC, super-enhancers), and an immunosuppressive TME that impairs antigen presentation and T-cell infiltration (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765, Aug 2024; URL: https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.08.16.504100, Aug 2024; URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-38239-5, May 2023; URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s44318-024-00206-1, Aug 2024) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3, burkert2024copynumberdosageregulates pages 18-24, thirant2023reversibletransitionsbetween pages 1-2, xu2024targetingswisnfatpases pages 1-2). - Dysregulated pathways: Telomere biology (TERT/ALT), chromatin remodeling (mSWI/SNF, PRC2 imbalance), super-enhancer–based transcriptional circuitry (ADRN/MES CRCs), immune checkpoint and innate checkpoint signaling (CD47, B7-H3, PD-L1), and myeloid-driven suppression (URL: https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.08.16.504100, Aug 2024; URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s44318-024-00206-1, Aug 2024; URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765, Aug 2024) (burkert2024copynumberdosageregulates pages 18-24, xu2024targetingswisnfatpases pages 1-2, persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3). - Affected cellular processes: DNA damage tolerance at telomeres, enhancer remodeling and TF occupancy, antigen processing/presentation, macrophage/NK/T-cell crosstalk, and lineage-state transitions under therapy pressure (URL: as above) (burkert2024copynumberdosageregulates pages 18-24, xu2024targetingswisnfatpases pages 1-2, persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3, thirant2023reversibletransitionsbetween pages 1-2).

2) Key Molecular Players - Genes/Proteins (HGNC): - MYCN (HGNC:7553): amplified oncogene driving proliferation and TERT transcription; tied to ADRN CRC and displaced from DNA by SMARCA2/4 degradation (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765; https://doi.org/10.1038/s44318-024-00206-1) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3, xu2024targetingswisnfatpases pages 1-2). - TERT (HGNC:11730): activated via rearrangement/copy-number and MYCN; defines telomerase-positive NB (URL: https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.08.16.504100) (burkert2024copynumberdosageregulates pages 18-24). - ATRX (HGNC:886): loss disrupts telomeric chromatin, promoting ALT (URL: https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.08.16.504100) (burkert2024copynumberdosageregulates pages 18-24). - SMARCA2/SMARCA4 (HGNC:11100/11103): mSWI/SNF ATPases required for plasticity-permissive chromatin; dual degradation reduces plasticity and invasion (URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s44318-024-00206-1) (xu2024targetingswisnfatpases pages 1-2). - PHOX2B, HAND2, GATA3 (HGNC:9140/4801/4172): ADRN CRC TFs defining noradrenergic identity (URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-38239-5; https://doi.org/10.1038/s44318-024-00206-1) (thirant2023reversibletransitionsbetween pages 1-2, xu2024targetingswisnfatpases pages 1-2). - Immune evasion mediators: CD47 (phagocytosis checkpoint), B7-H3 (CD276), PD-L1 (CD274), and MHC-I downregulation are implicated in immune exclusion (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3). - Chemical Entities (CHEBI): - Anti-GD2 monoclonal antibodies (therapeutic biologics) used clinically in HR-NB; activity conditioned by TME (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3). - Cell Types (CL): - Tumor cell states: adrenergic tumor cells; mesenchymal tumor cells (lineage-plastic cancer cell states) (URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-38239-5) (thirant2023reversibletransitionsbetween pages 1-2). - Immune/stromal: tumor-associated macrophages, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, regulatory T cells, NK cells (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3). - Anatomical locations (UBERON): - Adrenal medulla and sympathetic chain ganglia as common primaries; bone marrow as a key metastatic niche with immunosuppressive remodeling (review synthesis) (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3).

3) Biological Processes (GO annotation candidates, disrupted) - Telomere organization and maintenance (GO:0000723; GO:0001309): TERT activation or ALT engagement; copy-number dosage reshapes TMM pathways (URL: https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.08.16.504100) (burkert2024copynumberdosageregulates pages 18-24). - Chromatin organization and enhancer regulation (GO:0006325; GO:0032204): mSWI/SNF-dependent accessibility enabling CRC function; PRC2 imbalance in ALT contexts (URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s44318-024-00206-1; https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.08.16.504100) (xu2024targetingswisnfatpases pages 1-2, burkert2024copynumberdosageregulates pages 18-24). - Regulation of transcription by RNA polymerase II (GO:0006357): super-enhancer/CRC-driven lineage programs (URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-38239-5) (thirant2023reversibletransitionsbetween pages 1-2). - Antigen processing and presentation of peptide antigen via MHC class I (GO:0002474): downregulated in NB, contributing to immune coldness (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3). - Negative regulation of T cell activation (GO:0050868) and macrophage-mediated immunity (GO:0006955): checkpoint expression (CD47, PD-L1, B7-H3) and suppressive myeloid infiltration (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3). - Epithelial/mesenchymal program regulation (GO:0001837; GO:0001838 proxies for state changes): ADRN↔MES transitions under therapy pressure (URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-38239-5) (thirant2023reversibletransitionsbetween pages 1-2).

4) Cellular Components (where processes occur) - Telomere nucleoprotein complex (GO:0000781): site of ALT recombination or telomerase action (URL: https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.08.16.504100) (burkert2024copynumberdosageregulates pages 18-24). - Nuclear chromatin, enhancers/super-enhancers: mSWI/SNF-regulated cis-elements controlling CRC TF binding (URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s44318-024-00206-1; https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-38239-5) (xu2024targetingswisnfatpases pages 1-2, thirant2023reversibletransitionsbetween pages 1-2). - Plasma membrane: GD2 antigen display (therapeutic target), checkpoint molecules (PD-L1, CD47, B7-H3) (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3). - Tumor microenvironment extracellular space: cytokines and suppressive metabolites shaping immune exclusion (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3).

5) Disease Progression (sequence of events) - Developmental origin and transformation: sympathoadrenal progenitor with early segmental CNAs and oncogene activation (e.g., MYCN, TERT) establishes proliferative, ADRN-skewed tumor. Acquisition of telomere maintenance (telomerase or ALT) enables immortalization and genomic stability under replication stress (URL: https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.08.16.504100) (burkert2024copynumberdosageregulates pages 18-24). - Therapy pressure and plasticity: cytotoxic exposure enriches MES-like, chemoresistant states; microenvironmental signals can bias reversion to ADRN identity in vivo. Persistent plasticity enables relapse and resistance (URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-38239-5, May 2023) (thirant2023reversibletransitionsbetween pages 1-2). - Immune evasion and metastasis: MHC-I downregulation, myeloid suppression, and checkpoint signaling facilitate immune escape; bone marrow metastatic niches display pronounced immune suppression and T-cell dysfunction, limiting immunotherapy efficacy (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765, Aug 2024) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3).

6) Phenotypic Manifestations (clinical phenotypes and mechanism links) - Common phenotypes: abdominal mass (adrenal/sympathetic), bone/bone marrow metastases, opsoclonus–myoclonus in subsets; in high-risk disease, refractory/relapsed course and poor survival are linked to TMM activation and ADRN↔MES plasticity under therapy (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765, Aug 2024; URL: https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.08.16.504100, Aug 2024; URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-38239-5, May 2023) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3, burkert2024copynumberdosageregulates pages 18-24, thirant2023reversibletransitionsbetween pages 1-2).

Gene/protein annotations with ontology terms (examples) - MYCN (HGNC:7553) – Biological Process: positive regulation of transcription by RNA Pol II; cellular component: nucleus; Molecular Function: DNA-binding TF activity; Evidence: amplification and CRC occupancy in ADRN state; therapeutic vulnerability via mSWI/SNF ATPase degradation reducing TF DNA binding (URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s44318-024-00206-1) (xu2024targetingswisnfatpases pages 1-2). - TERT (HGNC:11730) – Biological Process: telomere maintenance via telomerase; Cellular Component: telomerase holoenzyme complex, telomere; Evidence: rearrangements/copy-number/MYCN drive TERT activation in NB (URL: https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.08.16.504100) (burkert2024copynumberdosageregulates pages 18-24). - ATRX (HGNC:886) – Biological Process: chromatin assembly at telomeres; ALT association; Cellular Component: nuclear chromatin; Evidence: ATRX dysfunction promotes ALT in NB (URL: https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.08.16.504100) (burkert2024copynumberdosageregulates pages 18-24). - SMARCA2/SMARCA4 (HGNC:11100/11103) – Biological Process: chromatin remodeling; Cellular Component: SWI/SNF complex; Evidence: dual degradation reduces plasticity and invasion (URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s44318-024-00206-1) (xu2024targetingswisnfatpases pages 1-2).

Phenotype associations (HP terms, examples) - HP:0002664 (Neoplasm of the adrenal gland)—common primary site; HP:0002667 (Metastatic neoplasm of the bone); mechanism links include immune suppression and lineage plasticity associated with progression and therapeutic resistance (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3).

Cell type involvement (CL terms) - CL:0000542 (neuron, sympathoadrenal lineage derivatives—tumor of neural crest origin); CL:0000798 (macrophage), CL:0000815 (T cell), CL:0000623 (natural killer cell)—constitute the immune TME implicated in immune evasion (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3).

Anatomical locations (UBERON terms) - UBERON:0002369 (adrenal medulla), UBERON:0001043 (sympathetic trunk), UBERON:0000178 (bone marrow) as sites of origin/metastasis with characteristic microenvironmental programs (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3).

Chemical entities (CHEBI) - Anti-GD2 antibody therapeutics (biologic drugs targeting disialoganglioside GD2) widely implemented in HR-NB; TME features modulate efficacy (URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13164765) (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3).

Notes on evidence scope and limitations - The core mechanistic claims above are supported by recent high-quality primary studies (Nature Communications 2023; EMBO Journal 2024) and integrative analyses (iScience 2024). Where comprehensive clinical statistics (incidence/survival trends) would usually be drawn from national registries, the present synthesis cites a 2024 clinical immunotherapy review for high-risk survival context because those were among the most relevant sources in the retrieved set (persaud2024highriskneuroblastomachallenges pages 2-3). Additional registry-based epidemiology could further refine survival estimates but was outside the current evidence set.
